chapters.title: Book I — The gods in council—Athena’s visit to Ithaca—the challenge from Telemachus to the suitors
paragraphs: Tell me, Muse, of that clever hero who wandered far and wide after he destroyed the famous city of Troy. He visited many cities and learned the customs of many peoples. He suffered greatly at sea while trying to save his own life and bring his men home safely. But no matter what he did, he could not save his companions—they died through their own reckless folly when they ate the cattle of the sun god Helios. So the god prevented them from ever reaching home. Tell me about all these things, daughter of Zeus, from whatever source you know them.

Now all those who had escaped death in battle or shipwreck had returned safely home—all except Odysseus. Though he longed to return to his wife and homeland, the goddess Calypso held him captive in her vast cave, wanting to marry him. But as the years passed, the time came when the gods decided he should return to Ithaca. Even then, when he was among his own people, his troubles would not be over. Nevertheless, all the gods had begun to pity him except Poseidon, who continued to persecute him relentlessly and would not let him reach home.

Now Poseidon had gone to the Ethiopians, who live at the world's edge and are divided in two groups, one facing west and the other east. He had gone there to receive an offering of a hundred sheep and oxen, and was enjoying himself at the feast. But the other gods gathered in the palace of Olympian Zeus, and the father of gods and men spoke first. At that moment he was thinking of Aegisthus, who had been killed by Agamemnon's son Orestes. So he said to the other gods:

"Look how mortals blame us gods for what is really nothing but their own foolishness. Take Aegisthus—he had to seduce Agamemnon's wife and then murder Agamemnon, even though he knew it would mean his death. I sent Hermes to warn him not to do either of these things, since Orestes would surely take revenge when he grew up and wanted to return home. Hermes gave him this warning with the best intentions, but Aegisthus wouldn't listen. Now he has paid the full price for everything."

Then Athena said, "Father, son of Cronos, king of kings, Aegisthus got what he deserved, and so would anyone else who acts as he did. But Aegisthus doesn't matter to me—it's Odysseus who breaks my heart when I think of his suffering on that lonely island surrounded by sea, far from all his friends. It's a forested island in the middle of the ocean, and a goddess lives there—the daughter of Atlas the magician, who watches over the ocean depths and holds up the great pillars that separate heaven and earth. This daughter of Atlas has trapped poor unhappy Odysseus and keeps trying with every kind of charm to make him forget his home. He's grown weary of life and thinks of nothing but seeing the smoke rising from his own chimneys once more. Yet you pay no attention to this. Didn't Odysseus honor you with many burnt offerings when he was at Troy? Why do you remain so angry with him?"

Zeus replied, "My child, what are you saying? How could I forget Odysseus? There's no mortal more capable than he, nor more generous in his offerings to the immortal gods who live in heaven. But remember that Poseidon is still furious with Odysseus for blinding the eye of Polyphemus, king of the Cyclopes. Polyphemus is Poseidon's son by the nymph Thoosa, daughter of the sea-king Phorcys. So while Poseidon won't kill Odysseus outright, he torments him by preventing him from reaching home. Still, let's put our heads together and figure out how to help him return. Then Poseidon will be appeased—if we're all in agreement, he can hardly stand against us alone."

Athena said, "Father, son of Cronos, king of kings, if the gods have now decided that Odysseus should return home, we should first send Hermes to the island of Ogygia to tell Calypso our decision—that Odysseus must be allowed to leave. Meanwhile, I'll go to Ithaca to encourage Odysseus's son Telemachus. I'll give him courage to call the Greeks to assembly and speak boldly to his mother Penelope's suitors, who keep devouring his flocks of sheep and herds of cattle. I'll also guide him to Sparta and Pylos to see if he can learn anything about his dear father's return—this will earn him a good reputation."

With that, she strapped on her gleaming golden sandals that carry her swift as the wind over land and sea. She grasped her mighty bronze-tipped spear, heavy and strong, with which she conquers ranks of warriors who displease her. Then she shot down from the heights of Olympus and appeared immediately in Ithaca, at the gateway of Odysseus's house. She disguised herself as a visitor—Mentes, chief of the Taphians—and held a bronze spear in her hand. There she found the arrogant suitors sitting on the hides of oxen they had slaughtered and eaten, playing board games in front of the house. Servants and attendants bustled about waiting on them—some mixing wine with water in the bowls, others wiping down tables with wet sponges and setting them again, still others carving great quantities of meat.

Telemachus spotted her long before anyone else did. He was sitting glumly among the suitors, thinking about his noble father and how he would drive them from the house if he were to return and reclaim his rightful place of honor. Lost in these thoughts among the suitors, he caught sight of Athena and went straight to the gate, annoyed that a stranger should be kept waiting for admission. He took her right hand in his and asked her to give him her spear. "Welcome to our house," he said, "and when you've shared our food, you can tell us what brings you here."

He led the way as he spoke, and Athena followed. Once inside, he took her spear and placed it in the spear rack against a sturdy pillar, alongside the many other spears belonging to his unfortunate father. He led her to a beautifully carved chair and spread a fine cloth beneath it. There was a footstool for her feet, and he placed another seat nearby for himself, away from the suitors, so she wouldn't be disturbed by their noise and rudeness while eating, and so he could ask her more freely about his father.

A maid brought them water in a beautiful golden pitcher and poured it into a silver basin for them to wash their hands. She set a polished table beside them. A housekeeper brought bread and offered them many delicious foods from the household stores. The carver served them portions of various meats and placed golden cups beside them, while a servant brought wine and poured it for them.

Then the suitors came in and took their places on the benches and chairs. Servants immediately poured water over their hands, maids distributed bread from baskets, and young men filled the mixing bowls with wine and water. Everyone reached for the good food set before them. When they had eaten and drunk their fill, they turned to music and dancing, which crown a feast. A servant brought a lyre to Phemius, whom they forced to sing for them. As soon as he touched his instrument and began to sing, Telemachus spoke quietly to Athena, leaning close so no one else could hear.

"I hope you won't be offended by what I'm about to say," he said. "These men find singing cheap entertainment since they don't pay for it—all this comes at the expense of a man whose bones are rotting in some wilderness or being ground to powder by the waves. If these men saw my father return to Ithaca, they'd pray for faster legs rather than more gold, because money wouldn't save them. But he has met with misfortune, and even when people sometimes say he's coming back, we no longer believe them. We'll never see him again. Now tell me truthfully who you are and where you come from. Tell me about your city and your parents, what kind of ship brought you here, how your crew got you to Ithaca, and what people they claim to be—you certainly couldn't have come on foot. Tell me honestly, because I want to know: are you a stranger to this house, or have you been here in my father's time? In the old days we had many visitors, for my father traveled widely himself."

Athena answered, "I'll tell you everything truthfully and completely. I am Mentes, son of Anchialus, and I rule the Taphians. I've come here with my ship and crew, sailing to foreign lands on a trading voyage to Temesa with a cargo of iron, and I'll bring back copper. My ship lies over there beyond the town in Rheithron harbor, beneath wooded Mount Neritum. Our fathers were friends before us, as old Laertes will tell you if you go ask him. But they say he no longer comes to town and lives alone in the countryside, struggling along with only an old woman to care for him and prepare his meals when he comes in exhausted from tending his vineyard. I came because they told me your father had returned home, but it seems the gods are still keeping him away. He's certainly not dead—not on the mainland. More likely he's trapped on some island surrounded by sea, held prisoner by savages against his will. I'm no prophet and know little about omens, but I speak as the thought comes to me from heaven: he won't be away much longer. He's so resourceful that even if he were bound in iron chains, he'd find some way to get home. But tell me honestly—can Odysseus really have such a handsome son? You look remarkably like him, especially around the head and eyes. We were close friends before he sailed for Troy with all the finest Greeks. Since then, neither of us has seen the other."

"My mother says I'm Odysseus's son," Telemachus replied, "but it's a wise child who knows his own father. I wish I were the son of someone who had grown old peacefully on his own estate. Since you ask, there's no man under heaven more unfortunate than the one they tell me is my father."

Athena said, "There's no danger of your family line dying out while Penelope has such a fine son as you. But tell me truly, what's the meaning of all this feasting? Who are these people? What's it all about? Is this some banquet, or is there a wedding in the family? No one seems to be bringing their own food. And the guests—how outrageously they're behaving! What a riot they're making throughout the house. It would disgust any decent person who came near them."

"Sir," Telemachus said, "regarding your question—as long as my father was here, all was well with us and our household. But the gods in their displeasure have willed otherwise and have hidden him away more completely than any mortal man has ever been hidden. I could bear it better even if he were dead—if he had fallen with his men at Troy, or died among friends when his fighting days were over. Then the Greeks would have built a tomb over his ashes, and I would have inherited his honor. But now the storm winds have swept him away to some unknown place. He's vanished without leaving a trace, and I inherit nothing but grief. Nor does my sorrow end simply with losing my father. Heaven has brought me troubles of another kind. All the nobles from our islands—Dulichium, Same, and wooded Zacynthus, as well as all the leading men of Ithaca itself—are consuming my household, pretending to court my mother. She neither refuses outright to marry nor brings the matter to an end. So they're destroying my inheritance, and soon they'll destroy me as well."

"Is that so?" exclaimed Athena. "Then you really do need Odysseus to come home. Give him his helmet, his shield, and a couple of spears, and if he's the man he was when I first knew him in our house, drinking and celebrating—he had just returned from Ephyra, where he'd gone to get poison for his arrows from Ilus, son of Mermerus. Ilus feared the eternal gods and wouldn't give him any, but my father provided some because he was very fond of Odysseus. If Odysseus is still that man, these suitors will have a quick end and a bitter wedding.

"But enough! It's up to heaven to decide whether he'll return and take revenge in his own house. However, I urge you to start planning how to get rid of these suitors immediately. Take my advice: call the Greek leaders to assembly tomorrow morning, present your case to them, and call on the gods to witness your words. Tell the suitors to go away, each to his own home. If your mother is determined to remarry, let her return to her father's house—he'll find her a husband and provide all the wedding gifts such a dear daughter deserves. As for yourself, let me persuade you to take the best ship you can get with a crew of twenty men and go searching for your long-missing father. Someone might tell you something, or you might hear some heaven-sent message—that's often how people learn things. First go to Pylos and question Nestor, then continue to Sparta to visit Menelaus, who returned home last of all the Greeks. If you hear that your father is alive and coming home, you can endure these suitors' waste for another year. But if you learn of his death, return home immediately, hold proper funeral rites, build a memorial mound, and see that your mother marries again. Then, having done all this, consider carefully how you might kill these suitors in your own house, whether by cunning or open force. You're too old to plead youth as an excuse any longer. Haven't you heard how people praise Orestes for killing Aegisthus, his father's murderer? You're a fine, handsome young man—show your courage and make a name for yourself. Now I must return to my ship and crew, who will be impatient if I keep them waiting longer. Think over what I've told you, and remember my words."

"Sir," Telemachus answered, "you've been very kind to speak to me as if I were your own son, and I'll do everything you've told me. I know you're eager to continue your voyage, but stay a little longer until you've bathed and refreshed yourself. Then I'll give you a gift—a beautiful and valuable keepsake, the kind that dear friends give each other—and you can go on your way rejoicing."

Athena replied, "Don't try to keep me—I need to leave at once. As for any gift you want to give me, save it until I return, and I'll take it home with me then. Give me a very fine one, and I'll give you one of equal value in return."

With these words she flew away like a bird into the air. But she had given Telemachus courage and made him think about his father more than ever. He felt the change, marveled at it, and knew that the stranger had been a god. So he went directly to where the suitors were sitting.

Phemius was still singing, and his audience sat in rapt silence as he told the sad story of the Greeks' return from Troy and the troubles Athena had brought upon them. Penelope, daughter of Icarius, heard his song from her room upstairs and came down the great staircase, not alone but accompanied by two of her maids. When she reached the suitors, she stood by one of the pillars supporting the roof of the hall, with a modest attendant on each side. She held a veil over her face and wept bitterly.

"Phemius," she cried, "you know many other tales of gods and heroes that poets love to sing. Sing one of those to the suitors and let them drink their wine in silence. But stop this sad song—it breaks my sorrowful heart and reminds me of my lost husband, whom I mourn constantly and whose name was renowned throughout Greece and central Argos."

"Mother," Telemachus answered, "let the singer sing whatever moves him. Singers don't create the troubles they sing about—Zeus does that, sending good fortune or bad to mortals as he pleases. This man means no harm by singing about the Greeks' ill-fated return from Troy. People always applaud the newest songs most enthusiastically. Steel yourself to bear it. Odysseus isn't the only man who never returned from Troy—many others died there too. Go back into the house and attend to your own work—your loom, your spinning, and managing the servants. Speech is men's business, and mine above all others, since I am master here."

She returned to the house in amazement, taking her son's words to heart. Going upstairs with her maids to her room, she mourned for her dear husband until Athena brought sweet sleep to her eyes. But the suitors grew rowdy throughout the covered halls, each praying that he might share her bed.

Then Telemachus spoke: "Shameless and arrogant suitors, let's feast peacefully now without fighting, for it's wonderful to hear a man sing with such a divine voice as Phemius has. But in the morning, meet me in full assembly so I can give you formal notice to leave and feast in each other's houses, taking turns at your own expense. But if you choose to keep devouring one man's livelihood, then heaven help me—Zeus will hold you accountable, and when you fall in my father's house, no one will avenge you."

The suitors bit their lips when they heard him and marveled at his bold speech. Then Antinous, son of Eupeithes, said, "The gods seem to have taught you to boast and talk big. May Zeus never make you king in Ithaca as your father was before you."

Telemachus replied, "Antinous, don't be angry with me, but if god wills it, I'll gladly be king too. Do you think that's the worst fate you can imagine for me? It's no bad thing to be a king—it brings both wealth and honor. Still, now that Odysseus is dead, there are many great men in Ithaca, both old and young, and someone else might become their leader. Nevertheless, I will be master in my own house and rule over the people Odysseus won for me."

Then Eurymachus, son of Polybus, answered, "It's up to heaven to decide who will be king among us, but you should be master of your own house and possessions. As long as there's a man left in Ithaca, no one will use force against you or rob you. Now, my good fellow, I want to know about this stranger. What country does he come from? What family is he from, and where are his lands? Did he bring you news about your father's return, or was he here on his own business? He seemed like a well-to-do man, but he left so suddenly—gone in a moment before we could get to know him."

"My father is dead and gone," Telemachus answered, "and even when some rumor reaches me, I no longer believe it. My mother does sometimes summon a prophet to question him, but I pay no attention to his predictions. As for the stranger, he was Mentes, son of Anchialus, chief of the Taphians, an old friend of my father's." But in his heart he knew it had been the goddess.

The suitors then returned to their singing and dancing until evening came. But when darkness fell on their revelry, they went home to bed, each to his own dwelling. Telemachus's bedroom was high up in a tower overlooking the courtyard. He went there, brooding and deep in thought. A loyal old woman, Eurycleia, daughter of Ops the son of Pisenor, went before him carrying two blazing torches. Laertes had bought her with his own money when she was quite young, paying the price of twenty oxen, and he honored her in his household as much as his own wife, though he never shared her bed for fear of his wife's anger. She was the one who now lit Telemachus's way to his room, and she loved him more than any of the other household women, for she had nursed him as a baby. He opened his bedroom door and sat on his bed. As he took off his soft tunic, he gave it to the good old woman, who folded it neatly and hung it on a peg beside his bed. Then she left the room, closed the door by its silver handle, and slid the bolt home with its leather strap. But Telemachus lay under his woolen blanket, thinking all night long about his planned journey and the advice Athena had given him.

chapters.title: Book II — Assembly of the people of Ithaca—speeches of Telemachus and of the suitors—Telemachus makes his preparations and starts for Pylos with Athena disguised as Mentor
paragraphs: When rosy-fingered Dawn, child of morning, appeared, Telemachus rose and dressed himself. He tied his sandals on his handsome feet, strapped his sword around his shoulder, and left his room looking like an immortal god. He immediately sent heralds around to call the people to assembly, so they made the announcement and the people gathered. When they had come together, he went to the meeting place with spear in hand—not alone, for his two dogs went with him. Athena gave him such divine grace that everyone marveled at him as he passed by, and when he took his place in his father's seat, even the oldest councilors made way for him.

Aegyptius, a man bent double with age and vast experience, was the first to speak. His son Antiphus had gone with Odysseus to Troy, land of noble horses, but the savage Cyclops had killed him when they were all trapped in the cave, and had made him his last meal. He had three sons left, two of whom still worked their father's land, while the third, Eurynomus, was one of the suitors. Nevertheless their father could not get over losing Antiphus, and was still weeping for him when he began his speech.

"Men of Ithaca," he said, "hear my words. From the day Odysseus left us there has been no meeting of our council until now. Who then can it be, whether old or young, who finds it so necessary to call us together? Has he heard of some army approaching, and does he wish to warn us, or would he speak about some other matter of public importance? I am sure he is an excellent person, and I hope Zeus will grant him his heart's desire."

Telemachus took this speech as a good omen and rose at once, for he was bursting with what he had to say. He stood in the middle of the assembly and the good herald Pisenor brought him his staff. Then, turning to Aegyptius, "Sir," he said, "it is I, as you will shortly learn, who have called you together, for it is I who am most wronged. I have not heard of any army approaching that I would warn you about, nor is there any matter of public importance I would discuss. My grievance is purely personal, and concerns two great misfortunes that have fallen upon my house. The first is the loss of my excellent father, who was chief among all you here present, and was like a father to every one of you. The second is much more serious, and will soon utterly ruin my estate. The sons of all the chief men among you are harassing my mother to marry them against her will. They are afraid to go to her father Icarius, asking him to choose the one he likes best, and to provide marriage gifts for his daughter. Instead, day by day they keep loitering around my father's house, slaughtering our cattle, sheep, and fat goats for their feasts, and never giving a thought to how much wine they drink. No estate can withstand such recklessness. We have no Odysseus now to protect our home from harm, and I cannot hold my own against them. I will never be as good a man as he was, but I would defend myself if I had the power to do so, for I cannot endure such treatment any longer. My house is being disgraced and ruined. Have respect, therefore, for your own consciences and for public opinion. Fear too the wrath of heaven, lest the gods should be displeased and turn upon you. I beg you by Zeus and Themis, who presides over councils, do not hold back, my friends, and leave me to face this alone—unless it be that my brave father Odysseus did some wrong to the Greeks which you would now avenge on me, by helping these suitors. Moreover, if I am to be eaten out of house and home at all, I would rather you did the eating yourselves, for then I could take action against you and demand payment from house to house until I was repaid in full, whereas now I have no remedy."

With this Telemachus threw his staff to the ground and burst into tears. Everyone felt very sorry for him, but they all sat still and no one dared to answer him angrily, except Antinous, who spoke thus:

"Telemachus, you arrogant braggart, how dare you try to blame us suitors? It is your mother's fault, not ours, for she is a very cunning woman. For three years now, almost four, she has been driving us out of our minds, encouraging each one of us and sending us messages without meaning a word of what she says. And then there was that other trick she played on us. She set up a great loom in her room and began working on an enormous piece of fine weaving. 'My dear suitors,' she said, 'Odysseus is indeed dead, but do not press me to marry again immediately. Wait—for I would not want my skill in needlework to go unremembered—until I have finished a burial shroud for the hero Laertes, to be ready when death takes him. He is very wealthy, and the women of the place will gossip if he is laid out without a proper shroud.'

"This was what she said, and we agreed. So we could see her working on her great web all day long, but at night she would unpick the stitches again by torchlight. She fooled us this way for three years without our knowing, but as time passed and she was in her fourth year, one of her maids who knew what she was doing told us, and we caught her in the act of undoing her work, so she had to finish it whether she wanted to or not. Therefore, the suitors give you this answer, so that both you and all the Greeks may understand: 'Send your mother away, and tell her to marry the man of her own and her father's choice.' For I do not know what will happen if she goes on tormenting us much longer with the airs she gives herself because of the skills Athena has taught her, and because she is so clever. We never heard of such a woman before. We know all about Tyro, Alcmene, Mycene, and the famous women of old, but not one of them could match your mother. It was not fair of her to treat us this way, and as long as she continues in the mind which heaven has given her, we will go on consuming your estate. And I do not see why she should change, for she gets all the honor and glory, and it is you who pay for it, not she. Understand, then, that we will not go back to our lands, neither here nor elsewhere, until she has made her choice and married one of us."

Telemachus answered, "Antinous, how can I drive the mother who bore me from my father's house? My father is abroad and we do not know whether he is alive or dead. It will be hard on me if I have to pay Icarius the large sum I would owe him if I insisted on sending his daughter back to him. Not only will he deal harshly with me, but heaven will also punish me, for my mother when she leaves the house will call on the Furies to avenge her. Besides, it would not be an honorable thing to do, and I will have nothing to do with it. If you choose to take offense at this, leave the house and feast elsewhere at one another's homes at your own expense, taking turns. If, on the other hand, you decide to persist in living off one man, heaven help me, but Zeus will settle accounts with you in full, and when you fall in my father's house there will be no one to avenge you."

As he spoke Zeus sent two eagles from the mountaintop, and they flew on and on with the wind, sailing side by side in their own majestic flight. When they were right over the middle of the assembly they wheeled and circled about, beating the air with their wings and glaring death into the eyes of those below. Then, fighting fiercely and tearing at one another, they flew off toward the right over the town. The people wondered as they watched them, and asked each other what this might mean. Then Halitherses, who was the best prophet and reader of omens among them, spoke to them plainly and honestly, saying:

"Hear me, men of Ithaca, and I speak especially to the suitors, for I see disaster brewing for them. Odysseus will not be away much longer. Indeed he is close at hand to bring death and destruction, not on them alone, but on many others of us who live in Ithaca. Let us then be wise in time, and put a stop to this wickedness before he comes. Let the suitors do so of their own accord—it will be better for them, for I am not prophesying without knowledge. Everything has happened to Odysseus as I foretold when the Greeks set out for Troy, and he with them. I said that after going through much hardship and losing all his men he would come home again in the twentieth year and that no one would recognize him. And now all this is coming true."

Eurymachus son of Polybus then said, "Go home, old man, and prophesy to your own children, or it may be worse for them. I can read these omens myself much better than you can. Birds are always flying about in the sunshine somewhere or other, but they seldom mean anything. Odysseus has died in a far country, and it is a pity you are not dead along with him, instead of babbling here about omens and adding fuel to the anger of Telemachus which is fierce enough as it is. I suppose you think he will give you something for your family, but I tell you—and it will surely happen—when an old man like you, who should know better, talks a young one into making trouble, in the first place his young friend will only fare worse—he will gain nothing by it, for the suitors will prevent this—and secondly, we will impose a heavier fine on you, sir, than you will like paying, for it will weigh heavily upon you. As for Telemachus, I warn him in the presence of you all to send his mother back to her father, who will find her a husband and provide her with all the marriage gifts so dear a daughter may expect. Until then we will go on pressing him with our suit, for we fear no man, and care neither for him, with all his fine speeches, nor for any fortune-telling of yours. You may preach as much as you please, but we will only hate you the more. We will go back and continue to consume Telemachus's estate without paying him, until his mother stops tormenting us by keeping us day after day in suspense, each competing with the other in his suit for a prize of such rare perfection. Besides we cannot pursue the other women we should marry in due course, because of the way she treats us."

Then Telemachus said, "Eurymachus, and you other suitors, I will say no more and beg you no further, for the gods and the people of Ithaca now know my story. Give me, then, a ship and a crew of twenty men to take me here and there, and I will go to Sparta and to Pylos in search of my father who has been missing so long. Someone may tell me something, or (and people often hear things this way) some heaven-sent message may guide me. If I can hear of him as alive and on his way home I will put up with the waste you suitors will make for yet another twelve months. If on the other hand I hear of his death, I will return at once, celebrate his funeral rites with all due ceremony, build a tomb to his memory, and make my mother marry again."

With these words he sat down, and Mentor who had been a friend of Odysseus, and had been left in charge of everything with full authority over the servants, rose to speak. He then addressed them plainly and honestly:

"Hear me, men of Ithaca, I hope that you may never have a kind and well-disposed ruler again, nor one who will govern you fairly. I hope that all your chiefs from now on may be cruel and unjust, for there is not one of you who remembers Odysseus, who ruled you as though he were your father. I am not nearly so angry with the suitors, for if they choose to act violently in the wickedness of their hearts, and gamble their lives that Odysseus will not return, they can take matters into their own hands and consume his estate. But as for you others I am shocked at the way you all sit still without even trying to stop such scandalous behavior—which you could do if you chose, for you are many and they are few."

Leocritus, son of Evenor, answered him saying, "Mentor, what folly is all this, that you should urge the people to stop us? It is a hard thing for one man to fight with many over his food. Even if Odysseus himself were to attack us while we are feasting in his house, and do his best to throw us out, his wife, who wants him back so badly, would have little cause for rejoicing, and his blood would be on his own head if he fought against such odds. There is no sense in what you have been saying. Now, therefore, you people go about your business, and let his father's old friends, Mentor and Halitherses, help this boy on his journey, if he goes at all—which I do not think he will, for he is more likely to stay where he is until someone comes and tells him something."
On this he broke up the assembly, and every man went back to his own home, while the suitors returned to the house of Odysseus.
Then Telemachus went all alone by the seashore, washed his hands in the gray waves, and prayed to Athena.

"Hear me," he cried, "you god who visited me yesterday, and told me to sail the seas in search of my father who has been missing so long. I would obey you, but the Greeks, and especially the wicked suitors, are preventing me from doing so."

As he prayed, Athena came close to him in the likeness and with the voice of Mentor. "Telemachus," she said, "if you are made of the same stuff as your father you will be neither fool nor coward from now on, for Odysseus never broke his word or left his work half done. If, then, you take after him, your voyage will not be fruitless, but unless you have the blood of Odysseus and of Penelope in your veins I see no likelihood of your succeeding. Sons are seldom as good as their fathers—they are generally worse, not better. Still, since you are not going to be either fool or coward from now on, and are not entirely without some share of your father's wise judgment, I have hope for your undertaking. But mind you never make common cause with any of those foolish suitors, for they have neither sense nor virtue, and give no thought to death and the doom that will shortly fall on one and all of them, so that they will perish on the same day. As for your voyage, it will not be long delayed. Your father was such an old friend of mine that I will find you a ship, and will come with you myself. Now, however, return home, and go among the suitors. Begin getting provisions ready for your voyage—see everything well stored, the wine in jars, and the barley meal, which is the staff of life, in leather bags, while I go around the town and gather volunteers at once. There are many ships in Ithaca both old and new. I will look them over for you and choose the best. We will get her ready and put out to sea without delay."

Thus spoke Athena daughter of Zeus, and Telemachus lost no time in doing as the goddess told him. He went home in a somber mood, and found the suitors skinning goats and roasting pigs in the outer court. Antinous came up to him at once and laughed as he took his hand in his own, saying, "Telemachus, my fine hothead, bear no more ill will either in word or deed, but eat and drink with us as you used to do. The Greeks will provide you with everything—a ship and a picked crew to boot—so that you can set sail for Pylos at once and get news of your noble father."

"Antinous," answered Telemachus, "I cannot eat in peace, nor take pleasure of any kind with such men as you are. Was it not enough that you should waste so much of my good property while I was still a boy? Now that I am older and know more about it, I am also stronger, and whether here among this people, or by going to Pylos, I will do you all the harm I can. I will go, and my going will not be in vain—though, thanks to you suitors, I have neither ship nor crew of my own, and must be passenger, not captain."
As he spoke he pulled his hand from that of Antinous. Meanwhile the others went on preparing dinner around the buildings, mocking him tauntingly as they did so.

"Telemachus," said one young man, "means to be the death of us. I suppose he thinks he can bring friends to help him from Pylos, or again from Sparta, where he seems bent on going. Or will he go to Ephyra as well, for poison to put in our wine and kill us?"

Another said, "Perhaps if Telemachus goes on board ship, he will be like his father and perish far from his friends. In this case we would have plenty to do, for we could then divide up his property among us. As for the house we can let his mother and the man who marries her have that."

This was how they talked. But Telemachus went down into the lofty and spacious storeroom where his father's treasure of gold and bronze lay heaped up upon the floor, and where the linen and spare clothes were kept in open chests. Here, too, there was a store of fragrant olive oil, while casks of old, well-aged wine, pure and fit for a god to drink, were ranged against the wall in case Odysseus should come home again after all. The room was secured with well-made doors opening in the middle. Moreover the faithful old housekeeper Eurycleia, daughter of Ops the son of Pisenor, was in charge of everything both night and day. Telemachus called her to the storeroom and said:

"Nurse, draw me off some of the best wine you have, after what you are keeping for my father's own drinking, in case, poor man, he should escape death and find his way home again after all. Let me have twelve jars, and see that they all have lids. Also fill me some well-sewn leather bags with barley meal—about twenty measures in all. Get these things put together at once, and say nothing about it. I will take everything away this evening as soon as my mother has gone upstairs for the night. I am going to Sparta and to Pylos to see if I can hear anything about the return of my dear father."

When Eurycleia heard this she began to cry, and spoke tenderly to him, saying, "My dear child, whatever can have put such a notion into your head? Where in the world do you want to go—you, who are the one hope of the house? Your poor father is dead and gone in some foreign country nobody knows where, and as soon as your back is turned these wicked ones here will be scheming to get you killed, and will share all your possessions among themselves. Stay where you are among your own people, and do not go wandering and worrying your life out on the barren ocean."

"Fear not, nurse," answered Telemachus, "my plan is not without heaven's approval. But swear that you will say nothing about all this to my mother, until I have been away some ten or twelve days, unless she hears of my having gone and asks you, for I do not want her to spoil her beauty by crying."

The old woman swore most solemnly that she would not, and when she had completed her oath, she began drawing off the wine into jars and getting the barley meal into the bags, while Telemachus went back to the suitors.

Then Athena thought of another matter. She took his shape, and went around the town to each one of the crew, telling them to meet at the ship by sundown. She went also to Noemon son of Phronius, and asked him to let her have a ship—which he was very ready to do. When the sun had set and darkness covered all the land, she got the ship into the water, put all the tackle on board that ships generally carry, and stationed her at the end of the harbor. Soon the crew came up, and the goddess spoke encouragingly to each of them.

Furthermore she went to the house of Odysseus, and cast the suitors into a deep sleep. She made their drink confuse them, and made them drop their cups from their hands, so that instead of sitting over their wine, they went back into the town to sleep, with their eyes heavy and full of drowsiness. Then she took the form and voice of Mentor, and called Telemachus to come outside.
"Telemachus," she said, "the men are on board and at their oars, waiting for you to give your orders, so hurry and let us be off."

On this she led the way, while Telemachus followed in her steps. When they got to the ship they found the crew waiting by the water's edge, and Telemachus said, "Now my men, help me get the stores on board. They are all gathered together in the storeroom, and my mother knows nothing about it, nor any of the maidservants except one."

With these words he led the way and the others followed after. When they had brought the things as he told them, Telemachus went on board, Athena going before him and taking her seat in the stern of the vessel, while Telemachus sat beside her. Then the men cast off the moorings and took their places on the benches. Athena sent them a fair wind from the West that whistled over the deep blue waves, and Telemachus told them to catch hold of the ropes and hoist sail, and they did as he told them. They set the mast in its socket in the crossbeam, raised it, and made it fast with the forestays. Then they hoisted their white sails aloft with ropes of twisted oxhide. As the sail bellied out with the wind, the ship flew through the deep blue water, and the foam hissed against her bow as she sped onward. Then they made all fast throughout the ship, filled the mixing bowls to the brim, and made drink offerings to the immortal gods that are from everlasting, but especially to the gray-eyed daughter of Zeus.
Thus, then, the ship sped on her way through the watches of the night from dark until dawn.

chapters.title: Book III — Telemachus visits Nestor at Pylos
paragraphs: As the sun rose from the beautiful sea into the heavens to bring light to mortals and immortals alike, they reached Pylos, the city of Neleus. The people of Pylos had gathered on the seashore to sacrifice black bulls to Poseidon, lord of earthquakes. There were nine groups of five hundred men each, with nine bulls for each group. As they ate the sacred meats and burned the thigh bones on the coals in Poseidon's honor, Telemachus and his crew arrived, furled their sails, anchored their ship, and came ashore.

Athena led the way with Telemachus following her. Soon she said, "Telemachus, you mustn't be shy or nervous at all. You've taken this voyage to try to find out where your father is buried and how he died, so go straight up to Nestor and see what he can tell us. Ask him to speak the truth, and he won't lie to you—he's an excellent man."

"But how, Mentor," Telemachus replied, "can I approach Nestor, and how should I address him? I've never been used to having long conversations with people, and I'm embarrassed to start questioning someone so much older than myself."
"Some things, Telemachus," Athena answered, "will come to you by instinct, and the gods will inspire you further. I'm certain that the gods have been with you from birth until now."

She then walked quickly ahead, and Telemachus followed her steps until they reached the place where the groups of Pylian people were assembled. There they found Nestor sitting with his sons, while his companions busily prepared dinner, putting pieces of meat on spits while other pieces cooked. When they saw the strangers, they crowded around them, took them by the hand, and invited them to sit down. Nestor's son Pisistratus immediately offered his hand to each of them and seated them on soft sheepskins that lay on the sand near his father and his brother Thrasymedes. Then he gave them portions of the sacred meat and poured wine into a golden cup, handing it first to Athena and greeting her respectfully.

"Offer a prayer, sir," he said, "to Lord Poseidon, for you're joining his feast. When you've properly prayed and made your drink offering, pass the cup to your friend so he can do the same. I'm sure he too lifts his hands in prayer, for no one can live without God in this world. Still, he's younger than you and about my own age, so I'll give you precedence."

As he spoke, he handed her the cup. Athena thought it very proper of him to have given it to her first. She began praying earnestly to Poseidon: "O you who encircle the earth, grant the prayers of your servants who call upon you. Especially we pray that you send down your grace on Nestor and his sons. Also give the rest of the Pylian people some worthy return for the fine sacrifice they're offering you. Finally, grant Telemachus and me success in the matter that brought us in our ship to Pylos."

When she finished praying, she handed the cup to Telemachus, and he prayed as well. Soon, when the outer meats were roasted and taken off the spits, the carvers gave everyone their portion and they all had an excellent dinner. As soon as they'd eaten and drunk enough, Nestor, the knight of Gerenia, began to speak.

"Now," he said, "that our guests have finished their dinner, it's time to ask who they are. Who are you, strangers, and from what port have you sailed? Are you traders, or do you sail the seas as pirates with your hand against every man, and every man's hand against you?"
Telemachus answered boldly, for Athena had given him courage to ask about his father and make a good name for himself.

"Nestor," he said, "son of Neleus, honor of the Greek people, you ask where we come from, and I'll tell you. We come from Ithaca below Mount Neriton, and what I want to discuss is a private matter, not public. I seek news of my unfortunate father Odysseus, who's said to have destroyed Troy alongside you. We know what fate befell each of the other heroes who fought at Troy, but regarding Odysseus, heaven has hidden from us even the knowledge that he's dead, for no one can tell us where he died, or whether he fell in battle on the mainland or was lost at sea in the waves. Therefore I come as a suppliant to you, hoping you might tell me of his sad end—whether you saw it with your own eyes or heard it from some other traveler, for he was born to suffer. Don't soften the truth out of pity for me, but tell me plainly exactly what you saw. If my brave father Odysseus ever served you loyally, either in word or deed, when you Greeks were hard-pressed among the Trojans, remember it now in my favor and tell me the truth."

"My friend," Nestor answered, "you bring back memories of great sorrow, for the brave Greeks suffered much both at sea while raiding under Achilles, and fighting before the great city of King Priam. All our best men fell there—Ajax, Achilles, Patroclus who was like a god in counsel, and my own dear son Antilochus, remarkably swift of foot and brave in battle. But we suffered much more than this. What mortal tongue could tell the whole story? Even if you stayed here questioning me for five or six years, I couldn't tell you all that the Greeks endured, and you'd turn homeward weary of my tale before it ended. For nine long years we tried every kind of strategy, but heaven's hand was against us. During all this time, no one could match your father in cleverness—if you are indeed his son—I can hardly believe my eyes—and you speak just like him too. No one would think people of such different ages could speak so similarly. He and I never disagreed from first to last, neither in camp nor council, but with one heart and purpose we advised the Greeks how everything might turn out for the best.

"However, when we had sacked Priam's city and were setting sail as heaven had scattered us, Zeus decided to torment the Greeks on their homeward voyage. They hadn't all been wise or understanding, so many came to a bad end through the anger of Zeus's daughter Athena, who caused a quarrel between the two sons of Atreus.

"The sons of Atreus called a meeting that wasn't properly done, for it was sunset and the Greeks were heavy with wine. When they explained why they'd gathered the people, it seemed Menelaus wanted to sail home immediately, which displeased Agamemnon, who thought we should wait until we'd offered sacrifices to appease Athena's anger. Fool that he was, he should have known he wouldn't prevail with her, for when the gods make up their minds, they don't change them lightly. So the two stood exchanging harsh words, while the Greeks leaped to their feet with a cry that split the air, divided in opinion about what to do.

"That night we rested and nursed our anger, for Zeus was plotting trouble for us. But in the morning, some of us launched our ships and put our goods and women aboard, while the rest—about half—stayed behind with Agamemnon. We, the other half, embarked and sailed, and the ships went well, for heaven had calmed the sea. When we reached Tenedos we offered sacrifices to the gods, longing to get home. But cruel Zeus didn't yet mean for us to do so, and raised a second quarrel during which some among us turned their ships back and sailed away under Odysseus to make peace with Agamemnon. But I and all the ships with me pressed forward, for I saw that trouble was brewing. Tydeus's son also went on with me, and his crews with him. Later Menelaus joined us at Lesbos and found us deciding our course—for we didn't know whether to go outside Chios by the island of Psyra, keeping it to our left, or inside Chios, past the stormy headland of Mimas. So we asked heaven for a sign and were shown that we'd be soonest out of danger if we headed our ships across the open sea to Euboea. This we did, and a fair wind sprang up that gave us a quick passage during the night to Geraestus, where we offered many sacrifices to Poseidon for helping us so far. Four days later Diomedes and his men stationed their ships in Argos, but I held on for Pylos, and the wind never failed from the day heaven first made it favorable for me.

"Therefore, my dear young friend, I returned without hearing anything about the others. I know neither who got home safely nor who were lost, but as duty requires, I'll give you freely the reports that have reached me since I've been here in my own house. They say the Myrmidons returned home safely under Achilles's son Neoptolemus; so did brave Philoctetes, son of Poias. Idomeneus lost no men at sea, and all his followers who escaped death in battle got safely home with him to Crete. No matter how remote you live, you'll have heard of Agamemnon and the terrible end he met at Aegisthus's hands—and what a fearful reckoning Aegisthus paid for it. See what a good thing it is for a man to leave a son behind him to do as Orestes did, who killed false Aegisthus, his noble father's murderer. You too—for you're a tall, handsome fellow—show your courage and make yourself famous in story."

"Nestor, son of Neleus," Telemachus answered, "honor of the Greek people, the Greeks praise Orestes and his name will live forever, for he nobly avenged his father. Would that heaven might grant me to take similar vengeance on the insolence of the wicked suitors who are mistreating me and plotting my ruin. But the gods have no such happiness in store for my father and me, so we must bear it as best we can."

"My friend," Nestor said, "now that you remind me, I remember hearing that your mother has many suitors who are hostile to you and destroying your estate. Do you submit to this meekly, or are public opinion and heaven's voice against you? Who knows but that Odysseus may return after all and pay these scoundrels in full, either alone or with a force of Greeks behind him? If Athena were to favor you as much as she did Odysseus when we were fighting before Troy—for I never saw the gods so openly fond of anyone as Athena was of your father—if she would take as good care of you as she did of him, some of these suitors would soon forget their courtship."

Telemachus answered, "I can't expect anything like that. It would be far too much to hope for. I don't dare think of it. Even if the gods themselves willed it, no such good fortune could happen to me."

At this Athena said, "Telemachus, what are you talking about? Heaven has a long reach when it wants to save a man. If it were me, I wouldn't care how much I suffered before getting home, as long as I could be safe once I was there. I'd rather that than get home quickly and then be killed in my own house as Agamemnon was by the treachery of Aegisthus and his wife. Still, death is certain, and when a man's time comes, not even the gods can save him, no matter how fond of him they are."

"Mentor," Telemachus answered, "let's not talk about it anymore. There's no chance of my father ever coming back—the gods long ago decided on his destruction. There's something else I'd like to ask Nestor about, since he knows much more than anyone else. They say he's ruled for three generations, so it's like talking to an immortal. Tell me, therefore, Nestor, and tell me truly: how did Agamemnon die that way? What was Menelaus doing? And how did false Aegisthus manage to kill a man so much better than himself? Was Menelaus away from Greek Argos, traveling elsewhere among mankind, so that Aegisthus took courage and killed Agamemnon?"

"I'll tell you truly," Nestor answered, "and you've already guessed how it all happened. If Menelaus had found Aegisthus still alive in his house when he returned from Troy, there would have been no burial mound heaped up for him—not even when he was dead. He would have been thrown outside the city for dogs and vultures, and no woman would have mourned him, for he had committed a terrible crime. But we were over there fighting hard at Troy, and Aegisthus, taking his ease quietly in the heart of Argos, seduced Agamemnon's wife Clytemnestra with constant flattery.

"At first she wanted nothing to do with his wicked scheme, for she was naturally good. Moreover, there was a bard with her whom Agamemnon had strictly ordered, when leaving for Troy, to guard his wife. But when heaven decreed her destruction, Aegisthus took this bard to a desert island and left him there for crows and seagulls to devour—after which she went willingly enough to Aegisthus's house. Then he offered many burnt sacrifices to the gods and decorated many temples with tapestries and gold, for he had succeeded far beyond his expectations.

"Meanwhile Menelaus and I were on our way home from Troy, on good terms with each other. When we reached Sunium, which is the point of Attica, Apollo with his painless arrows killed Phrontis, Menelaus's helmsman—no man knew better how to handle a vessel in rough weather—so he died right there with the helm in his hand. Menelaus, though very anxious to press on, had to wait to bury his comrade and give him proper funeral rites. When he could put to sea again and had sailed as far as the Malean headlands, Zeus plotted evil against him and made it blow hard until the waves ran mountain-high. Here he divided his fleet, taking half toward Crete where the Cydonians live around the waters of the river Iardanus. There's a high headland there stretching into the sea from a place called Gortyn, and all along this coast as far as Phaestus the sea runs high when there's a south wind blowing, but beyond Phaestus the coast is more protected, for a small headland can provide great shelter. Here this part of the fleet was driven onto the rocks and wrecked, but the crews just managed to save themselves. As for the other five ships, they were carried by winds and seas to Egypt, where Menelaus gathered much gold and treasure among people of foreign speech. Meanwhile Aegisthus here at home plotted his evil deed. For seven years after he killed Agamemnon, he ruled in Mycenae with the people obedient to him, but in the eighth year Orestes returned from Athens to be his doom, and killed his father's murderer. Then he held a funeral feast for his mother and false Aegisthus for the people of Argos, and on that very day Menelaus came home with as much treasure as his ships could carry.

"Take my advice then, and don't go traveling far from home for long, leaving your property with such dangerous people in your house. They'll devour everything you have, and you'll have been on a fool's errand. Still, I strongly advise you to go visit Menelaus, who has lately returned from a voyage among such distant peoples that no man could hope to return from, once the winds had carried him so far off course. Even birds can't fly such distances in a year, so vast and terrible are the seas they'd have to cross. Go to him by sea with your own men, or if you'd rather travel by land, you can have a chariot and horses, and here are my sons who can escort you to Lacedaemon where Menelaus lives. Ask him to speak the truth, and he'll tell you no lies, for he's an excellent man."

As he spoke, the sun set and darkness came on, so Athena said, "Sir, all you've said is well. Now, however, order the victims' tongues to be cut and mix wine so we may make drink-offerings to Poseidon and the other immortals, and then go to bed, for it's bedtime. People should leave early and not keep late hours at a religious festival."

Thus spoke Zeus's daughter, and they obeyed her words. Servants poured water over the guests' hands, while pages filled the mixing-bowls with wine and water and handed it around after giving everyone their drink-offering. Then they threw the victims' tongues into the fire and stood up to make their offerings. When they had made their offerings and drunk as much as they wanted, Athena and Telemachus were ready to go aboard their ship, but Nestor immediately stopped them.

"Heaven and the immortal gods forbid," he exclaimed, "that you should leave my house to go aboard a ship! Do you think I'm so poor and short of clothes, or have so few cloaks and blankets that I can't provide comfortable beds for myself and my guests? Let me tell you I have plenty of rugs and cloaks, and won't allow the son of my old friend Odysseus to sleep on a ship's deck—not while I live—nor will my sons after me, but they'll keep open house as I have done."

Then Athena answered, "Sir, you've spoken well, and it will be much better for Telemachus to do as you've said. He'll return with you and sleep at your house, but I must go back to give orders to my crew and keep up their spirits. I'm the only older person among them—the rest are all young men of Telemachus's age who've taken this voyage out of friendship. So I must return to the ship and sleep there. Moreover, tomorrow I must go to the Cauconians, where I have a large sum of money long owed to me. As for Telemachus, since he's now your guest, send him to Lacedaemon in a chariot with one of your sons as escort. Please also provide him with your best and fastest horses."

When she had spoken, she flew away in the form of an eagle, and everyone marveled at the sight. Nestor was astonished and took Telemachus by the hand. "My friend," he said, "I see you're going to be a great hero someday, since the gods attend you while you're still so young. This can have been none other than Zeus's formidable daughter, Athena, who showed such favor to your brave father among the Greeks. Holy queen," he continued, "grant your grace to myself, my good wife, and my children. In return, I'll sacrifice to you a broad-browed heifer, a year old, unbroken and never yet brought under the yoke by man. I'll gild her horns and offer her to you in sacrifice."

Thus he prayed, and Athena heard his prayer. He then led the way to his own house, followed by his sons and sons-in-law. When they'd arrived and taken their places on the benches and seats, he mixed them a bowl of sweet wine that was eleven years old when the housekeeper removed the lid from the jar that held it. As he mixed the wine, he prayed earnestly and made drink-offerings to Athena, daughter of Zeus who bears the aegis. Then, when they'd made their offerings and drunk as much as they wished, the others went home to bed in their own houses. But Nestor put Telemachus to sleep in the room over the gateway along with Pisistratus, who was the only unmarried son he had left. As for himself, he slept in an inner room of the house with the queen his wife beside him.

When rosy-fingered Dawn appeared, Nestor left his bed and took his seat on the benches of white polished marble that stood in front of his house. Here in former times sat Neleus, peer of gods in counsel, but he was now dead and had gone to Hades's house, so Nestor sat in his place with scepter in hand as guardian of the public good. His sons gathered around him as they left their rooms—Echephron, Stratius, Perseus, Aretus, and Thrasymedes. The sixth son was Pisistratus, and when Telemachus joined them, they seated him with them. Nestor then addressed them.

"My sons," he said, "hurry to do as I command you. I want first and foremost to honor the great goddess Athena, who appeared visibly to me during yesterday's festivities. Go, one of you to the plain—tell the herdsman to bring me a heifer and come here with it at once. Another must go to Telemachus's ship and invite all the crew, leaving only two men in charge of the vessel. Someone else will run and fetch Laerces the goldsmith to gild the heifer's horns. The rest of you stay here—tell the maids in the house to prepare an excellent dinner and to bring seats and firewood for a burnt offering. Tell them also to bring me some clear spring water."

At this they hurried off on their various tasks. The heifer was brought from the plain, and Telemachus's crew came from the ship. The goldsmith brought his anvil, hammer, and tongs with which he worked gold, and Athena herself came to accept the sacrifice. Nestor provided the gold, and the smith gilded the heifer's horns so the goddess might take pleasure in their beauty. Then Stratius and Echephron led her in by the horns. Aretus brought water from the house in a decorated pitcher, and in his other hand he held a basket of barley meal. Sturdy Thrasymedes stood by with a sharp ax, ready to strike the heifer, while Perseus held a bowl. Then Nestor began by washing his hands and sprinkling barley meal, offering many prayers to Athena as he threw a lock from the heifer's head into the fire.

When they'd finished praying and sprinkling barley meal, Thrasymedes struck his blow and brought the heifer down with a stroke that cut through the tendons at the base of her neck, at which Nestor's daughters and daughters-in-law, and his venerable wife Eurydice—eldest daughter of Clymenus—cried out with joy. Then they lifted the heifer's head from the ground, and Pisistratus cut her throat. When she'd finished bleeding and was quite dead, they butchered her. They cut out the thigh bones in proper order, wrapped them in two layers of fat, and placed some raw meat on top. Then Nestor laid them on the wood fire and poured wine over them, while the young men stood near him with five-pronged spits in their hands. When the thighs were burned and they'd tasted the inner organs, they cut up the rest of the meat small, put the pieces on spits, and roasted them over the fire.

Meanwhile lovely Polycaste, Nestor's youngest daughter, bathed Telemachus. When she'd washed him and anointed him with oil, she brought him a fine cloak and tunic, and he looked like a god as he came from the bath and took his seat beside Nestor. When the outer meats were done, they drew them off the spits and sat down to dinner, where worthy servants waited on them, pouring wine into golden cups. As soon as they'd eaten and drunk enough, Nestor said, "Sons, harness Telemachus's horses to the chariot so he can start at once."

Thus he spoke, and they did exactly as he said, yoking the swift horses to the chariot. The housekeeper packed them provisions of bread, wine, and delicacies fit for princes. Then Telemachus got into the chariot while Pisistratus gathered up the reins and took the seat beside him. He whipped the horses on, and they flew forward eagerly into the open country, leaving the high citadel of Pylos behind them. All day they traveled, with the yoke swaying on their necks, until the sun set and darkness covered the land. Then they reached Pherae, where Diocles lived—son of Ortilochus and grandson of Alpheus. Here they spent the night, and Diocles entertained them hospitably. When rosy-fingered Dawn appeared, they again harnessed their horses and drove out through the gateway under the echoing portico. Pisistratus whipped the horses on, and they flew forward eagerly. Soon they came to the wheat lands of the open country, and in due time completed their journey, so well did their steeds carry them.

Now when the sun had set and darkness covered the land, Nestor said, "It is getting late; it is time we were all in bed. The libations have been made and the prayers offered; let us go home to rest." Thus he spoke, and they did exactly as he said, yoking the swift horses to the chariot. The housekeeper packed them provisions of bread, wine, and delicacies fit for princes. Then Telemachus got into the chariot while Pisistratus gathered up the reins and took the seat beside him. He whipped the horses on, and they flew forward eagerly into the open country, leaving the high citadel of Pylos behind them. All day they traveled, with the yoke swaying on their necks, until the sun set and darkness covered the land. Then they reached Pherae, where Diocles lived—son of Ortilochus and grandson of Alpheus. Here they spent the night, and Diocles entertained them hospitably. When rosy-fingered Dawn appeared, they again harnessed their horses and drove out through the gateway under the echoing portico. Pisistratus whipped the horses on, and they flew forward eagerly. Soon they came to the wheat lands of the open country, and in due time completed their journey, so well did their steeds carry them.

chapters.title: Book IV — The visit to king Menelaus, who tells his story—meanwhile the suitors in Ithaca plot against Telemachus
paragraphs: They reached the low-lying city of Lacedaemon, where they drove straight to the palace of Menelaus and found him in his own house, celebrating with his many relatives in honor of his son's wedding, and also his daughter's, whom he was giving in marriage to the son of that brave warrior Achilles. He had promised her to him while still at Troy, and now the gods were bringing the marriage to pass, so he was sending her with chariots and horses to the city of the Myrmidons, where Achilles' son ruled. For his only son he had found a bride from Sparta, the daughter of Alector. This son, Megapenthes, was born to him by a slave woman, for heaven granted Helen no more children after she bore Hermione, who was as beautiful as golden Aphrodite herself.

So the neighbors and kinsmen of Menelaus were feasting and celebrating in his house. There was also a bard to sing for them and play his lyre, while two acrobats performed among them when the musician struck up his tune.

Telemachus and Nestor's son stopped their horses at the gate, and Eteoneus, Menelaus's servant, came out. As soon as he saw them, he ran hurrying back into the house to tell his master. He went close to him and said, "Menelaus, some strangers have arrived here—two men who look like sons of Zeus. What should we do? Should we unhitch their horses, or tell them to find lodging elsewhere as best they can?"

Menelaus was very angry and said, "Eteoneus, son of Boethous, you never used to be a fool, but now you're talking like an idiot. Unhitch their horses, of course, and show the strangers in so they can have supper. You and I have stayed at other people's houses often enough before we got back here, where heaven grant that we may rest in peace from now on."

So Eteoneus hurried back and told the other servants to come with him. They took the sweating horses from under the yoke, tied them to the mangers, and gave them a feed of mixed oats and barley. Then they leaned the chariot against the end wall of the courtyard and led the way into the house. Telemachus and Pisistratus were amazed when they saw it, for its splendor was like that of the sun and moon. After they had admired everything to their heart's content, they went to the bathroom and washed themselves.

When the servants had washed them and rubbed them with oil, they brought them woolen cloaks and tunics, and the two took their seats beside Menelaus. A maidservant brought them water in a beautiful golden pitcher and poured it into a silver basin for them to wash their hands, and she set a polished table beside them. A senior servant brought them bread and offered them many good things from what was available in the house, while the carver brought them plates of various meats and set golden cups beside them.

Menelaus then greeted them, saying, "Eat and welcome! When you've finished supper, I'll ask who you are, for men of your noble bearing cannot come from obscure lineage. You must be descended from a line of kings who carry scepters, for common people don't have sons like you."

With this he handed them a piece of fat roast beef that had been set near him as a choice portion, and they helped themselves to the good food before them. As soon as they had eaten and drunk their fill, Telemachus said to Nestor's son, leaning close so no one else could hear, "Look, Pisistratus, dear friend, see the gleam of bronze and gold—of amber, ivory, and silver. Everything is so magnificent that it's like seeing the palace of Zeus on Olympus. I'm overwhelmed with wonder."

Menelaus overheard him and said, "No one, my boys, can compete with Zeus, for his house and everything about him is immortal. But among mortal men—well, there may be another who has as much wealth as I do, or there may not. But in any case, I've traveled far and endured much hardship, for it took nearly eight years before I could get home with my fleet. I went to Cyprus, Phoenicia, and Egypt; I also went to the Ethiopians, the Sidonians, and the Erembians, and to Libya where the lambs grow horns as soon as they're born and the sheep give birth three times a year. Everyone in that country, whether master or servant, has plenty of cheese, meat, and good milk, for the ewes produce all year round. But while I was traveling and gathering great wealth among these peoples, my brother was secretly and brutally murdered through the treachery of his wicked wife, so I take no pleasure in being lord of all this wealth. Whoever your parents may be, they must have told you about all this, and about my terrible loss in the destruction of a stately mansion that was fully and magnificently furnished. I wish I had only a third of what I now possess, if only I had stayed home and all those men were still alive who died on the plain of Troy, far from Argos. I often grieve as I sit here in my house for each and every one of them. Sometimes I cry aloud in sorrow, but then I stop again, for weeping brings cold comfort and one soon grows tired of it. Yet however much I grieve for all of them, I mourn for one man more than all the rest. I can't even think of him without losing my appetite for food and sleep, so wretched does he make me feel, for none of the Greeks worked harder or risked more than he did. He gained nothing by it and left me a legacy of sorrow, for he's been gone so long that we don't know whether he's alive or dead. His old father, his long-suffering wife Penelope, and his son Telemachus, whom he left behind as an infant, are all plunged in grief on his account."

When Menelaus spoke these words, Telemachus's heart ached as he thought of his father. Tears fell from his eyes when he heard him mentioned, so he held his cloak before his face with both hands. When Menelaus saw this, he wondered whether to let him choose his own time to speak or to question him immediately and find out what it was all about.

While he was torn between these thoughts, Helen came down from her high, vaulted, and perfumed chamber, looking as lovely as Artemis herself. Adraste brought her a chair, Alcippe a soft woolen rug, while Phylo fetched her the silver work-box that Alcandra, wife of Polybus, had given her. Polybus lived in Egyptian Thebes, the richest city in the whole world. He gave Menelaus two silver baths, two tripods, and ten talents of gold. Besides all this, his wife gave Helen beautiful gifts: a golden spindle and a silver work-box on wheels with a gold rim around the top. Phylo now placed this beside her, filled with fine spun yarn, and a spindle loaded with violet-colored wool was laid on top of it. Then Helen took her seat, put her feet on the footstool, and began questioning her husband.

"Do we know, Menelaus," she said, "the names of these strangers who have come to visit us? Should I guess right or wrong? I can't help saying what I think. I have never seen any man or woman who looked so much like someone else—indeed, when I look at him I hardly know what to think—as this young man resembles Telemachus, whom Odysseus left as a baby when you Greeks went to Troy with war in your hearts, all because of my shameful behavior."

"My dear wife," replied Menelaus, "I see the resemblance just as you do. His hands and feet are just like Odysseus's, and so is his hair, the shape of his head, and the expression in his eyes. Moreover, when I was talking about Odysseus and saying how much he had suffered on my account, tears fell from his eyes and he hid his face in his cloak."

Then Pisistratus said, "Menelaus, son of Atreus, you're right in thinking this young man is Telemachus, but he's very modest and feels ashamed to come here and start a conversation with someone whose words are as divinely inspiring as yours. My father, Nestor, sent me to escort him here because he wanted to know whether you could give him any advice or help. A son always has trouble at home when his father has gone away leaving him without supporters, and this is how Telemachus is situated now, for his father is absent and there's no one among his own people to stand by him."

"Good heavens," replied Menelaus, "then I'm receiving a visit from the son of a very dear friend who suffered much hardship for my sake. I had always hoped to welcome him with the greatest honor when heaven granted us a safe return from overseas. I would have founded a city for him in Argos and built him a house. I would have made him leave Ithaca with his possessions, his son, and all his people, and would have conquered one of the neighboring cities under my rule for them. We could have seen each other constantly, and nothing but death could have interrupted such a close and happy friendship. But I suppose heaven begrudged us such great good fortune, for it has prevented the poor man from ever getting home at all."

His words set them all weeping. Helen wept, Telemachus wept, and so did Menelaus, nor could Pisistratus keep his eyes dry when he remembered his dear brother Antilochus, whom the son of bright Dawn had killed. Then he said to Menelaus:

"Sir, my father Nestor, when we used to talk about you at home, told me you were a person of rare and excellent wisdom. If it's possible, please do as I suggest. I don't enjoy crying while I'm eating my supper. Morning will come soon enough, and in the daylight I don't mind how much I weep for those who are dead and gone. This is all we can do for the poor souls—we can only cut our hair for them and let the tears flow from our cheeks. I had a brother who died at Troy; he was by no means the worst man there. You must have known him—his name was Antilochus. I never met him myself, but they say he was remarkably swift of foot and brave in battle."

"Your wisdom, my friend," answered Menelaus, "is beyond your years. It's clear you take after your father. One can easily see when a man is the son of someone heaven has blessed both in marriage and children—and it has blessed Nestor throughout his life, giving him a peaceful old age in his own house with sons who are both well-behaved and brave. Let's put an end to all this weeping and return to our supper. Let water be poured over our hands. Telemachus and I can talk together properly in the morning."
At this, Asphalion, one of the servants, poured water over their hands, and they helped themselves to the good food before them.

Then Zeus's daughter Helen thought of something else. She drugged the wine with a herb that banishes all care, sorrow, and bad feelings. Whoever drinks wine mixed with this drug cannot shed a single tear for the rest of the day, not even if both his father and mother died, or if he saw a brother or son cut down before his very eyes. This drug of such amazing power had been given to Helen by Polydamna, wife of Thon, a woman of Egypt, where all sorts of herbs grow—some good to put in the wine bowl and others poisonous. Moreover, everyone in that whole country is a skilled doctor, for they are descendants of Paeon. When Helen had put this drug in the bowl and told the servants to pour the wine, she said:

"Menelaus, son of Atreus, and you, my good friends, sons of noble men—which is as Zeus wills, for he gives both good and evil and can do whatever he chooses—feast here as you like and listen while I tell you a story for the occasion. I can't name every single one of Odysseus's exploits, but I can tell you what he did when he was at Troy and you Greeks were in all sorts of trouble. He covered himself with wounds and bruises, dressed in rags, and entered the enemy's city looking like a servant or beggar—completely different from how he appeared among his own people. In this disguise he entered Troy, and no one questioned him. I alone recognized him and began to ask him questions, but he was too clever for me. However, when I had bathed and anointed him and given him clothes, and after I had sworn a solemn oath not to betray him to the Trojans until he had safely returned to his camp and ships, he told me all the Greeks' plans. He killed many Trojans and gathered much information before reaching the Greek camp. For all this the Trojan women mourned, but I was glad, for my heart was beginning to long for home, and I regretted the wrong that Aphrodite had done me in bringing me there, away from my country, my daughter, and my lawful husband, who is certainly not lacking in either looks or intelligence."

Then Menelaus said, "Everything you've said, my dear wife, is true. I've traveled extensively and dealt with many heroes, but I've never seen another man like Odysseus. What endurance and courage he showed inside the wooden horse, where all the bravest Greeks were hiding, waiting to bring death and destruction to the Trojans! At that moment you came to us—some god who favored the Trojans must have prompted you, and Deiphobus was with you. Three times you walked around our hiding place and patted it, calling each of our leaders by name and imitating all our wives' voices. Diomedes, Odysseus, and I heard what a racket you made from inside. Diomedes and I couldn't decide whether to jump out right then or answer you from inside, but Odysseus kept us all in check, so we sat perfectly still. Only Anticlus started to answer you, but Odysseus clamped his strong hands over his mouth and kept them there. That's what saved us all, for he silenced Anticlus until Athena led you away."
"How sad," exclaimed Telemachus, "that none of this was enough to save him, despite his iron courage. But now, sir, please send us all to bed so we can lie down and enjoy the blessed gift of sleep."

At this, Helen told the maidservants to set up beds in the gatehouse room and make them with fine red blankets, spreading coverlets on top with woolen cloaks for the guests to wear. So the maids went out with torches and prepared the beds, and a manservant soon led the strangers there. Thus Telemachus and Pisistratus slept in the forecourt, while the son of Atreus lay in an inner room with lovely Helen beside him.

When rosy-fingered Dawn appeared, Menelaus rose and dressed himself. He fastened his sandals to his feet, girded his sword about his shoulders, and left his room looking like an immortal god. Then, taking a seat near Telemachus, he said:
"And what, Telemachus, has brought you on this long sea voyage to Sparta? Are you here on public business, or is this personal? Tell me everything."

"I have come, sir," Telemachus replied, "to see if you can tell me anything about my father. I'm being eaten out of house and home. My inheritance is being squandered, and my house is overrun with worthless men who keep slaughtering my sheep and cattle in great numbers, claiming they're courting my mother.
