So I come to you as a suppliant, hoping you might tell me about my father's sad fate—whether you witnessed it yourself or heard about it from another traveler. He was born for hardship. Don't soften the truth out of pity for me, but tell me plainly exactly what you saw. If my brave father Odysseus ever served you faithfully in word or deed when you Greeks were hard-pressed by the Trojans, remember that now and help me by telling me the whole truth."

When Menelaus heard this, he was deeply moved. "So," he exclaimed, "these cowards want to take over a brave man's bed! It's like a deer laying her newborn young in a lion's den, then wandering off to graze in the forest or some grassy valley—when the lion returns to his lair, he'll make quick work of both of them. And that's exactly what Odysseus will do to these suitors. By Zeus, Athena, and Apollo, if Odysseus is still the man he was when he wrestled with Philomeleides in Lesbos and threw him so hard that all the Greeks cheered—if he's still that strong and were to face these suitors, they'd have a quick death and a sorry wedding. But regarding your questions, I won't mislead or deceive you. I'll tell you without hiding anything all that the old man of the sea told me.

"I was trying to sail home, but the gods held me back in Egypt because my sacrifices hadn't fully satisfied them, and the gods are very strict about getting what's owed to them. Now off the coast of Egypt, about as far as a ship can sail in a day with a strong following wind, there's an island called Pharos. It has a good harbor where ships can reach open water after taking on supplies. Here the gods becalmed me for twenty days without even a breath of favorable wind to help me along. We would have run completely out of food and my men would have starved, if a goddess hadn't taken pity on me and saved me. This was Eidothea, daughter of Proteus, the old man of the sea, and she had taken quite a liking to me.

"She came to me one day when I was alone, as I often was, since my men would scatter across the island with their fishing hooks, hoping to catch a fish or two to stave off hunger. 'Stranger,' she said, 'it seems you actually enjoy starving like this—at least it doesn't seem to bother you much, since you just stay here day after day without even trying to leave, while your men are wasting away.'

"'Let me tell you,' I said, 'whichever goddess you may be, that I'm not staying here by choice. I must have angered the gods who rule the heavens. Tell me then—since the gods know everything—which of the immortals is blocking my way like this, and tell me how I can sail across the sea to reach my home.'

"'Stranger,' she replied, 'I'll explain everything clearly. There's an ancient immortal who lives beneath the sea in these parts, and his name is Proteus. He's Egyptian, and people say he's my father. He serves Poseidon and knows every inch of the ocean floor. If you can catch him and hold him tight, he'll tell you about your voyage—what route to take and how to sail the sea to reach your home. He'll also tell you, if you want to know, everything that's been happening at your house, both good and bad, while you've been away on this long and dangerous journey.'
"'Can you show me,' I asked, 'some trick by which I can catch this old god without him suspecting and discovering me? After all, a god isn't easily caught—not by a mortal man.'

"'Stranger,' she said, 'I'll make it all perfectly clear. Around the time when the sun reaches its peak, the old man of the sea rises from beneath the waves, announced by the west wind that ruffles the water above his head. As soon as he surfaces, he lies down and sleeps in a great sea cave, where the seals—Halosydne's children, as they're called—also emerge from the gray sea and sleep in groups all around him. And they bring with them a very strong, fishy smell. Early tomorrow morning I'll take you to this place and position you in ambush. So choose the three best men from your crew, and I'll tell you all the tricks the old man will try on you.

"'First he'll look over all his seals and count them. Then, when he's seen them and tallied them on his fingers, he'll go to sleep among them like a shepherd among his sheep. The moment you see he's asleep, grab him and use all your strength to hold him fast, because he'll do everything possible to escape from you. He'll transform himself into every kind of creature that walks the earth, and he'll also become both fire and water. But you must hold him tight and grip him even tighter, until he starts talking to you and returns to the form you saw when he fell asleep. Then you can relax your hold and release him, and you can ask him which god is angry with you and what you must do to reach your home across the seas.'

"Having said this, she dove beneath the waves, and I turned back to where my ships were drawn up on the shore. My heart was heavy with worry as I walked. When I reached my ship, we prepared supper, since night was falling, and we camped on the beach.

"When rosy-fingered Dawn appeared, I took the three men I could most rely on for every kind of courage and walked along the seashore, praying earnestly to heaven. Meanwhile, the goddess brought up four sealskins from the bottom of the sea, all freshly skinned, since she planned to trick her father. She dug four pits for us to lie in and sat down to wait for us to arrive. When we came close to her, she made us lie down in the pits one by one and threw a sealskin over each of us. Our hiding place would have been unbearable because the stench of the fishy seals was so disgusting—who would want to sleep next to a sea monster if they could avoid it? But here too the goddess helped us and thought of something that gave us great relief: she placed ambrosia under each man's nose, and its fragrance was so sweet that it overpowered the smell of the seals.

"We waited all morning and endured it, watching hundreds of seals come up to bask on the seashore, until at noon the old man of the sea also emerged. When he found his fat seals, he went among them and counted them. We were among the first he counted, and he never suspected any trickery, but lay down to sleep as soon as he finished counting. Then we rushed at him with a shout and seized him. He immediately began his old tricks, changing himself first into a great-maned lion, then suddenly into a dragon, a leopard, a wild boar. The next moment he was flowing water, and then again he was a tree. But we held on and never let go, until at last the cunning old creature grew tired and said, 'Which of the gods was it, son of Atreus, who devised this plot with you to trap and seize me against my will? What do you want?'

"'You know that yourself, old man,' I answered. 'You'll gain nothing by trying to put me off. It's because I've been trapped on this island so long and see no way to escape. I'm losing heart completely. Tell me then—since you gods know everything—which of the immortals is blocking my way, and tell me how I can sail the sea to reach my home.'

"'Then,' he said, 'if you want to complete your voyage and get home quickly, you must offer sacrifices to Zeus and the other gods before setting sail. For it's decreed that you won't return to your friends and your own house until you go back to the heaven-fed waters of Egypt and offer proper sacrifices to the immortal gods who rule in heaven. When you've done this, they'll let you complete your voyage.'

"I was heartbroken when I heard I had to make that entire long and terrible voyage back to Egypt. Nevertheless, I answered, 'I'll do everything you've commanded, old man. But now tell me truthfully whether all the Greeks that Nestor and I left behind when we sailed from Troy have returned home safely, or whether any of them met a bad end either aboard their own ships or among their friends after their fighting days were over.'

"'Son of Atreus,' he answered, 'why do you ask me this? You'd be better off not knowing what I can tell you, because your eyes will surely fill with tears when you hear my story. Many of those you ask about are dead and gone, but many still survive. Only two of the chief leaders among the Greeks died during their journey home. As for what happened on the battlefield—you were there yourself. A third Greek leader is still alive but stranded at sea, unable to return. Ajax was shipwrecked when Poseidon drove him onto the great rocks of Gyrae. Even so, Poseidon let him get safely out of the water, and despite all Athena's hatred, he would have escaped death if he hadn't ruined himself by boasting. He said the gods couldn't drown him even though they tried, and when Poseidon heard this arrogant talk, he grabbed his trident in both powerful hands and split the rock of Gyrae in two. The base remained where it was, but the part Ajax was sitting on fell headlong into the sea, carrying Ajax with it. So he swallowed salt water and drowned.

"'Your brother and his ships escaped because Hera protected him, but when he was just about to reach the high cape of Malea, a fierce gale caught him and carried him back out to sea against his will, driving him to the headland where Thyestes once lived but where Aegisthus was then ruling. Eventually, though, it seemed he would return safely after all, for the gods shifted the wind back to its proper quarter and they reached home. Agamemnon kissed his native soil and wept tears of joy at finding himself in his own country.

"'Now Aegisthus kept a watchman constantly on guard, promising him two talents of gold. This man had been watching for a full year to make sure Agamemnon didn't slip past him and prepare for war. So when this watchman saw Agamemnon arrive, he went and told Aegisthus, who immediately began plotting against him. He chose twenty of his bravest warriors and set them in ambush on one side of the hall, while on the other side he prepared a feast. Then he sent his chariots and horsemen to Agamemnon and invited him to the banquet, but he planned treachery. He got him there, completely unaware of the doom awaiting him, and killed him when the feast was over as if he were slaughtering an ox in a butcher shop. Not one of Agamemnon's men was left alive, nor any of Aegisthus's either—they were all killed there in the hall.'

"So spoke Proteus, and I was heartbroken as I listened. I sat down on the sand and wept, feeling as though I could no longer bear to live or look upon the sunlight. When I had my fill of weeping and writhing on the ground, the old man of the sea said, 'Son of Atreus, don't waste any more time crying so bitterly—it won't do any good. Find your way home as quickly as you can, for Aegisthus may still be alive, and even if Orestes has beaten you to killing him, you might still arrive in time for his funeral.'

"At this I took comfort despite all my grief and said, 'Now I know about those two. Tell me about the third man you mentioned—is he still alive but trapped at sea and unable to get home? Or is he dead? Tell me, no matter how much it grieves me.'

"'The third man,' he answered, 'is Odysseus who lives in Ithaca. I can see him on an island, grieving bitterly in the house of the nymph Calypso, who's keeping him prisoner. He can't reach his home because he has no ships or sailors to carry him across the sea. As for your own fate, Menelaus, you won't die in Argos. Instead, the gods will take you to the Elysian Fields at the world's end. There fair-haired Rhadamanthus rules, and people live more easily than anywhere else in the world, for in Elysium there's no rain, hail, or snow. Ocean constantly sends a gentle west wind that sings softly from the sea and brings fresh life to everyone. This will happen to you because you married Helen and are Zeus's son-in-law.'

"As he spoke, he dove beneath the waves, and I turned back to the ships with my companions, my heart heavy with worry as I walked. When we reached the ships, we prepared supper since night was falling, and we camped on the beach. When rosy-fingered Dawn appeared, we launched our ships into the water and set up our masts and sails. Then we boarded, took our places on the benches, and struck the gray sea with our oars. I sailed my ships back to the heaven-fed waters of Egypt and offered full and proper sacrifices. When I had appeased heaven's anger, I built a memorial mound for Agamemnon so his name would live forever. After that, I had a swift voyage home because the gods sent me favorable winds.

"Now as for you—stay here another ten or twelve days, and then I'll send you on your way. I'll give you a splendid gift of a chariot and three horses. I'll also give you a beautiful cup, so that as long as you live, you'll think of me whenever you pour drink offerings to the immortal gods."

"Son of Atreus," Telemachus replied, "don't urge me to stay longer. I'd be happy to remain with you for another twelve months—I find your conversation so delightful that I'd never miss being home with my parents. But my crew, whom I left at Pylos, are already getting restless, and you're keeping me from them. As for any gift you'd like to give me, I'd prefer it to be some piece of treasure. I won't take horses back to Ithaca—I'll leave them to grace your own stables, since you have plenty of flat land in your kingdom where clover grows, along with sweet grass, wheat, barley, and oats with their white spreading heads. But in Ithaca we have neither open fields nor racetracks. The country is better suited for goats than horses, and I like it better that way. None of our islands have much level ground suitable for horses, and Ithaca least of all."

Menelaus smiled and took Telemachus's hand in his own. "What you say shows that you come from good family. I both can and will make this exchange for you by giving you the finest and most precious piece in all my house. It's a mixing bowl made by Hephaestus himself, of pure silver except for the rim, which is inlaid with gold. Phaedimus, king of the Sidonians, gave it to me during a visit I paid him on my journey home. I'll give it to you as a gift."

So they talked together, while guests kept arriving at the king's house. They brought sheep and wine, and their wives had prepared bread for them to take along. The guests were busy cooking their dinners in the courtyards.

Meanwhile, the suitors were throwing discs and aiming spears at targets on the leveled ground in front of Odysseus's house, behaving with all their usual arrogance. Antinous and Eurymachus, who were their leaders and by far the most prominent among them, were sitting together when Noemon, son of Phronius, approached and said to Antinous,

"Do we have any idea, Antinous, when Telemachus returns from Pylos? He has a ship of mine, and I need it to cross over to Elis. I have twelve brood mares there with yearling mule foals at their side, not yet broken in, and I want to bring one of them back here to train."

They were shocked when they heard this, for they had been certain that Telemachus hadn't gone to Neleus's city. They thought he was only away somewhere on the farms, either with the sheep or with the swineherd. So Antinous said, "When did he leave? Tell me the truth. What young men did he take with him? Were they free men or his own servants—he could manage either? Tell me also, did you lend him the ship willingly because he asked, or did he take it without your permission?"

"I lent it to him," Noemon answered. "What else could I do when a man of his standing said he was in trouble and asked me for help? I couldn't possibly refuse. As for those who went with him, they were the best young men we have, and I saw Mentor go aboard as captain—or some god who looked exactly like him. I can't understand it, because I saw Mentor here myself yesterday morning, yet he was supposedly setting out for Pylos then."

Noemon then went back to his father's house, but Antinous and Eurymachus were furious. They told the others to stop playing and come sit with them. When they gathered, Antinous, son of Eupeithes, spoke in anger. His heart was black with rage, and his eyes flashed fire as he said,

"Good God, this voyage of Telemachus is serious business! We were sure it would come to nothing, but the young man has gotten away despite us, and with a picked crew too. He'll be causing us trouble soon. May Zeus strike him down before he's fully grown! Find me a ship with a crew of twenty men, and I'll lie in wait for him in the straits between Ithaca and Samos. Then he'll regret the day he set out trying to get news of his father."
So he spoke, and the others applauded his words. Then they all went inside the buildings.

It wasn't long before Penelope learned what the suitors were plotting. A servant named Medon overheard them from outside the outer court as they were laying their schemes within, and he went to tell his mistress. As he crossed the threshold of her room, Penelope said, "Medon, what have the suitors sent you here for? Is it to tell the maids to leave their master's work and cook dinner for them? I wish they would neither court me nor dine here anymore, neither here nor anywhere else. Let this be the very last time, considering all the waste you make of my son's estate. Didn't your fathers tell you when you were children how good Odysseus had been to them—never acting high-handed or speaking harshly to anyone? Kings may say harsh things sometimes, and they may favor one man and dislike another, but Odysseus never treated anyone unjustly—which shows what evil hearts you have, and that there's no such thing as gratitude left in this world."

Then Medon said, "I wish, my lady, that this were all, but they're plotting something much more terrible now—may heaven stop their plan. They're going to try to murder Telemachus as he returns home from Pylos and Sparta, where he's been to get news of his father."

Then Penelope's heart sank, and for a long time she was speechless. Her eyes filled with tears, and she couldn't find her voice. At last, however, she said, "Why did my son leave me? What business did he have sailing off in ships that make long voyages across the ocean like sea-horses? Does he want to die without leaving anyone behind to carry on his name?"
"I don't know," Medon answered, "whether some god prompted him to go, or whether he went on his own impulse to see if he could discover whether his father was dead or alive and on his way home."

Then he went downstairs again, leaving Penelope in agony. There were plenty of seats in the house, but she had no heart for sitting on any of them. She could only throw herself on the floor of her own room and weep, while all the maids in the house, both old and young, gathered around her and began crying too. Finally, in her overwhelming sorrow, she cried out,

"My dear women, heaven has chosen to burden me with more suffering than any other woman of my age and station. First I lost my brave and lion-hearted husband, who had every good quality under heaven and whose name was renowned throughout all Greece and central Argos. Now my darling son is at the mercy of the winds and waves, and I never even heard about his leaving home. You lazy girls, not one of you thought to wake me from my bed, though you all knew very well when he was departing. If I had known he planned this voyage, he would have had to give it up, no matter how determined he was, or leave me dead behind him—one or the other. Now go, some of you, and call old Dolius, who was given to me by my father when I married and who is my gardener. Tell him to go at once and inform Laertes of everything, who may be able to think of some plan for winning public sympathy to our side, against those who are trying to destroy his family line and that of Odysseus."

Then the dear old nurse Euryclea said, "You may kill me, my lady, or let me live on in your house, whichever you choose, but I'll tell you the truth. I knew all about it and gave him everything he needed—bread and wine—but he made me swear a solemn oath that I wouldn't tell you anything for ten or twelve days, unless you asked or happened to hear that he had gone. He didn't want you to ruin your beauty by crying. Now, my lady, wash your face, change your dress, and go upstairs with your maids to offer prayers to Athena, daughter of Zeus who carries the aegis, for she can save him even if he's in the jaws of death. Don't trouble Laertes—he has enough trouble already. Besides, I can't believe that the gods hate the family of Arceisius's son so much. There will be a descendant left to inherit both the house and the beautiful fields that stretch far around it."

With these words she made her mistress stop crying and dried the tears from her eyes. Penelope washed her face, changed her dress, and went upstairs with her maids. She put some ground barley into a basket and began praying to Athena.

"Hear me," she cried, "daughter of Zeus who carries the aegis, tireless one. If ever Odysseus burned fat thigh bones of sheep or cattle for you while he was here, remember it now in my favor and save my darling son from the evil of the suitors."
She cried aloud as she spoke, and the goddess heard her prayer. Meanwhile, the suitors were making noise throughout the covered colonnade, and one of them said,
"The queen is preparing for her marriage with one of us. Little does she know that her son has now been marked for death."

This was what they said, but they didn't know what was going to happen. Then Antinous said, "Friends, let's not talk so loudly, in case some of it carries inside. Let's get up and do what we're all agreed on, but quietly."

He then chose twenty men, and they went down to their ship and the seashore. They dragged the vessel into the water and put her mast and sails aboard. They fastened the oars to the oarlocks with twisted leather straps, all in proper order, and raised the white sails, while their servants brought them their weapons. Then they anchored the ship a short distance out, came back to shore, ate their supper, and waited for nightfall.

But Penelope lay in her room upstairs, unable to eat or drink, wondering whether her brave son would escape or be overpowered by the wicked suitors. Like a lioness caught in a trap with hunters surrounding her on all sides, she worried and worried until she fell into sleep, lying on her bed without thought or movement.

Then Athena thought of another plan and created a vision in the likeness of Penelope's sister Iphthime, daughter of Icarius, who had married Eumelus and lived in Pherae. She sent the vision to Odysseus's house to make Penelope stop crying. It entered her room through the hole where the strap went for pulling the door shut, and hovered over her head, saying,
"You're asleep, Penelope. The gods who live in comfort will not let you weep and be so sad. Your son has done them no wrong, so he will return to you."

Penelope, who was drifting peacefully at the edge of sleep, answered, "Sister, why have you come here? You don't visit very often, but I suppose that's because you live so far away. Am I supposed to stop crying and push away all the terrible thoughts that torment me? I've lost my brave and lion-hearted husband, who possessed every good quality imaginable, and whose reputation was renowned throughout all of Greece and the heartland of Argos. And now my beloved son has sailed away on a ship—that foolish boy who has never experienced hardship or mingled in the assemblies of men. I'm even more worried about him than about my husband. I tremble whenever I think of him, terrified that something will happen to him, either from the people he's gone to visit or at sea, because he has many enemies plotting against him who are determined to kill him before he can return home."

Then the vision said, "Take courage and don't be so frightened. Someone has gone with him whom many men would be grateful to have as their protector—I mean Athena. She feels compassion for you, and she's the one who sent me to bring you this message."

"Then," said Penelope, "if you are a goddess or have been sent here on divine orders, tell me also about that other unfortunate one—is he still alive, or is he already dead and in the realm of Hades?"
And the vision said, "I won't tell you for certain whether he's alive or dead—there's no point in meaningless chatter."
Then it vanished through the keyhole of the door and dissolved into thin air. But Penelope woke from her sleep feeling refreshed and comforted, so vivid had her dream been.

Meanwhile the suitors boarded their ship and sailed across the sea, intent on murdering Telemachus. There's a rocky island called Asteris, not very large, lying in the channel between Ithaca and Samos, with harbors on both sides where ships can anchor. There the Greeks positioned themselves in ambush.

chapters.title: Book V — Calypso—Odysseus reaches Scheria on a raft
paragraphs: As Dawn rose from her bed beside Tithonus, bringing light to both mortals and immortals, the gods gathered in council with Zeus, lord of thunder and their king. There Athena began telling them of Odysseus's many sufferings, for she pitied him trapped in the nymph Calypso's home.

"Father Zeus," she said, "and all you other gods who live in eternal bliss, I hope there's never again such a thing as a kind and fair-minded ruler, nor one who governs justly. I hope they'll all be cruel and unjust from now on, since not one of his subjects remembers Odysseus, who ruled them like a father. There he lies in great pain on an island where the nymph Calypso lives, and she won't let him go. He can't get back to his own country because he has no ships or sailors to carry him across the sea. And now wicked men are trying to murder his only son Telemachus, who's returning from Pylos and Sparta where he went seeking news of his father."

"What are you talking about, my dear?" her father replied. "Didn't you send him there yourself because you thought it would help Odysseus get home and punish the suitors? Besides, you're perfectly able to protect Telemachus and see him safely home, while the suitors will have to scurry back without killing him."

After speaking, he turned to his son Hermes. "Hermes, you are our messenger, so go tell Calypso that we've decided poor Odysseus must return home. He won't be escorted by gods or men, but after twenty perilous days on a raft he'll reach fertile Scheria, land of the Phaeacians, who are close to the gods and will honor him as one of us. They'll send him home in a ship and give him more bronze, gold, and clothing than he would have brought back from Troy if he'd had all his prize money and returned without disaster. This is how we've decided he shall return to his country and friends."

Zeus spoke, and Hermes the guide and guardian, slayer of Argus, obeyed. He immediately bound on his glittering golden sandals that let him fly like wind over land and sea. He took his wand that puts men to sleep or wakes them as he pleases, and holding it flew over Pieria, then swooped down through the sky until he reached sea level, skimming the waves like a cormorant fishing every corner of the ocean, drenching its thick feathers in spray. He flew over many weary waves until he finally reached the island that was his destination, left the sea, and went overland to the cave where the nymph Calypso lived.

He found her at home. A large fire burned on the hearth, and the fragrant smoke of burning cedar and sandalwood could be smelled from far away. She was busy at her loom, shooting her golden shuttle through the warp and singing beautifully. Around her cave grew a thick wood of alder, poplar, and sweet-smelling cypress trees where all kinds of birds had built their nests—owls, hawks, and chattering sea-crows that make their living from the waters. A vine heavy with grapes grew luxuriously around the cave's mouth. Four streams of water flowed in channels cut close together, winding here and there to water beds of violets and lush plants. Even a god couldn't help being charmed by such a lovely spot, so Hermes stood still and admired it before going inside the cave.

Calypso recognized him at once—the gods all know each other no matter how far apart they live—but Odysseus wasn't there. He was on the seashore as usual, staring at the barren ocean with tears in his eyes, groaning and breaking his heart with sorrow. Calypso offered Hermes a seat and said, "Why have you come to see me, Hermes—honored and always welcome—since you don't visit me often? Tell me what you want. I'll do it at once if I can and if it's possible. But come inside and let me offer you refreshment."
As she spoke, she drew up a table loaded with ambrosia and mixed him red nectar. Hermes ate and drank until he was satisfied, then said:

"We're speaking as god to goddess, and you ask why I've come, so I'll tell you truthfully as you wish. Zeus sent me—it wasn't my idea. Who would want to come all this way across the sea where there are no cities full of people to offer sacrifices or choice offerings? But I had to come, since none of us other gods can cross Zeus or disobey his orders. He says you have here the most cursed of all those who fought nine years before King Priam's city and sailed home in the tenth year after sacking it. On their way home they offended Athena, who raised wind and waves against them so that all his brave companions died, and he alone was carried here by wind and tide. Zeus says you must let this man go at once, for it's decreed that he won't die here far from his people, but will return to his house and country to see his friends again."

Calypso trembled with rage at these words. "You gods should be ashamed of yourselves," she cried. "You're always jealous and hate seeing a goddess fall for a mortal man and live with him openly. When rosy-fingered Dawn loved Orion, you precious gods were furious until Artemis killed him in Ortygia. When Demeter fell in love with Iasion and lay with him in a thrice-plowed field, Zeus heard about it quickly and killed Iasion with his thunderbolts. Now you're angry with me because I have a man here. I found the poor creature sitting alone on a ship's keel after Zeus struck his ship with lightning and sunk it mid-ocean, drowning his entire crew while he was driven by wind and waves to my island. I grew fond of him and cared for him, planning to make him immortal so he'd never age. But I can't cross Zeus or frustrate his plans. So if he insists, let the man sail beyond the seas again. But I can't send him anywhere myself since I have no ships or men to take him. Still, I'll gladly give him good advice that will help him reach his own country safely."
"Then send him away," said Hermes, "or Zeus will be angry and punish you."

With that he left, and Calypso went to find Odysseus, having heard Zeus's message. She found him sitting on the beach with his eyes full of tears, dying of homesickness. He'd grown tired of Calypso, and though he was forced to sleep with her in the cave at night, it was she, not he, who wanted it. During the day he spent time on the rocks and seashore, weeping and crying out in despair, always staring at the sea. Calypso approached him and said:

"Poor man, don't stay here grieving and wasting your life any longer. I'm going to send you away of my own free will. Go cut some logs and build yourself a large raft with a deck that can carry you safely across the sea. I'll put bread, wine, and water aboard to keep you from starving. I'll also give you clothes and send you a fair wind to take you home, if the gods in heaven will it—for they know more about these things and can manage them better than I can."

Odysseus shuddered at her words. "Now goddess," he answered, "there's something behind all this. You can't really mean to help me home when you tell me to do something as terrible as put to sea on a raft. Not even a well-built ship with fair wind would attempt such a distant voyage. Nothing you say or do will make me board a raft unless you first solemnly swear you mean me no harm."

Calypso smiled at this and stroked him with her hand. "You're very clever," she said, "but you're quite wrong here. Let heaven above and earth below witness, along with the waters of the river Styx—the most solemn oath a blessed god can take—that I mean you no harm and am only advising you to do exactly what I'd do in your place. I'm being completely honest with you. My heart isn't made of iron, and I feel very sorry for you."

After speaking she led the way quickly, and Odysseus followed until they reached Calypso's cave, where Odysseus took the seat Hermes had just left. Calypso set mortal food and drink before him while her maids brought ambrosia and nectar for herself. They ate the good food set before them. When they'd satisfied themselves, Calypso spoke:

"Odysseus, noble son of Laertes, so you want to go straight home to your own land? Good luck to you, but if you only knew how much suffering awaits you before you reach your country, you'd stay here, keep house with me, and let me make you immortal, no matter how anxious you are to see this wife you think about constantly. Yet I flatter myself that I'm no less tall or beautiful than she is, for no mortal woman should compare in beauty with an immortal."

"Goddess," replied Odysseus, "don't be angry about this. I know perfectly well that my wife Penelope is nothing like as tall or beautiful as you. She's only a woman, while you're an immortal. Still, I want to get home and can think of nothing else. If some god wrecks me at sea, I'll bear it and make the best of it. I've already had endless trouble on land and sea, so let this be added to the rest."
Soon the sun set and darkness fell, so the pair retired to the inner part of the cave and went to bed.

When rosy-fingered Dawn appeared, Odysseus put on his shirt and cloak while the goddess wore a dress of light, gossamer fabric, very fine and graceful, with a beautiful golden belt around her waist and a veil over her head. She immediately began thinking how to speed Odysseus on his way. She gave him a great bronze ax that fit his hands perfectly—sharpened on both sides with a beautiful olive-wood handle fitted firmly to it. She also gave him a sharp adze and led him to the far end of the island where the largest trees grew—alder, poplar, and pine reaching to the sky, very dry and well-seasoned to sail lightly on the water. After showing him the best trees, Calypso went home, leaving him to cut them, which he quickly finished. He cut down twenty trees and smoothed them with the adze, squaring them properly with good workmanship. Meanwhile Calypso returned with augers, so he drilled holes and fitted the timbers together with bolts and rivets. He made the raft as broad as a skilled shipwright makes a large vessel's beam, fixed a deck on top of the ribs, and ran a gunwale all around it. He also made a mast with a yardarm and a rudder to steer with. He fenced the raft with wicker hurdles as protection against waves, then threw on plenty of wood. Soon Calypso brought him linen for sails, and he made these excellently too, securing them with braces and sheets. Finally, using levers, he dragged the raft into the water.

In four days he'd completed the whole job, and on the fifth Calypso sent him from the island after washing him and giving him clean clothes. She gave him a goatskin full of dark wine and another larger one of water. She also gave him a bag full of provisions with plenty of good meat. Moreover, she made the wind fair and warm for him, and Odysseus gladly spread his sail, sitting and skillfully guiding the raft with the rudder. He never closed his eyes but kept them fixed on the Pleiades, late-setting Boötes, and the Bear—which men also call the Wagon, which turns around in place facing Orion and alone never dips into Ocean's stream—for Calypso had told him to keep this on his left. For seventeen days he sailed over the sea, and on the eighteenth the dim outlines of mountains on the nearest part of the Phaeacian coast appeared, rising like a shield on the horizon.

But King Poseidon, returning from the Ethiopians, spotted Odysseus from far off, from the Solymi mountains. He could see him sailing on the sea, and it made him furious. He shook his head and muttered to himself, "Good heavens, so the gods have changed their minds about Odysseus while I was away in Ethiopia, and now he's close to the Phaeacian land where he's destined to escape the troubles that have befallen him. Still, he'll have plenty more hardship before he's done."

Then he gathered his clouds, grasped his trident, stirred up the sea, and roused every wind to fury until earth, sea, and sky were hidden in cloud and night sprang from the heavens. Winds from east, south, north, and west struck him all at once, raising a tremendous sea that made Odysseus's heart fail. "Alas," he said to himself in dismay, "what will become of me? I'm afraid Calypso was right when she said I'd have trouble at sea before getting home. It's all coming true. How dark Zeus is making heaven with his clouds, and what a sea the winds are raising from every direction at once. Now I'm sure to die. Blessed and thrice blessed were those Greeks who fell before Troy fighting for the sons of Atreus. I wish I'd been killed the day the Trojans pressed me so hard around dead Achilles' body, for then I'd have had proper burial and the Greeks would have honored my name. But now it seems I'll come to the most wretched end."

As he spoke a wave broke over him with such terrible force that the raft spun around and he was hurled far overboard. He lost hold of the steering oar, and the hurricane's force was so great it snapped the mast in half, sending both sail and yardarm into the sea. For a long time Odysseus was underwater, barely able to surface again because the clothes Calypso had given him weighed him down. But finally he got his head above water and spat out the bitter brine streaming down his face. Despite everything, he didn't lose sight of his raft but swam as fast as he could toward it, grabbed hold, and climbed back aboard to escape drowning. The sea tossed the raft about like autumn winds whirling thistledown on a road. It was as if the south, north, east, and west winds were all playing battledore and shuttlecock with it at once.

While he was in this plight, Ino, daughter of Cadmus, also called Leucothea, saw him. She'd once been mortal but had since been raised to marine goddess rank. Seeing Odysseus's great distress, she took pity on him and, rising like a seagull from the waves, perched on the raft.

"My poor good man," she said, "why is Poseidon so furiously angry with you? He's giving you great trouble, but for all his bluster he won't kill you. You seem sensible, so do as I tell you: strip off your clothes, leave your raft to drift before the wind, and swim to the Phaeacian coast where better luck awaits you. Here, take my veil and wrap it around your chest—it's enchanted, and you can't be harmed while wearing it. As soon as you touch land, take it off, throw it as far as you can back into the sea, and then go away." With these words she removed her veil and gave it to him, then dove down like a seagull and vanished beneath the dark blue waters.

But Odysseus didn't know what to think. "Alas," he said to himself in dismay, "this is probably just another god trying to trick me into ruin by telling me to abandon my raft. I won't do it now, since the land where she said I'd escape all troubles still seems far away. I know what I'll do—I'm sure it's best—whatever happens, I'll stick to the raft as long as its timbers hold together. But when the sea breaks it up, I'll swim for it. I don't see how I can do better than this."

While he was torn between choices, Poseidon sent a terrible great wave that seemed to rear above his head before breaking right over the raft, which went to pieces like dry chaff tossed by a whirlwind. Odysseus straddled one plank and rode it like a horse. He then stripped off the clothes Calypso had given him, bound Ino's veil under his arms, and plunged into the sea, intending to swim to shore. King Poseidon watched him do this and shook his head, muttering, "There now, swim around as best you can until you meet some well-off people. I don't think you'll be able to say I let you off too lightly." With that he whipped his horses and drove to Aegae where his palace stands.

But Athena resolved to help Odysseus, so she stopped all winds except one and made them lie still. She raised a good stiff north wind that would calm the waters until Odysseus reached the Phaeacian land where he'd be safe.

So he floated for two nights and two days in heavy swells with death staring him in the face. But when the third day dawned, the wind died and there was dead calm without even a breath of air stirring. As he rose on a swell he looked eagerly ahead and could see land quite near. Then, as children rejoice when their dear father begins recovering after long suffering from some illness sent by an angry spirit, but the gods deliver him from evil, so Odysseus was thankful to see land and trees again, and swam with all his strength to set foot on dry ground once more. But when he got within earshot, he began hearing surf thundering against rocks, for swells still broke against them with a terrific roar. Everything was shrouded in spray—there were no harbors where a ship might anchor, no shelter of any kind, only headlands, jagged rocks, and mountain tops.

Odysseus's heart began to fail him, and he said despairingly to himself, "Alas, Zeus has let me see land after swimming so far that I'd given up all hope, but I can find no landing place. The coast is rocky and surf-beaten, the rocks are smooth and rise straight from the sea with deep water right under them, so I can't climb out for lack of footholds. I'm afraid some great wave will lift me up and dash me against the rocks as I leave the water—which would be a sorry landing indeed. If I swim further looking for some sloping beach or harbor, a hurricane may carry me back out to sea against my will, or heaven may send some great sea monster to attack me, for Amphitrite breeds many such, and I know Poseidon is very angry with me."

While he was torn between choices, a wave caught him and hurled him with such force against the rocks that he would have been smashed to pieces if Athena hadn't shown him what to do. He grabbed the rock with both hands and clung to it, groaning with pain until the wave receded—so he was saved that time. But then the wave came again and carried him far back into the sea, tearing his hands as the suckers of an octopus are torn when someone pulls it from its bed with stones still clinging—so the rocks tore skin from his strong hands, and the wave dragged him deep underwater.

Here poor Odysseus would certainly have died despite his destiny if Athena hadn't helped him keep his wits. He swam back out to sea, beyond reach of the surf beating against the land, while looking toward shore to find some haven or spit that might deflect the waves. Swimming on, he came to a river mouth, which seemed the best place since there were no rocks and it offered shelter from the wind. He felt a current, so he prayed inwardly:

"Hear me, O King, whoever you are, and save me from sea-god Poseidon's anger, for I approach you as a suppliant. Anyone who has lost his way has a claim on the gods, so in my distress I draw near to your stream and grasp the knees of your river-godhead. Have mercy on me, O King, for I declare myself your suppliant."

Then the god stopped his current and stilled the waves, making all calm before him and bringing him safely into the river mouth. Here at last Odysseus's knees and strong hands failed him, for the sea had completely broken him. His whole body was swollen, and seawater poured from his mouth and nostrils like a river, so he could neither breathe nor speak, lying unconscious from sheer exhaustion. When he'd caught his breath and come to himself again, he took off the scarf Ino had given him and threw it back into the river's salt stream, where Ino received it in her hands from the wave that bore it to her. Then he left the river, lay down among the rushes, and kissed the bountiful earth.

"Alas," he cried to himself in dismay, "what will become of me, and how will this all end? If I stay here on the riverbank through the long night watches, I'm so exhausted that the bitter cold and damp may finish me—for toward sunrise there'll be a keen wind blowing from the river. But if I climb the hillside, find shelter in the woods, and sleep in some thicket, I may escape the cold and get a good night's rest, though some wild beast may take advantage of me and devour me."

In the end he decided it was best to head for the woods, and he found one on high ground not far from the water. There he crept beneath two olive shoots growing from a single trunk—one wild, the other grafted. No wind, however fierce, could break through the cover they provided, nor could sun's rays pierce them, nor rain get through them, so closely did they grow together. Odysseus crawled under these and began making himself a bed, for there was a great pile of dead leaves lying about—enough to cover two or three men even in harsh winter weather. He was glad to see this, so he lay down and heaped leaves all around him. Then, like someone who lives alone in the country, far from any neighbor, who buries a burning brand in ashes to preserve fire and avoid having to get light elsewhere, so Odysseus covered himself with leaves. And Athena poured sweet sleep upon his eyes, closed his eyelids, and made him forget all his sorrows.

chapters.title: Book VI — The meeting between Nausicaa and Odysseus
paragraphs: So here Odysseus slept, overcome by exhaustion and weariness, but Athena traveled to the country and city of the Phaeacians—a people who used to live in the beautiful town of Hypereia, near the lawless Cyclopes. The Cyclopes were stronger than they were and constantly raided them, so their king Nausithous moved them away and settled them in Scheria, far from all other peoples. He built a wall around the city, constructed houses and temples, and distributed the land among his people. But he had died and gone to the realm of the dead, and King Alcinous, whose wisdom was blessed by heaven, now ruled. Athena went to his house to further Odysseus' return home.

She went straight to the beautifully decorated bedroom where a girl as lovely as a goddess was sleeping—Nausicaa, daughter of King Alcinous. Two maidservants slept near her, both very beautiful, one on each side of the doorway, which was closed with well-crafted folding doors. Athena took the form of the famous sea captain Dymas's daughter, who was Nausicaa's close friend and the same age. Then, approaching the girl's bedside like a gentle breeze, she hovered over her head and spoke:

"Nausicaa, how could your mother have raised such a lazy daughter? Here are your clothes lying around in complete disorder, yet you're going to be married very soon. You should not only dress well yourself, but also provide good clothes for those who will attend you. This is how you earn a good reputation and make your father and mother proud of you. Let's make tomorrow a washing day and start at dawn. I'll come and help you so you can have everything ready as quickly as possible, since all the best young men among your people are courting you, and you won't remain unmarried much longer. Ask your father to have a wagon and mules ready for us at daybreak to carry the blankets, robes, and sashes. You can ride too, which will be much more pleasant than walking, since the washing pools are quite far from town."

After saying this, Athena departed for Olympus, which they say is the eternal home of the gods. There no wind blows harshly, and neither rain nor snow can fall. Instead it remains in everlasting sunshine and great peaceful light, where the blessed gods live in radiance forever and ever. This was the place the goddess went after giving instructions to the girl.

Soon morning came and woke Nausicaa, who began wondering about her dream. She went to the other end of the house to tell her father and mother all about it, and found them in their room. Her mother was sitting by the fireplace spinning purple yarn with her maids around her, and she caught her father just as he was leaving to attend a meeting of the town council, which the Phaeacian leaders had called. She stopped him and said:

"Dear father, could you let me have a good large wagon? I want to take all our dirty clothes to the river and wash them. You're the chief here, so you should have a clean shirt when you attend council meetings. Besides, you have five sons at home—two married and three handsome bachelors. You know they always like clean clothes when they go to dances, and I've been thinking about all this."

She didn't mention her own wedding, since she felt too shy, but her father understood and said, "You can have the mules, my dear, and whatever else you need. Go ahead, and the men will get you a good strong wagon with a bed that will hold all your clothes."

He gave orders to the servants, who brought out the wagon, harnessed the mules, and hitched them up, while the girl brought the clothes down from the linen room and placed them in the wagon. Her mother packed her a basket of food with all sorts of good things and a goatskin full of wine. The girl climbed into the wagon, and her mother also gave her a golden flask of oil so she and her women could anoint themselves. Then she took the whip and reins and urged the mules forward. They set off with their hooves clattering on the road. They pulled steadily and carried not only Nausicaa and her load of clothes, but also the maids who went with her.

When they reached the waterside, they went to the washing pools, where pure water always flowed in sufficient quantity to wash any amount of linen, no matter how dirty. Here they unharnessed the mules and turned them loose to graze on the sweet, lush grass that grew by the water. They took the clothes from the wagon, put them in the water, and competed with each other in trampling them in the pools to get the dirt out. After they had washed them thoroughly and gotten them completely clean, they spread them out by the seashore, where the waves had built up a high beach of pebbles, and began washing and anointing themselves with olive oil. Then they had their meal beside the stream and waited for the sun to finish drying the clothes. When they had eaten, they threw off the veils covering their heads and began playing ball, while Nausicaa sang for them. Like the huntress Diana roaming the mountains of Taygetus or Erymanthus to hunt wild boars or deer, with the wood nymphs, daughters of Zeus, sporting alongside her—and then Leto feels proud seeing her daughter stand a full head taller than the others and outshine the most beautiful among a whole group of beauties—so did the girl surpass her handmaids.

When it was time to start home and they were folding the clothes and loading them into the wagon, Athena began considering how Odysseus should wake up and see the beautiful girl who would guide him to the city of the Phaeacians. So the girl threw a ball at one of the maids, but it missed her and fell into deep water. At this they all shouted, and the noise woke Odysseus, who sat up in his bed of leaves and began wondering what it could be.

"Oh no," he said to himself, "what kind of people have I come among? Are they cruel, savage, and uncivilized, or hospitable and decent? I seem to hear young women's voices, and they sound like nymphs that haunt mountaintops, or river springs and grassy meadows. At any rate, I'm among human beings. Let me see if I can get a look at them."

As he said this, he crept from under his bush and broke off a leafy branch to hide his nakedness. He looked like some wilderness lion that prowls about, glorying in his strength and defying both wind and rain. His eyes blaze as he hunts for cattle, sheep, or deer, driven by hunger, and he'll even dare to break into a well-protected farmyard to get at the livestock. That's how Odysseus appeared to the young women as he approached them, completely naked and desperate. Seeing someone so disheveled and crusted with salt water, the others scattered along the spits of land that jutted into the sea, but Alcinous's daughter stood firm, for Athena gave her courage and took away all fear. She stood right in front of Odysseus, and he wondered whether he should go up to her, throw himself at her feet, and clasp her knees as a suppliant, or stay where he was and plead with her from a distance to give him some clothes and show him the way to town. In the end, he decided it was best to appeal to her from afar, in case the girl took offense at his coming close enough to touch her knees, so he addressed her with honeyed and persuasive words.

"My lady," he said, "I beg for your help—but tell me, are you a goddess or a mortal woman? If you're a goddess who lives in heaven, I can only guess that you're Zeus's daughter Diana, for your face and figure resemble hers alone. If, on the other hand, you're mortal and live on earth, how blessed are your father and mother—how blessed too are your brothers and sisters. How proud and delighted they must feel when they see such a beautiful daughter going out to dance. But happiest of all will be the man whose wedding gifts win you and who takes you to his home. I've never seen anyone so beautiful, neither man nor woman, and I'm amazed as I look at you. I can only compare you to a young palm tree I saw when I was at Delos, growing near Apollo's altar—for I was there too, with many followers, on that journey which has been the source of all my troubles. Never did such a young plant shoot up from the ground as that one did, and I admired and marveled at it exactly as I now admire and marvel at you. I don't dare clasp your knees, but I'm in terrible distress. Yesterday was the twentieth day I've been tossing about on the sea. The winds and waves carried me all the way from Calypso's island, and now fate has thrown me on this shore to endure still more suffering. I don't think I've reached the end of it yet—heaven still has much evil in store for me.

"And now, my lady, have pity on me, for you're the first person I've met, and I know no one else in this country. Show me the way to your town, and give me something—anything you brought to wrap your clothes in—to cover myself. May heaven grant you everything your heart desires: a husband, a home, and a happy, harmonious marriage. Nothing in this world is better than when husband and wife live together in perfect accord. It frustrates their enemies, gladdens their friends' hearts, and they themselves know this joy better than anyone."

Nausicaa replied, "Stranger, you seem to be a sensible, well-meaning person. There's no accounting for fate—Zeus gives prosperity to rich and poor just as he chooses, so you must accept what he's given you and make the best of it. Now that you've come to our country, you won't lack for clothes or anything else that a distressed foreigner might reasonably expect. I'll show you the way to town and tell you our people's name: we're called Phaeacians, and I'm the daughter of Alcinous, who holds all the power in our state."

Then she called to her maids and said, "Stay where you are, girls. Why are you running away from a man? Do you think he's a robber or murderer? No one can come here to harm us Phaeacians, for we're dear to the gods and live apart on this remote land that juts into the sounding sea, having nothing to do with other peoples. This is just some poor man who's lost his way, and we must be kind to him. Strangers and foreigners in distress are under Zeus's protection and will be grateful for whatever they receive. So girls, give this poor fellow something to eat and drink, and let him wash in the stream at some place sheltered from the wind."

At this the maids stopped running and began calling each other back. They made Odysseus sit down in the shelter as Nausicaa had directed, and brought him a shirt and cloak. They also brought him a small golden flask of oil and told him to go wash in the stream. But Odysseus said, "Young women, please step aside a little so I can wash the salt from my shoulders and anoint myself with oil. It's been far too long since my skin has had a drop of oil on it. I can't wash while you're all standing there watching. I'm embarrassed to undress in front of a group of beautiful young women."

So they moved aside and went to tell the girl, while Odysseus washed himself in the stream and scrubbed the brine from his back and broad shoulders. When he had washed thoroughly and gotten all the salt out of his hair, he anointed himself with oil and put on the clothes the girl had given him. Then Athena made him look taller and stronger than before. She also made thick hair grow on his head and flow down in curls like hyacinth blossoms. She enhanced his head and shoulders the way a skilled craftsman who has learned his art from Hephaestus and Athena enriches a piece of silverware by overlaying it with gold—and his work is full of beauty. Then Odysseus went and sat down some distance away on the beach, looking quite handsome and youthful, and the girl gazed at him admiringly. Then she said to her maids:

"Listen, my dears, I want to say something. I believe the gods who live in heaven have sent this man to the Phaeacians. When I first saw him, I thought he looked ordinary, but now his appearance is like that of the gods who dwell in heaven. I wish my future husband could be just like him, if only he would stay here and not want to leave. But give him something to eat and drink."

They did as she ordered and set food before Odysseus, who ate and drank eagerly, since it had been a long time since he'd had any food. Meanwhile, Nausicaa thought of something else. She had the linen folded and placed in the wagon, then harnessed the mules, and as she took her seat, she called to Odysseus:

"Stranger," she said, "get up and let's head back to town. I'll take you to my excellent father's house, where I promise you'll meet all the best people among the Phaeacians. But be sure to do as I tell you, since you seem like a sensible person. While we're passing through the fields and farmland, follow quickly behind the wagon with the maids, and I'll lead the way. Soon, however, we'll reach the town, where you'll see a high wall running all around it, with a good harbor on each side and a narrow entrance to the city. The ships will be drawn up along the roadside, since everyone has a place where his own ship can dock. You'll see the marketplace with a temple of Poseidon in the center, paved with large stones set in the earth. Here people deal in all kinds of ship equipment—cables, sails, and this is also where oars are made. The Phaeacians aren't a nation of archers; they know nothing about bows and arrows, but are seafaring people who take pride in their masts, oars, and ships, with which they travel far across the sea.

"I'm worried about the gossip and scandal that might spread about me later, since the people here are very critical, and some lowlife, if he saw us, might say, 'Who's this handsome stranger walking with Nausicaa? Where did she find him? I suppose she's going to marry him. Maybe he's some vagrant sailor she picked up from a foreign ship, since we have no neighbors, or perhaps some god has finally come down from heaven to answer her prayers, and she'll live with him for the rest of her life. It would be good if she'd go find a husband somewhere else, since she won't look at any of the many excellent young Phaeacians who are in love with her.' That's the kind of nasty talk that would be said about me, and I couldn't complain, since I'd be scandalized myself to see any other girl do such a thing—going around with men despite what everyone thinks, while her father and mother are still alive, and without being properly married in front of everyone.

"So if you want my father to give you an escort and help you get home, do as I say. You'll see a beautiful grove of poplar trees by the roadside, sacred to Athena, with a well and a meadow all around it. My father has a fertile garden there, about as far from town as a man's voice can carry. Sit there and wait for a while until we can get into town and reach my father's house. Then, when you think we've had enough time to do this, come into town and ask for directions to my father Alcinous's house. You'll have no trouble finding it—any child can point it out to you, since no one else in the whole town has such a fine house as his. Once you've passed through the gates and outer courtyard, go straight across the inner court until you reach my mother. You'll find her sitting by the fire, spinning purple wool by firelight. It's a wonderful sight to see her leaning back against one of the pillars with all her maids arranged behind her. Close to her chair stands my father's, where he sits and drinks wine like an immortal god. Don't worry about him, but go straight to my mother and clasp her knees if you want to get home quickly. If you can win her over, you can hope to see your own country again, no matter how far away it may be."

With that, she whipped the mules and they left the river. The mules pulled steadily, their hooves beating rhythmically on the road. She was careful not to go too fast for Odysseus and the maids who were following on foot alongside the wagon, so she used her whip judiciously. As the sun was setting, they came to Athena's sacred grove, and there Odysseus sat down and prayed to Zeus's mighty daughter.

"Hear me," he cried, "daughter of Zeus who bears the aegis, tireless one, hear me now, for you paid no attention to my prayers when Poseidon was destroying me. Therefore, have pity on me now and grant that I may find friends and be welcomed hospitably by the Phaeacians."
So he prayed, and Athena heard his prayer, but she wouldn't show herself to him openly, for she feared her uncle Poseidon, who was still furious in his efforts to prevent Odysseus from reaching home.

chapters.title: Book VII — Reception of Odysseus at the palace of king Alcinous
paragraphs: So Odysseus waited and prayed, while the girl drove on to the city. When she reached her father's house, she stopped at the gateway. Her brothers—handsome as gods—gathered around her, unhitched the mules from the wagon, and carried the clothes inside, while she went to her own room. There an old servant, Eurynome of Apeira, lit the fire for her. This old woman had been brought by ship from Apeira and chosen as a prize for Alcinous because he was king over the Phaeacians, and the people obeyed him as if he were a god. She had been Nausicaa's nurse and now lit the fire and brought her supper to her room.

Soon Odysseus got up to go toward the city, and Athena wrapped him in a thick mist to hide him in case any proud Phaeacians he met might insult him or ask who he was. As he was entering the town, she came toward him disguised as a little girl carrying a water jar. She stood right in front of him, and Odysseus said:
"My child, would you be kind enough to show me the house of King Alcinous? I'm an unfortunate stranger in distress, and I don't know anyone in your town and country."

Then Athena said, "Yes, dear stranger, I'll show you the house you're looking for, since Alcinous lives quite close to my own father. I'll go ahead and show you the way, but don't say a word as you go, and don't look at anyone or ask questions. The people here can't stand strangers and don't like visitors from other places. They're seafaring folk who sail the seas by Poseidon's grace in ships that glide like thought itself, or like a bird through the air."

With that she led the way, and Odysseus followed behind her. Not one of the Phaeacians could see him as he passed through the city among them, for the great goddess Athena had hidden him in a thick cloud of darkness out of goodwill toward him. He marveled at their harbors, ships, meeting places, and the high walls of the city topped with palisades. When they reached the king's house, Athena said:

"This is the house, dear stranger, that you asked me to show you. You'll find many great people dining inside, but don't be afraid—go straight in, for the bolder a man is, the more likely he is to succeed, even if he's a stranger. First find the queen. Her name is Arete, and she comes from the same family as her husband Alcinous. They both descend from Poseidon, who fathered Nausithous by Periboea, a woman of great beauty. Periboea was the youngest daughter of Eurymedon, who once ruled over the giants, but he destroyed his ill-fated people and lost his own life as well.

"Poseidon, however, slept with his daughter, and she bore him a son, the great Nausithous, who ruled over the Phaeacians. Nausithous had two sons, Rhexenor and Alcinous. Apollo killed the first while he was still a bridegroom without male heirs, but he left a daughter, Arete, whom Alcinous married and honors as no other woman is honored among all those who keep house with their husbands.

"So she was then, and still is, respected beyond measure by her children, by Alcinous himself, and by all the people, who look upon her as a goddess and greet her whenever she walks through the city. She's a thoroughly good woman in both mind and heart, and when women are her friends, she'll help their husbands settle their disputes too. If you can win her favor, you may have every hope of seeing your friends again and getting safely back to your home and country."

Then Athena left Scheria and went away over the sea. She traveled to Marathon and the broad streets of Athens, where she entered Erechtheus's palace. But Odysseus went on to Alcinous's house, and he thought deeply as he paused before reaching the bronze threshold, for the palace's splendor was like that of the sun or moon. The walls on both sides were bronze from end to end, with a cornice of blue enamel. The doors were gold, hanging on silver pillars that rose from a bronze floor, while the lintel was silver and the door handle was gold.

On either side stood gold and silver mastiffs that Hephaestus had crafted with consummate skill to guard King Alcinous's palace. They were immortal and would never grow old. Seats lined the walls from one end to the other, covered with fine woven cloth that the women of the house had made. Here the leading Phaeacians sat to eat and drink, for there was abundance in every season. Golden figures of young men holding blazing torches stood on pedestals to give light at night to those dining. There were fifty maidservants in the house—some always grinding rich yellow grain at the mill, others working at the loom or sitting and spinning. Their shuttles moved back and forth like fluttering aspen leaves, while the linen was woven so tightly it would repel oil. As the Phaeacians were the world's best sailors, so their women excelled all others at weaving, for Athena had taught them every useful art, and they were highly skilled.

Outside the gate of the outer court lay a large garden of about four acres, surrounded by a wall. It was full of beautiful trees—pears, pomegranates, and the most delicious apples. There were luscious figs and thriving olive trees. The fruit never rotted or failed year-round, neither in winter nor summer, for the air was so mild that new crops ripened before the old ones fell. Pear grew upon pear, apple upon apple, fig upon fig, and the same with grapes, for there was an excellent vineyard. In one level section, grapes were being made into raisins; in another they were being harvested; some were being pressed in wine vats, while others had shed their blossoms and were beginning to fruit, and still others were just changing color. In the farthest part were beautifully arranged flower beds that bloomed year-round. Two streams flowed through it—one channeled in conduits throughout the garden, the other running underground to the house itself, where the townspeople drew water. Such were the splendors with which the gods had blessed King Alcinous's house.

So Odysseus stood there for a while, looking around, but when he had seen enough, he crossed the threshold and entered the house. There he found all the leading Phaeacians making drink offerings to Hermes, which they always did last thing before going to bed. He walked straight through the court, still hidden by the cloak of darkness that Athena had wrapped around him, until he reached Arete and King Alcinous. Then he grasped the queen's knees, and at that moment the miraculous darkness fell away from him and he became visible. Everyone was speechless with surprise at seeing a man there, but Odysseus immediately began his plea.

"Queen Arete," he exclaimed, "daughter of great Rhexenor, in my distress I humbly beg you, and also your husband and these guests of yours—may heaven grant them long life and happiness, and may they pass their possessions to their children along with all the honors the state has given them—to help me reach my own country as soon as possible, for I have long been in trouble and away from my friends."
Then he sat down on the hearth among the ashes, and they all remained silent. Finally the old hero Echeneus, an excellent speaker and elder among the Phaeacians, addressed them plainly and honestly:

"Alcinous," he said, "it's not right for you to have a stranger sitting among the ashes of your hearth. Everyone's waiting to hear what you'll say. Tell him to get up and take a seat on a silver-studded stool, and have your servants mix wine and water so we can make a drink offering to Zeus the Thunderer, who protects all worthy suppliants. And let the housekeeper give him supper from whatever's in the house."

When Alcinous heard this, he took Odysseus by the hand, raised him from the hearth, and had him take the seat of Laodamas, who had been sitting beside him and was his favorite son. A maidservant brought him water in a beautiful golden pitcher and poured it into a silver basin for him to wash his hands, and she set a polished table beside him. An upper servant brought bread and offered him many good things from what was in the house, and Odysseus ate and drank. Then Alcinous said to one of the servants, "Pontonous, mix a cup of wine and pass it around so we can make drink offerings to Zeus the Thunderer, who protects all worthy suppliants."
Pontonous mixed wine and water and served it after giving everyone their drink offering. When they had made their offerings and drunk as much as they wanted, Alcinous said:

"Leaders and councilors of the Phaeacians, hear my words. You've had your supper, so now go home to bed. Tomorrow morning I'll invite an even larger number of leaders and hold a sacrificial feast in honor of our guest. We can then discuss his escort and consider how to send him back rejoicing to his own country at once, without trouble or inconvenience to him, no matter how distant it may be. We must see that he comes to no harm on his journey home, but once he's there, he'll have to take whatever fate he was born to, for better or worse, like everyone else. It's possible, however, that this stranger is one of the immortals who has come down from heaven to visit us. But if so, the gods are changing their usual practice, for until now they've always appeared clearly to us when we've offered them sacrifices. They come and sit at our feasts just like one of us, and if any solitary traveler happens to meet one of them, they don't hide themselves, for we're as closely related to the gods as the Cyclopes and savage giants are."

Then Odysseus said: "Please, Alcinous, don't get any such idea in your head. There's nothing immortal about me, in body or mind, and I most resemble those among you who are most afflicted. Indeed, if I were to tell you everything heaven has seen fit to burden me with, you'd say I was even worse off than they are. Nevertheless, let me eat despite my sorrow, for an empty stomach is very demanding and forces itself on a man's attention no matter how terrible his distress. I'm in great trouble, yet it insists I eat and drink, commanding me to set aside all memory of my sorrows and think only of filling it properly. As for yourselves, do as you suggest, and at daybreak help me get home. I'll be content to die if I can just once more see my property, my servants, and all the grandeur of my house."

So he spoke. Everyone approved his words and agreed he should have his escort since he had spoken reasonably. After they made their drink offerings and drank as much as they wanted, they all went home to bed, each to his own house, leaving Odysseus in the colonnade with Arete and Alcinous while the servants cleared away the supper things. Arete was the first to speak, for she recognized the shirt, cloak, and fine clothes that Odysseus wore as the work of herself and her maids. So she said, "Stranger, before we go any further, I'd like to ask you something. Who are you and where do you come from, and who gave you those clothes? Didn't you say you came here from across the sea?"

And Odysseus answered, "It would be a long story, my lady, if I were to tell you the full tale of my misfortunes, for heaven's hand has been heavy upon me. But regarding your question, there's an island far away in the sea called Ogygia. There lives the cunning and powerful goddess Calypso, daughter of Atlas. She lives alone, far from all neighbors, human or divine. But fate brought me to her hearth, desolate and alone, for Zeus struck my ship with his thunderbolt and broke it apart in mid-ocean. My brave companions all drowned, but I clung to the keel and was carried here and there for nine days, until at last in the darkness of the tenth night the gods brought me to the Ogygian island where great Calypso lives. She took me in and treated me with the utmost kindness—indeed, she wanted to make me immortal so I would never grow old, but she couldn't persuade me to let her do so.

"I stayed with Calypso seven whole years, watering the fine clothes she gave me with my tears the entire time. But finally when the eighth year came, she told me to leave of her own free will, either because Zeus had ordered her to or because she had changed her mind. She sent me from her island on a raft that she supplied with plenty of bread and wine. She also gave me good sturdy clothing and sent a wind that blew both warm and favorable. I sailed for seventeen days over the sea, and on the eighteenth I caught sight of the shadowy outlines of the mountains on your coast—and glad indeed I was to see them. But there was still much trouble in store for me, for at that point Poseidon would let me go no further and raised a great storm against me. The sea was so terribly rough that I could no longer stay on my raft, which broke apart under the fury of the gale, and I had to swim until wind and current brought me to your shores.

"There I tried to land but couldn't, for it was a rocky place and the waves dashed me against the cliffs, so I swam on until I came to a river that seemed the best landing spot, since there were no rocks and it was sheltered from the wind. There I got out of the water and gathered my wits. Night was coming on, so I left the river and went into a thicket, where I covered myself completely with leaves, and presently heaven sent me into a very deep sleep. Sick and miserable as I was, I slept among the leaves all night and through the next day until afternoon, when I woke as the sun was setting and saw your daughter's maidservants playing on the beach, with your daughter among them looking like a goddess. I begged for her help, and she proved to have an excellent character, much more than could be expected from someone so young—for young people are often thoughtless. She gave me plenty of bread and wine, had me wash in the river, and also gave me the clothes you see me wearing. Now, though it pains me to do so, I've told you the whole truth."
Then Alcinous said, "Stranger, it was very wrong of my daughter not to bring you straight to my house with the maids, since you asked for her help first."

"Please don't scold her," replied Odysseus. "She's not to blame. She did tell me to follow along with the maids, but I was ashamed and afraid, thinking you might be displeased if you saw me. Every human being is sometimes a little suspicious and irritable."

"Stranger," replied Alcinous, "I'm not the kind of man to get angry over nothing—it's always better to be reasonable. But by Father Zeus, Athena, and Apollo, now that I see what kind of person you are and how much you think as I do, I wish you would stay here, marry my daughter, and become my son-in-law. If you'll stay, I'll give you a house and estate. But no one—heaven forbid—will keep you here against your will, and to assure you of this, I'll arrange your escort tomorrow. You can sleep during the entire voyage if you like, and my men will sail you over calm waters either to your own home or wherever you please, even if it's much farther than Euboea, which those of my people who saw it when they took golden-haired Rhadamanthus to visit Tityus, son of Earth, tell me is the most distant place—yet they made the whole voyage in a single day without tiring themselves and returned afterward. You'll see how much my ships excel all others and what magnificent oarsmen my sailors are."

Then Odysseus was glad and prayed aloud, saying, "Father Zeus, grant that Alcinous may do all as he has promised, for then he'll win an imperishable name among mankind, and at the same time I'll return to my country."

So they talked. Then Arete told her maids to set up a bed in the portico and make it with fine red rugs, and to spread coverlets on top with woolen cloaks for Odysseus to wear. The maids went out with torches in their hands, and when they had prepared the bed, they came to Odysseus and said, "Come, sir stranger, your bed is ready," and he was glad indeed to rest.
So Odysseus slept in a bed placed in the echoing portico, but Alcinous lay in the inner part of the house with the queen his wife beside him.

chapters.title: Book VIII — Banquet in the house of Alcinous—the games
paragraphs: When rosy-fingered Dawn appeared at daybreak, both Alcinous and Odysseus rose, and Alcinous led the way to the Phaeacian assembly place near the ships. They sat side by side on polished stone seats while Athena took the form of one of Alcinous's servants and went through the town to help Odysseus get home. She approached each citizen individually, saying, "Leaders and councilors of the Phaeacians, come to the assembly and listen to this stranger who has just arrived at King Alcinous's house after a long voyage. He looks like an immortal god."

With these words she inspired them all to come, and they flocked to the assembly until every seat and standing space was packed. Everyone was struck by Odysseus's appearance, for Athena had enhanced his head and shoulders, making him look taller and more imposing than he really was, so that he might favorably impress the Phaeacians as a remarkable man and perform well in the many contests they would challenge him to. When they had all gathered, Alcinous spoke:

"Listen to me, leaders and councilors of the Phaeacians, so I may speak my mind. This stranger, whoever he may be, has come to my house from somewhere east or west. He needs an escort and wants the matter settled. Let us prepare one for him, as we have done for others before. Indeed, no one who has ever come to my house has been able to complain that I was slow in speeding them on their way.
