Let us launch a ship—one that has never made a voyage—and crew it with fifty-two of our smartest young sailors. When you have secured your oars to your benches, leave the ship and come to my house for a feast. I will provide everything. These are my instructions to the young men who will form the crew. As for you leaders and councilors, you will join me in entertaining our guest in the courtyard. I will accept no excuses, and we will have Demodocus sing for us, for there is no bard like him, whatever he chooses to sing about."

Alcinous then led the way, and the others followed, while a servant went to fetch Demodocus. The fifty-two chosen oarsmen went to the seashore as instructed, and when they arrived they launched the ship into the water, set the mast and sails inside her, bound the oars to the oarlocks with twisted leather thongs, all in proper order, and spread the white sails aloft. They moored the vessel a little way offshore, then came ashore and went to King Alcinous's house. The courtyards, grounds, and all the surrounding areas were filled with crowds of men, both old and young, in great numbers. Alcinous slaughtered twelve sheep, eight full-grown pigs, and two oxen for them. These they skinned and prepared to provide a magnificent banquet.

A servant then brought in the famous bard Demodocus, whom the Muse had dearly loved but to whom she had given both good and evil—though she had blessed him with the divine gift of song, she had taken away his eyesight. Pontonous set a chair for him among the guests, leaning it against a pillar. He hung the lyre on a peg above his head and showed him where to reach for it with his hands. He also set a fine table beside him with a basket of food and a cup of wine from which he could drink whenever he wished.

The company then began eating the good food before them, but as soon as they had finished eating and drinking, the Muse inspired Demodocus to sing about the deeds of heroes, particularly a story that was then on everyone's lips—the quarrel between Odysseus and Achilles and the harsh words they exchanged while sitting together at a banquet. Agamemnon was pleased when he heard his chieftains quarreling with each other, for Apollo had prophesied this to him at Pytho when he crossed the stone floor to consult the oracle. This was the beginning of the disaster that Zeus's will brought upon both Greeks and Trojans.

So the bard sang, but Odysseus pulled his purple cloak over his head and covered his face, ashamed to let the Phaeacians see him weeping. When the bard stopped singing, he wiped away his tears, uncovered his face, and taking his cup, made a drink offering to the gods. But when the Phaeacians urged Demodocus to continue singing, for they delighted in his songs, Odysseus again drew his cloak over his head and wept bitterly. No one noticed his distress except Alcinous, who was sitting nearby and heard the heavy sighs he was making. So he immediately said, "Leaders and councilors of the Phaeacians, we have had enough of both the feast and the music that accompanies it. Let us now proceed to athletic competitions, so that our guest can tell his friends when he returns home how much we surpass all other nations in boxing, wrestling, jumping, and running."

With these words he led the way, and the others followed. A servant hung Demodocus's lyre on its peg, led him out of the courtyard, and set him on the same path that all the Phaeacian leaders were taking to watch the sports. A crowd of several thousand people followed them, and there were many excellent competitors for all the events. There was Acroneus, Ocyalus, Elatreus, Nauteus, Prymneus, Anchialus, Eretmeus, Ponteus, Proreus, Thoon, Anabesineus, and Amphialus son of Polyneus son of Tecton. There was also Euryalus son of Naubolus, who was like Mars himself and was the handsomest man among the Phaeacians except Laodamas. Three sons of Alcinous also competed: Laodamas, Halios, and Clytoneus.

The foot races came first. They set out the course from the starting line, and they raised dust on the plain as they all sprang forward at once. Clytoneus won by a wide margin, leaving everyone else behind by the length of furrow that a pair of mules can plow in a fallow field. They then turned to the grueling art of wrestling, and here Euryalus proved to be the best man. Amphialus excelled all others in jumping, while in discus throwing no one could approach Elatreus. Alcinous's son Laodamas was the best boxer, and when they had all been entertained by the games, he said, "Let's ask the stranger if he excels in any of these sports. He seems very powerfully built—his thighs, calves, hands, and neck show tremendous strength, and he's not old at all. But he has suffered much lately, and nothing wreaks havoc on a man like the sea, no matter how strong he is."
"You're absolutely right, Laodamas," replied Euryalus. "Go up to your guest and speak to him about it yourself."

When Laodamas heard this, he made his way into the middle of the crowd and said to Odysseus, "I hope, sir, that you will enter one or another of our competitions if you're skilled in any of them—and you must have participated in many before now. Nothing brings a man such lifelong credit as showing himself capable with his hands and feet. So please try something and banish all sorrow from your mind. Your journey home won't be delayed much longer, for the ship is already launched and the crew is ready."

Odysseus answered, "Laodamas, why do you taunt me this way? My mind is focused on troubles rather than contests. I have been through endless hardship and come among you now as a suppliant, asking your king and people to help me on my journey home."

Then Euryalus insulted him outright and said, "I gather you're unskilled in any of the many sports that men usually enjoy. I suppose you're one of those greedy traders who sail around in ships as captains or merchants, thinking of nothing but their outbound cargo and return freight. You don't seem to have much of the athlete about you."

"Shame on you, sir," answered Odysseus fiercely. "You're an insolent fellow—it's true that the gods don't bless all men equally in speech, appearance, and understanding. One man may have a weak presence, but heaven has blessed him with such good conversation that he charms everyone who sees him. His smooth eloquence wins over his listeners so that he leads in all assemblies of his peers, and wherever he goes he is looked up to. Another may be as handsome as a god, but his good looks aren't matched with wisdom. This is your case. No god could make a finer-looking man than you, but you're a fool. Your ill-judged remarks have made me extremely angry, and you're quite mistaken, for I excel in many athletic events. Indeed, as long as I had youth and strength, I was among the finest athletes of my time. Now, however, I'm worn out by hardship and sorrow, for I've endured much both on the battlefield and on the weary sea. Still, despite all this, I will compete, for your taunts have stung me to the core."

So he jumped up without even removing his cloak and seized a discus—larger, more massive, and much heavier than those the Phaeacians used when throwing among themselves. Then, swinging it back, he hurled it from his powerful hand, and it hummed through the air as he did so. The Phaeacians cowered beneath the rush of its flight as it sped gracefully from his hand and flew beyond any mark that had been made yet. Athena, in the form of a man, came and marked where it had fallen. "A blind man, sir," she said, "could easily find your mark by feeling for it—it's so far ahead of any other. You can set your mind at ease about this contest, for no Phaeacian can come near such a throw as yours."

Odysseus was glad when he found he had a friend among the spectators, so he began to speak more pleasantly. "Young men," he said, "match that throw if you can, and I'll throw another discus just as heavy or even heavier. If anyone wants to have a contest with me, let him come forward, for I'm extremely angry. I'll box, wrestle, or run—I don't care which—with any of you except Laodamas, but not with him because I'm his guest, and one can't compete with one's own host. At least I don't think it's wise or sensible for a guest to challenge his host's family at any game, especially in a foreign country. He'll undermine his own position if he does. But I make no exception for anyone else, for I want to settle this matter and see who's the best man. I'm skilled at every kind of athletic sport known to mankind. I'm an excellent archer. In battle I'm always the first to bring down a man with my arrow, no matter how many others are aiming at him alongside me. Philoctetes was the only man who could shoot better than I when we Greeks were before Troy and practicing. I far surpass everyone else in the whole world among those who still eat bread on the face of the earth, but I wouldn't want to compete against the mighty dead, such as Heracles or Eurytus of Oechalia—men who could shoot against the gods themselves. This is actually how Eurytus met his premature end, for Apollo was angry with him and killed him because he challenged the god as an archer. I can throw a spear farther than anyone else can shoot an arrow. Running is the only area where I fear some of the Phaeacians might beat me, for I've been brought very low at sea. My provisions ran short, and so I'm still weak."

They all remained silent except King Alcinous, who began, "Sir, we have had much pleasure hearing all you've told us, from which I understand you're willing to show your skill, having been displeased by some insolent remarks made by one of our athletes—remarks that could never have been uttered by anyone who knows how to speak properly. I hope you'll understand my meaning and will explain to any of your chief men who may be dining with you and your family when you get home, that we have a hereditary talent for accomplishments of all kinds. We're not particularly remarkable for boxing or wrestling, but we're exceptionally fast runners and excellent sailors. We're extremely fond of good dinners, music, and dancing. We also like frequent changes of clothing, warm baths, and comfortable beds. So now, please, some of you who are the best dancers, start dancing, so that our guest can tell his friends when he returns home how much we surpass all other nations as sailors, runners, dancers, and singers. Demodocus left his lyre at my house, so someone run and fetch it for him."

At this a servant hurried off to bring the lyre from the king's house, and nine men who had been chosen as officials stepped forward. It was their job to manage everything connected with the sports, so they smoothed the ground and marked out a wide space for the dancers. Soon the servant returned with Demodocus's lyre, and he took his place in their midst. Then the best young dancers in the town began to move and dance so nimbly that Odysseus was delighted with the merry twinkling of their feet.

Meanwhile the bard began to sing about the love affair of Mars and Venus, and how they first began their secret relationship in Vulcan's house. Mars gave Venus many gifts and defiled King Vulcan's marriage bed, so the Sun, who saw what they were doing, told Vulcan. Vulcan was furious when he heard such dreadful news, so he went to his forge planning mischief, set up his great anvil, and began making chains that none could either loosen or break, so they would stay trapped there. When he had finished his snare, he went into his bedroom and draped the bed-posts all over with chains like spider webs. He also hung many from the great ceiling beam. Not even a god could see them, so fine and subtle were they. As soon as he had spread the chains all over the bed, he pretended to set out for the fair land of Lemnos, which of all places in the world was his favorite. But Mars kept a sharp lookout, and as soon as he saw him leave, hurried off to his house, burning with love for Venus.

Now Venus had just returned from visiting her father Zeus and was about to sit down when Mars came inside the house and said as he took her hand in his own, "Come to Vulcan's bed—he's not at home, but has gone off to Lemnos among the Sintians, whose speech is foreign."

She was quite willing, so they went to the bed to rest, where they were caught in the trap that cunning Vulcan had set for them. They could neither get up nor move hand or foot, but realized too late that they were trapped. Then Vulcan returned to them, for he had turned back before reaching Lemnos when his spy the Sun told him what was happening. He was in a furious rage and stood in the entrance making a terrible noise as he shouted to all the gods.

"Father Zeus," he cried, "and all you other blessed gods who live forever, come here and see the ridiculous and disgraceful sight I'll show you. Zeus's daughter Venus is always dishonoring me because I'm lame. She's in love with Mars, who is handsome and well-built, while I'm a cripple—but my parents are to blame for that, not I. They should never have had me. Come and see the pair together asleep on my bed. It makes me furious to look at them. They're very fond of each other, but I don't think they'll lie there longer than they have to, nor do I think they'll sleep much. There, however, they'll stay until her father has repaid me the bride-price I gave him for his worthless daughter, who is beautiful but not faithful."

At this the gods gathered at Vulcan's house. Earth-shaking Poseidon came, and Hermes the luck-bringer, and King Apollo, but the goddesses all stayed home out of shame. Then the givers of all good things stood in the doorway, and the blessed gods roared with uncontrollable laughter as they saw how cunning Vulcan had been. One would turn to his neighbor saying:
"Evil deeds don't prosper, and the weak confound the strong. See how limping Vulcan, lame as he is, has caught Mars who is the swiftest god in heaven. Now Mars will have to pay heavy damages."
This is how they talked, but King Apollo said to Hermes, "Messenger Hermes, giver of good things, wouldn't you mind how strong the chains were if you could sleep with Venus?"

"King Apollo," answered Hermes, "I only wish I might get the chance, even if there were three times as many chains—and all of you gods and goddesses could watch—but I would sleep with her if I could."

The immortal gods burst out laughing when they heard him, but Poseidon took it all seriously and kept urging Vulcan to set Mars free again. "Let him go," he cried, "and I'll guarantee, as you require, that he'll pay you all the damages that are considered reasonable among the immortal gods."
"Don't," replied Vulcan, "ask me to do this. A bad man's promise is worthless security. What remedy could I enforce against you if Mars should leave and abandon his debts along with his chains?"
"Vulcan," said Poseidon, "if Mars goes away without paying his damages, I'll pay you myself." So Vulcan answered, "In that case I cannot and must not refuse you."

Then he loosened the bonds that held them, and as soon as they were free they rushed off—Mars to Thrace and laughter-loving Venus to Cyprus and to Paphos, where her grove and altar fragrant with offerings are located. There the Graces bathed her and anointed her with ambrosial oil such as the immortal gods use, and they clothed her in the most enchanting garments.
So the bard sang, and both Odysseus and the seafaring Phaeacians were charmed as they listened to him.

Then Alcinous told Laodamas and Halius to dance alone, since there was no one to compete with them. So they took a red ball that Polybus had made for them, and one bent backward and threw it up toward the clouds while the other jumped from the ground and caught it easily before it came down again. When they had finished throwing the ball straight up into the air, they began to dance while simultaneously tossing it back and forth to each other, as all the young men in the circle applauded and stamped their feet loudly. Then Odysseus said:
"King Alcinous, you said your people were the nimblest dancers in the world, and indeed they have proved themselves to be so. I was amazed as I watched them."

The king was delighted at this and exclaimed to the Phaeacians, "Leaders and town councilors, our guest seems to be a person of exceptional judgment. Let us give him such proof of our hospitality as he may reasonably expect. There are twelve chief men among you, and counting myself there are thirteen. Each of you contribute a clean cloak, a shirt, and a talent of fine gold. Let us give him all this together at once, so when he has his dinner he may do so with a light heart. As for Euryalus, he will have to make a formal apology and give a present too, for he has been rude."

So he spoke, and the others all applauded his words and sent their servants to fetch the presents. Then Euryalus said, "King Alcinous, I will give the stranger all the satisfaction you require. He shall have my sword, which is bronze except for the hilt, which is silver. I'll also give him the scabbard of newly carved ivory that it fits into. It will be worth a great deal to him."

As he spoke he placed the sword in Odysseus's hands and said, "Good luck to you, respected stranger. If anything has been said inappropriately, may the winds blow it away, and may heaven grant you a safe return, for I understand you've been long away from home and have endured much hardship."
To which Odysseus answered, "Good luck to you too, my friend, and may the gods grant you every happiness. I hope you won't miss the sword you've given me along with your apology."

With these words he strapped the sword to his shoulders, and toward sunset the presents began to arrive as the servants of the donors kept bringing them to King Alcinous's house. His sons received them and placed them in their mother's care. Then Alcinous led the way to the house and had his guests take their seats.

"Wife," he said, turning to Queen Arete, "go fetch the finest chest we have and put a clean cloak and shirt in it. Also, put a pot on the fire and heat some water. Our guest will take a warm bath. See also to the careful packing of the presents that the noble Phaeacians have given him. This way he'll better enjoy both his dinner and the singing that will follow. I'll personally give him this golden goblet—which is exquisitely crafted—so he'll be reminded of me for the rest of his life whenever he makes a drink offering to Zeus or any of the gods."

Then Arete told her maids to put a large tripod on the fire as quickly as they could, so they set a tripod full of bath water over a clear fire. They threw on sticks to make it blaze, and the water became hot as the flame played around the belly of the tripod. Meanwhile Arete brought a magnificent chest from her own room, and inside it she packed all the beautiful presents of gold and clothing that the Phaeacians had brought. Finally she added a cloak and a fine shirt from Alcinous and said to Odysseus:
"See to the lid yourself and have the whole thing tied up at once, in case anyone should rob you while you're sleeping in your ship."

When Odysseus heard this, he put the lid on the chest and secured it with a knot that Circe had taught him. He had barely finished when a servant told him to come to the bath and wash himself. He was very glad of a warm bath, for he had had no one to wait on him ever since he left Calypso's house, who had taken as good care of him as if he were a god as long as he stayed with her. When the servants had finished washing and anointing him with oil and had given him a clean cloak and shirt, he left the bathroom and joined the guests who were sitting over their wine. Lovely Nausicaa stood by one of the pillars supporting the roof of the courtyard and admired him as she saw him pass. "Farewell, stranger," she said. "Don't forget me when you're safe at home again, for it's to me first that you owe thanks for saving your life."

And Odysseus said, "Nausicaa, daughter of great Alcinous, may Zeus the mighty husband of Hera grant that I reach my home. Then I shall bless you as my guardian angel all my days, for it was you who saved me."

When he had said this, he seated himself beside Alcinous. Dinner was then served, and wine was mixed for drinking. A servant led in the celebrated bard Demodocus and seated him in the middle of the company, near one of the pillars supporting the courtyard, so he could lean against it. Then Odysseus cut off a piece of roast pork with plenty of fat (for there was abundance left on the joint) and said to a servant, "Take this piece of pork to Demodocus and tell him to eat it. Despite any pain his songs may cause me, I will honor him nonetheless. Bards are honored and respected throughout the world, for the Muse teaches them their songs and loves them."

The servant carried the pork over to Demodocus, who took it and was very pleased. They then began eating the good food before them, and as soon as they had finished eating and drinking, Odysseus said to Demodocus, "Demodocus, there is no one in the world I admire more than you. You must have studied under the Muse, Zeus's daughter, and under Apollo, so accurately do you sing about the Greeks' return with all their sufferings and adventures. If you weren't there yourself, you must have heard it all from someone who was. Now, however, change your song and tell us about the wooden horse that Epeus made with Athena's help, which Odysseus got by trickery into Troy's fortress after filling it with the men who later sacked the city. If you sing this tale properly, I'll tell all the world how magnificently heaven has blessed you."

The heaven-inspired bard took up the story at the point where some of the Greeks set fire to their tents and sailed away while others, hidden within the horse, were waiting with Odysseus in Troy's assembly place. For the Trojans themselves had dragged the horse into their fortress, and it stood there while they sat in council around it, unable to decide what to do. Some wanted to break it up then and there; others would have it dragged to the top of the rock where the fortress stood and then thrown down the cliff; while still others wanted to let it remain as an offering to appease the gods. And this is how they decided in the end, for the city was doomed when it accepted that horse, within which were all the bravest Greeks waiting to bring death and destruction to the Trojans. Then he sang how the Greeks emerged from the horse and sacked the town, breaking out from their hiding place. He sang how they overran the city in all directions and ravaged it, and how Odysseus went raging like Mars along with Menelaus to Deiphobus's house. It was there that the fighting was fiercest, but nevertheless with Athena's help he was victorious.

All this he told, but Odysseus was overcome as he heard him, and his cheeks were wet with tears. He wept as a woman weeps when she throws herself on the body of her husband who has fallen before his own city and people, fighting bravely to defend his home and children. She screams aloud and throws her arms around him as he lies gasping for breath and dying, but her enemies beat her from behind on the back and shoulders and carry her off into slavery, to a life of labor and sorrow, and the beauty fades from her cheeks. Just as pitifully did Odysseus weep, but none of those present noticed his tears except Alcinous, who was sitting near him and could hear the sobs and sighs he was making. The king therefore immediately rose and said:

"Leaders and town councilors of the Phaeacians, let Demodocus stop his song, for there are those present who don't seem to enjoy it. From the moment we finished dinner and Demodocus began to sing, our guest has been groaning and lamenting the whole time. He's evidently in great distress, so let the bard stop, that we may all enjoy ourselves, hosts and guest alike. This will be much more appropriate, for all these festivities—the escort and the presents we're giving so willingly—are entirely in his honor, and anyone with even a modest sense of propriety knows he should treat a guest and suppliant as if he were his own brother.

"Therefore, sir, don't maintain any more secrecy or reserve about what I'm going to ask you. It would be more courteous of you to give me a straight answer. Tell me the name your father and mother used to call you, and by which you were known among your neighbors and fellow citizens. No one, neither rich nor poor, is completely without a name, for people's parents give them names as soon as they're born. Tell me also your country, nation, and city, so our ships may set their course accordingly and take you there. For the Phaeacians have no pilots; their vessels have no rudders like those of other nations, but the ships themselves understand what we're thinking and want. They know all the cities and countries in the whole world and can cross the sea just as well even when it's covered with mist and cloud, so there's no danger of being wrecked or coming to harm. Still, I do remember hearing my father say that Poseidon was angry with us for being too generous in giving people escorts. He said that one day he would wreck one of our ships as it was returning from escorting someone and bury our city under a high mountain. This is what my father used to say, but whether the god will carry out his threat is a matter he will decide for himself.

"And now, tell me truthfully: Where have you been wandering, and what countries have you traveled through? Tell us about the peoples themselves and their cities—who were hostile, savage, and uncivilized, and who, on the other hand, were hospitable and humane. Tell us also why you're made so unhappy by hearing about the return of the Greek warriors from Troy. The gods arranged all this and sent them their misfortunes so that future generations might have something to sing about. Did you lose some brave relative of your wife's when you were at Troy? A son-in-law or father-in-law—who are a man's nearest relations outside his own flesh and blood? Or was it some brave and kind-hearted comrade—for a good friend is as dear to a man as his own brother?"

chapters.title: Book IX — Odysseus declares himself and begins his story—-the Cicons, Lotophagi, and Cyclopes
paragraphs: And Odysseus answered, "King Alcinous, it is a wonderful thing to hear a singer with such a divine voice as this man has. There is nothing better or more delightful than when a whole people celebrate together, with the guests sitting in order to listen, while the table is loaded with bread and meat, and the cup-bearer draws wine and fills each man's cup. This is truly as beautiful a sight as anyone can see. Now, however, since you want to hear the story of my sorrows, and rekindle my own sad memories of them, I don't know how to begin, or how to continue and end my tale, for the hand of heaven has weighed heavily upon me.

"First, then, I will tell you my name so that you too may know it, and one day, if I survive this time of sorrow, you may become my guests though I live so far away from all of you. I am Odysseus son of Laertes, known among mankind for all kinds of cunning, so that my fame reaches to heaven. I live in Ithaca, where there is a high mountain called Neritum, covered with forests; and not far from it there is a group of islands very close to one another—Dulichium, Same, and the wooded island of Zacynthus. It lies low on the horizon, farthest out in the sea toward the sunset, while the others lie away from it toward dawn. It is a rugged island, but it breeds brave men, and my eyes know nothing they love better to look upon. The goddess Calypso kept me with her in her cave, and wanted me to marry her, as did also the cunning goddess Circe of Aeaea; but neither of them could persuade me, for there is nothing dearer to a man than his own country and his parents, and however splendid a home he may have in a foreign country, if it is far from father or mother, he doesn't care about it. Now, however, I will tell you of the many dangerous adventures which by Zeus's will I met with on my return from Troy.

"When I had set sail from there the wind took me first to Ismarus, which is the city of the Cicones. There I sacked the town and put the people to the sword. We took their wives and also much treasure, which we divided fairly among us, so that no one could complain. I then said that we had better leave at once, but my men very foolishly would not obey me, so they stayed there drinking much wine and killing great numbers of sheep and cattle on the seashore. Meanwhile the Cicones called out for help to other Cicones who lived inland. These were greater in number, and stronger, and they were more skilled in the art of war, for they could fight either from chariots or on foot as the situation required; in the morning, therefore, they came as thick as leaves and flowers in summer, and the hand of heaven was against us, so that we were hard pressed. They arranged the battle near the ships, and both armies hurled their bronze-tipped spears at one another. As long as the day grew and it was still morning, we held our own against them, though they outnumbered us; but as the sun went down, toward the time when men unyoke their oxen, the Cicones got the better of us, and we lost six men from every ship we had; so we escaped with those who were left.

"From there we sailed onward with sorrow in our hearts, but glad to have escaped death though we had lost our comrades, and we didn't leave until we had called three times upon each one of the poor fellows who had died by the hands of the Cicones. Then Zeus raised the North wind against us until it blew a hurricane, so that land and sky were hidden in thick clouds, and night sprang forth from the heavens. We let the ships run before the gale, but the force of the wind tore our sails to shreds, so we took them down for fear of shipwreck, and rowed our hardest toward the land. There we lay two days and two nights suffering much from both toil and distress of mind, but on the morning of the third day we again raised our masts, set sail, and took our places, letting the wind and helmsmen direct our ship. I should have reached home at that time unharmed had not the North wind and the currents been against me as I was rounding Cape Malea, and set me off my course near the island of Cythera.

"I was driven from there by foul winds for nine days upon the sea, but on the tenth day we reached the land of the Lotus-eaters, who live on a food that comes from a kind of flower. Here we landed to take on fresh water, and our crews got their midday meal on the shore near the ships. When they had eaten and drunk I sent two of my company to see what kind of people lived in that place, and they had a third man with them. They started at once, and went among the Lotus-eaters, who did them no harm, but gave them lotus to eat, which was so delicious that those who ate it stopped caring about home, and didn't even want to go back and report what had happened to them, but wanted to stay and eat lotus with the Lotus-eaters without thinking any more of their return; nevertheless, though they wept bitterly I forced them back to the ships and tied them up under the benches. Then I told the rest to go on board at once, in case any of them should taste the lotus and stop wanting to get home, so they took their places and struck the gray sea with their oars.

"We sailed from there, always in great distress, until we came to the land of the lawless and savage Cyclopes. Now the Cyclopes neither plant nor plow, but trust in providence, and live on such wheat, barley, and grapes as grow wild without any cultivation, and their wild grapes yield them wine as the sun and rain may make them grow. They have no laws or assemblies of the people, but live in caves on the tops of high mountains; each is lord and master in his own family, and they pay no attention to their neighbors.

"Now off their harbor there lies a wooded and fertile island not quite close to the land of the Cyclopes, but still not far. It is overrun with wild goats, that breed there in great numbers and are never disturbed by human foot; for hunters—who as a rule will endure so much hardship in forest or among mountain cliffs—don't go there, nor is it ever plowed or grazed, but it lies a wilderness untilled and unsown from year to year, and has no living thing upon it but only goats. For the Cyclopes have no ships, nor shipwrights who could make ships for them; they cannot therefore go from city to city, or sail over the sea to one another's country as people who have ships can do; if they had these they would have colonized the island, for it is a very good one, and would yield everything in due season. There are meadows that in some places come right down to the seashore, well watered and full of rich grass; grapes would do excellently there; there is level land for plowing, and it would always yield heavily at harvest time, for the soil is deep. There is a good harbor where no cables are needed, nor anchors, nor need a ship be moored, but all one has to do is beach one's vessel and stay there until the wind becomes fair for putting out to sea again. At the head of the harbor there is a spring of clear water coming out of a cave, and there are poplars growing all around it.

"Here we entered, but so dark was the night that some god must have brought us in, for there was nothing whatever to be seen. A thick mist hung all around our ships; the moon was hidden behind a mass of clouds so that no one could have seen the island if he had looked for it, nor were there any breakers to tell us we were close to shore before we found ourselves upon the land itself; when, however, we had beached the ships, we took down the sails, went ashore and camped upon the beach until daybreak.

"When the child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn appeared, we admired the island and wandered all over it, while the nymphs Zeus's daughters roused the wild goats so that we might get some meat for our dinner. At this we fetched our spears and bows and arrows from the ships, and dividing ourselves into three bands began to shoot the goats. Heaven sent us excellent sport; I had twelve ships with me, and each ship got nine goats, while my own ship had ten; thus through the whole day until the sun went down we ate and drank our fill, and we had plenty of wine left, for each one of us had taken many jars when we sacked the city of the Cicones, and this had not yet run out. While we were feasting we kept turning our eyes toward the land of the Cyclopes, which was nearby, and saw the smoke of their fires. We could almost imagine we heard their voices and the bleating of their sheep and goats, but when the sun went down and it grew dark, we camped down upon the beach, and next morning I called a council.

"'Stay here, my brave fellows,' said I, 'all the rest of you, while I go with my ship and explore these people myself: I want to see if they are uncivilized savages, or a hospitable and civilized race.'

"I went on board, telling my men to do so also and loose the cables; so they took their places and struck the gray sea with their oars. When we got to the land, which was not far, there, on the face of a cliff near the sea, we saw a great cave overhung with laurels. It was a shelter for a great many sheep and goats, and outside there was a large yard, with a high wall around it made of stones set deep in the ground and of trees both pine and oak. This was the home of a huge monster who was then away from home shepherding his flocks. He would have nothing to do with other people, but led the life of an outlaw. He was a horrible creature, not like a human being at all, but resembling rather some crag that stands out boldly against the sky on the top of a high mountain.

"I told my men to draw the ship ashore, and stay where they were, all but the twelve best among them, who were to go along with me. I also took a goatskin of sweet black wine which had been given me by Maron, son of Euanthes, who was priest of Apollo the patron god of Ismarus, and lived within the sacred precincts of the temple. When we were sacking the city we respected him, and spared his life, as well as his wife and child; so he made me some presents of great value—seven talents of fine gold, and a bowl of silver, with twelve jars of sweet wine, unblended, and of the most exquisite flavor. Not a man or woman in the house knew about it, but only himself, his wife, and one housekeeper: when he drank it he mixed twenty parts of water to one of wine, and yet the fragrance from the mixing-bowl was so wonderful that it was impossible to resist drinking. I filled a large skin with this wine, and took a bag full of provisions with me, for my mind warned me that I might have to deal with some savage who would be of great strength, and would respect neither right nor law.

"We soon reached his cave, but he was out shepherding, so we went inside and looked at everything we could see. His cheese-racks were loaded with cheeses, and he had more lambs and kids than his pens could hold. They were kept in separate flocks; first there were the yearlings, then the older of the younger lambs and lastly the very young ones all kept apart from one another; as for his dairy, all the vessels, bowls, and milk pails into which he milked, were swimming with whey. When they saw all this, my men begged me to let them first steal some cheeses, and make off with them to the ship; they would then return, drive down the lambs and kids, put them on board and sail away with them. It would have been much better if we had done so but I would not listen to them, for I wanted to see the owner himself, in the hope that he might give me a gift. When, however, we saw him my poor men found him terrible to deal with.

"We lit a fire, offered some of the cheeses in sacrifice, ate others of them, and then sat waiting until the Cyclops should come in with his sheep. When he came, he brought in with him a huge load of dry firewood to light the fire for his supper, and this he threw with such a crash onto the floor of his cave that we hid ourselves in fear at the far end of the cavern. Meanwhile he drove all the ewes inside, as well as the female goats that he was going to milk, leaving the males, both rams and he-goats, outside in the yards. Then he rolled a huge stone to the mouth of the cave—so huge that twenty-two strong four-wheeled wagons would not be enough to draw it from its place against the doorway. When he had done this he sat down and milked his ewes and goats, all in proper order, and then let each of them have her own young. He curdled half the milk and set it aside in wicker strainers, but the other half he poured into bowls that he might drink it for his supper. When he had finished all his work, he lit the fire, and then caught sight of us, whereupon he said:
"'Strangers, who are you? Where do you sail from? Are you traders, or do you sail the sea as pirates, with your hands against every man, and every man's hand against you?'

"We were terrified by his loud voice and monstrous form, but I managed to say, 'We are Achaeans on our way home from Troy, but by the will of Zeus, and stress of weather, we have been driven far out of our course. We are the people of Agamemnon, son of Atreus, who has won infinite fame throughout the whole world, by sacking so great a city and killing so many people. We therefore humbly pray you to show us some hospitality, and otherwise make us such gifts as visitors may reasonably expect. May your excellency fear the wrath of heaven, for we are your suppliants, and Zeus protects all respectable travelers, for he is the avenger of all suppliants and foreigners in distress.'

"To this he gave me a pitiless answer, 'Stranger,' said he, 'you are a fool, or else you know nothing of this country. Talk to me about fearing the gods or avoiding their anger? We Cyclopes don't care about Zeus or any of your blessed gods, for we are ever so much stronger than they. I shall not spare either yourself or your companions out of any regard for Zeus, unless I am in the mood to do so. And now tell me where you made your ship fast when you came on shore. Was it around the point, or is she lying straight off the land?'

"He said this to draw me out, but I was too cunning to be caught in that way, so I answered with a lie; 'Poseidon,' said I, 'sent my ship onto the rocks at the far end of your country, and wrecked it. We were driven onto them from the open sea, but I and those who are with me escaped the jaws of death.'

"The cruel wretch gave me not one word of answer, but with a sudden grab he seized two of my men at once and dashed them down upon the ground as though they had been puppies. Their brains were scattered upon the ground, and the earth was wet with their blood. Then he tore them limb from limb and ate them for supper. He devoured them like a lion in the wilderness, flesh, bones, marrow, and entrails, without leaving anything uneaten. As for us, we wept and lifted up our hands to heaven on seeing such a horrible sight, for we didn't know what else to do; but when the Cyclops had filled his huge belly, and had washed down his meal of human flesh with a drink of pure milk, he stretched himself full length upon the ground among his sheep, and went to sleep. I was at first inclined to seize my sword, draw it, and drive it into his heart, but I reflected that if I did we would all certainly be lost, for we would never be able to move the stone which the monster had put in front of the door. So we stayed sobbing and sighing where we were until morning came.

"When the child of morning, rosy-fingered dawn, appeared, he again lit his fire, milked his goats and ewes, all quite properly, and then let each have her own young one; as soon as he had finished all his work, he grabbed two more of my men, and began eating them for his morning meal. Presently, with the utmost ease, he rolled the stone away from the door and drove out his sheep, but he at once put it back again—as easily as though he were merely putting the lid on a quiver full of arrows. As soon as he had done so he shouted, and cried 'Shoo, shoo,' after his sheep to drive them on to the mountain; so I was left to scheme some way of taking my revenge and covering myself with glory.

"In the end I decided it would be the best plan to do as follows: The Cyclops had a great club which was lying near one of the sheep pens; it was of green olive wood, and he had cut it intending to use it for a staff as soon as it should be dry. It was so huge that we could only compare it to the mast of a twenty-oared merchant vessel of large size, able to venture out into open sea. I went up to this club and cut off about six feet of it; I then gave this piece to the men and told them to smooth it evenly at one end, which they proceeded to do, and lastly I brought it to a point myself, hardening the end in the fire to make it stronger. When I had done this I hid it under dung, which was lying about all over the cave, and told the men to cast lots to see which of them should venture along with me to lift it and bore it into the monster's eye while he was asleep. The lot fell upon the very four whom I would have chosen, and I myself made five. In the evening the wretch came back from shepherding, and drove his flocks into the cave—this time driving them all inside, and not leaving any in the yards; I suppose some fancy must have taken him, or a god must have prompted him to do so. As soon as he had put the stone back in its place against the door, he sat down, milked his ewes and his goats all quite properly, and then let each have her own young one; when he had finished all this work, he seized two more of my men, and made his supper off them. So I went up to him with an ivy-wood bowl of black wine in my hands:

"'Look here, Cyclops,' said I, 'you have been eating a great deal of human flesh, so take this and drink some wine, that you may see what kind of drink we had on board my ship. I was bringing it to you as a drink-offering, in the hope that you would take pity upon me and help me on my way home, whereas all you do is to go on raging and ranting most intolerably. You ought to be ashamed of yourself; how can you expect people to come see you any more if you treat them in this way?'

"He then took the cup and drank. He was so delighted with the taste of the wine that he begged me for another bowl full. 'Be so kind,' he said, 'as to give me some more, and tell me your name at once. I want to make you a present that you will be glad to have. We have wine even in this country, for our soil grows grapes and the sun ripens them, but this tastes like nectar and ambrosia all in one.'

"I then gave him some more; three times did I fill the bowl for him, and three times did he drain it without thought or care; then, when I saw that the wine had gotten into his head, I said to him as persuasively as I could: 'Cyclops, you ask my name and I will tell it to you; give me, therefore, the present you promised me; my name is Nobody; this is what my father and mother and my friends have always called me.'
"But the cruel wretch said, 'Then I will eat all Nobody's comrades before Nobody himself, and will keep Nobody for the last. This is the present that I will make him.'

"As he spoke he swayed, and fell sprawling face upward on the ground. His great neck hung heavily backward and a deep sleep took hold of him. Presently he turned sick, and threw up both wine and the chunks of human flesh on which he had been gorging, for he was very drunk. Then I thrust the beam of wood far into the embers to heat it, and encouraged my men lest any of them should lose heart. When the wood, green though it was, was about to blaze, I drew it out of the fire glowing with heat, and my men gathered around me, for heaven had filled their hearts with courage. We drove the sharp end of the beam into the monster's eye, and bearing upon it with all my weight I kept turning it around and around as though I were boring a hole in a ship's plank with an auger, which two men with a wheel and strap can keep on turning as long as they choose. Even thus did we bore the red hot beam into his eye, until the boiling blood bubbled all over it as we worked it around and around, so that the steam from the burning eyeball scalded his eyelids and eyebrows, and the roots of the eye sputtered in the fire. As a blacksmith plunges an axe or hatchet into cold water to temper it—for it is this that gives strength to the iron—and it makes a great hiss as he does so, even thus did the Cyclops' eye hiss around the beam of olive wood, and his hideous yells made the cave ring again. We ran away in fright, but he plucked the beam all covered with gore from his eye, and hurled it from him in a frenzy of rage and pain, shouting as he did so to the other Cyclopes who lived on the bleak headlands near him; so they gathered from all quarters around his cave when they heard him crying, and asked what was the matter with him.

"'What ails you, Polyphemus,' said they, 'that you make such a noise, breaking the stillness of the night, and preventing us from being able to sleep? Surely no one is carrying off your sheep? Surely no one is trying to kill you either by trickery or by force?'
"But Polyphemus shouted to them from inside the cave, 'Nobody is killing me by trickery; nobody is killing me by force.'
"'Then,' said they, 'if no one is attacking you, you must be ill; when Zeus makes people ill, there is no help for it, and you had better pray to your father Poseidon.'

"Then they went away, and I laughed inwardly at the success of my clever trick, but the Cyclops, groaning and in agony of pain, felt about with his hands until he found the stone and took it from the door; then he sat in the doorway and stretched his hands in front of it to catch anyone going out with the sheep, for he thought I might be foolish enough to attempt this.

"As for myself I kept on puzzling to think how I could best save my own life and those of my companions; I schemed and schemed, as one who knows that his life depends upon it, for the danger was very great. In the end I decided that this plan would be the best; the male sheep were well grown, and carried a heavy black fleece, so I bound them noiselessly in threes together, with some of the willow branches on which the wicked monster used to sleep. There was to be a man under the middle sheep, and the two on either side were to cover him, so that there were three sheep to each man. As for myself there was a ram finer than any of the others, so I caught hold of him by the back, tucked myself in the thick wool under his belly, and hung on patiently to his fleece, face upward, keeping a firm hold on it all the time.

"Thus, then, did we wait in great fear of mind until morning came, but when the child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn, appeared, the male sheep hurried out to feed, while the ewes remained bleating about the pens waiting to be milked, for their udders were full to bursting; but their master in spite of all his pain felt the backs of all the sheep as they stood upright, without being sharp enough to find out that the men were underneath their bellies. As the ram was going out, last of all, heavy with its fleece and with the weight of my cunning self, Polyphemus laid hold of it and said:

"'My good ram, what is it that makes you the last to leave my cave this morning? You are not used to letting the ewes go before you, but lead the flock at a run whether to flowery meadow or bubbling fountain, and are the first to come home again at night; but now you lag last of all. Is it because you know your master has lost his eye, and are sorry because that wicked Nobody and his horrible crew got him down in his drink and blinded him? But I will have his life yet. If you could understand and talk, you would tell me where the wretch is hiding, and I would dash his brains upon the ground until they flew all over the cave. I would thus have some satisfaction for the harm this no-good Nobody has done me.'

"As he spoke he drove the ram outside, but when we were a little way out from the cave and yards, I first got from under the ram's belly, and then freed my comrades; as for the sheep, which were very fat, by constantly heading them in the right direction we managed to drive them down to the ship. The crew rejoiced greatly at seeing those of us who had escaped death, but wept for the others whom the Cyclops had killed. However, I made signs to them by nodding and frowning that they were to stop their crying, and told them to get all the sheep on board at once and put out to sea; so they went aboard, took their places, and struck the gray sea with their oars. Then, when I had gotten as far out as my voice would reach, I began to taunt the Cyclops.

"'Cyclops,' said I, 'you should have taken better measure of your man before eating up his comrades in your cave. You wretch, eat up your visitors in your own house? You might have known that your sin would find you out, and now Zeus and the other gods have punished you.'

"He got more and more furious as he heard me, so he tore the top from a high mountain, and flung it just in front of my ship so that it was within a little of hitting the end of the rudder. The sea quaked as the rock fell into it, and the wash of the wave it raised carried us back toward the mainland, and forced us toward the shore. But I snatched up a long pole and kept the ship off, making signs to my men by nodding my head, that they must row for their lives, whereupon they rowed with all their strength. When we had gotten twice as far as we were before, I was for taunting the Cyclops again, but the men begged and pleaded with me to hold my tongue.

"'Don't,' they exclaimed, 'be mad enough to provoke this savage creature further; he has thrown one rock at us already which drove us back again to the mainland, and we made sure it had been the death of us; if he had then heard any further sound of voices he would have pounded our heads and our ship's timbers into a pulp with the rugged rocks he would have heaved at us, for he can throw them a long way.'

"But I would not listen to them, and shouted out to him in my rage, 'Cyclops, if anyone asks you who it was that put your eye out and spoiled your beauty, say it was the valiant warrior Odysseus, son of Laertes, who lives in Ithaca.'

"At this he groaned, and cried out, 'Alas, alas, then the old prophecy about me is coming true. There was a prophet here, at one time, a man both brave and of great stature, Telemus son of Eurymus, who was an excellent seer, and did all the prophesying for the Cyclopes until he grew old; he told me that all this would happen to me some day, and said I should lose my sight by the hand of Odysseus. I have been all along expecting someone of imposing presence and superhuman strength, whereas he turns out to be a little insignificant weakling, who has managed to blind my eye by taking advantage of me in my drink; come here, then, Odysseus, that I may make you presents to show my hospitality, and urge Poseidon to help you forward on your journey—for Poseidon and I are father and son. He, if he so chooses, shall heal me, which no one else neither god nor man can do.'
"Then I said, 'I wish I could be as sure of killing you outright and sending you down to the house of Hades, as I am that it will take more than Poseidon to cure that eye of yours.'

"At this he lifted up his hands to the vault of heaven and prayed, saying, 'Hear me, great Poseidon; if I am indeed your own true son, grant that Odysseus may never reach his home alive; or if he must get back to his friends at last, let him do so late and in terrible condition after losing all his men, let him reach his home in another man's ship and find trouble in his house.'

"Thus did he pray, and Poseidon heard his prayer. Then he picked up a rock much larger than the first, swung it aloft and hurled it with tremendous force. It fell just short of the ship, but was within a little of hitting the end of the rudder. The sea quaked as the rock fell into it, and the wash of the wave it raised drove us onward on our way toward the shore of the island.

"When at last we got to the island where we had left the rest of our ships, we found our comrades lamenting us, and anxiously awaiting our return. We ran our vessel upon the sands and got out of her onto the seashore; we also landed the Cyclops' sheep, and divided them fairly among us so that no one could complain. As for the ram, my companions agreed that I should have it as an extra share; so I sacrificed it on the seashore, and burned its thigh bones to Zeus, who is the lord of all. But he paid no attention to my sacrifice, and only thought how he might destroy both my ships and my comrades.

"Thus through the whole day until the sun went down we feasted our fill on meat and drink, but when the sun went down and it grew dark, we camped upon the beach. When the child of morning rosy-fingered Dawn appeared, I told my men to go on board and loose the cables. Then they took their places and struck the gray sea with their oars; so we sailed on with sorrow in our hearts, but glad to have escaped death though we had lost our comrades.

chapters.title: Book X — Aeolus, the Laestrygones, Circe
paragraphs: From there we sailed to the floating island of Aeolus, son of Hippotas, beloved by the immortal gods. It's an island that seems to drift on the sea, surrounded by an unbreakable wall of bronze. Aeolus had six daughters and six strong sons, and he married the sons to the daughters, so they all lived together with their parents in constant celebration, enjoying every luxury imaginable. All day long the house filled with the rich smell of roasting meat, and the courtyard echoed with the sounds of feasting. At night they slept in their fine beds, each man with his wife beside him. These were the people we had come among.

Aeolus entertained me for a full month, asking me endless questions about Troy, the Greek fleet, and how the Greeks had returned home. I told him everything exactly as it had happened, and when I said I needed to leave and asked him to help me on my way, he agreed without hesitation and set about helping me at once. He skinned a prime ox-hide to hold the paths of the roaring winds, which he trapped inside the hide like a sack—for Zeus had made him master of the winds, and he could calm or stir each one as he pleased. He put the sack in my ship and bound its mouth so tightly with silver wire that not even the slightest breeze could escape from any direction. Only the West Wind, which would carry us home, did he allow to blow freely. But it all came to nothing, because we were ruined by our own stupidity.

For nine days and nights we sailed, and on the tenth day we could see our homeland on the horizon. We came so close that we could see the fires burning in the fields, and I, completely exhausted, fell into a light sleep—I had never let the steering oar leave my hands, hoping we'd reach home faster. Then my men began talking among themselves, saying I was bringing back gold and silver in the bag Aeolus had given me. "Look at that," one would say to another, "how this man gets honored and makes friends wherever he goes. See what fine treasures he's bringing back from Troy, while we, who traveled just as far as he did, return empty-handed—and now Aeolus has given him even more. Quick, let's see what's in there, and how much gold and silver is in that bag he gave him."

So they talked, and their evil plan won out. They opened the bag, and the winds came howling out, raising a storm that swept us weeping back out to sea, away from our own country. When I woke up, I didn't know whether to throw myself into the sea or bear it and go on living. But I endured it, covered my head, and lay down in the ship while my men wailed bitterly as the fierce winds carried our fleet back to Aeolus's island.

When we reached it, we went ashore to get fresh water and ate a meal beside the ships. Right after we finished eating, I took a herald and one of my men and went straight to Aeolus's house, where I found him feasting with his wife and family. We sat down as suppliants at his threshold. They were amazed when they saw us and said, "Odysseus, what brings you here? What god has been tormenting you? We took such care to send you on your way home to Ithaca, or wherever else you wanted to go."
They spoke like this, but I answered sadly, "My men have destroyed me—they and cursed sleep have ruined me. My friends, please fix this disaster for me, since you have the power to do so."

I spoke as persuasively as I could, but they said nothing until their father answered, "Get out of here at once, you vilest of men! I will not help someone whom heaven hates. Leave now, for you come here as one the gods despise." And with those words he sent me away from his door in sorrow.

From there we sailed on miserably until the men were worn out from long and useless rowing, since there was no longer any wind to help them. For six days and nights we struggled, and on the seventh day we reached the rocky fortress of Lamus—Telepylus, city of the Laestrygonians, where the shepherd driving his flocks home for milking greets the one driving his animals out to pasture, and the other returns the greeting. In that country, a man who never slept could earn double wages—one as a cattle herder and another as a shepherd, since they work almost the same hours by night as by day.

When we reached the harbor, we found it completely enclosed by steep cliffs, with only a narrow entrance between two headlands. All my other captains took their ships inside and moored them close together, since there wasn't even a breath of wind inside—it was always perfectly calm. I kept my own ship outside and tied it to a rock at the very tip of the point. Then I climbed a high rock to scout around, but I could see no signs of people or livestock, only some smoke rising from the ground. So I sent two of my men with an attendant to find out what kind of people lived there.

When my men reached the shore, they followed a smooth road that the people used to bring firewood down from the mountains to the town. Soon they met a young woman who had come out to fetch water—she was the daughter of a Laestrygonian named Antiphates. She was going to the spring called Artacia, where the people got their water, and when my men approached her, they asked who ruled that land and what kind of people lived there. She directed them to her father's house, but when they got there, they found his wife was a giantess as huge as a mountain, and they were horrified at the sight of her.

She immediately called for her husband Antiphates from the assembly place, and he set about killing my men at once. He grabbed one of them and began making his dinner of him right there, while the other two ran back to the ships as fast as they could. But Antiphates raised a war cry, and thousands of mighty Laestrygonians sprang up from everywhere—giants, not men. They hurled massive boulders at us from the cliffs as if they were pebbles, and I heard the horrible sound of ships being crushed together and the death cries of my men as the Laestrygonians speared them like fish and carried them off to eat. While they were slaughtering my men in the harbor, I drew my sword, cut my ship's anchor rope, and told my crew to row with all their strength if they didn't want to share the same fate. So they rowed for their lives, and we were grateful when we reached open water beyond the range of the rocks they hurled at us. As for the others, not one of them survived.

From there we sailed on sadly, glad to have escaped death though we had lost our comrades, and came to the island of Aeaea, where Circe lives—a great and cunning goddess, sister to the sorcerer Aeetes. Both are children of the Sun by Perse, who is Ocean's daughter. We brought our ship into a safe harbor without a word, guided there by some god, and after landing we lay there for two days and nights, exhausted in body and spirit. When the morning of the third day came, I took my spear and sword and left the ship to scout around, hoping to find signs of human activity or hear voices. Climbing to the top of a high lookout, I spotted smoke rising from Circe's house through the dense forest. When I saw this, I wondered whether I should go investigate immediately, but in the end I decided it was better to return to the ship, give the men their meal, and send some of them instead of going myself.

As I was nearly back to the ship, some god took pity on my loneliness and sent a magnificent stag with great antlers right into my path. He was coming down from his pasture in the forest to drink from the river, driven by the heat of the sun, and as he passed I struck him in the middle of his back. The bronze spear point went clean through him, and he fell groaning in the dust until he died. Then I set my foot on him, pulled my spear from the wound, and laid it aside. I also gathered rough grass and rushes and twisted them into about six feet of strong rope, with which I tied the noble creature's four legs together. Having done this, I slung him around my neck and walked back to the ship leaning on my spear, since the stag was far too big for me to carry on my shoulder while steadying him with one hand. When I threw him down in front of the ship, I called to my men and spoke encouragingly to each one. "Look here, my friends," I said, "we're not going to die before our time after all, and we won't starve as long as we have something to eat and drink aboard." At this they uncovered their heads on the seashore and admired the stag, for he was indeed a magnificent animal. Then, after they had gazed at him enough, they washed their hands and began preparing him for dinner.

So all day long until sunset we stayed there eating and drinking our fill, but when the sun went down and darkness came, we camped on the seashore. When rosy-fingered Dawn appeared, I called a meeting and said, "My friends, we're in serious trouble. Listen to me. We have no idea where the sun sets or rises, so we don't even know east from west. I see no way out of this, but we must try to find one. We're definitely on an island, for I climbed as high as I could this morning and saw the sea stretching to the horizon all around us. The island lies low, but toward the center I saw smoke rising from a thick forest."

Their hearts sank when they heard me, remembering how they had been treated by the Laestrygonian Antiphates and by the savage giant Polyphemus. They wept bitterly in their despair, but crying wouldn't help, so I divided them into two groups and appointed a leader for each. I put Eurylochus in charge of one group while I commanded the other. Then we drew lots in a helmet, and the lot fell to Eurylochus. So he set out with his twenty-two men, and they wept, as did we who were left behind.

When they reached Circe's house, they found it built of polished stones in a clearing that could be seen from far off, in the middle of the forest. Wild mountain wolves and lions prowled all around it—poor enchanted creatures that she had tamed with her magic and drugged into submission. They didn't attack my men, but wagged their great tails, fawned on them, and rubbed against them lovingly. Just as dogs crowd around their master when they see him coming back from dinner—knowing he'll bring them scraps—so these wolves and lions with their great claws fawned on my men, though the men were terrified at seeing such strange beasts. Soon they reached the gates of the goddess's house, and standing there they could hear Circe inside, singing beautifully as she worked at her loom, weaving cloth so fine, so soft, and of such brilliant colors that only a goddess could make. Then Polites, whom I valued and trusted more than any of my other men, said, "Someone inside is working at a loom and singing beautifully—the whole place echoes with it. Let's call out and see whether it's a woman or goddess."

They called to her and she came down, opened the door, and invited them in. Suspecting nothing, they all followed her except Eurylochus, who sensed trouble and stayed outside. Once she had them in her house, she seated them on benches and chairs and mixed them a drink with cheese, honey, meal, and Pramnian wine, but she drugged it with evil potions to make them forget their homeland. After they drank it, she struck them with her wand and turned them into pigs, then shut them up in her pigsties. They had pigs' heads, hair, and voices, and grunted just like pigs, but their minds remained the same as before, and they remembered everything.

So there they were, locked up and squealing, while Circe threw them acorns and beech nuts and other pig food. But Eurylochus rushed back to tell me about our comrades' terrible fate. He was so overwhelmed with horror that though he tried to speak, he couldn't find words. His eyes filled with tears and he could only sob and sigh, until finally we forced the story out of him, and he told us what had happened to the others.

"We went through the forest as you told us," he said, "and in the middle of it we found a beautiful house built of polished stones in a place that could be seen from far away. There we found a woman—or perhaps she was a goddess—working at her loom and singing sweetly. The men shouted and called to her, and she came down at once, opened the door, and invited us in. The others didn't suspect any treachery, so they followed her into the house, but I stayed where I was, thinking there might be some trick. From that moment I never saw them again, for not one of them came back out, though I sat watching for them for a long time."

Then I took my bronze sword and slung it over my shoulder. I also took my bow and told Eurylochus to come back with me and show me the way. But he grabbed me with both hands and spoke desperately: "Sir, don't force me to go with you—let me stay here, because I know you won't bring any of them back, and you won't even return alive yourself. Let's see if we can't escape with at least the few of us who are left, for we might still save our lives."
"Stay here then," I answered, "eating and drinking at the ship, but I must go, for I feel absolutely compelled to do so."

With that I left the ship and went inland. When I had passed through the enchanted grove and was near the great house of the sorceress Circe, I met Hermes with his golden wand, disguised as a handsome young man in the prime of youth, with the first down just appearing on his face. He came up to me and took my hand, saying, "My poor unfortunate man, where are you going over this mountain peak, alone and not knowing the way? Your men are shut up in Circe's pigsties like wild boars in their dens. You surely don't think you can free them? I can tell you that you'll never get back and will have to stay there with them. But never mind—I'll protect you and get you out of trouble. Take this herb, which has great power, and keep it with you when you go to Circe's house. It will protect you against every kind of harm.

"I'll tell you about all the wicked magic that Circe will try to use on you. She'll mix a drink for you and drug the food she puts in it, but she won't be able to enchant you, because this herb I'm giving you will prevent her spells from working. I'll tell you exactly what to do. When Circe strikes you with her wand, draw your sword and rush at her as if you're going to kill her. She'll be frightened and will want you to sleep with her. Don't refuse her outright, because you want her to free your companions and take good care of you too, but make her swear solemnly by all the blessed gods that she won't plot any more mischief against you, or else when she has you naked she'll rob you of your courage and manhood."

As he spoke, he pulled the herb from the ground and showed me what it looked like. The root was black, while the flower was white as milk. The gods call it moly, and mortal men cannot uproot it, but the gods can do whatever they please.

Then Hermes went back to high Olympus, passing over the wooded island, while I continued to Circe's house with a troubled heart. When I reached her gates I stood there and called to the goddess, and as soon as she heard me she came down, opened the door, and asked me to come in. So I followed her, deeply worried. She seated me on a richly decorated chair inlaid with silver, with a footstool beneath my feet, and mixed a drink for me in a golden cup, but she drugged it, intending me harm. When she gave it to me and I had drunk it without being enchanted, she struck me with her wand. "There," she cried, "go to the pigsty and make your bed with the rest of them!"

But I rushed at her with my sword drawn as if I would kill her. She fell back with a loud scream, grabbed my knees, and spoke desperately: "Who are you and where do you come from? What place and people are you from? How can it be that my drugs have no power over you? No man has ever been able to resist even a taste of the potion I gave you—you must be protected by magic! Surely you can be none other than the resourceful hero Odysseus, whom Hermes always said would come here someday in his ship while returning home from Troy. So be it then—put away your sword and let's go to bed, so we can learn to trust each other."

I answered, "Circe, how can you expect me to be friendly when you've just turned all my men into pigs? And now that you have me here, you mean me harm when you ask me to sleep with you—you'll rob me of my courage and manhood. I certainly won't consent to go to bed with you unless you first swear a solemn oath not to plot any more harm against me."
So she swore immediately as I had demanded, and when she had completed her oath, I went to bed with her.

Meanwhile her four servants, who were her maids, set about their work. They are the daughters of the springs and groves and the sacred waters that flow down to the sea. One spread a beautiful purple cloth over a chair and laid a carpet beneath it. Another brought silver tables to the seats and set golden baskets on them. A third mixed sweet wine with water in a silver bowl and placed golden cups on the tables, while the fourth brought water and set it to boil in a large cauldron over a good fire she had lit. When the water in the cauldron was boiling, she mixed in cold water until it was just the right temperature, then put me in a bath and began washing me, pouring the water over my head and shoulders to take away the weariness and stiffness from my limbs. When she had finished washing and anointing me with oil, she dressed me in a fine cloak and tunic and led me to a richly decorated chair inlaid with silver, with a footstool beneath my feet. A servant then brought me water in a beautiful golden pitcher and poured it into a silver basin so I could wash my hands, and she set a polished table beside me. The housekeeper brought bread and offered me many of the good things in the house, and then Circe told me to eat. But I wouldn't eat and sat there paying no attention to what was in front of me, still gloomy and suspicious.

When Circe saw me sitting there without eating, in great distress, she came to me and said, "Odysseus, why do you sit there like a mute, eating your heart out, refusing both food and drink? Are you still suspicious? You shouldn't be, for I've already sworn solemnly that I won't hurt you."

I said, "Circe, no man with any sense of right and wrong can think of eating or drinking in your house until you've freed his friends and let him see them. If you want me to eat and drink, free my men and bring them to me so I can see them with my own eyes."

When I said this, she went straight through the courtyard with her wand in hand and opened the pigsty doors. My men came out looking like fat hogs and stood facing her, but she went among them and rubbed each one with a different drug. Then the bristles that the evil potion had given them fell off, and they became men again—younger than before, and much taller and more handsome. They recognized me at once, each one grasped my hand, and wept for joy until the whole house rang with their cries. Even Circe herself was moved by their emotion and came to me saying, "Noble Odysseus, son of Laertes, go back to the shore where you left your ship at once. First drag it up onto the beach, then hide all your ship's equipment and treasure in some cave, and come back here with your men."

I agreed to this, so I went back to the seashore and found my men at the ship weeping and wailing pitifully. When they saw me, the dear fools began frisking around me like calves that break out of their pen and gambol around their mothers when they see them coming home to be milked after feeding all day, and the farmyard echoes with their lowing. They seemed as glad to see me as if they had reached their own rugged Ithaca, where they were born and raised. "Sir," said the devoted men, "we're as happy to see you back as if we had safely reached Ithaca itself! But tell us what happened to our comrades."

I spoke comfortingly to them: "We must drag our ship onto the beach and hide all our gear and treasure in some cave. Then come with me, all of you, as quickly as you can to Circe's house, where you'll find your comrades eating and drinking in the midst of great plenty."

At this the men were ready to come with me immediately, but Eurylochus tried to hold them back, saying, "Poor fools, what will become of us? Don't rush to your doom by going to Circe's house, where she'll turn us all into pigs or wolves or lions, and we'll have to guard her palace. Remember how the Cyclops treated us when our comrades went into his cave with Odysseus. It was entirely due to his recklessness that those men lost their lives."

When I heard this, I was torn between drawing the sharp blade that hung at my side and cutting off his head, even though he was my own relative. But my men intervened and said, "Sir, if you wish, let this man stay here and guard the ship, but take the rest of us with you to Circe's house."
So we all went inland, and Eurylochus wasn't left behind after all—he came too, frightened by the harsh rebuke I had given him.

Meanwhile, Circe had been bathing the men who had been left behind and rubbing them with olive oil. She had also given them woolen cloaks and tunics, and when we arrived we found them all dining comfortably in her house. As soon as the men saw each other face to face and recognized one another, they wept for joy and cried out so loudly that the whole palace rang. Then Circe came to me and said, "Noble Odysseus, son of Laertes, tell your men to stop crying. I know how much you've all suffered at sea, and how badly you've been treated by cruel savages on land, but that's over now. So stay here and eat and drink until you're as strong and vigorous as you were when you left Ithaca. Right now you're weakened in both body and spirit—you keep dwelling on the hardships you've endured during your travels, so that you have no joy left in you."

She spoke like this and we agreed. We stayed with Circe for a full year, feasting on unlimited quantities of meat and wine. But when the year had passed with the waning of the moons and the long days had come round again, my men called me aside and said, "Sir, it's time you started thinking about going home, if you're destined to be spared to see your house and native country at all."

They spoke like this and I agreed. So all day long until sunset we feasted on meat and wine, but when the sun went down and darkness fell, the men lay down to sleep in the covered porches. But I went to Circe's bed and begged her by her knees, and the goddess listened to what I had to say. "Circe," I said, "please keep the promise you made to help me on my journey home. I want to get back, and so do my men—they're always pestering me with complaints whenever you're not around."

The goddess answered, "Noble Odysseus, son of Laertes, none of you need stay here any longer against your will, but there's another journey you must make before you can sail home. You must go to the house of Hades and dread Persephone to consult the spirit of the blind Theban prophet Tiresias, whose mind is still sound. To him alone has Persephone left his understanding even in death, while the other ghosts flit about mindlessly."

I was dismayed when I heard this. I sat up in bed and wept, and would have been glad never again to see the light of the sun. But when I was finally tired of weeping and tossing about, I said, "Who will guide me on this voyage? For the realm of Hades is a port that no ship can reach."

"You won't need a guide," she answered. "Raise your mast, set your white sails, sit still, and the North Wind will blow you there by itself. When your ship has crossed the waters of Ocean, you'll reach the fertile shore of Persephone's land with its groves of tall poplars and willows that drop their fruit before it ripens. Beach your ship there on the shore of Ocean and go straight to the dark house of Hades. You'll find it near the place where the rivers Pyriphlegethon and Cocytus—which is a branch of the river Styx—flow into Acheron, and you'll see a rock there, right where the two roaring rivers meet.

"When you reach that spot, as I'm telling you, dig a trench about eighteen inches square and deep, and pour into it drink offerings to all the dead—first honey mixed with milk, then wine, and third water, sprinkling white barley meal over it all.
