You must also offer many prayers to the powerless ghosts and promise them that when you return to Ithaca you'll sacrifice your best barren heifer to them and load the pyre with good things. Especially promise that Tiresias will have a black ram all to himself, the finest in your flocks.

"After you've made these prayers to the ghosts, sacrifice a ram and a black ewe, turning their heads toward Erebus while you yourself face away from them as if heading toward the river. Then many spirits of the dead will come to you, and you must tell your men to skin the two sheep you've just killed and burn them as sacrifices with prayers to Hades and Persephone. Then draw your sword and sit there, preventing any other ghost from approaching the spilled blood until Tiresias has answered your questions. The prophet will come to you soon and tell you about your voyage—what stages you must make and how you must sail the sea to reach your home."

It was daybreak by the time she finished speaking, so she dressed me in my shirt and cloak. As for herself, she threw a beautiful, light, shimmering fabric over her shoulders, fastening it with a golden belt around her waist, and covered her head with a veil. Then I went among my men throughout the house and spoke kindly to each one: "You can't lie here sleeping any longer," I told them. "We must be going, for Circe has told me everything." And they did as I commanded.

Even so, I didn't get them all away without accident. We had with us a young man named Elpenor, not particularly notable for good sense or courage, who had gotten drunk and was lying on the rooftop away from the other men, sleeping off his wine in the cool air. When he heard the noise of the men bustling about, he jumped up suddenly and forgot to come down by the main staircase, so he fell straight off the roof and broke his neck, and his soul went down to the house of Hades.

When I had gathered the men together, I said to them, "You think you're about to sail home, but Circe has explained to me that instead we must go to the house of Hades and Persephone to consult the spirit of the Theban prophet Tiresias."

The men were heartbroken when they heard me and threw themselves on the ground, groaning and tearing their hair, but their crying didn't help anything. When we reached the seashore, weeping and lamenting our fate, Circe brought the ram and ewe and tethered them near the ship. She passed through our midst without us knowing it, for who can see the comings and goings of a god when the god doesn't wish to be seen?

chapters.title: Book XI — The visit to the dead
paragraphs: When we reached the seashore, we dragged our ship into the water and loaded her mast and sails. We put the sheep aboard and took our places, weeping with heavy hearts. Circe, that great and cunning goddess, sent us a fair wind that blew steadily behind us, keeping our sails filled. We did whatever work the ship required and let her sail as the wind and helmsman directed. All day her sails stayed full as she held course across the sea, but when the sun set and darkness covered the earth, we entered the deep waters of the river Ocean, where lies the land and city of the Cimmerians. They live wrapped in mist and darkness that the sun's rays never pierce, neither when he rises nor when he sets again in the heavens. Those wretched people live in eternal, melancholy night. When we arrived there, we beached the ship, unloaded the sheep, and walked along the waters of Ocean until we came to the place Circe had described.

Here Perimedes and Eurylochus held the sacrificial animals while I drew my sword and dug a trench a cubit square. I made drink offerings to all the dead—first with honey and milk, then with wine, and finally with water. I sprinkled white barley meal over everything, praying earnestly to the helpless ghosts and promising them that when I returned to Ithaca, I would sacrifice my best barren heifer for them and load the funeral pyre with fine offerings. I especially promised Teiresias the finest black sheep from my flocks. When I had finished praying to the dead, I cut the throats of the two sheep and let their blood flow into the trench. Then the ghosts came streaming up from the underworld—young brides, unmarried men, old men worn out by toil, maidens who had died for love, and brave warriors killed in battle with their armor still stained with blood. They came from every direction and flitted around the trench with a strange, unearthly wailing that made me pale with fear. When I saw them approaching, I ordered my men to quickly skin the dead sheep and burn them as offerings while reciting prayers to Hades and Persephone. But I sat with my drawn sword, refusing to let the helpless ghosts near the blood until Teiresias had answered my questions.

The first ghost to appear was my companion Elpenor, for his body had not yet been buried. We had left him unwaked and unburied in Circe's house because we had too much else to do. I felt terrible sorrow when I saw him and cried out, "Elpenor, how did you get down here into this gloom and darkness? You reached this place on foot faster than I did with my ship."

"Sir," he answered with a groan, "it was bad luck and my own terrible drunkenness. I was sleeping on the roof of Circe's house and forgot to use the long staircase when I woke. I fell straight off the roof and broke my neck, so my soul came down to Hades' realm. Now I beg you by everyone you left behind—though they're not here—by your wife, by the father who raised you as a child, and by Telemachus, who is your house's only hope, do what I'm about to ask. I know that when you leave this underworld, you'll sail your ship back to the island of Aeaea. Don't leave me there unwaked and unburied, or I might bring heaven's anger upon you. Burn me with whatever armor I have, build a burial mound for me on the seashore that will tell future generations what an unlucky man I was, and plant over my grave the oar I used to row with when I was alive among my companions." And I replied, "My poor friend, I will do everything you've asked."

So we sat holding this sad conversation, I on one side of the trench with my sword held over the blood, and my comrade's ghost speaking to me from the other side. Then came the ghost of my dead mother Anticleia, daughter of Autolycus. I had left her alive when I set out for Troy and was moved to tears when I saw her, but even in my grief, I wouldn't let her approach the blood until I had questioned Teiresias.

Then came the ghost of Theban Teiresias with his golden scepter in his hand. He recognized me and said, "Odysseus, noble son of Laertes, why have you left the light of day to visit the dead in this sorrowful place? Step back from the trench and put away your sword so I may drink the blood and give you true answers."
So I stepped back and sheathed my sword. When he had drunk the blood, he began his prophecy.

"You want to know about your homecoming, but the gods will make this difficult for you. I don't think you'll escape Poseidon's notice—he still nurses his bitter grudge against you for blinding his son. Still, after much suffering, you may reach home if you can restrain yourself and your companions when your ship reaches the island of Thrinacia, where you'll find the sheep and cattle belonging to the sun god, who sees and hears everything. If you leave these flocks unharmed and think only of getting home, you may yet reach Ithaca after much hardship. But if you harm them, I warn you of destruction for both your ship and your men. Even if you escape yourself, you'll return in terrible condition after losing all your men, aboard another man's ship, and you'll find trouble in your house, which will be overrun by arrogant men who are consuming your wealth while pretending to court your wife.

When you get home, you'll take revenge on these suitors. After you've killed them by force or cunning in your own house, you must take a well-made oar and carry it until you reach a country where people have never heard of the sea and don't even salt their food, nor do they know anything about ships and oars that serve as a ship's wings. I'll give you a sure sign you can't miss: a traveler will meet you and say that what you carry on your shoulder must be a winnowing fan. At that spot you must plant the oar in the ground and sacrifice a ram, a bull, and a boar to Poseidon. Then go home and offer grand sacrifices to all the heavenly gods, one after another. As for yourself, death will come to you from the sea, and your life will ebb away very gently when you're full of years and at peace, and your people will be blessed. All that I've said will come true."

"This must be as heaven wills," I answered, "but tell me truly—I see my poor mother's ghost nearby. She sits by the blood without saying a word, and though I'm her own son, she doesn't recognize me or speak to me. Tell me, sir, how can I make her know me?"
"That I can easily explain," he said. "Any ghost you allow to taste the blood will speak to you rationally, but those you don't give blood to will go away again."

With that, Teiresias's ghost returned to Hades' house, his prophecies complete. But I remained where I was until my mother came forward and tasted the blood. Then she recognized me at once and spoke lovingly, saying, "My son, how did you come down to this realm of darkness while still alive? It's hard for the living to see these places, for between us and them lie great and terrible waters, and there is Ocean, which no one can cross on foot—they must have a good ship to carry them. Have you been wandering all this time trying to find your way home from Troy? Haven't you reached Ithaca yet or seen your wife in your own house?"

"Mother," I said, "I was forced to come here to consult the ghost of the Theban prophet Teiresias. I've never yet come near Greek lands or set foot in my native country. I've had nothing but one long series of misfortunes from the very first day I sailed with Agamemnon to horse-breeding Troy to fight the Trojans. But tell me truly, how did you die? Did you have a long illness, or did heaven grant you a gentle, easy passage to eternity? Tell me also about my father and the son I left behind—is my property still in their hands, or has someone else seized it, thinking I won't return to claim it? Tell me what my wife intends to do and what she's thinking. Does she stay with my son and guard my estate safely, or has she made the best match she could and married again?"

My mother answered, "Your wife remains in your house, but she's in great distress and spends all her time weeping, both night and day. No one has yet taken possession of your fine property, and Telemachus still holds your lands undisturbed. He has to host many guests, as he must, considering his position as a magistrate and how everyone invites him. Your father remains at his old place in the country and never goes near the town. He has no comfortable bed or bedding. In winter he sleeps on the floor by the fire with the servants and wears rags, but in summer, when warm weather returns, he lies outside in the vineyard on a bed of vine leaves scattered on the ground. He grieves constantly about your failure to return home and suffers more and more as he grows older. As for my own death, it happened this way: heaven didn't take me swiftly and painlessly in my own house, nor was I struck by any illness that typically wears people down and kills them. Rather, my longing to know what you were doing and the force of my love for you—that's what killed me."

Then I tried to find some way to embrace my poor mother's ghost. Three times I sprang toward her and tried to clasp her in my arms, but each time she slipped from my embrace like a dream or phantom. Deeply hurt, I said to her, "Mother, why don't you stay still when I try to embrace you? If we could put our arms around each other, we might find sad comfort in sharing our sorrows even here in Hades' house. Does Persephone want to burden me with even more grief by mocking me with only a phantom?"

"My son," she answered, "most unfortunate of all mankind, Persephone isn't deceiving you—this is simply how all people are when they're dead. The sinews no longer hold flesh and bones together. These perish in the fierce heat of consuming fire as soon as life leaves the body, and the soul flits away like a dream. Now go back to the light of day as quickly as you can, and remember all these things so you can tell your wife later."

As we talked this way, Persephone sent up the ghosts of the wives and daughters of all the most famous men. They gathered in crowds around the blood, and I considered how I might question them individually. Finally I decided it would be best to draw the sharp blade from my sturdy thigh and prevent them all from drinking the blood at once. So they approached one by one, and each told me her lineage and family as I questioned her.

The first I saw was Tyro, daughter of Salmoneus and wife of Cretheus, son of Aeolus. She fell in love with the river Enipeus, the most beautiful river in the whole world. Once when she was walking by its banks as usual, Poseidon, disguised as her beloved river, made love to her at the river's mouth, and a huge blue wave arched itself like a mountain over them to hide both woman and god. Then he loosened her virgin belt and made her sleep deeply. When the god had completed his act of love, he took her hand and said, "Tyro, rejoice in good will—the embraces of gods are not fruitless, and around this time next year you'll have fine twin sons. Take great care of them. I am Poseidon, so now go home, but keep silent and don't tell anyone."

Then he dove under the sea, and in due time she bore Pelias and Neleus, both of whom served Zeus with all their might. Pelias became a great sheep breeder and lived in Iolcus, while the other lived in Pylos. Her other children were by Cretheus: Aeson, Pheres, and Amythaon, who was a mighty warrior and charioteer.

Next I saw Antiope, daughter of Asopus, who could boast of having slept in Zeus's arms and bore him two sons, Amphion and Zethus. These founded seven-gated Thebes and built walls around it, for strong as they were, they couldn't hold Thebes without fortifying it.
Then I saw Alcmene, wife of Amphitryon, who also bore invincible Heracles to Zeus, and Megara, daughter of great King Creon, who married Amphitryon's formidable son.

I also saw fair Epicaste, mother of King Oedipus, whose awful fate it was to marry her own son unknowingly. He married her after killing his father, but the gods revealed the whole story to the world. He remained king of Thebes in great grief for the gods' spite against him, but Epicaste went to mighty Hades' house, having hanged herself in her anguish, leaving behind avenging spirits to torment him for his outraged mother—bringing him bitter regret thereafter.

Then I saw Chloris, whom Neleus married for her beauty, giving priceless gifts for her. She was the youngest daughter of Amphion, son of Iasus and king of Minyan Orchomenus, and became queen of Pylos. She bore Nestor, Chromius, and Periclymenus, and also that marvelously lovely woman Pero, who was courted by all the surrounding country. But Neleus would only give her to whoever could steal Iphicles' cattle from the grazing grounds of Phylace—a difficult task. The only man willing to attempt this cattle raid was a certain excellent seer, but heaven's will was against him. The cattle guards captured and imprisoned him. Nevertheless, when a full year had passed and the same season came again, Iphicles freed him after he had interpreted all of heaven's oracles. Thus Zeus's will was accomplished.

I saw Leda, wife of Tyndareus, who bore him two famous sons: Castor the horse-tamer and Pollux the mighty boxer. Both these heroes lie beneath the earth, though they're still alive, for by Zeus's special dispensation, they die and come back to life alternately, each living every other day throughout all time, and they have the rank of gods.

After her I saw Iphimedeia, wife of Aloeus, who boasted of Poseidon's embrace. She bore two sons, Otus and Ephialtes, but both were short-lived. They were the finest and best-looking children ever born in this world, except for Orion. At nine years old they were nine fathoms tall and nine cubits around the chest. They threatened to make war on the Olympian gods and tried to pile Mount Ossa on top of Mount Olympus, and Mount Pelion on top of Ossa, so they could scale heaven itself. They would have succeeded if they'd reached maturity, but Apollo, son of Leto, killed them both before they had even a trace of hair on their cheeks or chins.

Then I saw Phaedra, Procris, and fair Ariadne, daughter of the magician Minos, whom Theseus was carrying from Crete to Athens. But he didn't enjoy her, for before he could, Diana killed her on the island of Dia because of what Bacchus had said against her.

I also saw Maera, Clymene, and hateful Eriphyle, who sold her own husband for gold. But it would take me all night to name every single wife and daughter of heroes I saw, and it's time for me to sleep, either aboard ship with my crew or here. As for my escort home, heaven and you yourselves will arrange it.
Here he finished, and all the guests sat enthralled and speechless throughout the covered hall. Then Arete said to them:

"What do you think of this man, Phaeacians? Isn't he tall and handsome, and isn't he clever? True, he's my guest, but all of you share in the honor. Don't be hasty to send him away, and don't be stingy with gifts to someone in such great need, for heaven has blessed all of you with great wealth."

Then spoke aged hero Echeneus, one of the oldest men among them: "My friends, what our noble queen has just said is both reasonable and appropriate, so be persuaded by it. But the final decision, whether in word or deed, rests with King Alcinous."

"It will be done," declared Alcinous, "as surely as I still live and rule the Phaeacians. Our guest is indeed eager to get home, but we must persuade him to stay with us until tomorrow, by which time I'll be able to gather the full amount I intend to give him. His escort will be everyone's concern, but especially mine as your chief."

Odysseus answered, "King Alcinous, if you asked me to stay here for a full twelve months and then speed me on my way loaded with your noble gifts, I would gladly obey, and it would be greatly to my advantage, for I would return home richer and thus be more respected and beloved by all who see me when I reach Ithaca."

"Odysseus," replied Alcinous, "none of us who see you think you're a charlatan or swindler. I know many people go around telling such believable stories that it's hard to see through them, but there's a quality in your speech that assures me of your good character. Moreover, you've told the story of your own misfortunes and those of the Greeks as skillfully as a practiced bard. But tell me truly, did you see any of the mighty heroes who went to Troy with you and died there? The evenings are still long, and it's not yet bedtime—continue with your divine story, for I could stay here listening until tomorrow morning, as long as you keep telling us of your adventures."

"Alcinous," answered Odysseus, "there's a time for speeches and a time for sleep. Nevertheless, since you wish it, I won't refrain from telling you the even sadder tale of those companions who didn't fall fighting the Trojans but perished on their return through a wicked woman's treachery.

When Persephone had dismissed the female ghosts in all directions, the ghost of Agamemnon, son of Atreus, came sadly toward me, surrounded by those who had died with him in Aegisthus's house. As soon as he tasted the blood, he recognized me and, weeping bitterly, stretched out his arms to embrace me. But he had no strength or substance anymore, and I too wept and pitied him. 'How did you die, King Agamemnon?' I asked. 'Did Poseidon raise winds and waves against you at sea, or did your enemies kill you on land while you were stealing cattle or sheep, or while fighting to defend their wives and city?'

'Odysseus, noble son of Laertes,' he answered, 'I wasn't lost at sea in any storm Poseidon raised, nor did enemies kill me on the mainland. Aegisthus and my wicked wife murdered me together. He invited me to his house, feasted me, then butchered me as miserably as a fat beast in a slaughterhouse, while all around me my companions were slain like sheep or pigs for a wedding feast, banquet, or celebration of some great lord. You must have seen many men killed in battle or single combat, but you never saw anything as truly pitiful as how we fell in that hall, with the wine bowl and loaded tables lying about and the ground reeking with our blood. I heard Priam's daughter Cassandra scream as Clytemnestra killed her beside me. I lay dying on the ground with a sword in my body and raised my hands to strike the murderous slut, but she slipped away from me. She wouldn't even close my lips or eyes as I died, for nothing in this world is as cruel and shameless as a woman who has fallen into such guilt as hers. Imagine murdering her own husband! I thought I'd be welcomed home by my children and servants, but her abominable crime has brought disgrace on herself and all women who come after—even the good ones.'

'Truly Zeus has hated the house of Atreus from first to last because of their women's schemes,' I said. 'See how many of us died for Helen's sake, and now it seems Clytemnestra plotted against you during your absence.'

'Therefore be careful,' continued Agamemnon, 'and don't be too trusting even with your own wife. Don't tell her everything you know perfectly well. Tell her part of it and keep the rest to yourself. Not that your wife Odysseus is likely to murder you, for Penelope is a very admirable woman with an excellent character. We left her a young bride with an infant at her breast when we set out for Troy. That child is doubtless now grown to manhood, and he and his father will have a joyful meeting and embrace each other as they should, whereas my wicked wife didn't even let me see my son before killing me. Furthermore I say—and take my words to heart—don't announce your arrival when you bring your ship to Ithaca, but come secretly, for after all this, women can't be trusted. But tell me truly, can you give me any news of my son Orestes? Is he in Orchomenus, or Pylos, or at Sparta with Menelaus? I assume he's still living.'
'Agamemnon, why do you ask me?' I said. 'I don't know whether your son is alive or dead, and it's wrong to speak when one doesn't know.'

As we sat weeping and talking sadly together, the ghost of Achilles approached with Patroclus, Antilochus, and Ajax, who was the finest and most handsome of all the Greeks after Peleus's son. The fleet descendant of Aeacus recognized me and spoke mournfully: 'Odysseus, noble son of Laertes, what daring deed will you attempt next, that you venture down to Hades among us mindless dead, who are merely ghosts of those who can no longer work?'

'Achilles, son of Peleus, greatest champion of the Greeks,' I said, 'I came to consult Teiresias to see if he could advise me about returning home to Ithaca, for I've never yet been able to reach Greek lands or set foot in my own country, but have been in trouble constantly. As for you, Achilles, no one was ever as fortunate as you've been, nor ever will be, for all of us Greeks honored you like a god while you lived, and now that you're here, you're a great prince among the dead. Don't take it so hard that you've died.'

'Don't speak to me of death's consolations,' he answered. 'I'd rather be a hired laborer working for a poor man on earth than king of all the dead. But give me news about my son—has he gone to war and will he be a great soldier, or not? Tell me also if you've heard anything about my father Peleus—does he still rule among the Myrmidons, or do they show him no respect throughout Greece and Phthia now that age has weakened his limbs? If I could stand beside him in the sunlight with the same strength I had when I killed the bravest of our foes on the plain of Troy—if I could be as I was then and go even briefly to my father's house, anyone who tried to harm him or depose him would soon regret it.'

'I've heard nothing about Peleus,' I answered, 'but I can tell you all about your son Neoptolemus, for I brought him in my own ship from Scyros to join the Greeks. In our war councils before Troy, he was always first to speak, and his judgment was flawless. Only Nestor and I could surpass him. When it came to fighting on Troy's plain, he would never stay with the main body of troops but would dash far ahead, foremost of all in courage. He killed many men in battle—I can't name every single one he slew while fighting for the Greeks, but I'll mention how he killed that brave hero Eurypylus, son of Telephus, the handsomest man I ever saw except Memnon. Many other Ceteans fell around Eurypylus because of a woman's bribes. Moreover, when all the bravest Greeks went inside the horse Epeus had built, and it fell to me to decide when we should open our ambush or stay hidden, though all the other leaders and chief men among the Greeks were wiping their eyes and trembling in every limb, I never once saw him turn pale or brush a tear from his cheek. He kept urging me to break out from the horse, gripping his sword handle and bronze-tipped spear, breathing fury against the enemy. Yet when we had sacked Priam's city, he received his fair share of the prize money and boarded his ship (such is war's fortune) without a wound, neither from a thrown spear nor in close combat, for the rage of war is very unpredictable.'
When I had told him this, Achilles's ghost strode away across a meadow full of asphodel, rejoicing in what I'd said about his son's prowess.

The ghosts of other dead men stood near me, each telling his own sad story. But Ajax, son of Telamon, alone held back—still angry with me for winning our dispute over Achilles's armor. Thetis had offered it as a prize, and the Trojan prisoners and Athena were the judges. I wish I had never won in such a contest, for it cost Ajax's life—he who was greatest of all the Greeks after Peleus's son in both stature and prowess.

When I saw him, I tried to appease him, saying, 'Ajax, won't you forget and forgive even in death? Must the judgment about that cursed armor still anger you? It cost us Greeks dearly to lose such a tower of strength as you were. We mourned you as much as we mourned Achilles, son of Peleus himself. The blame lies only with Zeus's spite against the Greeks, for that's what made him plan your destruction. Come here, master your proud spirit, and hear what I have to tell you.'

He wouldn't answer but turned away to the underworld and the other ghosts. Nevertheless, I might have made him speak despite his anger, or I might have continued talking to him, except that there were still others among the dead I wanted to see.
Then I saw Minos, son of Zeus, with his golden scepter, sitting in judgment on the dead. The ghosts were gathered sitting and standing around him in Hades' spacious house, learning his verdicts.
After him I saw huge Orion in a meadow full of asphodel, driving the ghosts of wild beasts he had killed in the mountains, holding a great bronze club in his hands, unbreakable forever.

I saw Tityus, son of Earth, stretched across the plain and covering about nine acres. Two vultures on either side were digging their beaks into his liver, and he kept trying to beat them off with his hands but couldn't, for he had violated Zeus's lover Leto as she traveled through Panopeus on her way to Pytho.

I also saw Tantalus's dreadful fate. He stood in a lake that reached his chin, dying of thirst but never able to reach the water. Whenever the poor wretch bent down to drink, it dried up and vanished, leaving nothing but parched ground—withered by heaven's spite. Tall trees hung their fruit over his head—pears, pomegranates, apples, sweet figs, and juicy olives—but whenever the poor creature reached out to take some, the wind tossed the branches back up to the clouds.

I saw Sisyphus at his endless task, pushing his enormous stone with both hands. With hands and feet he struggled to roll it up the hill, but always, just before he could push it over to the other side, its weight overcame him, and the pitiless stone would thunder back down to the plain. Then he would start trying to push it uphill again, sweat pouring off him and steam rising from his body.

After him I saw mighty Heracles, but it was only his phantom, for he himself feasts eternally with the immortal gods and has lovely Hebe as his wife, daughter of Zeus and Hera. The ghosts were screaming around him like frightened birds flying in all directions. He looked black as night with his bare bow in his hands and an arrow on the string, glaring around as if always about to shoot. Around his chest was a wondrous golden belt decorated most marvelously with bears, wild boars, and lions with gleaming eyes. There was also war, battle, and death depicted on it. The craftsman who made that belt could never, no matter what he tried, make another like it. Heracles recognized me immediately and spoke sorrowfully: 'Poor Odysseus, noble son of Laertes, are you too living the same miserable kind of life I lived when I was above ground? I was Zeus's son, but I endured infinite suffering, for I became enslaved to someone far beneath me—a worthless man who set me all kinds of labors. He once sent me here to fetch the hell-hound, thinking he couldn't find anything harder for me than this. But I brought the hound out of Hades and delivered him, for Hermes and Athena helped me.'

With that, Heracles went back down into Hades' house, but I stayed where I was in case some other mighty dead might come to me. I would have seen still others who are gone—Theseus and Pirithous, glorious children of the gods—but so many thousands of ghosts gathered around me uttering such terrifying cries that I was struck with panic, fearing Persephone might send up from Hades' house the head of that awful monster, the Gorgon. At this I hurried back to my ship and ordered my men to board immediately and cast off the mooring ropes. So they embarked and took their places, and the ship went down the stream of the river Ocean. We had to row at first, but soon a fair wind sprang up.

chapters.title: Book XII — The Sirens, Scylla and Charybdis, the cattle of the sun
paragraphs: After we cleared the river Oceanus and reached the open sea, we sailed until we came to Aeaea, the island where dawn and sunrise occur just as they do everywhere else. We beached our ship on the sand and climbed out onto the shore, where we slept and waited for daybreak.

When rosy-fingered Dawn appeared, I sent some men to Circe's house to retrieve Elpenor's body. We gathered firewood from where the headland jutted into the sea, and after we had wept and mourned for him, we performed his funeral rites. Once his body and armor had been burned to ashes, we built a burial mound, placed a stone marker on it, and at the top we planted the oar he had used for rowing.

While we were busy with all this, Circe—who knew we had returned from Hades—dressed herself and came to us as quickly as she could. Her servants came with her, bringing bread, meat, and wine. She stood among us and said, "You have accomplished something bold by going down alive to the house of Hades. You will have died twice while others die only once. Now stay here for the rest of the day, eat your fill, and continue your voyage at dawn tomorrow. Meanwhile, I will tell Odysseus about your route and explain everything so you won't suffer any disasters by land or sea."

We agreed to do as she suggested and feasted all day until sunset. When the sun went down and darkness fell, the men lay down to sleep beside the ship's stern cables. Then Circe took me by the hand and had me sit apart from the others. She reclined beside me and asked about all our adventures.

"So far, so good," she said when I had finished my story. "Now pay attention to what I'm about to tell you—heaven itself will help you remember it. First, you'll come to the Sirens, who enchant everyone who approaches them. Anyone who carelessly draws too close and hears the Sirens singing will never see his wife and children welcome him home again, for the Sirens sit in a flowery meadow and bewitch him to death with the sweetness of their song. Around them lies a great heap of men's bones with flesh still rotting on them. So sail past these Sirens, and stop your men's ears with wax so none of them can hear. But if you want to listen yourself, have your men bind you upright to the mast's crossbeam, and they must tie the rope ends to the mast itself so you can enjoy listening. If you beg and plead with them to untie you, they must bind you even tighter.

"After your crew takes you past the Sirens, I cannot give you clear directions about which of two routes to take. I'll present both alternatives, and you must decide for yourself. On one side are towering rocks against which the deep blue waves crash with terrible fury—the blessed gods call these the Wandering Rocks. Not even birds can pass here, not even the gentle doves that bring ambrosia to Father Zeus. The sheer rock always destroys one of them, and Father Zeus must send another to replace it. No ship that has ever reached these rocks has escaped. The waves and fiery whirlwinds carry away wreckage and men's bodies. Only one vessel ever sailed through safely—the famous Argo returning from Aeetes' land, and she would have been dashed against those mighty rocks if Hera hadn't guided her past them for love of Jason.

"Of the two rocks, one reaches to heaven, its peak lost in dark clouds that never leave it, so the summit is never clear, not even in summer and early autumn. No man, even with twenty hands and twenty feet, could find a foothold and climb it, for it rises straight up, smooth as if polished. Halfway up is a large cave facing west toward the underworld. You must steer your ship past this way, but the cave is so high that even the strongest archer couldn't shoot an arrow into it. Inside, Scylla sits howling with a voice like a young puppy's, but she is actually a dreadful monster that no one—not even a god—could face without terror. She has twelve misshapen feet and six necks of enormous length. At the end of each neck is a hideous head with three rows of closely packed teeth that could crush anyone to death instantly. She sits deep in her shadowy cave, thrusting out her heads and scanning the rock all around, fishing for dolphins, sharks, or any larger sea creature she can catch from the thousands that swarm in these waters. No ship has ever passed her without losing men, for she shoots out all her heads at once and carries off a man in each mouth.

"The other rock lies lower, but they're so close together there's barely a bowshot between them. A large fig tree grows on it in full leaf, and beneath it lies Charybdis' sucking whirlpool. Three times each day she spits up the waters, and three times she sucks them down again. Make sure you're not there when she's sucking them down, for if you are, not even Poseidon could save you. You must hug Scylla's side and drive your ship past as fast as possible, because it's better to lose six men than your entire crew."
"Is there no way," I asked, "to escape Charybdis while also keeping Scylla from harming my men?"

"You daredevil," the goddess replied, "you're always looking for a fight with someone or something. You won't admit defeat even to the immortals. Scylla isn't mortal—she's savage, monstrous, fierce, cruel, and invincible. There's no help for it. Your best chance is to get past her as quickly as possible. If you linger near her rock putting on armor, she might strike again with her six heads and snatch up another half dozen of your men. Drive your ship past at full speed, and shout loudly to Crataiis, Scylla's mother—curse her—and she'll stop Scylla from attacking you a second time.

"Next you'll reach the island of Thrinacia, where you'll see many herds of cattle and flocks of sheep belonging to the sun god—seven herds of cattle and seven flocks of sheep, fifty animals in each group. They never breed or decrease in number, and they're tended by the goddesses Phaethusa and Lampetia, daughters of the sun god Helios and the nymph Neaera. After bearing and nursing them, their mother sent them to distant Thrinacia to live there and watch over their father's flocks and herds. If you leave these animals unharmed and focus only on reaching home, you may still reach Ithaca after great hardship. But if you harm them, I predict the destruction of both your ship and your companions. Even if you yourself escape, you'll return home late, in miserable condition, having lost all your men."

With that, she finished speaking, and golden-throned Dawn began to appear in the sky. She returned inland while I went aboard and told my men to untie the ship from its moorings. They immediately boarded, took their positions, and began striking the gray sea with their oars. Soon the great and clever goddess Circe sent us a favorable wind that blew steadily from behind, filling our sails nicely. We took care of the ship's rigging and let her sail as the wind and helmsman directed.

Then, deeply troubled, I spoke to my men: "My friends, it's not right that only one or two of us should know the prophecies Circe gave me. I'll tell you everything so that whether we live or die, we'll do so with full knowledge. First, she said we must avoid the Sirens, who sit singing beautifully in a flowery field. She said I alone could listen to them as long as no one else did. So tie me to the crossbeam halfway up the mast—bind me upright with bonds so tight I can't possibly break free, and fasten the rope ends to the mast itself. If I beg and plead with you to release me, tie me up even more securely."

I had barely finished explaining everything to the men when we reached the island of the two Sirens, carried by favorable winds. Suddenly the wind died completely—there wasn't a breath of air or a ripple on the water. The men furled the sails and stowed them, then took up their oars and churned the water white with foam. Meanwhile, I took a large wheel of wax and cut it into small pieces with my sword. I kneaded the wax in my strong hands until it became soft, which happened quickly between the kneading and the rays of the sun god. Then I plugged all my men's ears, and they bound me hand and foot to the mast as I stood upright on the crossbeam, then continued rowing. When we got within earshot of the land and the ship was moving at good speed, the Sirens spotted us approaching shore and began their song.

"Come here," they sang, "famous Odysseus, glory of the Greeks, and listen to our voices. No one has ever sailed past us without stopping to hear the enchanting sweetness of our song—and whoever listens goes on his way not only delighted but wiser, for we know all the suffering the gods inflicted on Greeks and Trojans at Troy, and we can tell you everything that will happen throughout the world."

They sang these words with such beautiful music that I longed to hear more. I signaled with frowning gestures for my men to untie me, but they rowed harder, and Eurylochus and Perimedes bound me with even stronger ropes until we had passed out of hearing range. Then my men removed the wax from their ears and untied me.

Immediately after passing the island, I saw a great wave with spray rising from it, and I heard loud roaring. The men were so frightened they dropped their oars, and the whole sea echoed with the rushing waters, but the ship stayed where it was because the men had stopped rowing. I went around encouraging each man not to lose heart.

"My friends," I said, "this isn't the first time we've faced danger, and we're in nothing like as bad a situation as when the Cyclops trapped us in his cave. Yet my courage and wise planning saved us then, and we'll live to remember this too. Now do as I say: trust in Zeus and row with all your might. Helmsman, these are your orders—pay attention, since you control the ship. Steer away from these boiling rapids and hug the rock, or the ship will slip away toward the other side before you know it, and you'll destroy us all."

They did as I commanded, but I said nothing about the terrible monster Scylla, knowing the men would stop rowing if I did and would huddle together in the hold instead. I disobeyed only one of Circe's strict instructions—I put on my armor. Then, gripping two strong spears, I took position at the ship's bow, expecting to first spot the rock monster who would harm my men so badly. But I couldn't see her anywhere, though I strained my eyes searching every part of that gloomy cliff.

We entered the strait in great fear, with Scylla on one side and dread Charybdis on the other, sucking down the salt water. When she vomited it up, it was like water boiling in a cauldron over a great fire, and the spray reached the tops of the rocks on both sides. When she began sucking again, we could see all the water inside whirling around, making a deafening sound as it crashed against the rocks. We could see the bottom of the whirlpool, black with sand and mud, and the men were terrified out of their wits. While we were distracted by this, expecting each moment to be our last, Scylla suddenly swooped down and snatched up my six best men. Looking back at both ship and crew, I saw their hands and feet high above me, flailing in the air as Scylla carried them off, and I heard them call out my name in one final, desperate cry. Like a fisherman sitting on a jutting rock with his rod, throwing bait into the water to fool small fish, then spearing them with his ox-horn-tipped spear and tossing them gasping onto land as he catches them one by one—just so did Scylla carry these struggling men to her rock and devour them at the mouth of her den while they screamed and reached out their hands to me in mortal agony. This was the most sickening sight I witnessed in all my voyages.

After we passed the Wandering Rocks with Scylla and terrible Charybdis, we reached the noble island of the sun god, where the fine cattle and sheep belonging to Helios lived. While still at sea in my ship, I could hear the cattle lowing as they came home to their pens and the sheep bleating. Then I remembered what the blind Theban prophet Tiresias had told me, and how carefully Circe had warned me to avoid the island of the blessed sun god. Deeply troubled, I said to my men, "Men, I know you're exhausted, but listen while I tell you Tiresias's prophecy and how carefully Circe warned me to avoid the island of the blessed sun god. She said our worst danger would be here. Therefore, steer the ship away from this island."

The men were dismayed, and Eurylochus immediately gave me an insolent answer: "Odysseus, you're heartless. You're very strong yourself and never get tired—you seem made of iron. Now, though your men are worn out from labor and lack of sleep, you won't let them land and cook themselves a good meal on this island, but order them to put back to sea and wander aimlessly through the watches of the swift night. Night brings the strongest, most destructive winds—how can we escape if one of those sudden squalls springs up from the southwest or west, which often wreck ships when the lord gods are hostile? Now let's obey the demands of night and prepare our dinner here by the ship. Tomorrow morning we'll board again and put out to sea."

So spoke Eurylochus, and the men approved his words. I saw that heaven meant to harm us and said, "You force me to give in, since you're many against one. But each of you must swear a solemn oath that if you encounter a herd of cattle or large flock of sheep, you won't be so mad as to kill a single animal, but will be satisfied with the food Circe gave us."

They all swore as I required, and when they completed their oath, we moored the ship in a harbor near a freshwater stream. The men went ashore and prepared their supper. After they had eaten and drunk their fill, they began talking about their poor comrades whom Scylla had snatched up and devoured. This made them weep, and they cried until they fell into deep sleep.

In the third watch of the night, when the stars had shifted position, Zeus raised a great gale that blew like a hurricane, covering both land and sea with thick clouds, and darkness burst from the heavens. When rosy-fingered Dawn appeared, we brought the ship to land and dragged her into a cave where sea nymphs hold their gatherings and dances. I called the men together for a meeting.

"Friends," I said, "we have food and drink on the ship, so let's be careful not to touch the cattle, or we'll suffer for it. These cattle and sheep belong to the mighty sun god, who sees and hears everything." Again they promised to obey.

For a whole month the wind blew steadily from the south, with no other wind except south and east. As long as grain and wine lasted, the men didn't touch the cattle when hungry. But when they had consumed everything on the ship, they were forced to roam farther, catching birds with hooks and lines and taking whatever they could find, for they were starving. One day I went inland to pray to heaven to show me some means of escape. When I had gone far enough to be away from all my men and found a place well sheltered from the wind, I washed my hands and prayed to all the Olympian gods until they sent me into sweet sleep.

Meanwhile, Eurylochus was giving bad advice to the men: "Listen to me, poor comrades. All deaths are terrible, but none is worse than starvation. Why shouldn't we drive in the best of these cattle and sacrifice them to the immortal gods? If we ever return to Ithaca, we can build a splendid temple to the sun god and fill it with every kind of offering. But if he's determined to sink our ship in revenge for these horned cattle, and the other gods agree with him, I'd rather drink salt water once and for all and be done with it than slowly starve to death on such a deserted island."

So spoke Eurylochus, and the men agreed. The beautiful, fine cattle were grazing not far from the ship. The men drove in the best ones and stood around them praying, using young oak shoots instead of barley meal, since no barley remained. After praying, they killed the cattle and prepared the carcasses. They cut out the thigh bones, wrapped them in two layers of fat, and placed pieces of raw meat on top. They had no wine for drink offerings during the sacrifice, so they kept sprinkling water while the inner organs grilled. When the thigh bones were burned and they had tasted the inner meat, they cut up the rest and put the pieces on spits.

By this time my deep sleep had left me, and I headed back to the ship and seashore. As I approached, I began to smell hot roasted meat and groaned out a prayer to the immortal gods: "Father Zeus, and all you other gods who live in eternal bliss, you've played a cruel trick on me by sending me that sleep. See what terrible work my men have done in my absence!"

Meanwhile, Lampetia went straight to the sun god and told him we had been killing his cattle. He flew into a great rage and said to the immortals: "Father Zeus, and all you other gods who live in eternal bliss, I must have vengeance on Odysseus's crew. They've had the audacity to kill my cattle, which were the one thing I loved to look upon, whether I was going up to heaven or coming back down. If they don't pay me proper compensation for my cattle, I'll go down to Hades and shine there among the dead."
"Sun," said Zeus, "continue shining on us gods and on mankind over the fertile earth. I'll shatter their ship into little pieces with a white lightning bolt as soon as they put out to sea."
I learned all this from Calypso, who said she had heard it from Hermes.

As soon as I reached my ship and the seashore, I scolded each man individually, but we could see no way out of it—the cattle were already dead. Indeed, the gods immediately began showing signs and portents among us: the cattle hides crawled about, the joints on the spits began to low like living cows, and the meat, whether cooked or raw, kept making noises just like cattle.

For six days my men kept driving in the finest cattle and feasting on them. But when Zeus had added a seventh day, the fury of the gale subsided. We immediately boarded, raised our mast, spread sail, and put out to sea. As soon as we were well away from the island with nothing visible but sky and sea, Zeus raised a black cloud over our ship, and the sea grew dark beneath it. We didn't travel much farther before we were caught by a terrific squall from the west that snapped the mast's forestays so it fell backward, while all the ship's rigging tumbled into the vessel's bottom. The mast struck the helmsman's head at the ship's stern, crushing his skull completely, and he fell overboard as if diving, with no life left in him.

Then Zeus let loose his thunderbolts, and the ship spun around and filled with fire and sulfur as lightning struck it. All the men fell into the sea, carried about in the water around the ship like sea gulls, but the god quickly deprived them of any chance of reaching home again.

I clung to the ship until the sea knocked her sides away from her keel, which drifted by itself, and struck the mast free in the direction of the keel. But a strong ox-hide backstay was still attached to it, and with this I lashed the mast and keel together. Getting astride them, I was carried wherever the winds chose to take me.

The western gale had now spent its force, and the wind shifted to the south again, which frightened me because I might be carried back to terrible Charybdis. This is exactly what happened—I was borne along by the waves all night, and by sunrise had reached Scylla's rock and the whirlpool. Charybdis was then sucking down the salt water, but I was lifted up toward the fig tree, which I grabbed and clung to like a bat. I couldn't plant my feet anywhere to stand securely because the roots were far below and the branches that overshadowed the entire pool were too high, too massive, and too far apart to reach. So I hung on patiently, waiting for the pool to discharge my mast and raft again—and it seemed like forever. A juror is no more eager to get home to dinner after being detained in court by troublesome cases than I was to see my raft beginning to work its way out of the whirlpool again. At last I let go with hands and feet and fell heavily into the sea, close to my raft. I climbed onto it and began rowing with my hands. As for Scylla, the father of gods and men prevented her from seeing me again—otherwise I would certainly have been lost.

From there I drifted for nine days until on the tenth night the gods washed me ashore on Ogygia, where the great and powerful goddess Calypso lives. She took me in and treated me kindly, but I need say no more about this since I told you and your noble wife all about it yesterday, and I hate repeating the same story over and over.

chapters.title: Book XIII — Odysseus leaves Scheria and returns to Ithaca
paragraphs: He finished speaking, and everyone fell silent throughout the covered hall, spellbound by the charm of his story, until Alcinous finally spoke up.

"Odysseus," he said, "now that you've reached my house, I'm confident you'll get home without any more trouble, no matter how much you've suffered before. But to the rest of you who come here night after night to drink my finest wine and listen to my bard, I want to say this: Our guest has already packed up the clothes, wrought gold, and other treasures you've brought as gifts for him. Let's now give him even more—each of us should contribute a large tripod and cauldron. We'll reimburse ourselves through a general tax, since private individuals can't be expected to bear the cost of such generous presents alone."

Everyone agreed with this proposal, and then they all went home to bed. When rosy-fingered Dawn appeared, they hurried down to the ship carrying their cauldrons. Alcinous came aboard and made sure everything was securely stowed beneath the ship's benches so nothing could break loose and injure the rowers. Then they went to Alcinous's house for dinner, where he sacrificed a bull in honor of Zeus, lord of all. They grilled the meat and enjoyed an excellent feast, after which the inspired bard Demodocus, who was everyone's favorite, sang for them. But Odysseus kept turning his eyes toward the sun, as if trying to make it set faster, for he was eager to be on his way. Like a man who has spent all day plowing a field with his oxen and thinks constantly of his supper, glad when night comes so he can go eat it—for his legs can barely carry him—just so did Odysseus rejoice when the sun went down. He immediately addressed the Phaeacians, speaking particularly to King Alcinous:

"My lord, and all of you, farewell. Pour your libations and send me on my way with joy, for you've fulfilled my heart's desire by giving me safe passage and these generous gifts. May the gods grant that I put them to good use. May I find my noble wife living peacefully among friends, and may you who remain here bring happiness to your own wives and children. May heaven grant you every blessing, and may no evil come to your people."

Everyone approved his words and agreed he should have his escort since he had spoken so reasonably. Alcinous then said to his servant, "Pontonous, mix the wine and serve it to everyone, so we can pray to father Zeus and send our guest safely on his way."

Pontonous mixed the wine and served it to each person in turn. The others poured their drink offerings to the blessed gods from where they sat, but Odysseus rose and placed his cup in Queen Arete's hands.

"Farewell, queen," he said, "from now and forever, until old age and death—mankind's common fate—claim you. I take my leave now. Be happy in this house with your children, your people, and King Alcinous."

With these words he crossed the threshold, and Alcinous sent a man to escort him to his ship at the seashore. Arete also sent some maidservants with him—one carrying a clean shirt and cloak, another his strongbox, and a third with grain and wine. When they reached the water's edge, the crew took these items and loaded them aboard along with all the food and drink. For Odysseus they spread a rug and linen sheet on the stern deck so he could sleep comfortably. Then he too came aboard and lay down without a word, while the crew took their positions and cast off the hawser from the mooring stone. As soon as they began rowing out to sea, Odysseus fell into a deep, sweet, almost deathlike sleep.

The ship bounded forward like a four-horse chariot racing across the plain when the horses feel the whip. Her prow rose and fell like a stallion's neck, and a great wave of dark blue water churned in her wake. She held steadily to her course, and even a falcon—swiftest of all birds—couldn't have kept pace with her. So she cut through the water, carrying a man as cunning as the gods themselves, who now slept peacefully, forgetting all he had suffered both on the battlefield and on the restless sea.

When the bright star that heralds dawn's approach began to show, the ship drew near to land. Now there is a harbor in Ithaca belonging to the old sea-god Phorcys, lying between two headlands that jut into the sea and shelter the harbor. These protect it from the storms and rough seas that rage outside, so that once inside, a ship can lie safely without even needing to be moored. At the head of this harbor stands a large olive tree, and nearby is a beautiful arching cave sacred to the nymphs called Naiads. Inside are stone mixing bowls and wine jars, and bees make their hives there. There are also great stone looms where the nymphs weave their sea-purple robes—a wondrous sight to see—and fresh water always flows within. The cave has two entrances: one facing north, by which mortals can enter, while the other faces south and is more mysterious—mortals cannot possibly enter by it, as it's the path used by the gods.

Into this harbor they steered their ship, for they knew the place well. She had so much momentum that she ran halfway up onto the shore. Once they had landed, the first thing they did was lift Odysseus, still wrapped in his rug and linen sheet, out of the ship and lay him on the sand, still fast asleep. Then they unloaded the presents that Athena had persuaded the Phaeacians to give him for his homeward journey. They placed all these together by the olive tree's roots, away from the road, in case some passerby might steal them before Odysseus woke up. Then they set off for home.

But Poseidon hadn't forgotten the threats he had made against Odysseus, so he consulted with Zeus. "Father Zeus," he said, "I'll no longer be respected among the gods if mortals like the Phaeacians—who are my own descendants—show me so little regard. I said I would let Odysseus reach home after he had suffered enough. I didn't say he should never get home at all, for I knew you had already nodded your agreement and promised he would. But now they've brought him home in a ship while he slept and landed him in Ithaca after loading him with more magnificent presents of bronze, gold, and fine clothing than he would ever have brought back from Troy, even if he'd gotten his fair share of the spoils and returned home without mishap."

Zeus answered, "What are you talking about, Lord of Earthquakes? The gods certainly don't lack respect for you. It would be outrageous for them to insult one so ancient and honored as you. As for mortals, if any of them treats you disrespectfully or acts insolently, you're always free to deal with them as you see fit. Do whatever you please."

"I would have acted at once," replied Poseidon, "if I weren't concerned about displeasing you. Now, however, I'd like to wreck the Phaeacian ship as it returns from its escort mission. This will stop them from escorting people in the future. I'd also like to bury their city under a huge mountain."

"My good friend," Zeus answered, "here's what I'd recommend: at the very moment when people from the city are watching the ship return, turn it into a rock near the shore that looks like a ship. This will amaze everyone, and then you can bury their city under the mountain."

When earth-encircling Poseidon heard this, he went to Scheria where the Phaeacians live and waited until the ship, which was making good speed, had gotten close to shore. Then he approached it, turned it to stone, and drove it down with his palm, rooting it firmly in the seabed. After this, he departed.

The Phaeacians began talking among themselves, and one would turn to his neighbor, saying, "Good heavens, who could have rooted our ship in the sea just as she was entering port? We could see all of her just a moment ago."

This was how they spoke, but they knew nothing about what had really happened. Then Alcinous said, "I remember now the old prophecy my father told me. He said Poseidon would be angry with us for safely escorting everyone across the sea, and would one day wreck a Phaeacian ship returning from an escort mission and bury our city under a high mountain. That's what my old father used to say, and now it's all coming true. So let's all do as I suggest: first, we must stop giving escorts to people who come here, and second, let's sacrifice twelve choice bulls to Poseidon so he might have mercy on us and not bury our city under that high mountain." When the people heard this, they were afraid and prepared the bulls.

So the chiefs and rulers of the Phaeacians prayed to King Poseidon, standing around his altar. At the same time, Odysseus woke up once more on his native soil. He had been away so long that he didn't recognize it. Moreover, Zeus's daughter Athena had made it a foggy day so people wouldn't know of his arrival, and so she could tell him everything without his wife, fellow citizens, or friends recognizing him until he had taken revenge on the wicked suitors. Everything looked completely different to him—the long straight paths, the harbors, the cliffs, and the noble trees all appeared changed as he got up and looked upon his homeland. He struck his thighs with his palms and cried out in despair.

"Alas," he exclaimed, "what kind of people have I fallen among? Are they savage and uncivilized, or hospitable and kind? Where shall I put all this treasure, and which way should I go? I wish I had stayed with the Phaeacians, or I could have gone to some other great chief who would have treated me well and given me safe passage. As it is, I don't know where to put my treasure, and I can't leave it here for fear someone else might take it. Truly, the chiefs and rulers of the Phaeacians haven't dealt fairly with me—they've left me in the wrong country! They said they would take me back to Ithaca, but they haven't done so. May Zeus, protector of suppliants, punish them, for he watches over everyone and punishes wrongdoers. Still, I suppose I should count my goods and see if the crew took any of them."

He counted his fine bronze vessels and cauldrons, his gold and all his clothes, but nothing was missing. Still, he kept grieving about not being in his own country and wandered up and down along the shore of the loud-roaring sea, lamenting his harsh fate. Then Athena approached him, disguised as a young shepherd with a delicate, princely appearance. She wore a fine cloak folded double about her shoulders, had sandals on her lovely feet, and carried a spear in her hand. Odysseus was glad when he saw her and went straight to her.

"My friend," he said, "you're the first person I've met in this country. I greet you and ask you to be kind to me. Protect both these goods of mine and me as well, for I clasp your knees and pray to you as if you were a god. Tell me truly—what land and country is this? Who lives here? Am I on an island, or is this the coastline of some continent?"

Athena answered, "Stranger, you must be very naive, or you must come from somewhere far away, not to know what country this is. It's a very famous place, and everyone knows it, both east and west. It's rugged and not good for driving horses, but it's not a bad island for what it is. It grows plenty of grain and wine, for it gets both rain and dew. It breeds cattle and goats too. All kinds of trees grow here, and there are springs where the water never runs dry. So, stranger, the name of Ithaca is known even as far as Troy, which I understand is a long way from this Greek land."
Odysseus was delighted to find himself, as Athena told him, in his own country, and he began to reply. But he didn't tell the truth, instead making up a lying story with his instinctive cunning.

"I heard of Ithaca," he said, "when I was in Crete across the sea, and now it seems I've reached it with all these treasures. I left just as much behind for my children, but I'm fleeing because I killed Orsilochus, son of Idomeneus, the fastest runner in Crete. I killed him because he tried to rob me of the spoils I'd won from Troy through so much trouble and danger, both on the battlefield and on the restless sea. He said I hadn't served his father loyally at Troy as a vassal, but had set myself up as an independent ruler. So I ambushed him with one of my followers by the roadside and speared him as he was coming into town from the countryside. It was a very dark night and nobody saw us, so no one knew I had killed him. As soon as I'd done it, I went to a ship and begged the owners, who were Phoenicians, to take me aboard and set me down in Pylos or Elis where the Epeans rule, offering them spoils that satisfied them. They meant no harm, but the wind drove them off course, and we sailed until we arrived here by night. We could barely get into the harbor, and none of us mentioned supper though we badly wanted it. We all just went ashore and lay down as we were. I was exhausted and fell asleep immediately, so they took my goods from the ship and placed them beside me where I was lying on the sand. Then they sailed away to Sidonia, leaving me here in great distress."

Such was his story, but Athena smiled and stroked him with her hand. Then she took the form of a woman—beautiful, tall, and wise. "He would have to be quite a shifty, lying fellow," she said, "who could surpass you in all kinds of trickery, even if he were a god competing against you. You daredevil, full of schemes, never tiring of deception—can't you drop your tricks and instinctive lies, even now that you're back in your own country? But let's say no more about this, since we can both deceive when the occasion calls for it. You're the most accomplished counselor and speaker among all mortals, while I have no equal among the gods for diplomacy and cunning. Didn't you recognize Zeus's daughter Athena—me, who has always been with you, who watched over you through all your troubles, and who made the Phaeacians like you so much? And now I've come here again to discuss plans with you and help you hide the treasure I made the Phaeacians give you. I want to tell you about the troubles awaiting you in your own house. You'll have to face them, but don't tell anyone—man or woman—that you've returned home. Bear everything silently and endure every man's insolence without a word."

Odysseus answered, "A man may know a great deal, goddess, but you're constantly changing your appearance, so when he meets you it's hard to know whether it's really you or not. This much I know for certain: you were very kind to me as long as we Greeks were fighting before Troy. But from the day we boarded our ships after sacking Priam's city and heaven scattered us—from that day, Athena, I saw no more of you and can't remember you ever coming to my ship to help me in trouble. I had to wander on, sick and sorry, until the gods delivered me from evil and I reached the Phaeacians' city, where you encouraged me and led me into town. Now I beg you in your father's name, tell me the truth, for I don't believe I'm really back in Ithaca. I must be in some other country, and you're mocking and deceiving me with everything you've said. Tell me truly—have I really returned to my own land?"

"You're always thinking something like that," Athena replied, "and that's why I can't abandon you in your troubles—you're so persuasive, shrewd, and clever. Anyone else returning from such a long voyage would immediately rush home to see his wife and children, but you don't seem to care about asking after them or hearing news about them until you've tested your wife, who stays home constantly grieving for you, having no peace night or day for the tears she sheds on your account. As for my not coming near you, I was never worried about you, for I was certain you'd get home safely, though you'd lose all your men. I didn't want to quarrel with my uncle Poseidon, who never forgave you for blinding his son. But now I'll show you Ithaca's landscape, and then perhaps you'll believe me. This is the harbor of old Phorcys the sea-god, and here's the olive tree that grows at its head. Near it is the cave sacred to the Naiads, and here's the arching cavern where you've offered many acceptable sacrifices to the nymphs, and this is wooded Mount Neritum."

As she spoke, the goddess dispersed the mist and the land appeared clearly. Then Odysseus rejoiced at finding himself in his own land again and kissed the fertile soil. He raised his hands and prayed to the nymphs, saying, "Naiad nymphs, daughters of Zeus, I was sure I would never see you again, so now I greet you with all loving salutations, and I'll bring you offerings as in the old days, if Zeus's formidable daughter grants me life and lets my son reach manhood."
"Take heart and don't worry about that," Athena replied. "Let's focus on storing your things safely in the cave right away. Let's figure out how to manage this best."

With that, she went down into the cave to look for the safest hiding places, while Odysseus brought up all the treasure of gold, bronze, and fine clothing the Phaeacians had given him. They stored everything carefully, and Athena placed a stone against the cave's entrance. Then the two sat down by the great olive tree's roots and planned how to destroy the wicked suitors.

"Odysseus," Athena said, "noble son of Laertes, think about how you can deal with these shameless men who have been ruling your house for three years, courting your wife and offering her wedding gifts, while she does nothing but mourn your absence, giving each of them hope and sending encouraging messages to all of them, but meaning the opposite of everything she says."

Odysseus answered, "Truly, goddess, it seems I would have met the same terrible end in my own house as Agamemnon did, if you hadn't given me this timely information. Advise me how I can best get my revenge. Stand by my side and fill my heart with courage, as you did on the day when we stripped Troy of her fair crown. Help me now as you did then, and I'll fight three hundred men, if you, goddess, will be with me."

"Trust me for that," she said. "I won't lose sight of you once we begin, and I imagine some of those who are devouring your wealth will then splatter the floor with their blood and brains. I'll start by disguising you so no human will recognize you. I'll cover your body with wrinkles, make you lose all your golden hair, clothe you in a garment that will fill everyone who sees it with disgust, dim your bright eyes, and make you a repulsive sight to the suitors, your wife, and the son you left behind. Then go immediately to the swineherd who tends your pigs—he has always been loyal to you and devoted to Penelope and your son. You'll find him feeding his pigs near the rock called Raven by the spring Arethusa, where they're fattening on acorns and spring water as is their way. Stay with him and find out how things stand, while I go to Sparta to see your son, who is with Menelaus in Lacedaemon, where he's gone to try to learn whether you're still alive."
"But why," Odysseus said, "didn't you tell him, since you knew everything? Did you want him too to go sailing around facing all kinds of hardships while others devour his inheritance?"

Athena answered, "Don't worry about him. I sent him so he'd gain a good reputation for having made the journey. He's in no danger at all, but is staying quite comfortably with Menelaus, surrounded by every kind of abundance. The suitors have put out to sea and are waiting to ambush him, planning to kill him before he can get home. But I don't think they'll succeed—rather, some of those now devouring your estate will find their graves first."

As she spoke, Athena touched him with her wand and covered him with wrinkles, took away all his golden hair, and withered the flesh all over his body. She dimmed his eyes, which were naturally very fine, changed his clothes and threw a tattered old cloak around him, along with a tunic that was torn, filthy, and stained with smoke. She also gave him an undressed deerskin as an outer garment and provided him with a staff and a torn wallet with a twisted strap to sling over his shoulder.
When the two had made their plans, they parted, and the goddess went straight to Lacedaemon to fetch Telemachus.

chapters.title: Book XIV — Odysseus in the hut with Eumaeus
paragraphs: Odysseus now left the harbor and took the rough track up through the wooded countryside and over the mountain crest until he reached the place where Athena had told him he would find the swineherd, who was his most reliable servant. He found him sitting in front of his hut, which was near the pig yards he had built on a site that could be seen from far away. He had made them spacious and impressive to look at, with plenty of room for the pigs to roam around them. He had built them while his master was away, using stones he had gathered from the ground without telling Penelope or Laertes, and he had topped them with thorn bush fencing. Outside the yard he had built a strong fence of split oak posts set close together, while inside he had constructed twelve pens next to each other for the sows to lie in. There were fifty pigs wallowing in each pen, all breeding sows, but the boars slept outside and were much fewer in number because the suitors kept eating them, forcing the swineherd to continuously send them his best animals. There were three hundred and sixty boar pigs, and the herdsman's four hounds, fierce as wolves, always slept with them. The swineherd was at that moment cutting out a pair of sandals from good thick ox hide. Three of his men were out herding the pigs in various places, and he had sent the fourth to town with a boar he had been forced to send the suitors so they could sacrifice it and feast on the meat.

When the hounds saw Odysseus, they set up furious barking and rushed at him, but Odysseus was clever enough to sit down and drop the stick he held in his hand. Still, he would have been torn apart by them in his own homestead if the swineherd hadn't dropped his ox hide, rushed at full speed through the yard gate, and driven the dogs off by shouting and throwing stones at them. Then he said to Odysseus, "Old man, the dogs nearly made short work of you, and then you would have gotten me into trouble. The gods have given me quite enough worries without that, since I've lost the best of masters and am in constant grief over him. I have to tend swine for other people to eat, while he, if he still lives to see daylight, is starving in some distant land. But come inside, and when you've had your fill of bread and wine, tell me where you come from and all about your troubles."

With that, the swineherd led the way into the hut and told him to sit down. He spread a good thick bed of rushes on the floor, and on top of this he threw the shaggy chamois skin—a great thick one—that he used to sleep on at night. Odysseus was pleased at being welcomed so warmly and said, "May Zeus, sir, and the rest of the gods grant you your heart's desire in return for the kind way you've received me."

To this you answered, swineherd Eumaeus, "Stranger, even if a poorer man than you came here, it wouldn't be right for me to insult him, for all strangers and beggars come from Zeus. You must take what you can get and be thankful, because servants live in fear when they have young lords for masters—and this is my misfortune now, since heaven has prevented the return of him who would have always been good to me and given me something of my own: a house, a piece of land, a good-looking wife, and everything else that a generous master gives a servant who has worked hard for him, and whose labor the gods have blessed as they have mine in the position I hold. If my master had grown old here, he would have done great things for me, but he is gone, and I wish Helen's whole family were utterly destroyed, for she has been the death of many a good man. It was this matter that took my master to Troy, the land of noble horses, to fight the Trojans for King Agamemnon's cause."

As he spoke, he tied his belt around him and went to the pens where the young suckling pigs were kept. He picked out two, brought them back, and sacrificed them. He singed them, cut them up, and put them on spits. When the meat was cooked, he brought it all in and set it before Odysseus, hot and still on the spit, and Odysseus sprinkled it with white barley meal. The swineherd then mixed wine in a bowl of ivy wood, and taking a seat across from Odysseus told him to begin eating.

"Dig in, stranger," he said, "to a dish of servant's pork. The fat pigs have to go to the suitors, who eat them up without shame or restraint, but the blessed gods don't love such shameful behavior and respect those who do what is lawful and right. Even fierce raiders who go plundering other people's lands, and Zeus gives them their spoils—even they, when they've filled their ships and returned home, live with troubled consciences and look fearfully for judgment. But some god seems to have told these people that Odysseus is dead and gone. They won't go back to their own homes and make their marriage proposals in the usual way, but waste his estate by force, without fear or limit. Not a single day or night passes but they sacrifice not just one victim but two, and they freely help themselves to his wine, for he was extremely rich. No other great man either in Ithaca or on the mainland is as wealthy as he was—he had as much as twenty men put together. I'll tell you what he owned. There are twelve herds of cattle on the mainland and as many flocks of sheep, plus twelve droves of pigs, while his own men and hired foreigners tend twelve widely scattered herds of goats. Here in Ithaca he runs eleven large flocks of goats on the far end of the island, and they're in the charge of excellent goatherds. Each one of these sends the suitors the best goat in the flock every day. As for myself, I'm in charge of the pigs you see here, and I have to keep picking out the best I have and sending them to the suitors."

This was his story, but Odysseus went on eating and drinking hungrily without a word, brooding over his revenge. When he had eaten enough and was satisfied, the swineherd took the bowl he usually drank from, filled it with wine, and gave it to Odysseus, who was pleased and said as he took it in his hands, "My friend, who was this master of yours who bought you and paid for you, so rich and powerful as you tell me? You say he died in King Agamemnon's cause—tell me who he was, in case I may have met such a person. Zeus and the other gods know, but I may be able to give you news of him, for I have traveled much."

Eumaeus answered, "Old man, no traveler who comes here with news will get Odysseus' wife and son to believe his story. Nevertheless, tramps looking for lodging keep coming with their mouths full of lies and not a word of truth. Everyone who finds his way to Ithaca goes to my mistress and tells her falsehoods, and she takes them in, treats them well, and asks them all sorts of questions, crying all the time as women do when they've lost their husbands. And you too, old man, would doubtless make up a very pretty story for a shirt and cloak. But the wolves and birds of prey have long since torn Odysseus to pieces, or the fish of the sea have eaten him, and his bones are lying buried deep in sand on some foreign shore. He is dead and gone, and it's a bad business for all his friends—especially for me. Wherever I go, I'll never find so good a master, not even if I were to return home to my mother and father where I was born and raised. I don't care so much about my parents now, though I'd dearly love to see them again in my own country. It's the loss of Odysseus that grieves me most. I can't speak of him without reverence even though he's no longer here, for he was very fond of me and took such care of me that wherever he may be, I'll always honor his memory."

"My friend," replied Odysseus, "you are very certain and very skeptical about your master's homecoming, but I will not merely say but will swear that he is coming. Don't give me anything for my news until he has actually returned—you may then give me a shirt and cloak of good quality if you will. I'm in great need, but I won't take anything at all until then, for I hate a man, as much as I hate the fires of hell, who lets his poverty tempt him into lying. I swear by King Zeus, by the laws of hospitality, and by that hearth of Odysseus to which I have now come, that everything will surely happen as I have said.
