Odysseus will return in this very year—with the end of this moon and the beginning of the next, he will be here to take vengeance on all those who are mistreating his wife and son."

To this you answered, swineherd Eumaeus, "Old man, you will neither get paid for bringing good news, nor will Odysseus ever come home. Drink your wine in peace and let us talk about something else. Don't keep reminding me of all this—it always pains me when anyone speaks about my honored master. As for your oath, we'll let it alone, but I only wish he may come, as do Penelope, his old father Laertes, and his son Telemachus. I'm terribly unhappy about this boy of his too. He was growing fast into manhood and promised to be no worse a man, in face and figure, than his father, but someone, either god or man, has been unsettling his mind, so he has gone off to Pylos to try to get news of his father, and the suitors are lying in wait for him as he returns home, hoping to leave the house of Arceisius without a name in Ithaca. But let's say no more about him and leave him to be taken or else to escape if the son of Saturn holds his hand over him for protection. And now, old man, tell me your own story. Tell me also, for I want to know, who you are and where you come from. Tell me about your town and parents, what kind of ship you came in, how your crew brought you to Ithaca, and what country they claimed to come from—for you cannot have come by land."

And Odysseus answered, "I will tell you all about it. If there were meat and wine enough, and we could stay here in the hut with nothing to do but eat and drink while the others go to their work, I could easily talk on for a whole twelve months without ever finishing the story of the sorrows that heaven has been pleased to visit upon me.

"I am by birth a Cretan. My father was a well-to-do man who had many sons born in marriage, whereas I was the son of a slave woman he had bought as a concubine. Nevertheless, my father Castor, son of Hylax—whose lineage I claim and who was held in the highest honor among the Cretans for his wealth, prosperity, and the valor of his sons—put me on the same level as my brothers who had been born in wedlock. When death took him to the house of Hades, his sons divided his estate and cast lots for their shares, but to me they gave a holding and little else. Nevertheless, my valor enabled me to marry into a rich family, for I was not given to boasting or shirking on the battlefield. It's all over now, but if you look at the straw you can see what the grain was like, for I have had trouble enough and to spare. Mars and Athena made me mighty in war. When I had picked my men to surprise the enemy with an ambush, I never gave death so much as a thought but was the first to leap forward and spear all whom I could overtake. Such was I in battle, but I didn't care about farm work or the frugal home life of those who would raise children. My delight was in ships, fighting, javelins, and arrows—things that most men shudder to think of. But one man likes one thing and another likes another, and this was what I was most naturally inclined to. Before the Greeks went to Troy, nine times I was in command of men and ships on foreign service, and I accumulated much wealth. I had my pick of the spoils first, and much more was allotted to me later on.

"My house grew rapidly and I became a great man among the Cretans, but when Zeus planned that terrible expedition in which so many died, the people required me and Idomeneus to lead their ships to Troy, and there was no way out of it, for they insisted on our doing so. There we fought for nine whole years, but in the tenth we sacked Priam's city and sailed home again as heaven scattered us. Then Zeus devised evil against me. I spent only one month happily with my children, wife, and property, and then I conceived the idea of making a descent on Egypt, so I fitted out a fine fleet and manned it. I had nine ships, and the people flocked to fill them. For six days my men and I feasted, and I provided them many victims both for sacrifice to the gods and for themselves, but on the seventh day we went on board and set sail from Crete with a fair north wind behind us, sailing as smoothly as if we were going down a river. Nothing went wrong with any of our ships, and we had no sickness on board, but sat where we were and let the ships go as the wind and steersmen took them. On the fifth day we reached the Nile River. There I stationed my ships in the river, ordering my men to stay by them and keep guard over them while I sent out scouts to reconnoiter from every vantage point.

"But the men disobeyed my orders, followed their own devices, and ravaged the land of the Egyptians, killing the men and taking their wives and children captive. The alarm was soon carried to the city, and when they heard the war cry, the people came out at daybreak until the plain was filled with horsemen and foot soldiers and the gleam of armor. Then Zeus spread panic among my men, and they would no longer face the enemy, for they found themselves surrounded. The Egyptians killed many of us and took the rest alive to do forced labor for them. Zeus, however, put it in my mind to do this—and I wish I had died then and there in Egypt instead, for there was much sorrow in store for me—I took off my helmet and shield and dropped my spear from my hand, then I went straight up to the king's chariot, clasped his knees and kissed them. He spared my life, told me to get into his chariot, and took me weeping to his own home. Many came at me with their ash spears and tried to kill me in their fury, but the king protected me, for he feared the wrath of Zeus the protector of strangers, who punishes those who do evil.

"I stayed there for seven years and accumulated much money among the Egyptians, for they all gave me something. But when it was going on for eight years, there came a certain Phoenician, a cunning rascal who had already committed all sorts of villainy, and this man talked me into going with him to Phoenicia, where his house and possessions lay. I stayed there for a whole twelve months, but at the end of that time when months and days had gone by until the same season had come round again, he put me on board a ship bound for Libya, pretending that I was to take cargo along with him to that place, but really intending to sell me as a slave and take the money I would bring. I suspected his intention but went on board with him, for I could not help it.

"The ship ran before a fresh north wind until we had reached the sea that lies between Crete and Libya. There, however, Zeus planned their destruction, for as soon as we were well out from Crete and could see nothing but sea and sky, he raised a black cloud over our ship and the sea grew dark beneath it. Then Zeus let fly with his thunderbolts and the ship spun round and round and was filled with fire and brimstone as the lightning struck it. The men all fell into the sea and were carried about in the water around the ship, looking like so many seagulls, but the god soon deprived them of all chance of getting home again. I was dismayed, but Zeus sent the ship's mast within my reach, which saved my life, for I clung to it and drifted before the fury of the gale. For nine days I drifted, but in the darkness of the tenth night a great wave bore me onto the Thesprotian coast. There Pheidon, king of the Thesprotians, entertained me hospitably without charging me anything at all—for his son found me when I was nearly dead with cold and fatigue, lifted me by the hand, took me to his father's house, and gave me clothes to wear.

"There it was that I heard news of Odysseus, for the king told me he had entertained him and shown him much hospitality while he was on his homeward journey. He showed me also the treasure of gold and wrought iron that Odysseus had gathered. There was enough to keep his family for ten generations, so much had he left in the house of King Pheidon. But the king said Odysseus had gone to Dodona so he might learn Zeus's will from the god's high oak tree and know whether after so long an absence he should return to Ithaca openly or in secret. Moreover, the king swore in my presence, making drink offerings in his own house as he did so, that the ship was by the water's side and the crew found that would take him to his own country. He sent me off, however, before Odysseus returned, for there happened to be a Thesprotian ship sailing for the wheat-growing island of Dulichium, and he told those in charge of her to be sure to take me safely to King Acastus.

"These men hatched a plot against me that would have reduced me to the depths of misery, for when the ship had gotten some way out from land, they decided to sell me as a slave. They stripped me of the shirt and cloak I was wearing and gave me instead the tattered old rags you now see me in. Then, toward nightfall, they reached the cultivated lands of Ithaca, and there they bound me with a strong rope fast in the ship while they went ashore to get supper by the seaside. But the gods soon undid my bonds for me, and having drawn my rags over my head, I slid down the rudder into the sea, where I struck out and swam until I was well clear of them and came ashore near a thick wood in which I lay hidden. They were very angry at my having escaped and went searching for me, until at last they thought it was no further use and went back to their ship. The gods, having hidden me so easily, then took me to a good man's door—for it seems I am not to die yet."

To this you answered, swineherd Eumaeus, "Poor unhappy stranger, I have found the story of your misfortunes extremely interesting, but that part about Odysseus is not right, and you will never get me to believe it. Why should a man like you go about telling lies in this way? I know all about the return of my master. The gods, one and all of them, hate him, or they would have taken him before Troy or let him die with friends around him when his fighting days were done—for then the Greeks would have built a mound over his ashes and his son would have inherited his renown, but now the storm winds have spirited him away we know not where.

"As for me, I live out of the way here with the pigs and never go to town unless Penelope sends for me when some news arrives about Odysseus. Then they all sit around and ask questions, both those who grieve over the king's absence and those who rejoice at it because they can eat up his property without paying for it. For my own part, I have never cared about asking anyone else since the time I was taken in by an Aetolian who had killed a man and traveled a long way until at last he reached my station, and I was very kind to him. He said he had seen Odysseus with Idomeneus among the Cretans, refitting his ships which had been damaged in a gale. He said Odysseus would return in the following summer or autumn with his men, bringing back much wealth. And now you, you unfortunate old man, since fate has brought you to my door, do not try to flatter me in this way with vain hopes. It is not for any such reason that I shall treat you kindly, but only out of respect for Zeus the god of hospitality, as I fear him and pity you."

Odysseus answered, "I see that you are skeptical and will not believe anything about your master's homecoming. Nevertheless, I will not merely say but will swear that he is coming. Do not give me anything for my news until he has actually come—you may then give me a cloak and shirt of good quality if you will. I am in great need, but I will not take anything at all until then, for I hate a man, as much as I hate hell fire, who lets his poverty tempt him into lying. I swear by King Zeus, by the laws of hospitality, and by that hearth of Odysseus to which I have now come, that all will surely happen as I have said it will. Odysseus will return in this very year—with the end of this moon and the beginning of the next, he will be here to take vengeance on all those who are mistreating his wife and son."

"And a pretty figure I would cut then," replied Eumaeus, "both now and hereafter, if I were to kill you after receiving you into my hut and showing you hospitality. I would have to say my prayers in earnest if I did that. But it's just supper time and I hope my men will come in directly, so we may cook something tasty for supper."

Thus they talked, and presently the swineherds came up with the pigs, which were then shut up for the night in their pens, and they made a tremendous squealing as they were being driven into them. But Eumaeus called to his men and said, "Bring in the best pig you have, so I may sacrifice him for this stranger, and we will feast on him ourselves. We have had trouble enough this long time feeding pigs while others reap the fruit of our labor."

With that he began chopping firewood while the others brought in a fine fat five-year-old boar and set it at the altar. Eumaeus did not forget the gods, for he was a man of good principles, so the first thing he did was cut bristles from the pig's face and throw them into the fire, praying to all the gods as he did so that Odysseus might return home again. Then he clubbed the pig with a piece of oak he had kept back when he was chopping the firewood and stunned it, while the others slaughtered and singed it. Then they cut it up, and Eumaeus began by putting raw pieces from each joint onto some of the fat. These he sprinkled with barley meal and laid upon the embers. They cut the rest of the meat up small, put the pieces on spits, and roasted them until they were done. When they had taken them off the spits, they threw them onto the serving table in a heap. The swineherd, who was a most fair-minded man, then stood up to give everyone his share. He made seven portions—one of these he set apart for Hermes the son of Maia and the nymphs, praying to them as he did so, and the others he distributed to the men one by one. He gave Odysseus some slices cut lengthwise down the loin as a mark of special honor, and Odysseus was much pleased. "I hope, Eumaeus," said he, "that Zeus will be as well disposed toward you as I am, for the respect you are showing to an outcast like myself."
To this you answered, swineherd Eumaeus, "Eat, my good fellow, and enjoy your supper, such as it is. God grants this and withholds that, just as he thinks right, for he can do whatever he chooses."

As he spoke he cut off the first piece and offered it as a burnt sacrifice to the immortal gods, then he made them a drink offering, put the cup in the hands of Odysseus, and sat down to his own portion. Mesaulius brought them their bread—the swineherd had bought this man on his own account from among the Taphians during his master's absence and had paid for him with his own money without telling either his mistress or Laertes. They then laid their hands on the good things that were before them, and when they had had enough to eat and drink, Mesaulius took away what was left of the bread, and they all went to bed after having made a hearty supper.

Now the night came on stormy and very dark, for there was no moon. It poured without ceasing, and the wind blew strong from the west, which brings wet weather, so Odysseus thought he would see whether Eumaeus, in the excellent care he took of him, would take off his own cloak and give it to him, or make one of his men give him one. "Listen to me," said he, "Eumaeus and the rest of you. When I have said a prayer I will tell you something. It is the wine that makes me talk in this way—wine will make even a wise man fall to singing, will make him chuckle and dance and say many a word that he had better leave unspoken. Still, as I have begun, I will go on. Would that I were still young and strong as when we set up an ambush before Troy. Menelaus and Odysseus were the leaders, but I was in command also, for the other two insisted on it. When we had come up to the wall of the city, we crouched down beneath our armor and lay there under cover of the reeds and thick brushwood that grew about the swamp. It came on to freeze with a north wind blowing—the snow fell small and fine like frost, and our shields were coated thick with ice. The others all had cloaks and shirts and slept comfortably enough with their shields about their shoulders, but I had carelessly left my cloak behind me, not thinking that I would be too cold, and had gone off in nothing but my shirt and shield. When the night was two-thirds through and the stars had shifted their places, I nudged Odysseus who was close to me with my elbow, and he at once gave me his attention.
"'Odysseus,' said I, 'this cold will be the death of me, for I have no cloak. Some god fooled me into setting off with nothing on but my shirt, and I don't know what to do.'
"Odysseus, who was as crafty as he was brave, came up with the following plan:
"'Keep still,' said he in a low voice, 'or the others will hear you.' Then he raised his head on his elbow.
"'My friends,' said he, 'I have had a dream from heaven in my sleep. We are a long way from the ships—I wish someone would go down and tell Agamemnon to send us up more men at once.'

"At this Thoas, son of Andraemon, threw off his cloak and set out running to the ships, and I took the cloak and lay in it comfortably enough till morning. Would that I were still young and strong as I was in those days, for then some one of you swineherds would give me a cloak both out of good will and for the respect due to a brave soldier. But now people look down on me because my clothes are shabby."

And Eumaeus answered, "Old man, you have told us an excellent story and have said nothing so far but what is quite satisfactory. For the present, therefore, you shall want neither clothing nor anything else that a stranger in distress may reasonably expect, but tomorrow morning you will have to wrap your own old rags about your body again, for we don't have many spare cloaks or shirts up here—every man has only one. When Odysseus' son comes home again, he will give you both cloak and shirt and send you wherever you may want to go."

With this he got up and made a bed for Odysseus by throwing some goatskins and sheepskins on the ground in front of the fire. Here Odysseus lay down, and Eumaeus covered him over with a great heavy cloak that he kept for a change in case of extraordinarily bad weather.

Thus Odysseus slept, and the young men slept beside him. But the swineherd did not like sleeping away from his pigs, so he got ready to go outside, and Odysseus was glad to see that he looked after his property during his master's absence. First he slung his sword over his strong shoulders and put on a thick cloak to keep out the wind. He also took the skin of a large and well-fed goat and a javelin in case of attack from men or dogs. Thus equipped he went to his rest where the pigs were camping under an overhanging rock that gave them shelter from the north wind.

chapters.title: Book XV — Athena summons Telemachus from Lacedaemon—he meets with Theoclymenus at Pylos and brings him to Ithaca—on landing he goes to the hut of Eumaeus
paragraphs: But Athena went to the beautiful city of Lacedaemon to tell Odysseus's son that he must return home immediately. She found him and Pisistratus sleeping in the forecourt of Menelaus's house. Pisistratus was fast asleep, but Telemachus couldn't rest all night, thinking about his troubled father. So Athena came close to him and said:

"Telemachus, you shouldn't stay so far from home any longer, or leave your property with such dangerous people in your house. They'll devour everything you own, and your journey will have been pointless. Ask Menelaus to send you home at once if you want to find your noble mother still there when you return. Her father and brothers are already urging her to marry Antinous, who has offered her more gifts than any of the others and keeps increasing his wedding presents. I hope nothing valuable has been stolen from the house while you've been gone, but you know how women are—they always want to do their best for the man who marries them, and never give another thought to the children of their first husband, or to their father once he's dead and gone. Go home, therefore, and put everything in the care of the most trustworthy woman servant you have, until heaven sees fit to send you a wife of your own. Let me also tell you something else you should know. The leading suitors are lying in wait for you in the strait between Ithaca and Samos, planning to kill you before you can reach home. I don't think they'll succeed—it's more likely that some of those who are now devouring your property will find their own graves. Sail day and night, and keep your ship well away from the islands. The god who watches over and protects you will send you favorable winds. As soon as you reach Ithaca, send your ship and crew on to the town, but go straight to the swineherd who tends your pigs. He's loyal to you—stay with him for the night, then send him to Penelope to tell her you've returned safely from Pylos."
Then she returned to Olympus. But Telemachus stirred Pisistratus with his heel to wake him, saying, "Wake up, Pisistratus, and harness the horses to the chariot. We must head for home."

But Pisistratus said, "No matter how urgent this is, we can't drive in the dark. Morning will come soon. Wait until Menelaus brings his gifts and loads them in the chariot for us, and let him say goodbye properly. A guest should never forget a host who has shown him kindness, as long as he lives."

As he spoke, dawn began to break, and Menelaus, who had already risen and left Helen in bed, came toward them. When Telemachus saw him, he quickly put on his tunic, threw a great cloak over his shoulders, and went out to meet him. "Menelaus," he said, "let me return now to my own country, for I want to get home."

Menelaus answered, "Telemachus, if you insist on leaving, I won't detain you. I don't like to see a host who's either too clingy with his guests or too rude to them. Moderation is best in all things—not letting a man go when he wants to leave is as bad as telling him to go if he'd rather stay. A host should treat his guest well while he's in the house and help him on his way when he wants to leave. Wait, then, until I can load your beautiful presents into your chariot, and until you've seen them yourself. I'll tell the women to prepare a proper meal from what we have in the house. It will be both more fitting and more economical for you to eat before setting out on such a long journey. Moreover, if you'd like to tour Greece or the Peloponnese, I'll harness my horses and escort you personally through all our principal cities. No one will send us away empty-handed—everyone will give us something: a bronze tripod, a pair of mules, or a golden cup."

"Menelaus," replied Telemachus, "I want to go home at once. When I left, I abandoned my property without protection, and I'm afraid that while searching for my father, I'll be ruined myself, or discover that something valuable has been stolen in my absence."

When Menelaus heard this, he immediately told his wife and servants to prepare a proper meal from what was available in the house. At that moment Eteoneus joined him, since he lived nearby and had just gotten up. Menelaus told him to light the fire and cook some meat, which he did at once. Then Menelaus went down to his fragrant storeroom, not alone—Helen went too, along with Megapenthes. When he reached the place where his household treasures were kept, he selected a double cup and told his son Megapenthes to bring a silver mixing bowl as well. Meanwhile, Helen went to the chest where she kept the lovely dresses she had made with her own hands. She took out the largest and most beautifully embroidered one, which glittered like a star and lay at the very bottom of the chest. Then they all returned through the house until they reached Telemachus, and Menelaus said, "Telemachus, may Zeus, Hera's mighty husband, bring you safely home as you desire. I now present you with the finest and most precious piece of metalwork in all my house. It's a mixing bowl of pure silver, except for the rim, which is inlaid with gold, and it's the work of Hephaestus. King Phaedimus of the Sidonians gave it to me during a visit I paid him on my way home. I'd like to give it to you."
With these words he placed the double cup in Telemachus's hands, while Megapenthes brought the beautiful mixing bowl and set it before him. Nearby stood lovely Helen with the robe ready in her hands.

"I too, my son," she said, "have something for you as a keepsake from Helen's hand—it's for your bride to wear on her wedding day. Until then, have your dear mother keep it for you. May you return rejoicing to your own country and home."

So saying, she gave him the robe, and he received it gladly. Then Pisistratus put the presents into the chariot, admiring them all as he did so. Presently Menelaus led Telemachus and Pisistratus into the house, where they both sat down to eat. A maid servant brought them water in a beautiful golden pitcher and poured it into a silver basin for them to wash their hands. She drew a clean table beside them, and a senior servant brought them bread and offered them many good things from what was available in the house. Eteoneus carved the meat and gave them each their portions, while Megapenthes poured the wine. Then they helped themselves to the good food before them. But as soon as they had eaten and drunk their fill, Telemachus and Pisistratus harnessed the horses and took their places in the chariot. They drove out through the inner gateway and under the echoing gatehouse of the outer courtyard, and Menelaus followed them with a golden cup of wine in his right hand so they could make a drink offering before departing. He stood in front of the horses and toasted them, saying, "Farewell to both of you. Be sure to tell Nestor how I've treated you, for he was as kind to me as any father could be while we Greeks were fighting before Troy."

"We'll certainly tell him everything as soon as we see him, sir," answered Telemachus. "I wish I could be as certain of finding Odysseus returned when I get back to Ithaca, so I could tell him of your great kindness and of the many beautiful presents I'm taking with me."

As he was speaking, a bird flew on their right—an eagle carrying a great white goose in its talons that it had snatched from the farmyard, while all the men and women ran after it, shouting. It came quite close to them and flew away on their right, in front of the horses. When they saw it, they were glad and took heart, and Pisistratus said, "Tell me, Menelaus, has heaven sent this omen for us or for you?"

Menelaus was thinking what would be the most appropriate response, but Helen was quicker and said, "I'll interpret this sign as heaven has put it in my heart, and as I'm sure it will come to pass. The eagle came from the mountain where it was bred and has its nest, and likewise Odysseus, after traveling far and suffering much, will return to take his revenge—if indeed he isn't back already, plotting mischief for the suitors."
"May Zeus grant it," replied Telemachus. "If that proves to be so, I'll make vows to you as though you were a goddess, even when I'm at home."

As he spoke, he whipped his horses, and they started off at full speed through the town toward the open country. They swayed the yoke on their necks and traveled all day long until the sun set and darkness covered the land. Then they reached Pherae, where Diocles lived, son of Ortilochus, grandson of Alpheus. There they spent the night and were treated hospitably. When rosy-fingered Dawn appeared, they again harnessed their horses and took their places in the chariot. They drove out through the inner gateway and under the echoing gatehouse of the outer court. Then Pisistratus urged his horses forward, and they flew ahead eagerly. Before long they came to Pylos, and Telemachus said:

"Pisistratus, I hope you'll promise to do what I'm about to ask you. You know our fathers were old friends, and we're both the same age. This journey has brought us even closer together. So don't take me past my ship—leave me there. If I go to your father's house, he'll try to keep me out of goodwill toward me, and I must go home at once."

Pisistratus considered how to do as requested, and finally decided it would be best to turn his horses toward the ship and put Menelaus's beautiful presents of gold and clothing in the stern of the vessel. Then he said, "Go aboard at once and tell your men to do the same before I can reach home to tell my father. I know how stubborn he is, and I'm sure he won't let you go. He'll come down here to fetch you himself and won't go back without you. But he'll be very angry."

With this he drove his fine horses back to the city of the Pylians and soon reached his home. But Telemachus called his men together and gave his orders. "Now, men," he said, "get everything ready on board the ship, and let's set out for home."

They did as he said and went aboard. But as Telemachus was busy making prayers and sacrifices to Athena in the ship's stern, there came to him a man from a distant country—a prophet fleeing from Argos because he had killed a man. He was descended from Melampus, who used to live in Pylos, the land of sheep. Melampus had been rich and owned a great house, but was driven into exile by the great and powerful king Neleus. Neleus seized his goods and held them for a whole year, during which Melampus was imprisoned in the house of King Phylacus, suffering greatly both because of Neleus's daughter and because he was haunted by a great sorrow that the dread Fury had laid upon him. In the end, however, he escaped with his life, drove the cattle from Phylace to Pylos, avenged the wrong done to him, and gave Neleus's daughter to his brother. Then he left the country and went to Argos, where he was destined to rule over many people. There he married, established himself, and had two famous sons: Antiphates and Mantius. Antiphates became father of Oecleus, and Oecleus of Amphiaraus, who was dearly loved by both Zeus and Apollo, but didn't live to old age, for he was killed in Thebes because of a woman's bribes. His sons were Alcmaeon and Amphilochus. Mantius, Melampus's other son, was father to Polypheides and Cleitus. Golden-throned Dawn carried off Cleitus for his beauty, so he might dwell among the immortals, but Apollo made Polypheides the greatest prophet in the world now that Amphiaraus was dead. He quarreled with his father and went to live in Hyperesia, where he remained and prophesied for all people.

His son, Theoclymenus, was the one who now approached Telemachus as he was making drink offerings and praying in his ship. "Friend," he said, "since I find you sacrificing in this place, I beg you by your sacrifices and by the god to whom you make them, and by your own head and those of your followers—tell me the truth and nothing but the truth. Who are you and where do you come from? Tell me also about your city and parents."

Telemachus said, "I'll answer you truthfully. I'm from Ithaca, and my father is Odysseus—or was, if he ever lived. But he's come to some miserable end. That's why I've taken this ship and gathered my crew, to see if I can hear any news of him, for he's been away a long time."

"I too am an exile," answered Theoclymenus, "for I've killed a man of my own people. He has many brothers and kinsmen in Argos who have great power among the Argives. I'm fleeing to escape death at their hands, and am thus doomed to wander the earth. I'm your suppliant—take me aboard your ship so they won't kill me, for I know they're pursuing me."
"I won't refuse you," replied Telemachus, "if you wish to join us. Come then, and in Ithaca we'll treat you hospitably with what we have."

At this he took Theoclymenus's spear and laid it on the ship's deck. He went aboard and sat in the stern, telling Theoclymenus to sit beside him. Then the men cast off the mooring ropes. Telemachus told them to catch hold of the rigging, and they hurried to obey. They set the mast in its socket in the crossbeam, raised it and secured it with the forestays, and hoisted their white sails with sheets of twisted oxhide. Athena sent them a fair wind that blew fresh and strong to carry the ship on her course as fast as possible. So they passed by Crouni and Chalcis.

Soon the sun set and darkness covered all the land. The vessel made quick passage to Pheae and then on to Elis, where the Epeans rule. Telemachus then headed toward the outlying islands, wondering whether he would escape death or be taken prisoner.

Meanwhile, Odysseus and the swineherd were eating their supper in the hut, and the men ate with them. As soon as they had finished eating and drinking, Odysseus began testing the swineherd to see whether he would continue treating him kindly and ask him to stay at the station, or send him away to the city. So he said:

"Eumaeus, and all of you—tomorrow I want to go away and start begging around the town, so I won't be more trouble to you or your men. Give me your advice, and let me have a good guide to go with me and show me the way. I'll make the rounds of the city begging, as I must, to see if anyone will give me a drink and a piece of bread. I'd also like to go to Odysseus's house and bring news of her husband to Queen Penelope. I could then move among the suitors and see if, out of all their abundance, they'll give me dinner. I'd soon make them an excellent servant in all kinds of ways. Listen and believe me when I tell you that by the blessing of Hermes, who gives grace and good reputation to all men's work, there's no one living who would make a handier servant than I would—to put fresh wood on the fire, chop fuel, carve meat, cook, pour wine, and do all those services that poor men must do for their betters."

The swineherd was very disturbed when he heard this. "Heaven help me," he exclaimed, "whatever could have put such an idea into your head? If you go near the suitors, you'll surely be destroyed, for their pride and arrogance reach the very heavens. They would never think of taking a man like you as a servant. Their servants are all young men, well-dressed, wearing good cloaks and shirts, with handsome faces and well-groomed hair. The tables are kept spotless and loaded with bread, meat, and wine. Stay where you are—you're not in anyone's way. I don't mind you being here, and neither do any of the others. When Telemachus comes home, he'll give you a shirt and cloak and send you wherever you want to go."

Odysseus answered, "May you be as dear to the gods as you are to me, for saving me from wandering about and getting into trouble. There's nothing worse than always being on the road. Still, when men have fallen low in the world, they'll endure a great deal for the sake of their miserable bellies. Since you urge me to stay here and await Telemachus's return, tell me about Odysseus's mother and his father, whom he left on the threshold of old age when he set out for Troy. Are they still living, or are they already dead and in the house of Hades?"

"I'll tell you all about them," replied Eumaeus. "Laertes is still living and prays to heaven to let him die peacefully in his own house, for he's terribly distressed about his son's absence and also about his wife's death, which grieved him greatly and aged him more than anything else. She came to an unhappy end through sorrow for her son—may no friend or neighbor who has been kind to me suffer such an end as she did. As long as she was still alive, though she was always grieving, I enjoyed seeing her and asking how she was, for she raised me along with her daughter Ctimene, the youngest of her children. We grew up together as boy and girl, and she treated us almost the same. When we both came of age, they sent Ctimene to Same and received a splendid dowry for her. As for me, my mistress gave me a good shirt and cloak with a pair of sandals for my feet, and sent me to work in the country, but she was just as fond of me as ever. This is all over now. Still, it has pleased heaven to bless my work in the position I now hold. I have enough to eat and drink, and can provide for any respectable stranger who comes here. But there's no getting a kind word or deed from my mistress now, for the house has fallen into the hands of wicked people. Servants sometimes want to see their mistress and talk with her—they like to have something to eat and drink at the house, and something to take back with them to the country. This is what keeps servants content."

Odysseus answered, "Then you must have been just a little boy, Eumaeus, when you were taken so far from your home and parents. Tell me truthfully: was the city where your father and mother lived sacked and pillaged, or did enemies carry you off when you were alone tending sheep or cattle, ship you here, and sell you for whatever your master paid them?"

"Stranger," replied Eumaeus, "regarding your question: sit still, make yourself comfortable, drink your wine, and listen to me. The nights are at their longest now—there's plenty of time for both sleeping and sitting up talking together. You shouldn't go to bed until it's time—too much sleep is as bad as too little. If any of the others want to go to bed, let them leave us and do so. Then they can take my master's pigs out after breakfast in the morning. We'll sit here eating and drinking in the hut, telling each other stories about our misfortunes. When a man has suffered much and been knocked about in the world, he takes pleasure in recalling sorrows that have long passed. So regarding your question, my story is as follows:

"You may have heard of an island called Syra that lies beyond Ortygia, where the land begins to curve around and face another direction. It's not very heavily populated, but the soil is good, with much pasture suitable for cattle and sheep, and it abounds with wine and wheat. Famine never comes there, nor are the people plagued by sickness, but when they grow old, Apollo comes with Artemis and kills them with his painless arrows. It contains two communities, and the whole country is divided between them. My father, Ctesias son of Ormenus, a man comparable to the gods, ruled over both.

"Now some cunning traders from Phoenicia came to this place (for the Phoenicians are great sailors) in a ship they had loaded with trinkets of all kinds. There happened to be a Phoenician woman in my father's house—very tall and beautiful, and an excellent servant. These scoundrels got hold of her one day when she was washing near their ship, seduced her, and sweet-talked her in ways no woman can resist, no matter how virtuous she may be by nature. The man who had seduced her asked who she was and where she came from, and she told him her father's name. 'I come from Sidon,' she said, 'and am daughter to Arybas, a man rolling in wealth. One day as I was coming into town from the countryside, some Taphian pirates seized me and brought me here over the sea, where they sold me to the man who owns this house, and he paid them their price for me.'
"The man who had seduced her then said, 'Would you like to come with us to see your parents' house and your parents themselves? They're both alive and said to be well off.'
"'I'll do so gladly,' she answered, 'if you men will first swear a solemn oath that you'll do me no harm along the way.'

"They all swore as she demanded, and when they had completed their oath, the woman said, 'Be quiet now, and if any of your men meets me in the street or at the well, don't let him speak to me, for fear someone might go and tell my master. If he suspects something, he'll put me in chains and have all of you killed. Keep this to yourselves—buy your merchandise as quickly as you can, and send me word when you've finished loading. I'll bring as much gold as I can get my hands on, and there's something else I can do to help pay my passage. I'm nurse to the master's son, a clever little fellow just old enough to run around. I'll carry him off in your ship, and you'll get a great deal of money for him if you take him and sell him in foreign lands.'

"With that she returned to the house. The Phoenicians stayed a whole year until they had loaded their ship with precious merchandise. When they had enough cargo, they sent word to the woman. Their messenger, a very cunning fellow, came to my father's house bringing a gold necklace strung with amber beads. While my mother and the servants were handling it, admiring it and bargaining over it, he quietly signaled to the woman and then returned to the ship. She took me by the hand and led me out of the house. In the front part of the house she saw tables set with cups from guests who had been feasting with my father in his official capacity—these men had now all gone to a public assembly. She snatched up three cups and hid them in the folds of her dress while I followed her, knowing no better. The sun had now set and darkness covered all the land, so we hurried as fast as we could until we reached the harbor, where the Phoenician ship was moored. When they got aboard, they sailed away over the sea, taking us with them, and Zeus sent them favorable winds. We sailed six days, both night and day, but on the seventh day Artemis struck the woman and she fell heavily into the ship's hold like a seagull dropping to the water. So they threw her overboard to the seals and fish, and I was left all sorrowful and alone. Eventually the winds and waves carried the ship to Ithaca, where Laertes traded various possessions for me, and that's how I came to set eyes on this country."

Odysseus answered, "Eumaeus, I've listened to the story of your misfortunes with the deepest interest and sympathy, but Zeus has given you good as well as evil. Despite everything, you have a good master who sees that you always have enough to eat and drink, and you lead a good life, while I'm still wandering from city to city, begging my way."

So they talked, and they had only a little time left for sleep, for dawn was soon coming. Meanwhile, Telemachus and his crew were nearing land, so they lowered the sails, took down the mast, and rowed the ship into the harbor. They dropped their anchor stones and secured the mooring lines, then got out on the seashore, mixed their wine, and prepared breakfast. As soon as they had eaten and drunk enough, Telemachus said, "Take the ship on to the town, but leave me here, for I want to check on the herdsmen at one of my farms. In the evening, when I've seen everything I need to see, I'll come down to the city, and tomorrow morning I'll give you all a good feast with meat and wine in return for your service."
Then Theoclymenus said, "And what's to become of me, my dear young friend? To whose house, among all your leading men, should I go? Or shall I go straight to your own house and to your mother?"

"At any other time," replied Telemachus, "I would invite you to my own house, for you'd find no lack of hospitality. At the present moment, however, you wouldn't be comfortable there, since I'll be away and my mother won't see you. She doesn't often show herself even to the suitors, but sits at her loom weaving in an upper chamber, keeping out of their way. But I can tell you whose house you can go to—I mean Eurymachus, son of Polybus, who is held in the highest regard by everyone in Ithaca. He's by far the best man and the most persistent suitor among all those courting my mother and trying to take Odysseus's place. Zeus alone in heaven knows whether they'll come to a bad end before the marriage takes place."

As he was speaking, a bird flew by on his right—a hawk, Apollo's messenger. It held a dove in its talons, and as it tore the feathers off, they fell to the ground midway between Telemachus and the ship. At this, Theoclymenus called him aside and grasped his hand. "Telemachus," he said, "that bird didn't fly on your right without being sent there by some god. As soon as I saw it, I knew it was an omen. It means you'll remain in power and that no house in Ithaca will be more royal than your own."
"I hope it proves true," answered Telemachus. "If it does, I'll show you such goodwill and give you so many gifts that everyone who meets you will congratulate you."

Then he said to his friend Piraeus, "Piraeus, son of Clytius, you've shown yourself most willing to serve me of all those who accompanied me to Pylos. I want you to take this stranger to your own house and entertain him hospitably until I can come for him."
Piraeus answered, "Telemachus, you may stay away as long as you like, but I'll look after him for you, and he'll find no lack of hospitality."

As he spoke, he went aboard and told the others to do the same and cast off the mooring lines. So they took their places in the ship. But Telemachus strapped on his sandals and took a long, sturdy spear with a sharp bronze point from the ship's deck. Then they cast off the lines, pushed the ship away from shore, and headed toward the city as they had been told, while Telemachus strode away as fast as he could until he reached the homestead where his countless herds of swine were feeding, and where lived the excellent swineherd, who was such a devoted servant to his master.

chapters.title: Book XVI — Odysseus reveals himself to Telemachus
paragraphs: Meanwhile Odysseus and the swineherd had lit a fire in the hut and were preparing breakfast at daybreak, having sent the men out with the pigs. When Telemachus arrived, the dogs didn't bark but wagged their tails at him, so Odysseus, hearing footsteps and noticing that the dogs weren't barking, said to Eumaeus:
"Eumaeus, I hear footsteps. I think one of your men or someone you know is coming here, because the dogs are being friendly and not barking."

The words had barely left his mouth when his son appeared at the door. Eumaeus jumped to his feet, and the bowls he was using to mix wine fell from his hands as he rushed toward his young master. He kissed his head and both his bright eyes, weeping with joy. A father couldn't be more delighted at the return of an only son, a child of his old age, after ten years away in a foreign land and much suffering. He embraced him, kissed him all over as if he had returned from the dead, and spoke lovingly to him:

"So you've come back, Telemachus, light of my eyes. When I heard you'd gone to Pylos, I was sure I'd never see you again. Come in, dear boy, and sit down so I can get a good look at you now that you're home. You don't visit us country folk very often—you usually stay close to town. I suppose you think it's better to keep an eye on what the suitors are doing."

"That's true, old friend," Telemachus replied, "but I've come now because I want to see you and find out whether my mother is still in her old home, or if someone else has married her, leaving Odysseus's bed empty and covered with cobwebs."
"She's still at the house," Eumaeus answered, "grieving and heartbroken, doing nothing but weep both night and day."

As he spoke, he took Telemachus's spear, and the young man crossed the stone threshold and entered. Odysseus rose from his seat to make room as he came in, but Telemachus stopped him. "Sit down, stranger," he said. "I can easily find another seat, and someone here will prepare it for me."

Odysseus returned to his place, and Eumaeus spread fresh brushwood on the floor and threw a sheepskin on top for Telemachus to sit on. Then the swineherd brought them plates of cold meat left over from the day before, and filled bread baskets as quickly as he could. He also mixed wine in wooden bowls and sat down facing Odysseus. They helped themselves to the good food before them, and when they had eaten and drunk their fill, Telemachus said to Eumaeus, "Old friend, where does this stranger come from? How did his crew bring him to Ithaca, and who were they? He certainly didn't come here on foot."

To this you replied, swineherd Eumaeus: "My boy, I'll tell you the truth. He says he's from Crete and has traveled widely. Right now he's escaped from a Thesprotian ship and has taken refuge at my station, so I'm putting him in your hands. Do whatever you think best with him, but remember he's come to you for protection."

"I'm very troubled by what you've told me," said Telemachus. "How can I take this stranger into my house? I'm still young and not strong enough to defend myself if anyone attacks me. My mother can't decide whether to stay where she is and look after the house out of respect for public opinion and her husband's memory, or whether it's time to choose the best of her suitors—the one who'll make her the most generous offer. Still, since the stranger has come to your station, I'll provide him with a good cloak and tunic, a sword and sandals, and send him wherever he wants to go. Or if you prefer, you can keep him here at the station, and I'll send clothes and food so he won't be a burden on you and your men. But I won't let him go near the suitors—they're very arrogant and would surely mistreat him in a way that would pain me greatly. No matter how brave a man is, he can't fight against so many, for they'd overpower him."

Then Odysseus said, "Sir, it's right that I should speak up. I'm deeply shocked by what you've said about how insolently the suitors are behaving despite a man like you being here. Tell me, do you submit to this treatment quietly, or has some god turned your people against you? Can't you count on your brothers for support—for those are the ones a man looks to for help, no matter how serious his quarrel? I wish I were as young as you and in my present frame of mind. If I were Odysseus's son, or indeed Odysseus himself, I'd rather have someone cut off my head than not go to that house and destroy every one of those men. If they outnumbered me—being alone—I'd rather die fighting in my own house than witness such disgraceful scenes day after day: strangers brutally mistreated, serving women dragged around the house improperly, wine wasted recklessly, and bread squandered pointlessly for an end that will never come."

Telemachus answered, "I'll tell you the whole truth. There's no hostility between me and my people, nor can I complain about brothers who might support me in any quarrel. Zeus has made us a line of only sons. Laertes was Arceisius's only son, and Odysseus was Laertes's only son. I'm Odysseus's only son, left behind when he went away, so I've never been any help to him. That's why my house is overrun with countless enemies. All the nobles from the neighboring islands—Dulichium, Same, Zacynthus—as well as all the leading men of Ithaca itself are devouring my household under the pretense of courting my mother. She won't flatly refuse to remarry, but she won't bring the matter to an end either, so they're destroying my estate and will soon destroy me as well. The outcome, however, rests with heaven. But you, old friend Eumaeus, go at once and tell Penelope that I'm safe and have returned from Pylos. Tell her alone, then come back here without letting anyone else know, for many are plotting against me."

"I understand and will obey," replied Eumaeus. "You need say no more. But since I'm going that way, should I also let poor Laertes know you've returned? He used to oversee the farm work despite his bitter grief over Odysseus, and would eat and drink normally with his servants. But they tell me that since the day you left for Pylos, he's neither eaten nor drunk properly, nor does he tend his farm, but sits weeping and wasting away."

"That's unfortunate," answered Telemachus, "and I'm sorry for him, but we must leave him alone for now. If people could have everything they wanted, the first thing I'd choose would be my father's return. But go and deliver your message, then hurry back without making a detour to tell Laertes. Have my mother send one of her women secretly with the news right away—let him hear it from her."

So he urged the swineherd. Eumaeus put on his sandals and set off for town. Athena watched him leave the station, then approached in the form of a woman—beautiful, tall, and wise. She stood by the entrance, revealing herself to Odysseus, but Telemachus couldn't see her and didn't know she was there, for the gods don't show themselves to everyone. Odysseus saw her, as did the dogs, who didn't bark but whimpered and slunk away to the far side of the yard. She nodded and signaled to Odysseus with her eyebrows, so he left the hut and stood before her outside the main wall of the courtyard. Then she said:

"Odysseus, noble son of Laertes, it's time to tell your son the truth. Don't keep him in the dark any longer, but make your plans for destroying the suitors, then head for town. I won't be long in joining you, for I too am eager for battle."

As she spoke, she touched him with her golden wand. First she draped a clean shirt and cloak over his shoulders, then made him younger and more impressive in appearance. She restored his color, filled out his cheeks, and let his beard become dark again. Then she departed, and Odysseus returned to the hut. His son was amazed when he saw him and looked away, fearing he might be gazing upon a god.

"Stranger," he said, "how suddenly you've changed from what you were just moments ago! You're dressed differently and your appearance has completely altered. Are you one of the gods who live in heaven? If so, be kind to me until I can make proper sacrifices and offerings of fine gold. Have mercy on me."
Odysseus replied, "I'm no god—why do you mistake me for one? I am your father, for whose sake you grieve and suffer so much at the hands of lawless men."
As he spoke, he kissed his son, and a tear fell from his cheek to the ground, for he had held back all tears until now. But Telemachus still couldn't believe it was his father, and said:

"You're not my father, but some god is deceiving me with false hopes so I'll grieve even more later. No mortal man could do what you've just done—make himself old and young in an instant—unless a god were helping him. A moment ago you were old and dressed in rags, and now you look like a god come down from heaven."

Odysseus answered, "Telemachus, you shouldn't be so amazed that I'm really here. No other Odysseus will come after this. I am who I am—after long wandering and great hardship, I've come home in the twentieth year to my own country. What amazes you is the work of the great goddess Athena, who does with me whatever she wishes, for she can do anything. One moment she makes me look like a beggar, the next I'm a young man in fine clothes. It's easy for the gods who live in heaven to make any man appear rich or poor."

As he spoke, he sat down, and Telemachus threw his arms around his father and wept. They were both so moved that they cried aloud like eagles or vultures with hooked claws whose half-grown young have been stolen by farmers. They wept so pitifully that the sun would have set on their tears if Telemachus hadn't suddenly asked, "What ship brought you here to Ithaca, dear father? What crew did they claim to be? You certainly couldn't have come on foot."

"I'll tell you the truth, my son," replied Odysseus. "The Phaeacians brought me here. They're great sailors who escort anyone who reaches their shores. They carried me across the sea while I slept and landed me in Ithaca, giving me many gifts of bronze, gold, and clothing. By heaven's grace, these are hidden in a cave, and I've come here on Athena's advice so we can plan the destruction of our enemies. First, give me a count of the suitors and their numbers, so I can consider whether we two can fight them all ourselves, or if we need to find others to help us."

Telemachus answered, "Father, I've always heard of your fame both in battle and in counsel, but what you're suggesting is enormous—I'm awed just thinking about it. Two men can't fight many brave ones. There aren't just ten suitors, or even twenty, but many times that. Listen to their numbers: fifty-two chosen young men from Dulichium with six servants; twenty-four from Same; twenty young Achaeans from Zacynthus; and twelve from Ithaca itself, all well-born. They have with them a servant named Medon, a bard, and two carvers. If we face such numbers, you may bitterly regret coming here for revenge. See if you can think of someone willing to help us."
"Listen to me," replied Odysseus, "and consider whether Athena and her father Zeus might be sufficient, or if I should try to find someone else as well."
"Those you've named," answered Telemachus, "are certainly good allies. Though they dwell high among the clouds, they have power over both gods and mortals."

"These two," continued Odysseus, "won't stay out of the fight long when the suitors and we clash in my house. Now, go home early tomorrow morning and mingle with the suitors as before. Later, the swineherd will bring me to the city disguised as a wretched old beggar. If you see them mistreating me, steel your heart against my suffering. Even if they drag me from the house by my feet or throw things at me, just watch and do nothing except gently try to make them behave more reasonably. But they won't listen to you, for their day of reckoning has come. Furthermore, remember this carefully: when Athena puts it in my mind, I'll nod to you, and when you see me do this, gather all the weapons in the house and hide them in the strong storeroom. When the suitors ask why you're removing them, make some excuse—say you've taken them away from the smoke, since they're no longer what they were when Odysseus left, but have become stained and blackened with soot. Add especially that you're afraid Zeus might make them quarrel over their wine and harm each other, which would disgrace both the feast and the courtship, for the sight of weapons sometimes tempts people to use them. But leave a sword and spear each for you and me, and a couple of oxhide shields so we can grab them at any moment. Zeus and Athena will soon quiet these people. There's also another matter: if you're truly my son and my blood runs in your veins, let no one know that Odysseus is in the house—not Laertes, not the swineherd, not any of the servants, not even Penelope herself. Let just you and me test the women, and let's also try some of the male servants to see who's on our side and who's against us."

"Father," replied Telemachus, "you'll come to know my character in time, and when you do, you'll find I can keep your secrets. But I don't think the plan you suggest will work well for either of us. Consider this: it will take us a long time to go around to all the farms and test the men, and meanwhile the suitors will be wasting your estate freely and without remorse. By all means test the women to see who are disloyal and who are innocent, but I'm not in favor of going around testing the men. We can deal with that later, if you really have some sign from Zeus that he'll support you."

While they talked, the ship that had brought Telemachus and his crew from Pylos reached the town of Ithaca. When they entered the harbor, they pulled the ship onto land. Their servants took their weapons, and they left all the gifts at Clytius's house. Then they sent a messenger to tell Penelope that Telemachus had gone to the country but had sent the ship to town to keep her from worrying. This messenger and Eumaeus happened to meet while both were on the same errand of informing Penelope. When they reached the house, the messenger stood up and announced to the queen in front of the waiting women, "Your son, my lady, has returned from Pylos." But Eumaeus went directly to Penelope and privately told her everything her son had instructed him to say. After delivering his message, he left the house and grounds and returned to his pigs.

The suitors were surprised and angry at what had happened, so they went outside the great wall surrounding the outer courtyard and held a meeting near the main gate. Eurymachus, son of Polybus, spoke first.

"Friends," he said, "this voyage of Telemachus is a serious matter. We were sure it would come to nothing. Now let's launch a ship and gather a crew to send after the others, telling them to return as quickly as possible."

He had barely finished speaking when Amphinomus turned and saw the ship in the harbor with the crew lowering the sails and stowing their oars. He laughed and said to the others, "We don't need to send any message—they're already here. Some god must have warned them, or they saw the ship pass and couldn't catch up."

At this they rose and went to the waterside. The crew pulled the ship ashore, their servants took their weapons, and they all went up to the assembly place, not allowing anyone old or young to sit with them. Antinous, son of Eupeithes, spoke first.

"Damn it," he said, "see how the gods have saved this man from destruction! We kept scouts posted on the headlands all day, and when the sun set we didn't go ashore to sleep but waited in the ship all night until morning, hoping to capture and kill him. But some god has brought him home despite us. Let's figure out how to finish him off. He must not escape us—our plan will never succeed while he's alive, for he's very clever, and public opinion isn't entirely on our side. We must act quickly before he can call the Achaeans to assembly. He'll waste no time doing so, for he'll be furious with us and will tell everyone how we plotted to kill him but failed. The people won't like this when they learn of it. We must make sure they don't harm us or drive us from our own country into exile. Let's try to catch him either on his farm away from town or on the road here. Then we can divide his property among ourselves and let his mother and whoever marries her keep the house. If this doesn't appeal to you and you want Telemachus to live and keep his father's property, then we shouldn't gather here eating up his goods this way, but should make our offers to Penelope each from his own house. She can marry whoever offers the most and has the best luck."

They all remained silent until Amphinomus rose to speak. He was the son of Nisus, who was King Aretias's son, and he was the leading suitor from the wheat-growing, well-pastured island of Dulichium. His conversation pleased Penelope more than that of any other suitor, for he was a man of good character. "Friends," he said, speaking plainly and honestly, "I'm not in favor of killing Telemachus. It's a terrible thing to kill someone of noble blood. Let's first consult the gods, and if Zeus's oracles advise it, I'll help kill him myself and urge everyone else to do so. But if they discourage us, I say we should hold back."
His words pleased them, so they rose immediately and went to Odysseus's house, where they took their usual seats.

Then Penelope decided to show herself to the suitors. She knew of the plot against Telemachus, for the servant Medon had overheard their plans and told her. So she went down to the courtyard with her maids, and when she reached the suitors, she stood by one of the pillars supporting the roof, holding a veil before her face, and scolded Antinous:

"Antinous, you arrogant and evil schemer, they say you're the best speaker and advisor of any man your age in Ithaca, but you're nothing of the sort. Madman, why do you try to bring about Telemachus's death, showing no respect for suppliants, whose witness is Zeus himself? It's wrong for you to plot against each other this way. Don't you remember how your father fled to this house in fear of the people, who were enraged at him for joining Taphian pirates and raiding the Thesprotians, who were at peace with us? They wanted to tear him apart and devour everything he owned, but Odysseus restrained them despite their fury. Now you're consuming his property without payment, courting his wife, and trying to kill his son. Stop this behavior and make the others stop too."

Eurymachus, son of Polybus, answered, "Take heart, Queen Penelope, daughter of Icarius, and don't worry about these matters. The man isn't yet born, and never will be, who will lay hands on your son Telemachus while I still live to see the light of day. I tell you—and it will surely happen—that my spear will be red with his blood, for many times Odysseus took me on his knees, put wine to my lips, and placed meat in my hands. Therefore Telemachus is my dearest friend, and he has nothing to fear from us suitors. Of course, if death comes to him from the gods, he cannot escape it." He said this to calm her, but he was actually plotting against Telemachus.

Then Penelope went upstairs again and mourned her husband until Athena brought sleep to her eyes. In the evening Eumaeus returned to Odysseus and his son, who had just sacrificed a year-old pig and were preparing supper together. Athena came to Odysseus, struck him with her wand to make him look like an old man again, and dressed him in his ragged clothes, fearing the swineherd might recognize him and fail to keep the secret by telling Penelope.
Telemachus spoke first. "So you're back, Eumaeus," he said. "What's the news from town? Have the suitors returned, or are they still waiting somewhere to ambush me on my way home?"

"I didn't think to ask about that when I was in town," replied Eumaeus. "I thought I'd deliver my message and get back as quickly as possible. I met a messenger sent by those who sailed with you to Pylos, and he was first to tell your mother the news. But I can tell you what I saw with my own eyes: I had just reached the crest of Hermes's hill above the town when I saw a ship entering the harbor with many men aboard. They had numerous shields and spears, and I thought it was the suitors, but I can't be certain."
Hearing this, Telemachus smiled at his father, though Eumaeus couldn't see him.

When they had finished their work and the meal was ready, they ate, and everyone had a full portion so all were satisfied. As soon as they had eaten and drunk enough, they lay down to rest and enjoyed the gift of sleep.

chapters.title: Book XVII — Telemachus and his mother meet—Odysseus and Eumaeus come down to the town, and Odysseus is insulted by Melanthius—he is recognised by the dog Argos—he is insulted and presently struck by Antinous with a stool—Penelope desires that he shall be sent to her
paragraphs: When dawn appeared with her rosy fingers, Telemachus strapped on his sandals and picked up a sturdy spear that fit well in his hands, ready to head into the city. "Old friend," he said to the swineherd, "I'm going to town now to show myself to my mother—she won't stop grieving until she sees me. As for this unfortunate stranger, take him to town and let him beg there from anyone willing to give him food and drink. I have enough troubles of my own without being burdened by other people's problems. If this angers him, that's his business, but I prefer to speak plainly."

Then Odysseus said, "Sir, I don't want to stay here anyway. A beggar always does better in town than in the countryside—anyone who wants to can give him something. I'm too old to care about staying here at some master's beck and call. So let this man do as you've told him and take me to town, once I've warmed myself by the fire and the day gets a bit warmer. My clothes are terribly thin, and in this cold morning I'll freeze to death, especially since you say the city is quite far off."

With that, Telemachus strode off through the farmyard, his mind focused on revenge against the suitors. When he reached home, he leaned his spear against a pillar of the colonnade, crossed the stone floor, and went inside.

Nurse Eurycleia saw him long before anyone else did. She was spreading fleeces on the chairs, and she burst into tears as she ran to him. All the other maids gathered around too, covering his head and shoulders with kisses. Penelope came out of her room looking like Artemis or Aphrodite, weeping as she threw her arms around her son. She kissed his forehead and both his beautiful eyes. "Light of my life," she cried as she spoke tenderly to him, "you've come home! I was sure I'd never see you again. To think you went off to Pylos without telling me or getting my permission! But come, tell me what you saw."

"Don't scold me, mother," Telemachus replied, "or upset me, considering what a narrow escape I've had. Instead, wash your face, change your dress, go upstairs with your maids, and promise full sacrifices to all the gods if Zeus will only grant us revenge on the suitors. I need to go to the assembly now to invite a stranger who came back with me from Pylos. I sent him ahead with my crew and told Piraeus to take him home and look after him until I could come for him myself."
She listened to her son's words, washed her face, changed her dress, and vowed full sacrifices to all the gods if they would grant her revenge on the suitors.

Telemachus went through and out of the colonnade, spear in hand—not alone, for his two swift dogs went with him. Athena blessed him with such divine presence that everyone marveled at him as he passed, and the suitors gathered around him with fair words on their lips but malice in their hearts. But he avoided them and went to sit with Mentor, Antiphus, and Halitherses, old friends of his father's house, and they made him tell them everything that had happened. Then Piraeus came up with Theoclymenus, whom he had escorted through town to the assembly, and Telemachus immediately joined them. Piraeus spoke first: "Telemachus," he said, "I wish you'd send some of your women to my house to collect the gifts Menelaus gave you."

"We don't know what might happen, Piraeus," Telemachus answered. "If the suitors kill me in my own house and divide my property among themselves, I'd rather you had the presents than let any of those people get their hands on them. But if I manage to kill them, I'll be very grateful if you'll kindly bring me my gifts."

With these words he took Theoclymenus to his own house. When they arrived, they laid their cloaks on the benches and chairs, went to the baths, and washed themselves. After the maids had washed and anointed them and given them fresh cloaks and tunics, they took their places at the table. A maid brought them water in a beautiful golden pitcher and poured it into a silver basin for them to wash their hands, then drew up a polished table beside them. A senior servant brought them bread and offered them many good things from what was available in the house. Across from them sat Penelope, reclining on a couch by one of the colonnade pillars, spinning. Then they began eating the good food set before them, and when they had eaten and drunk their fill, Penelope said:

"Telemachus, I'm going upstairs to lie down on that sorrowful bed, which I haven't stopped watering with my tears since the day Odysseus left for Troy with the sons of Atreus. But you failed to make it clear to me, before the suitors returned to the house, whether you'd been able to hear anything about your father's return."

"I'll tell you the truth," her son replied. "We went to Pylos and saw Nestor, who took me to his house and treated me as hospitably as if I were his own son returning after a long absence—his sons did the same. But he said he hadn't heard a word from anyone about Odysseus, whether he was alive or dead. So he sent me with a chariot and horses to Menelaus. There I saw Helen, for whose sake so many Greeks and Trojans were destined by heaven's will to suffer. Menelaus asked what had brought me to Sparta, and I told him everything. Then he said, 'So these cowards want to take over a brave man's bed? A deer might as well lay her newborn fawns in a lion's den, then go off to graze in the forest or meadow. When the lion returns to his lair, he'll make short work of them both—and so will Odysseus with these suitors. By Zeus, Athena, and Apollo, if Odysseus is still the man he was when he wrestled with Philomeleides in Lesbos and threw him so hard that all the Greeks cheered—if he's still like that and came near these suitors, they'd have a quick death and a bitter wedding. But regarding your question, I won't lie or mislead you. What the old man of the sea told me, I'll tell you exactly. He said he could see Odysseus on an island, grieving bitterly in the house of the nymph Calypso, who was holding him prisoner. He couldn't reach home because he had no ships or sailors to carry him across the sea.' That's what Menelaus told me, and after hearing his story I left. The gods then gave me fair winds and brought me safely home."
These words stirred Penelope's heart. Then Theoclymenus said to her:

"Madam, wife of Odysseus, Telemachus doesn't understand these things. Listen to me instead, for I can read the signs clearly and will hide nothing from you. May Zeus the king of heaven be my witness, along with the laws of hospitality and the hearth of Odysseus which I now approach—Odysseus himself is already here in Ithaca. Whether moving about the country or staying in one place, he's investigating all these evil deeds and planning a day of reckoning for the suitors. I saw an omen when I was on the ship that meant exactly this, and I told Telemachus about it."
"May it be so," Penelope answered. "If your words prove true, you'll receive such gifts and friendship from me that everyone who sees you will call you blessed."

So they talked. Meanwhile the suitors were throwing discus or aiming spears at targets on the level ground in front of the house, behaving with all their usual arrogance. But when it was time for dinner, and the flocks of sheep and goats had come into town from all the surrounding countryside with their usual shepherds, then Medon, their favorite servant who waited on them at table, said, "Now then, young masters, you've had enough sport. Come inside so we can prepare dinner. There's nothing wrong with eating when it's mealtime."

They left their games as he told them, and once inside the house, they laid their cloaks on the benches and chairs, then sacrificed some sheep, goats, pigs, and a heifer—all of them fat and well-fed. So they prepared their meal. Meanwhile Odysseus and the swineherd were getting ready to leave for town, and the swineherd said, "Stranger, I suppose you still want to go to town today, as my master said you should. For my part, I'd have liked you to stay here as a farmhand, but I must do as my master tells me, or he'll scold me later—and a scolding from one's master is no small matter. Let's go then, since it's broad daylight now. It'll be evening again soon and then you'll find it colder."
"I know and understand," Odysseus replied. "You don't need to say more. Let's go, but if you have a walking stick ready, let me have it, since you say the road is very rough."

As he spoke, he slung his shabby, tattered bag over his shoulders by its cord, and Eumaeus gave him a suitable stick. The two then started out, leaving the farm in charge of the dogs and herdsmen who stayed behind. The swineherd led the way with his master following, looking like some broken-down old tramp leaning on his staff, his clothes all in rags. When they had crossed the rough, steep ground and were approaching the city, they reached the fountain where the citizens drew their water. This had been built by Ithacus, Neritus, and Polyctor. A grove of water-loving poplars grew in a circle around it, and clear cold water flowed down to it from a high rock. Above the fountain was an altar to the nymphs where all travelers made sacrifices. Here Melanthius, son of Dolius, overtook them as he drove down some goats—the best in his flock—for the suitors' dinner, with two shepherds accompanying him. When he saw Eumaeus and Odysseus, he insulted them with outrageous and offensive language that made Odysseus very angry.

"There you go," he cried, "what a precious pair you are! See how heaven brings birds of a feather together. Where are you taking this miserable wretch, master swineherd? The sight of such a creature at table would make anyone sick. A fellow like this never won a prize for anything in his life, but goes around rubbing his shoulders against every doorpost, begging—not for swords and cauldrons like a man, but just for scraps not worth begging for. If you gave him to me as a hand at my station, he might clean out the pens or bring fodder to the kids, and he could fatten his thighs as much as he liked on whey. But he's taken to bad ways and won't do any kind of work—he'll do nothing but beg for food all over town to feed his greedy belly. I tell you this, and it will surely happen—if he goes near Odysseus' house, he'll get his head cracked by the stools they'll throw at him until they drive him out."

As he passed, he kicked Odysseus in the hip out of pure malice, but Odysseus stood firm and didn't budge from the path. For a moment he wondered whether to attack Melanthius and kill him with his staff, or grab him and beat his brains out. But he decided to endure it and control himself. The swineherd looked straight at Melanthius and scolded him, raising his hands and praying to heaven.

"Fountain nymphs," he cried, "daughters of Zeus, if Odysseus ever burned offerings to you—thigh bones covered with fat from lambs or kids—grant my prayer that heaven may send him home. He would soon put an end to the swaggering threats that men like you make, insulting people while wandering all over town as your flocks go to ruin through bad shepherding."

Then Melanthius the goatherd answered, "Listen to this ill-bred cur! What are you talking about? Someday I'll put you on a ship and take you to a foreign country where I can sell you and pocket the money. I wish I were as sure that Apollo would strike Telemachus dead today, or that the suitors would kill him, as I am that Odysseus will never come home again."

With that he left them to follow at their own pace while he went quickly ahead and soon reached his master's house. When he got there, he went in and took his seat among the suitors opposite Eurymachus, who liked him better than any of the others. The servants brought him a portion of meat, and a senior maid set bread before him to eat. Soon Odysseus and the swineherd approached the house and stopped beside it, hearing the sound of music as Phemius was just beginning to sing to the suitors. Then Odysseus took the swineherd's hand and said:

"Eumaeus, this house of Odysseus is truly magnificent. No matter how far you travel, you'll find few like it. One building connects to another. The courtyard has a wall with battlements all around it, the doors are double and well-made—it would be hard to take by force. I can tell there are many people feasting inside because I smell roasted meat and hear music, which the gods have made to accompany feasting."

Then Eumaeus said, "You've observed correctly, as you usually do. But let's think about our best course. Will you go inside first and join the suitors while I stay here, or will you wait here and let me go in first? But don't wait long, or someone might see you loitering outside and throw something at you. Please consider this."

And Odysseus answered, "I understand and will be careful. Go in first and leave me here. I'm quite used to being beaten and having things thrown at me. I've been so battered by war and sea that I'm hardened to it, and this can be added to the rest. But a man can't hide the demands of a hungry belly—this is an enemy that causes much trouble to all men. It's because of this that ships are built to sail the seas and make war on other people."

As they were talking, a dog that had been lying asleep raised his head and pricked up his ears. This was Argos, whom Odysseus had raised before leaving for Troy, but he had never gotten any use from him.
