In the old days the young men used to take him when they went hunting wild goats, deer, or rabbits, but now that his master was gone, he lay neglected on the heaps of mule and cow dung in front of the stable doors, waiting for the men to come and cart it away to fertilize the fields. He was covered with fleas. As soon as he saw Odysseus standing there, he dropped his ears and wagged his tail, but he couldn't get close to his master. When Odysseus saw the dog across the yard, he wiped away a tear without Eumaeus seeing it and said:

"Eumaeus, what a noble dog that is over there on the manure pile. His build is splendid—is he as fine as he looks, or is he just one of those dogs that hang around tables and are kept merely for show?"

"This dog," Eumaeus answered, "belonged to the man who died in a distant land. If he were what he was when Odysseus left for Troy, he would soon show you what he could do. There wasn't a wild beast in the forest that could escape him once he picked up its trail. But now he's fallen on hard times, since his master is dead and gone, and the women don't care for him. Servants never do their work properly when their master's hand is no longer over them—Zeus takes away half a man's worth when he makes him a slave."
As he spoke, he went inside the buildings to the colonnade where the suitors were, but Argos died as soon as he had recognized his master.

Telemachus saw Eumaeus long before anyone else did and beckoned him to come sit beside him. The swineherd looked around, picked up a stool that was lying near where the server sat distributing portions to the suitors, brought it to Telemachus' table, and sat down across from him. Then the servant brought him his portion and gave him bread from the basket.

Immediately afterward, Odysseus came inside, looking like a poor, miserable old beggar, leaning on his staff with his clothes all in rags. He sat down on the ash-wood threshold just inside the doors leading from the outer to the inner court, against a cypress-wood pillar that the carpenter had skillfully planed and fitted with perfect precision. Telemachus took a whole loaf from the bread basket, along with as much meat as he could hold in both hands, and said to Eumaeus, "Take this to the stranger and tell him to go around to all the suitors and beg from them—a beggar shouldn't be ashamed."
So Eumaeus went up to him and said, "Stranger, Telemachus sends you this and says you should go around begging from the suitors, since beggars shouldn't be ashamed."
Odysseus answered, "May King Zeus grant Telemachus all happiness and fulfill his heart's desire."

Then with both hands he took what Telemachus had sent him and laid it on the filthy old bag at his feet. He continued eating while the bard was singing, and had just finished his meal when the song ended. The suitors applauded the bard, and then Athena came to Odysseus and urged him to beg pieces of bread from each of the suitors, so he could see what kind of people they were and distinguish the good from the bad—though she wasn't going to save a single one of them regardless. So Odysseus made his rounds, going from left to right, stretching out his hands to beg as if he were a real beggar. Some of them pitied him and were curious about him, asking each other who he was and where he came from. Then the goatherd Melanthius said, "Suitors of my noble mistress, I can tell you something about him, since I've seen him before. The swineherd brought him here, but I know nothing about the man himself or where he comes from."

At this, Antinous began abusing the swineherd. "You fool," he shouted, "what did you bring this man to town for? Don't we have enough tramps and beggars already pestering us while we eat? Do you think it's nothing that such people gather here to waste your master's property—and you had to bring this one too?"

Eumaeus answered, "Antinous, your birth may be noble, but your words are evil. It wasn't my idea to bring him here. Who would invite a stranger from a foreign country unless he were someone useful—a prophet, a healer, a carpenter, or a bard who can charm us with his singing? Such men are welcome everywhere, but no one invites a beggar who will only be a nuisance. You're always harder on Odysseus' servants than any of the other suitors, especially on me, but I don't care as long as Telemachus and Penelope are alive and here."
But Telemachus said, "Quiet, don't answer him. Antinous has the sharpest tongue of all the suitors, and he makes the others worse."

Then turning to Antinous he said, "Antinous, you look after my interests as if I were your son. Why do you want this stranger thrown out of the house? Heaven forbid! Take something and give it to him yourself—I don't begrudge it, I encourage it. Never mind my mother or any of the other servants in the house. But I know you won't do what I say, because you prefer eating things yourself to giving them to others."
"What do you mean, Telemachus," Antinous replied, "with this arrogant talk? If all the suitors gave him as much as I will, he wouldn't come here again for another three months."

As he spoke, he lifted the footstool that supported his delicate feet from under the table and made as if to throw it at Odysseus. But the other suitors all gave him something and filled his bag with bread and meat. He was about to return to the threshold and eat what the suitors had given him, but first he went up to Antinous and said:

"Sir, give me something. You're surely not the poorest man here—you look like a chief, the foremost among them all, so you should be a better giver, and I'll spread word of your generosity far and wide. I too was once a wealthy man with a fine house of my own. In those days I gave to many a tramp like I am now, no matter who he was or what he needed. I had countless servants and all the other things that make people prosperous and respected. But Zeus chose to take it all away from me. He sent me with a band of raiders to Egypt—it was a long voyage that ruined me. I stationed my ships in the Nile River and ordered my men to stay with them and keep guard while I sent out scouts to survey from every vantage point.

"But the men disobeyed my orders, followed their own impulses, and ravaged the land of the Egyptians, killing the men and taking their wives and children as slaves. The alarm quickly reached the city, and when they heard the war cry, people came out at dawn until the plain was filled with foot soldiers, cavalry, and gleaming bronze. Then Zeus sent panic among my men, and they would no longer face the enemy, finding themselves surrounded. The Egyptians killed many of us and took the rest alive for forced labor. As for me, they gave me to a friend they met, to take to Cyprus—Dmetor by name, son of Iasus, who was a powerful man in Cyprus. From there I've come here in great misery."

Then Antinous said, "What god sent such a plague to ruin our dinner? Get out into the open courtyard, or I'll give you Egypt and Cyprus all over again for your insolence and pestering. You've begged from everyone else, and they've given you plenty, since they have abundance around them and it's easy to be generous with other people's property when there's plenty of it."

At this, Odysseus began to move away, saying, "Your looks, sir, are better than your manners. If you were in your own house, you wouldn't give a poor man even a pinch of salt, yet here you are in another man's house, surrounded by abundance, and you can't find it in yourself to give him even a piece of bread."

This made Antinous furious, and he glared at him, saying, "You'll pay for this before you get out of this hall." With these words he hurled a footstool at him, hitting him on the right shoulder blade near the top of his back. Odysseus stood firm as a rock—the blow didn't even stagger him, but he shook his head silently as he planned his revenge. Then he went back to the threshold and sat down, setting his well-filled bag at his feet.

"Listen to me," he called out, "you suitors of Queen Penelope, so I can speak my mind. A man feels no pain or ache when he's hit while fighting for his money, his sheep, or his cattle. So too Antinous has struck me while I serve my wretched belly, which always gets people into trouble. Still, if the poor have gods and avenging spirits at all, I pray that Antinous meets a bad end before his wedding day."

"Sit there and eat your food in silence, or get out," Antinous shouted. "If you say another word, I'll have you dragged hand and foot through the halls, and the servants will strip the skin from your body."

The other suitors were very displeased at this, and one of the young men said, "Antinous, you did wrong in striking that poor wretch of a beggar. It will be worse for you if he turns out to be some god—we know the gods disguise themselves in all sorts of ways as people from foreign countries and travel around the world to see who acts wrongly and who righteously."

So the suitors spoke, but Antinous paid them no attention. Meanwhile Telemachus was furious about the blow struck against his father, and though no tear fell from his eyes, he shook his head in silence and brooded on revenge.

When Penelope heard that the beggar had been struck in the banquet hall, she said to her maids, "May Apollo strike you the same way, Antinous," and her waiting woman Eurynome answered, "If our prayers were answered, not one of the suitors would ever see another sunrise." Then Penelope said, "Nurse, I hate every single one of them because they mean nothing but harm, but I hate Antinous like death itself. A poor unfortunate tramp came begging around the house from sheer need. Everyone else gave him something for his bag, but Antinous hit him on the right shoulder blade with a footstool."

So she talked with her maids as she sat in her room, while Odysseus was eating his meal. Then she called for the swineherd and said, "Eumaeus, go and tell the stranger to come here. I want to see him and ask him some questions. He seems to have traveled widely, and he might have seen or heard something of my unfortunate husband."

To this you answered, swineherd Eumaeus, "If only these Greeks would keep quiet, madam, you would be enchanted by the story of his adventures. I had him three days and three nights in my hut, which was the first place he reached after escaping from his ship, and he still hasn't finished telling the story of his misfortunes. If he had been the most divinely inspired minstrel in the world, on whose lips all listeners hang spellbound, I couldn't have been more charmed as I sat in my hut listening to him. He says there's an old friendship between his house and that of Odysseus, and that he comes from Crete where the descendants of Minos live, after being driven here and there by every kind of misfortune. He also claims that he's heard Odysseus is alive and nearby among the Thesprotians, and that he's bringing great wealth home."

"Call him here then," said Penelope, "so I too can hear his story. As for the suitors, let them enjoy themselves indoors or out as they please—they have nothing to worry about. Their grain and wine remain untouched in their houses with only servants to consume them, while they keep hanging around our house day after day, slaughtering our cattle, sheep, and fat goats for their feasts, never giving a thought to how much wine they drink. No estate can survive such recklessness, since we no longer have Odysseus to protect us. If he were to return, he and his son would quickly have their revenge."

As she spoke, Telemachus sneezed so loudly that the whole house echoed with it. Penelope laughed when she heard this and said to Eumaeus, "Go and call the stranger—didn't you hear how my son sneezed just as I was speaking? This can only mean that all the suitors are going to die, and not one of them will escape. Furthermore, I tell you this and take it to heart: if I'm satisfied that the stranger is telling the truth, I'll give him a tunic and cloak of good quality."

When Eumaeus heard this, he went straight to Odysseus and said, "Father stranger, my mistress Penelope, mother of Telemachus, has sent for you. She's in great sorrow, but she wants to hear anything you can tell her about her husband. If she's satisfied that you're telling the truth, she'll give you a tunic and cloak, which are exactly what you need most. As for food, you can get enough to fill your belly by begging around town from those who are willing to give."

"I will tell Penelope," Odysseus answered, "nothing but the absolute truth. I know all about her husband and have shared his sufferings, but I'm afraid of passing through this crowd of cruel suitors—their pride and violence reach the heavens. Just now, as I was going around the house doing no harm, a man struck me painfully, but neither Telemachus nor anyone else defended me. Tell Penelope, therefore, to be patient and wait until sunset. Let her give me a seat close to the fire, since my clothes are very thin—you know they are, as you've seen them ever since I first asked for your help—and then she can ask me about her husband's return."

The swineherd went back when he heard this, and Penelope said as she saw him cross the threshold, "Why don't you bring him, Eumaeus? Is he afraid someone will mistreat him, or is he simply shy about coming inside the house? Beggars shouldn't be ashamed."

To this you answered, swineherd Eumaeus, "The stranger is being quite reasonable. He's avoiding the suitors, and he's only doing what anyone else would do. He asks you to wait until sunset, and it would be much better, madam, for you to have him all to yourself when you can hear him and talk to him as you wish."
"The man is no fool," Penelope replied. "It would very likely be as he says, for there are no more abominable people in the whole world than these men."

When she finished speaking, Eumaeus went back to the suitors, having explained everything. Then he went up to Telemachus and said quietly in his ear so no one could overhear, "My dear sir, I'll now go back to the pigs to look after your property and my own business. You'll watch what's happening here, but above all be careful to stay out of danger, for there are many who wish you ill. May Zeus destroy them before they harm us."
"Very well," Telemachus replied. "Go home after you've eaten, and in the morning come here with the animals we're to sacrifice for the day. Leave the rest to heaven and me."

At this, Eumaeus took his seat again, and when he had finished his dinner, he left the courtyard and colonnade with the men still at table and went back to his pigs. As for the suitors, they soon began amusing themselves with singing and dancing, for evening was now approaching.

chapters.title: Book XVIII — The fight with Irus—Odysseus warns Amphinomus—Penelope gets presents from the suitors—the braziers—Odysseus rebukes Eurymachus
paragraphs: Now there came a common vagrant who wandered all over the city of Ithaca, begging for food, notorious as an incorrigible glutton and drunkard. This man had no strength or substance in him, but he was a big, hulking fellow to look at. His real name, the one his mother gave him, was Arnaeus, but the young men called him Irus because he would run errands for anyone who would send him. As soon as he arrived, he began insulting Odysseus and trying to drive him from his own house.

"Get away from this doorway, old man," he shouted, "or you'll be dragged out by your neck and heels! Can't you see they're all winking at me, wanting me to throw you out by force? I just don't like doing it. Get up and leave on your own, or we'll come to blows."

Odysseus frowned at him and said, "Friend, I'm not harming you in any way. People give you plenty, and I'm not jealous. There's room enough in this doorway for both of us, and you don't need to begrudge me things that aren't yours to give. You seem to be just another tramp like me, but perhaps the gods will give us better luck later. However, don't talk too much about fighting, or you'll anger me. Old as I am, I'll cover your mouth and chest with blood. I'll have more peace tomorrow if I do, because you won't come to Odysseus's house anymore."

Irus grew very angry and answered, "You filthy glutton! You chatter away like an old fishwife. I have a mind to lay both hands on you and knock your teeth out of your head like boar's tusks. Get ready, then, and let these people stand by and watch. You'll never be able to fight someone so much younger than yourself."

This is how they insulted each other on the smooth pavement in front of the doorway, and when Antinous saw what was happening, he laughed heartily and said to the others, "This is the finest entertainment you ever saw! Heaven never sent anything like it to this house. The stranger and Irus have quarreled and are going to fight. Let's encourage them to do it right now."

The suitors all came up laughing and gathered around the two ragged tramps. "Listen to me," said Antinous. "There are some goats' stomachs down by the fire, which we've filled with blood and fat and set aside for supper. Whoever wins and proves himself the better man can have his pick of them. He'll be welcome at our table, and we won't allow any other beggar around the house at all."

The others all agreed, but Odysseus, to throw them off the scent, said, "Sirs, an old man like me, worn out with suffering, can't hold his own against a young one. But my demanding belly urges me on, though I know it can only end in my getting a beating. You must swear, however, that none of you will give me a foul blow to help Irus win."

They swore as he asked, and when they had completed their oath, Telemachus spoke up and said, "Stranger, if you're determined to settle with this fellow, you needn't fear anyone here. Whoever strikes you will have to fight more than one person. I'm the host, and the other chiefs, Antinous and Eurymachus, both sensible men, agree with me."

Everyone agreed, and Odysseus tucked his old rags around his waist, revealing his strong thighs, broad chest and shoulders, and mighty arms. But Athena came to him and made his limbs even stronger still. The suitors were amazed beyond measure, and one would turn to his neighbor saying, "The stranger has revealed such a powerful build from under his old rags that there'll soon be nothing left of Irus."

Irus began to feel very uneasy when he heard this, but the servants forced him forward and brought him into the open part of the court in such fear that his limbs were trembling. Antinous scolded him and said, "You swaggering bully, you should never have been born if you're afraid of such an old, broken-down creature as this tramp. I tell you now—and it will surely happen—if he beats you and proves himself the better man, I'll pack you off on a ship to the mainland and send you to King Echetus, who kills everyone who comes near him. He'll cut off your nose and ears and pull out your guts for the dogs to eat."

This frightened Irus even more, but they brought him into the middle of the court, and both men raised their hands to fight. Then Odysseus considered whether he should strike so hard as to kill him on the spot, or give him a lighter blow that would only knock him down. In the end he decided on the lighter blow, fearing the Greeks might begin to suspect who he was. Then they began to fight. Irus hit Odysseus on the right shoulder, but Odysseus struck Irus on the neck under the ear, crushing the bones of his skull. Blood gushed from his mouth as he fell groaning in the dust, gnashing his teeth and kicking on the ground. The suitors threw up their hands and nearly died of laughter as Odysseus grabbed him by the foot and dragged him to the outer court as far as the gatehouse. There he propped him against the wall and put his staff in his hands. "Sit here," he said, "and keep the dogs and pigs away. You're a pitiful creature, and if you try to make yourself king of the beggars again, you'll fare even worse."

Then he threw his dirty old wallet, all tattered and torn, over his shoulder by its cord and went back to sit on the threshold. The suitors went inside the colonnade, laughing and congratulating him. "May Zeus and all the other gods," they said, "grant you whatever you want for putting an end to this insufferable tramp's pestering. We'll take him to the mainland soon, to King Echetus, who kills everyone who comes near him."

Odysseus took this as a good omen, and Antinous set a large goat's stomach before him, filled with blood and fat. Amphinomus took two loaves from the bread basket and brought them to him, toasting him with a golden cup of wine. "Good luck to you, father stranger," he said. "You're in a bad way now, but I hope you'll have better times ahead."

Odysseus answered, "Amphinomus, you seem to be a man of good sense, as you well might be, considering whose son you are. I've heard your father spoken of well—he is Nisus of Dulichium, both brave and wealthy. They tell me you're his son, and you appear to be a decent person. Listen, therefore, and pay attention to what I'm saying. Man is the most foolish of all creatures that live on earth. As long as heaven grants him health and strength, he thinks no harm will ever come to him. Even when the blessed gods bring sorrow upon him, he bears it as he must and makes the best of it, for God Almighty gives men their daily thoughts day by day. I know all about it, for I was once a rich man and did much wrong in my stubborn pride, confident that my father and brothers would support me. Therefore let a man fear God in all things always, and accept the good that heaven may send him without vanity. Consider the shameful way these suitors are acting—see how they're wasting the estate and dishonoring the wife of one who is certain to return someday, and soon. No, he'll be here shortly. May heaven send you home safely before you meet him when he comes, for once he's here, the suitors and he will not part without bloodshed."

With these words he made a drink offering, and after drinking, he put the gold cup back into Amphinomus's hands. Amphinomus walked away serious and bowing his head, for he sensed trouble coming. But even so he could not escape destruction, for Athena had doomed him to fall by Telemachus's hand. So he returned to his seat where he had been before.

Then Athena put it into Penelope's mind to show herself to the suitors, so that she might make them even more infatuated with her and win greater honor from her son and husband. She gave a mocking laugh and said, "Eurynome, I've changed my mind and have a desire to show myself to the suitors, though I detest them. I'd also like to give my son a hint that he'd better have nothing more to do with them. They speak pleasantly enough, but they mean harm."

"My dear child," answered Eurynome, "everything you've said is true. Go and tell your son about it, but first wash yourself and anoint your face. Don't go around with your cheeks covered with tears—it's not right for you to grieve so constantly. Telemachus, whom you always prayed you might live to see grown up, already has a beard."

"I know, Eurynome," replied Penelope, "that you mean well, but don't try to persuade me to wash and anoint myself, for heaven took away all my beauty the day my husband sailed away. Nevertheless, tell Autonoe and Hippodamia that I want them. They must be with me when I'm in the hall—I won't go among the men alone, as that wouldn't be proper."

The old woman left the room to call the maids to their mistress. Meanwhile, Athena had another plan and sent Penelope into a sweet sleep. She lay down on her couch and her limbs grew heavy with slumber. Then the goddess poured grace and beauty over her so that all the Greeks would admire her. She washed her face with the divine loveliness that Aphrodite wears when she dances with the Graces. She made her taller and more commanding, and her complexion became whiter than carved ivory. When Athena had finished all this, she departed, and the maids came in from the women's quarters and woke Penelope with their chatter.

"What a wonderfully sweet sleep I've had," she said, passing her hands over her face, "despite all my misery. I wish Artemis would let me die so peacefully right now, so I wouldn't waste away in despair over losing my dear husband, who had every good quality and was the most distinguished man among the Greeks."

With these words she came down from her upper room, not alone but attended by two of her maids. When she reached the suitors, she stood by one of the pillars supporting the roof of the hall, holding a veil before her face, with a faithful maid on either side of her. When they saw her, the suitors were overwhelmed and became so desperately infatuated that each one prayed he might win her as his wife.

"Telemachus," she said, addressing her son, "I'm afraid you're no longer as wise and well-behaved as you used to be. When you were younger, you had better judgment. Now, however, though you're grown up—and a stranger looking at you would think you were the son of a wealthy father, judging by your size and good looks—your conduct is far from what it should be. What is all this commotion that's been going on? How could you allow a stranger to be so disgracefully mistreated? What would have happened if he had been seriously injured while seeking shelter in our house? Surely this would have brought great shame on you."

"I'm not surprised at your displeasure, dear mother," replied Telemachus. "I understand everything and know when things aren't as they should be, which I couldn't do when I was younger. I can't, however, behave perfectly at all times. One after another of these wicked people keeps driving me out of my mind, and I have no one to support me. After all, though, this fight between Irus and the stranger didn't turn out as the suitors intended, for the stranger got the better of it. I wish Father Zeus, Athena, and Apollo would break the neck of every one of your suitors, some inside the house and some outside. I wish they could all be as helpless as Irus is over there by the gate of the outer court. See how his head lolls like a drunk man's—he's been beaten so badly that he can't stand up or get back to his home, wherever that may be, because he has no strength left."

This is how they talked. Then Eurymachus came forward and said, "Queen Penelope, daughter of Icarius, if all the Greeks in Argos could see you at this moment, you would have even more suitors in your house by tomorrow morning, for you are the most admirable woman in the whole world, both in personal beauty and wisdom."

Penelope replied, "Eurymachus, heaven robbed me of all my beauty, whether of face or figure, when the Greeks set sail for Troy with my dear husband among them. If he were to return and look after my affairs, I would be more respected and present a better appearance to the world. As it is, I'm oppressed with care and the afflictions heaven has seen fit to heap upon me. My husband foresaw it all, and when he was leaving home, he took my right hand in his. 'Wife,' he said, 'not all of us will come home safely from Troy, for the Trojans fight well with both bow and spear. They're also excellent at fighting from chariots, and nothing decides a battle's outcome faster than that. I don't know, therefore, whether heaven will send me back to you, or whether I might fall at Troy. Meanwhile, you look after things here. Take care of my father and mother as you do now, and even more so during my absence. But when you see our son growing a beard, then marry whomever you choose and leave this house.' This is what he said, and now it's all coming true. A night will come when I must submit to a marriage I detest, for Zeus has taken from me all hope of happiness. This further grief, moreover, cuts me to the heart. You suitors are not courting me according to my country's custom. When men court a woman they think will make a good wife and who is of noble birth, and when each is trying to win her for himself, they usually bring cattle and sheep to feast the lady's friends, and they give her magnificent gifts, instead of eating up other people's property without paying for it."
This is what she said, and Odysseus was pleased when he heard her trying to get presents from the suitors and flattering them with fair words that he knew she didn't mean.

Then Antinous said, "Queen Penelope, daughter of Icarius, accept as many presents as you like from anyone who will give them to you—it's not right to refuse a gift. But we won't go about our business or leave this place until you've married the best man among us, whoever he may be."

The others applauded what Antinous said, and each sent his servant to bring his gift. Antinous's man returned with a large and lovely dress, beautifully embroidered, with twelve exquisite golden brooches to fasten it. Eurymachus immediately brought her a magnificent chain of gold and amber beads that gleamed like sunlight. Eurydamas's two men returned with earrings fashioned into three brilliant pendants that sparkled beautifully, while King Pisander, son of Polyctor, gave her a necklace of the finest workmanship. Everyone else brought her a beautiful present of some kind.

Then the queen went back upstairs to her room, and her maids carried the presents after her. Meanwhile the suitors turned to singing and dancing and stayed until evening came. They danced and sang until it grew dark, then brought in three braziers to give light and piled them with chopped firewood, very old and dry. They lit torches from them, which the maids held up in turns. Then Odysseus said:

"Maids, servants of Odysseus who has been absent so long, go to the queen inside the house. Sit with her and entertain her, or spin and prepare wool. I'll hold the light for all these people. They may stay until morning, but they won't defeat me, for I can endure a great deal."

The maids looked at each other and laughed, while pretty Melantho began mocking him contemptuously. She was Dolius's daughter but had been raised by Penelope, who used to give her toys and cared for her as a child. Despite all this, she showed no consideration for her mistress's sorrows and was having an affair with Eurymachus, with whom she was in love.

"Poor fool," she said, "have you completely lost your mind? Go sleep in some blacksmith's shop or public gathering place instead of chattering here. Aren't you ashamed to open your mouth in front of your betters—so many of them too? Has the wine gone to your head, or do you always babble this way? You seem to have lost your wits because you beat that tramp Irus. Be careful that a better man doesn't come and beat you about the head until he drives you bleeding from the house."
"Vixen," replied Odysseus, glaring at her, "I'll go tell Telemachus what you've been saying, and he'll have you torn limb from limb."

With these words he frightened the women, and they hurried off into the main part of the house, trembling all over, for they thought he would do as he said. But Odysseus took his position near the burning braziers, holding up torches and watching the people—brooding all the while on things that would surely come to pass.

But Athena wouldn't let the suitors stop their insolence for even a moment, for she wanted Odysseus to become even more bitter against them. So she prompted Eurymachus, son of Polybus, to mock him, which made the others laugh. "Listen to me," he said, "you suitors of Queen Penelope, so I can speak my mind. It's not for nothing that this man has come to Odysseus's house. I believe the light isn't coming from the torches but from his own head—for his hair is completely gone, every bit of it."

Then, turning to Odysseus, he said, "Stranger, would you work as a servant if I sent you to the countryside and saw that you were well paid? Can you build a stone wall or plant trees? I'll feed you all year round and provide you with shoes and clothing. Will you go then? No, you won't, because you've gotten into bad habits and don't want to work. You'd rather fill your belly by going around the country begging."

"Eurymachus," answered Odysseus, "if you and I were to work against each other in early summer when the days are longest—give me a good scythe and take another yourself, and let's see which of us lasts longer or mows stronger, from dawn to dark when there's grass to cut. Or if you want to plow against me, let's each take a yoke of strong, well-matched oxen of great strength and endurance. Put me in a four-acre field and see whether you or I can cut a straighter furrow. If war broke out today, give me a shield, a couple of spears, and a helmet that fits well on my head—you'd find me in the front ranks and would stop your jokes about my belly. You are insolent and cruel and think yourself important because you live in a small world, and a bad one at that. If Odysseus returns to reclaim his property, his house's doors are wide, but you'll find them narrow when you try to escape through them."

Eurymachus was furious at all this. He scowled and cried, "You wretch, I'll soon pay you back for daring to say such things to me, and in public too! Has the wine gone to your head, or do you always babble like this? You seem to have lost your wits because you beat that tramp Irus." With this he grabbed a footstool, but Odysseus sought protection at Amphinomus of Dulichium's knees, for he was afraid. The stool hit the cupbearer on his right hand and knocked him down. The man fell flat on his back with a cry, and his wine jug fell ringing to the ground. The suitors in the covered hall were now in an uproar, and one would turn to his neighbor saying, "I wish the stranger had gone somewhere else—bad luck to him for all the trouble he causes us. We can't allow such disturbance over a beggar. If such poor judgment prevails, we'll have no more pleasure at our feast."

At this Telemachus stepped forward and said, "Sirs, are you mad? Can't you handle your food and drink properly? Some evil spirit has possessed you. I don't wish to drive any of you away, but you've had your dinner, and the sooner you all go home to bed, the better."

The suitors bit their lips and marveled at his bold speech, but Amphinomus, son of Nisus, who was son of Aretias, said, "Let's not take offense—that's reasonable, so let's not argue. Don't let us harm the stranger or any of Odysseus's servants. Let the cupbearer go around with the drink offerings so we can make them and go home to rest. As for the stranger, let's leave Telemachus to deal with him, since he has come to his house."

This is what he said, and his words pleased them well. So Mulius of Dulichium, Amphinomus's servant, mixed them a bowl of wine and water and passed it around to each man in turn. They made their drink offerings to the blessed gods, and after making their offerings and drinking as each desired, they went their separate ways, each to his own home.

chapters.title: Book XIX — Telemachus and Odysseus remove the armour—Odysseus interviews Penelope—Euryclea washes his feet and recognises the scar on his leg—Penelope tells her dream to Odysseus
paragraphs: Odysseus was left in the courtyard, pondering on the means whereby with Athena's help he might be able to kill the suitors. Presently he said to Telemachus, "Telemachus, we must gather the weapons together and take them down inside. Make some excuse when the suitors ask you why you have removed them. Say that you have taken them to be out of the way of the smoke, since they are no longer what they were when Odysseus went away, but have become soiled and begrimed with soot. Add to this more particularly that you are afraid Zeus may set them on to quarrel over their wine, and that they may do each other some harm which may disgrace both banquet and wooing, for the sight of arms sometimes tempts people to use them."

Telemachus approved of what his father had said, so he called nurse Euryclea and said, "Nurse, shut the women up in their room, while I take the armor that my father left behind him down into the storeroom. No one looks after it now my father is gone, and it has gotten all smirched with soot during my own boyhood. I want to take it down where the smoke cannot reach it."

"I wish, child," answered Euryclea, "that you would take the management of the house into your own hands altogether, and look after all the property yourself. But who is to go with you and light you to the storeroom? The maids would have done so, but you would not let them."
"The stranger," said Telemachus, "shall show me a light; when people eat my bread they must earn it, no matter where they come from."

Euryclea did as she was told, and bolted the women inside their room. Then Odysseus and his son made all haste to take the helmets, shields, and spears inside; and Athena went before them with a gold lamp in her hand that shed a soft and brilliant radiance, whereon Telemachus said, "Father, my eyes behold a great marvel: the walls, with the rafters, crossbeams, and the supports on which they rest are all aglow as with a flaming fire. Surely there is some god here who has come down from heaven."

"Hush," answered Odysseus, "hold your peace and ask no questions, for this is the manner of the gods. Get you to your bed, and leave me here to talk with your mother and the maids. Your mother in her grief will ask me all sorts of questions."

On this Telemachus went by torch-light to the other side of the inner court, to the room in which he always slept. There he lay in his bed till morning, while Odysseus was left in the courtyard pondering on the means whereby with Athena's help he might be able to kill the suitors.

Then Penelope came down from her room looking like Aphrodite or Artemis, and they set her a seat inlaid with scrolls of silver and ivory near the fire in her accustomed place. It had been made by Icmalius and had a footstool all in one piece with the seat itself; and it was covered with a thick fleece: on this she now sat, and the maids came from the women's room to join her. They set about removing the tables at which the wicked suitors had been dining, and took away the bread that was left, with the cups from which they had drunk. They emptied the embers out of the braziers, and heaped much wood upon them to give both light and heat; but Melantho began to rail at Odysseus a second time and said, "Stranger, do you mean to plague us by hanging about the house all night and spying upon the women? Be off, you wretch, outside, and eat your supper there, or you shall be driven out with a firebrand."

Odysseus scowled at her and answered, "My good woman, why should you be so angry with me? Is it because I am not clean, and my clothes are all in rags, and because I am obliged to go begging about after the manner of tramps and beggars generally? I too was a rich man once, and had a fine house of my own; in those days I gave to many a tramp such as I now am, no matter who he might be nor what he wanted. I had any number of servants, and all the other things which people have who live well and are accounted wealthy, but it pleased Zeus to take all away from me; therefore, woman, beware lest you too come to lose that pride and place in which you now wanton above your fellows; have a care lest you get out of favor with your mistress, and lest Odysseus should come home, for there is still a chance that he may do so. Moreover, though he be dead as you think he is, yet by Apollo's will he has left a son behind him, Telemachus, who will note anything done amiss by the maids in the house, for he is now no longer in his boyhood."

Penelope heard what he was saying and scolded the maid, "Impudent baggage," said she, "I see how abominably you are behaving, and you shall smart for it. You knew perfectly well, for I told you myself, that I was going to see the stranger and ask him about my husband, for whose sake I am in such continual sorrow."

Then she said to her head waiting woman Eurynome, "Bring a seat with a fleece upon it, for the stranger to sit upon while he tells his story, and listens to what I have to say. I wish to ask him some questions."

Eurynome brought the seat at once and set a fleece upon it, and as soon as Odysseus had sat down Penelope began by saying, "Stranger, I shall first ask you who and whence are you? Tell me of your town and parents."

"Madam," answered Odysseus, "who on the face of the whole earth can dare to chide with you? Your fame reaches the firmament of heaven itself; you are like some blameless king, who upholds righteousness, as the monarch over a great and valiant nation: the earth yields its wheat and barley, the trees are loaded with fruit, the ewes bring forth lambs, and the sea abounds with fish by reason of his virtues, and his people do good deeds under him. Nevertheless, as I sit here in your house, ask me some other question and do not seek to know my race and family, or you will recall memories that will yet more increase my sorrow. I am full of heaviness, but I ought not to sit weeping and wailing in another person's house, nor is it well to be thus grieving continually. I shall have one of the servants or even yourself complaining of me, and saying that my eyes swim with tears because I am heavy with wine."

Then Penelope answered, "Stranger, heaven robbed me of all beauty, whether of face or figure, when the Argives set sail for Troy and my dear husband with them. If he were to return and look after my affairs I should be both more respected and should show a better presence to the world. As it is, I am oppressed with care, and with the afflictions which heaven has seen fit to heap upon me. The chiefs from all our islands—Dulichium, Same, and Zacynthus, as also from Ithaca itself, are wooing me against my will and are wasting my estate. I can therefore show no attention to strangers, nor suppliants, nor to people who say that they are skilled artisans, but am all the time broken-hearted about Odysseus. They want me to marry again at once, and I have to invent stratagems in order to deceive them. In the first place heaven put it in my mind to set up a great loom in my room, and to begin working upon an enormous piece of fine needlework. Then I said to them, 'Sweethearts, Odysseus is indeed dead, still, do not press me to marry again immediately; wait—for I would not have my skill in needlework perish unrecorded—till I have finished making a shroud for the hero Laertes, to be ready against the time when death shall take him. He is very rich, and the women of the place will talk if he is laid out without a shroud.' This was what I said, and they assented; whereon I used to keep working at my great web all day long, but at night I would unpick the stitches again by torch light. I fooled them in this way for three years without their finding it out, but as time wore on and I was now in my fourth year, in the waning of moons, and many days had been accomplished, those good for nothing hussies my maids betrayed me to the suitors, who broke in upon me and caught me; they were very angry with me, so I was forced to finish my work whether I would or no. And now I do not see how I can find any further shift for getting out of this marriage. My parents are putting great pressure upon me, and my son chafes at the ravages the suitors are making upon his estate, for he is now old enough to understand all about it and is perfectly able to look after his own affairs, for heaven has blessed him with an excellent disposition. Still, notwithstanding all this, tell me who you are and where you come from—for you must have had father and mother of some sort; you cannot be the son of an oak or of a rock."

Then Odysseus answered, "Madam, wife of Odysseus, since you persist in asking me about my family, I will answer, no matter what it costs me: people must expect to be pained when they have been exiles as long as I have, and suffered as much among as many peoples. Nevertheless, as regards your question I will tell you all you ask. There is a fair and fruitful island in mid-ocean called Crete; it is thickly peopled and there are ninety cities in it: the people speak many different languages which overlap one another, for there are Achaeans, brave Eteocretans, Dorians of three-fold race, and noble Pelasgians. There is a great town there, Knossos, where Minos reigned who every nine years had a conference with Zeus himself. Minos was father to Deucalion, whose son I am, for Deucalion had two sons Idomeneus and myself. Idomeneus sailed for Troy, and I, who am the younger, am called Aethon; my brother, however, was at once the older and the more valiant of the two; hence it was in Crete that I saw Odysseus and showed him hospitality, for the winds took him there as he was on his way to Troy, carrying him out of his course from cape Malea and leaving him in Amnisus off the cave of Eileithyia, where the harbors are difficult to enter and he could hardly find shelter from the winds that were then raging. As soon as he got there he went into the town and asked for Idomeneus, claiming to be his old and valued friend, but Idomeneus had already set sail for Troy some ten or twelve days earlier, so I took him to my own house and showed him every kind of hospitality, for I had abundance of everything. Moreover, I fed the men who were with him with barley meal from the public store, and got subscriptions of wine and oxen for them to sacrifice to their heart's content. They stayed with me twelve days, for there was a gale blowing from the North so strong that one could hardly keep one's feet on land. I suppose some unfriendly god had raised it for them, but on the thirteenth day the wind dropped, and they got away."

Many a plausible tale did Odysseus further tell her, and Penelope wept as she listened, for her heart was melted. As the snow wastes upon the mountain tops when the winds from South East and West have breathed upon it and thawed it till the rivers run bank full with water, even so did her cheeks overflow with tears for the husband who was all the time sitting by her side. Odysseus felt for her and was sorry for her, but he kept his eyes as hard as horn or iron without letting them so much as quiver, so cunningly did he restrain his tears. Then, when she had relieved herself by weeping, she turned to him again and said: "Now, stranger, I shall put you to the test and see whether or no you really did entertain my husband and his men, as you say you did. Tell me, then, how he was dressed, what kind of a man he was to look at, and so also with his companions."

"Madam," answered Odysseus, "it is such a long time ago that I can hardly say. Twenty years are come and gone since he left my home, and went elsewhither; but I will tell you as well as I can recollect. Odysseus wore a mantle of purple wool, double lined, and it was fastened by a gold brooch with two catches for the pin. On the face of this there was a device that showed a dog holding a spotted fawn between his fore paws, and watching it as it lay panting upon the ground. Every one marveled at the way in which these things had been done in gold, the dog looking at the fawn, and strangling it, while the fawn was struggling convulsively to escape. As for the shirt that he wore next his skin, it was so soft that it fitted him like the skin of an onion, and glistened in the sunlight to the admiration of all the women who beheld it. Furthermore I say, and lay my saying to your heart, that I do not know whether Odysseus wore these clothes when he left home, or whether one of his companions had given them to him while he was on his voyage; or possibly someone at whose house he was staying made him a present of them, for he was a man of many friends and had few equals among the Achaeans. I myself gave him a sword of bronze and a beautiful purple mantle, double lined, with a shirt that went down to his feet, and I sent him on board his ship with every mark of honor. He had a servant with him, a little older than himself, and I can tell you what he was like; his shoulders were hunched, he was dark, and he had thick curly hair. His name was Eurybates, and Odysseus treated him with greater familiarity than he did any of the others, as being the most like-minded with himself."

Penelope was moved still more deeply as she heard the indisputable proofs that Odysseus laid before her; and when she had again found relief in tears she said to him, "Stranger, I was already disposed to pity you, but henceforth you shall be honored and made welcome in my house. It was I who gave Odysseus the clothes you speak of. I took them out of the store room and folded them up myself, and I gave him also the gold brooch to wear as an ornament. Alas! I shall never welcome him home again. It was by an ill fate that he ever set out for that detested city whose very name I cannot bring myself even to mention."

Then Odysseus answered, "Madam, wife of Odysseus, do not disfigure yourself further by grieving thus bitterly for your loss, though I can hardly blame you for doing so. A woman who has loved her husband and borne him children, would naturally be grieved at losing him, even though he were a worse man than Odysseus, who they say was like a god. Still, cease your tears and listen to what I can tell you. I will hide nothing from you, and can say with perfect truth that I have lately heard of Odysseus as being alive and on his way home; he is among the Thesprotians, and is bringing back much valuable treasure that he has begged from one and another of them; but his ship and all his crew were lost as they were leaving the Thrinacian island, for Zeus and the sun-god were angry with him because his men had slaughtered the sun-god's cattle, and they were all drowned to a man. But Odysseus stuck to the keel of the ship and was drifted on to the land of the Phaeacians, who are near of kin to the immortals, and who treated him as though he had been a god, giving him many presents, and wishing to escort him home safe and sound. In fact Odysseus would have been here long ago, had he not thought better to go from land to land gathering wealth; for there is no man living who is so wily as he is; there is no one can compare with him. Pheidon king of the Thesprotians told me all this, and he swore to me—making drink-offerings in his house as he did so—that the ship was by the water side and the crew found who would take Odysseus to his own country. He sent me off first, for there happened to be a Thesprotian ship sailing for the wheat-growing island of Dulichium, but he showed me all the treasure Odysseus had got together, and he had enough lying in the house of king Pheidon to keep his family for ten generations; but the king said Odysseus had gone to Dodona that he might learn Zeus's mind from the high oak tree, and know whether after so long an absence he should return to Ithaca openly or in secret. So you may know he is safe and will be here shortly; he is close at hand and cannot remain away from home much longer; nevertheless I will confirm my words with an oath, and call Zeus who is the first and mightiest of all gods to witness, as also that hearth of Odysseus to which I have now come, that all I have spoken shall surely come to pass. Odysseus will return in this self same year; with the end of this moon and the beginning of the next he will be here."

"May it be even so," answered Penelope; "if your words come true you shall have such gifts and such good will from me that all who see you shall congratulate you; but I know very well how it will be. Odysseus will not return, neither will you get your escort hence, for so surely as that Odysseus ever was, there are now no longer any such masters in the house as he was, to receive honorable strangers or to further them on their way home. And now, you maids, wash his feet for him, and make him a bed on a couch with rugs and blankets, that he may be warm and quiet till morning. Then, at day break wash him and anoint him again, that he may sit in the courtyard and take his meals with Telemachus. It shall be the worse for any one of these hateful people who is uncivil to him; like it or not, he shall have no more to do in this house. For how, sir, shall you be able to learn whether or no I am superior to others of my sex both in goodness of heart and understanding, if I let you dine in my courtyards squalid and ill clad? Men live but for a little season; if they are hard, and deal hardly, people wish them ill so long as they are alive, and speak contemptuously of them when they are dead, but he that is righteous and deals righteously, the people tell of his praise among all lands, and many shall call him blessed."

Odysseus answered, "Madam, I have foresworn rugs and blankets from the day that I left the snowy ranges of Crete to go on shipboard. I will lie as I have lain on many a sleepless night hitherto. Night after night have I passed in any rough sleeping place, and waited for morning. Nor, again, do I like having my feet washed; I shall not let any of the young hussies about your house touch my feet; but, if you have any old and respectable woman who has gone through as much trouble as I have, I will allow her to wash them."

To this Penelope said, "My dear sir, of all the guests who ever yet came to my house there never was one who spoke in all things with such admirable propriety as you do. There happens to be in the house a most respectable old woman—the same who received my poor dear husband in her arms the night he was born, and nursed him in infancy. She is very feeble now, but she shall wash your feet." "Come here," said she, "Euryclea, and wash your master's age-mate; I suppose Odysseus' hands and feet are very much the same now as his are, for trouble ages all of us dreadfully fast."

On these words the old woman covered her face with her hands; she began to weep and made lamentation saying, "My dear child, I cannot think whatever I am to do with you. I am certain no one was ever more god-fearing than yourself, and yet Zeus hates you. No one in the whole world ever burned him more thigh bones, nor gave him finer sacrifices when you prayed you might come to a green old age yourself and see your son grow up to take after you: yet see how he has prevented you alone from ever getting back to your own home. I have no doubt the women in some foreign palace which Odysseus has got to are gibing at him as all these sluts here have been gibing at you. I do not wonder at your not choosing to let them wash you after the manner in which they have insulted you; I will wash your feet myself gladly enough, as Penelope has said that I am to do so; I will wash them both for Penelope's sake and for your own, for you have raised the most lively feelings of compassion in my mind; and let me say this moreover, which pray attend to; we have had all kinds of strangers in distress come here before now, but I make bold to say that no one ever yet came who was so like Odysseus in figure, voice, and feet as you are."
"Those who have seen us both," answered Odysseus, "have always said we were wonderfully like each other, and now you have noticed it too."

Then the old woman took the cauldron in which she was going to wash his feet, and poured plenty of cold water into it, adding hot till the bath was warm enough. Odysseus sat by the fire, but ere long he turned away from the light, for it occurred to him that when the old woman had hold of his leg she would recognize a certain scar which it bore, whereon the whole truth would come out. And indeed as soon as she began washing her master, she at once knew the scar as one that had been given him by a wild boar when he was hunting on Mt. Parnassus with his excellent grandfather Autolycus—who was the most accomplished thief and perjurer in the whole world—and with the sons of Autolycus. Hermes himself had endowed him with this gift, for he used to burn the thigh bones of goats and kids to him, so he took pleasure in his companionship. It happened once that Autolycus had gone to Ithaca and had found the child of his daughter just born. As soon as he had done supper Euryclea set the infant upon his knees and said, "Autolycus, you must find a name for your grandson; you greatly wished that you might have one."

"Son-in-law and daughter," replied Autolycus, "call the child thus: I am highly displeased with a large number of people in one place and another, both men and women; so name the child 'Odysseus,' or the child of anger. When he grows up and comes to visit his mother's family on Mt. Parnassus, where my possessions lie, I will make him a present and will send him on his way rejoicing."

Odysseus, therefore, went to Parnassus to get the presents from Autolycus, who with his sons shook hands with him and gave him welcome. His grandmother Amphithea threw her arms about him, and kissed his head, and both his beautiful eyes, while Autolycus desired his sons to get dinner ready, and they did as he told them. They brought in a five year old bull, flayed it, made it ready and divided it into joints; these they then cut carefully up into smaller pieces and spitted them; they roasted them sufficiently and served the portions round. Thus through the livelong day to the going down of the sun they feasted, and every man had his full share so that all were satisfied; but when the sun set and it came on dark, they went to bed and enjoyed the boon of sleep.

When the child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn, appeared, the sons of Autolycus went out with their hounds hunting, and Odysseus went too. They climbed the wooded slopes of Parnassus and soon reached its breezy upland valleys; but as the sun was beginning to beat upon the fields, fresh-risen from the slow still currents of Oceanus, they came to a mountain dell. The dogs were in front searching for the tracks of the beast they were chasing, and after them came the sons of Autolycus, among whom was Odysseus, close behind the dogs, and he had a long spear in his hand. Here was the lair of a huge boar among some thick brushwood, so dense that the wind and rain could not get through it, nor could the sun's rays pierce it, and the ground underneath lay thick with fallen leaves. The boar heard the noise of the men's feet, and the hounds baying on every side as the huntsmen came up to him, so he rushed from his lair, raised the bristles on his neck, and stood at bay with fire flashing from his eyes. Odysseus was the first to raise his spear and try to drive it into the brute, but the boar was too quick for him, and charged him sideways, ripping him above the knee with a gash that tore deep though it did not reach the bone. As for the boar, Odysseus hit him on the right shoulder, and the point of the spear went right through him, so that he fell groaning in the dust until the life went out of him. The sons of Autolycus busied themselves with the carcass of the boar, and bound Odysseus' wound; then, after saying a spell to stop the bleeding, they went home as fast as they could. But when Autolycus and his sons had thoroughly healed Odysseus, they made him some splendid presents, and sent him back to Ithaca with much mutual good will. When he got back, his father and mother were rejoiced to see him, and asked him all about it, and how he had hurt himself to get the scar; so he told them how the boar had ripped him when he was out hunting with Autolycus and his sons on Mt. Parnassus.

As soon as Euryclea had got the scarred limb in her hands and had well hold of it, she recognized it and dropped the foot at once. The leg fell into the bath, which rang out and was overturned, so that all the water was spilt on the ground; Euryclea's eyes between her joy and her grief filled with tears, and she could not speak, but she caught Odysseus by the beard and said, "My dear child, I am sure you must be Odysseus himself, only I did not know you till I had actually touched and handled you."

As she spoke she looked towards Penelope, as though wanting to tell her that her dear husband was in the house, but Penelope was unable to look in that direction and observe what was going on, for Athena had diverted her attention; so Odysseus caught Euryclea by the throat with his right hand and with his left drew her close to him, and said, "Nurse, do you wish to be the ruin of me, you who nursed me at your own breast, now that after twenty years of wandering I am at last come to my own home again? Since it has been borne in upon you by heaven to recognize me, hold your tongue, and do not say a word about it to any one else in the house, for if you do I tell you—and it shall surely be—that if heaven grants me to take the lives of these suitors, I will not spare you, though you are my own nurse, when I am killing the other women."

"My child," answered Euryclea, "what are you talking about? You know very well that nothing can either bend or break me. I will hold my tongue like a stone or a piece of iron; furthermore let me say, and lay my saying to your heart, when heaven has delivered the suitors into your hand, I will give you a list of the women in the house who have been ill-behaved, and of those who are guiltless."
And Odysseus answered, "Nurse, you ought not to speak in that way; I am well able to form my own opinion about one and all of them; hold your tongue and leave everything to heaven."

As he said this Euryclea left the courtyard to fetch some more water, for the first had been all spilt; and when she had washed him and anointed him with oil, Odysseus drew his seat nearer to the fire to warm himself, and hid the scar under his rags. Then Penelope began talking to him and said:

"Stranger, I should like to speak with you briefly about another matter. It is indeed nearly bed time—for those, at least, who can sleep in spite of sorrow. As for myself, heaven has given me a life of such unmeasurable woe, that even by day when I am attending to my duties and looking after the servants, I am still weeping and lamenting during the whole time; then, when night comes, and we all of us go to bed, I lie awake thinking, and my heart becomes a prey to the most incessant and cruel tortures. As the dun nightingale, daughter of Pandareus, sings in the early spring from her seat in shadiest covert hid, and with many a plaintive trill pours out the tale how by mishap she killed her own child Itylus, son of king Zethus, even so does my mind toss and turn in its uncertainty whether I ought to stay with my son here, and safeguard my substance, my bondsmen, and the greatness of my house, out of regard to public opinion and the memory of my late husband, or whether it is not now time for me to go with the best of these suitors who are wooing me and making me such magnificent presents. As long as my son was still young, and unable to understand, he would not hear of my leaving my husband's house, but now that he is full grown he begs and prays me to do so, being incensed at the way in which the suitors are eating up his property. Listen, then, to a dream that I have had and interpret it for me if you can. I have twenty geese about the house that eat mash out of a trough, and of which I am exceedingly fond. I dreamed that a great eagle came swooping down from a mountain, and dug his curved beak into the neck of each of them till he had killed them all. Presently he soared off into the sky, and left them lying dead about the yard; whereon I wept in my dream till all my maids gathered round me, so piteously was I grieving because the eagle had killed my geese. Then he came back again, and perching on a projecting rafter spoke to me with human voice, and told me to leave off crying. 'Be of good courage,' he said, 'daughter of Icarius; this is no dream, but a vision of good omen that shall surely come to pass. The geese are the suitors, and I am no longer an eagle, but your own husband, who am come back to you, and who will bring these suitors to a disgraceful end.' On this I woke, and when I looked out I saw my geese at the trough eating their mash as usual."

"This dream, Madam," replied Odysseus, "can admit but of one interpretation, for had not Odysseus himself told you how it shall be fulfilled? The death of the suitors is portended, and not one single one of them will escape."

And Penelope answered, "Stranger, dreams are very curious and unaccountable things, and they do not by any means invariably come true. There are two gates through which these unsubstantial fancies proceed; the one is of horn, and the other ivory. Those that come through the gate of ivory are fatuous, but those from the gate of horn mean something to those that see them. I do not think, however, that my own dream came through the gate of horn, though I and my son should be most thankful if it proves to have done so. Furthermore I say—and lay my saying to your heart—the coming dawn will usher in the ill-omened day that is to sever me from the house of Odysseus, for I am about to hold a tournament of axes. My husband used to set up twelve axes in the court, one in front of the other, like the stays upon which a ship is built; he would then go back from them and shoot an arrow through the whole twelve. I shall make the suitors try to do the same thing, and whichever of them can string the bow most easily, and send his arrow through all the twelve axes, him will I follow, and quit this house of my lawful husband, so goodly and so abounding in wealth. But even so, I doubt not that I shall remember it in my dreams."

Then Odysseus answered, "Madam, wife of Odysseus, you need not defer your tournament, for Odysseus will return ere ever they can string the bow, handle it how they will, and send their arrows through the iron."

To this Penelope said, "As long, sir, as you will sit here and talk to me, I can have no desire to go to bed. Still, people cannot do permanently without sleep, and heaven has appointed us dwellers on earth a time for all things. I will therefore go upstairs and recline upon that couch which I have never ceased to flood with my tears from the day Odysseus set out for the city with a hateful name."
She then went upstairs to her own room, not alone, but attended by her maidens, and when there, she lamented her dear husband till Athena shed sweet sleep over her eyelids.

chapters.title: Book XX — Odysseus cannot sleep—Penelope’s prayer to Diana—the two signs from heaven—Eumaeus and Philoetius arrive—the suitors dine—Ctesippus throws an ox’s foot at Odysseus—Theoclymenus foretells disaster and leaves the house
paragraphs: Odysseus slept in the courtyard on a raw bull's hide, with several sheepskins thrown over it from the animals the suitors had devoured. Eurynome covered him with a cloak after he lay down. There Odysseus lay sleepless, brooding over how he would kill the suitors. Soon the servant women who had been sleeping with the suitors came giggling and laughing out of the house together. This made Odysseus furious, and he wondered whether to leap up and kill every one of them on the spot, or let them enjoy one final night with the suitors. His heart growled within him like a mother dog protecting her puppies, baring her teeth at a stranger. But he struck his chest and said, "Heart, be still. You endured worse than this when the terrible Cyclops devoured your brave companions. Yet you bore it in silence until your cunning got you safely out of that cave, though you thought you were doomed."

He scolded his heart this way and forced it to endurance, but he tossed restlessly like someone turning a stomach full of blood and fat over a hot fire, flipping it from side to side to cook it quickly. So he turned from side to side, wondering how he alone could manage to kill so many wicked suitors. Then Athena came down from heaven in the form of a woman and hovered over his head, saying, "My poor, troubled man, why do you lie awake like this? This is your house. Your wife is safe inside, and so is your son—a young man any father would be proud of."

"Goddess," Odysseus replied, "everything you say is true, but I'm uncertain how I can kill these wicked suitors single-handedly, considering how many there are. And there's an even greater problem: even if Zeus and you help me succeed in killing them, where can I escape to from their families' revenge afterward?"

"Shame on you!" Athena replied. "Anyone else would trust a weaker ally than me, even if that ally were only mortal and less wise than I am. Am I not a goddess? Haven't I protected you through all your troubles? I tell you plainly that even if fifty bands of armed men surrounded us, eager to kill us, you would still drive off all their sheep and cattle. Now go to sleep—staying awake all night does no good, and you'll be free of your troubles soon."
As she spoke, she poured sleep over his eyes and returned to Olympus.

While Odysseus surrendered to deep sleep that eased his sorrows, his noble wife awakened. Sitting up in bed, she began to weep. After crying, she prayed to Artemis: "Great goddess Artemis, daughter of Zeus, shoot an arrow through my heart and kill me, or let some whirlwind snatch me up and carry me through dark paths until it drops me into the flowing depths of Ocean, as happened to Pandareus's daughters. Those daughters lost their parents when the gods killed them, leaving them orphans. But Aphrodite cared for them, feeding them cheese, honey, and sweet wine. Hera taught them to surpass all women in beauty and wisdom. Artemis gave them dignity, and Athena blessed them with every accomplishment. But when Aphrodite went to Olympus to ask Zeus about arranging their marriages—for he knows what will and won't happen to everyone—storm winds swept them away to serve the dread Furies. Just so, I wish the heavenly gods would hide me from mortal sight, or that Artemis would strike me down. I would gladly go beneath the sorrowful earth if I could do so while still faithful to Odysseus alone, without having to accept a lesser man. Besides, no matter how much people grieve during the day, they can bear it as long as they can sleep at night, for when eyes close in slumber, people forget both joy and sorrow. But my misery haunts me even in dreams. Just tonight I dreamed someone lay beside me who looked exactly like Odysseus when he left with his army. I rejoiced, believing it was no dream but reality itself."

At daybreak, Odysseus heard the sound of her weeping, and it puzzled him—it seemed as if she already knew him and was beside him. He gathered up the cloak and fleeces he'd slept on and placed them on a seat in the courtyard, but took the bull's hide outside. He raised his hands to heaven and prayed: "Father Zeus, since you saw fit to bring me home over land and sea after all the suffering you laid on me, give me a sign from someone now waking in the house, and let me have another sign from outside."

Zeus heard his prayer and immediately thundered from the brightness of Olympus, high above the clouds. Odysseus was glad to hear it. At the same time, a mill-woman working nearby in the mill room lifted her voice and gave him another sign. Twelve mill-women worked there, grinding wheat and barley—the staff of life. The others had finished their work and gone to rest, but this one hadn't finished because she wasn't as strong as the others. When she heard the thunder, she stopped grinding and spoke to her master: "Father Zeus, ruler of heaven and earth, you've thundered from a clear sky without a cloud in sight—this means something for someone. Grant the prayer of your poor servant who calls on you: let this be the very last day the suitors dine in Odysseus's house. They've worn me out grinding meal for them, and I hope they never eat another dinner anywhere."
Odysseus was glad to hear these omens—the woman's words and the thunder—for he knew they meant he would have his revenge on the suitors.

The other maids in the house got up and lit the fire on the hearth. Telemachus also rose and dressed, strapping his sword over his shoulder, binding sandals on his feet, and taking a sharp bronze-pointed spear. He went to the courtyard threshold and said to Eurycleia, "Nurse, did you make the stranger comfortable with bed and food, or did you let him fend for himself? My mother is a good woman, but she has a way of paying great attention to lesser people while neglecting those who are actually much better."

"Don't find fault, child," Eurycleia said, "when there's no cause. The stranger sat and drank wine as long as he wanted. Your mother asked if he wanted more bread, but he said no. When he wanted to sleep, she told the servants to make him a bed, but he said he was such a wretched outcast that he wouldn't sleep on a bed with blankets. He insisted on having a raw bull's hide and sheepskins in the courtyard, and I threw a cloak over him myself."

Then Telemachus left the courtyard for the place where the Achaeans held assembly, carrying his spear and accompanied by his two dogs. Eurycleia called the maids: "Come, wake up! Start sweeping the courtyards and sprinkling them with water to settle the dust. Put covers on the seats. Some of you wipe down the tables with wet sponges. Clean the mixing bowls and cups, and fetch water from the spring right away. The suitors will be here soon—they'll come early since it's a feast day."

She spoke, and they did exactly as she ordered. Twenty went to the spring for water while others busied themselves around the house. The men who served the suitors also arrived and began chopping firewood. Soon the women returned from the spring, followed by the swineherd with the three finest pigs he could find. He let them feed around the grounds, then said cheerfully to Odysseus, "Stranger, are the suitors treating you any better now, or are they still as arrogant as ever?"
"May heaven," Odysseus replied, "punish them for the wickedness with which they act so shamelessly in another man's house."

While they talked, Melanthius the goatherd arrived, bringing his best goats for the suitors' dinner, with two shepherds helping him. They tied the goats under the gatehouse, and then Melanthius began taunting Odysseus: "Are you still here, stranger, pestering people by begging around the house? Why don't you go somewhere else? You and I won't reach an understanding until we've traded some blows. You beg without any decency—aren't there other feasts among the Achaeans besides this one?"

Odysseus made no reply but bowed his head in brooding silence. Then a third man, Philoetius, joined them, bringing a barren heifer and some goats. The ferrymen had brought them across. Philoetius secured his animals under the gatehouse, then approached the swineherd. "Swineherd," he said, "who is this stranger who just arrived? Is he one of your men? What's his background? Where does he come from? Poor fellow, he looks like he was once a great man, but the gods bring sorrow to whomever they choose—even to kings, if it pleases them."

He went up to Odysseus and took his right hand: "Good day, father stranger. You seem very unfortunate now, but I hope you'll have better times ahead. Father Zeus, you're the most cruel of all gods. We're your own children, yet you show us no mercy in our misery and suffering. I broke into a sweat when I saw this man, and my eyes filled with tears, because he reminds me of Odysseus, who I fear is wandering in just such rags as these, if he's still alive. If he's already dead in Hades' house, then alas for my good master, who made me his herdsman when I was young among the Cephallenians. Now his cattle are countless—no one could have done better with them than I have, for they've multiplied like ears of grain. Yet I must keep bringing them for others to eat, men who don't care about his son though he's in the house, and don't fear heaven's wrath, but are already eager to divide Odysseus's property since he's been gone so long. I've often thought—though it wouldn't be right while his son lives—of taking the cattle to some foreign country. As bad as that would be, it's harder to stay here and be mistreated over other people's herds. My situation is unbearable, and I would have run away long ago to serve another master, except I believe my poor lord will return and send all these suitors flying from the house."

"Herdsman," Odysseus replied, "you seem like a good and sensible man. So I'll tell you something and swear an oath to it: By Zeus, chief of all gods, and by Odysseus's hearth that I've now reached, Odysseus will return before you leave this place. If you wish, you'll see him killing the suitors who now rule here."
"If Zeus brought this to pass," the herdsman replied, "you'd see how I'd do my utmost to help him."
Eumaeus likewise prayed that Odysseus might return home.

While they talked, the suitors were plotting to murder Telemachus. But a bird flew past on their left—an eagle carrying a dove in its talons. Seeing this, Amphinomus said, "Friends, our plot to kill Telemachus won't succeed. Let's go to dinner instead."

The others agreed, so they went inside and laid their cloaks on the benches and seats. They sacrificed sheep, goats, pigs, and the heifer. When the inner organs were cooked, they served them around. They mixed wine in the bowls, the swineherd gave each man his cup, Philoetius distributed bread from baskets, and Melanthius poured the wine. Then they began eating the good food before them.

Telemachus deliberately seated Odysseus in the stone-paved part of the courtyard, giving him a shabby seat at a small table by himself. He had a portion of the inner meat brought to him with wine in a gold cup. "Sit there," he said, "and drink wine among the nobles. I'll put a stop to the insults and blows from the suitors. This isn't a public tavern—it belongs to Odysseus and has passed from him to me. Therefore, suitors, keep your hands and tongues to yourselves, or there'll be trouble."

The suitors bit their lips, amazed at his bold speech. Then Antinous said, "We don't like such language, but we'll tolerate it, since Telemachus is seriously threatening us. If Zeus had allowed us, we would have silenced his brave talk by now."
Antinous spoke, but Telemachus ignored him. Meanwhile, heralds were bringing the sacred offering through the city, and the Achaeans gathered under Apollo's shady grove.

They roasted the outer meat, drew it off the spits, gave each man his portion, and feasted to their hearts' content. The servers gave Odysseus exactly the same portion as the others, for Telemachus had ordered it.

But Athena wouldn't let the suitors drop their insolence for a moment—she wanted Odysseus to become even more bitter against them. Among them was a crude fellow named Ctesippus from Same. Confident in his great wealth, he was courting Odysseus's wife. He said to the suitors, "Listen to what I say. The stranger has already received as large a portion as anyone else, which is proper—it's not right to mistreat any guest of Telemachus who comes here. But I'll give him a present of my own, so he'll have something to give the bath-woman or another of Odysseus's servants."

As he spoke, he picked up a cow's hoof from the meat basket and hurled it at Odysseus. But Odysseus ducked slightly and avoided it, smiling grimly like a Sardinian as he did so. The hoof hit the wall instead of him. Telemachus spoke angrily to Ctesippus: "It's lucky for you that the stranger moved his head and you missed. If you'd hit him, I would have run you through with my spear, and your father would be arranging your funeral instead of your wedding in this house. So I want no more disgraceful behavior from any of you. I'm grown up now and understand good and evil instead of being the child I was before.
