I've long watched you killing my sheep and consuming my grain and wine. I've endured this because one man can't match many, but do me no more violence. Still, if you want to kill me, go ahead—I'd rather die than see such shameful scenes day after day: guests insulted and servant women dragged around the house improperly."

Everyone fell silent until finally Agelaus, son of Damastor, said, "No one should take offense at what was just said or argue with it—it's quite reasonable. Stop mistreating the stranger or any other servants in the house. I'd like to say something friendly to Telemachus and his mother, which I hope both will accept: 'As long as you had reason to hope Odysseus would return someday, no one could blame you for waiting and allowing the suitors in your house. It would have been better if he had returned, but it's now clear enough that he never will. So discuss this quietly with your mother and tell her to marry the best man who makes her the most advantageous offer. Then you'll be able to manage your inheritance and eat and drink in peace, while your mother looks after some other man's house, not yours.'"

Telemachus replied, "By Zeus and by my unhappy father's sufferings—whether he's died far from Ithaca or wanders in some distant land—I put no obstacles in my mother's way regarding marriage. On the contrary, I urge her to choose whoever she will, and I'll give her countless gifts besides. But I dare not force her to leave the house against her wishes. Heaven forbid I should do that."

Athena now made the suitors burst into uncontrollable laughter and addled their wits, but they laughed with forced mirth. Their meat became smeared with blood, their eyes filled with tears, and their hearts grew heavy with foreboding. Seeing this, Theoclymenus said, "Unhappy men, what's wrong with you? Darkness shrouds you from head to foot, your cheeks are wet with tears, the air rings with wailing voices, the walls and beams drip blood, the gateway and courtyard beyond are full of ghosts streaming down into hell's night. The sun is blotted from heaven, and a cursed gloom covers all the land."
He spoke, and they all laughed heartily. Eurymachus said, "This stranger who just arrived has lost his mind. Servants, escort him to the street, since he finds it so dark in here."

But Theoclymenus replied, "Eurymachus, you needn't send anyone with me. I have eyes, ears, feet, and a sound mind. I'll take these out of the house myself, for I see disaster hanging over you. Not one of you men who insult people and plot evil in Odysseus's house will escape it."

He left the house as he spoke and returned to Piraeus, who welcomed him. But the suitors kept looking at each other and provoking Telemachus by mocking the strangers. One insolent fellow said, "Telemachus, you're unlucky with your guests. First you have this persistent beggar who wants bread and wine but has no skill for work or fighting—completely useless. Now here's another setting himself up as a prophet. Let me persuade you—it would be much better to put them on a ship and send them to Sicily to sell for whatever they'll bring."
Telemachus paid him no attention but sat silently watching his father, expecting any moment that he would begin his attack on the suitors.

Meanwhile, wise Penelope, Icarius's daughter, had a fine seat placed facing the court and colonnades so she could hear everything being said. The dinner had indeed been prepared with much celebration—it was both good and plentiful, for they had sacrificed many animals. But the supper was yet to come, and nothing could be more gruesome than the meal a goddess and a brave man would soon set before them—for they had brought their doom upon themselves.

chapters.title: Book XXI — The trial of the axes, during which Odysseus reveals himself to Eumaeus and Philoetius
paragraphs: Athena now put it into Penelope's mind to make the suitors test their skill with the bow and iron axes in a contest among themselves, as a way to bring about their destruction. She went upstairs and got the storeroom key, which was made of bronze with an ivory handle. Then she went with her servants to the storeroom at the end of the house, where her husband's treasures of gold, bronze, and wrought iron were kept, and where his bow was also stored, along with the quiver full of deadly arrows that had been given to him by a friend he had met in Lacedaemon—Iphitus, son of Eurytus. The two had encountered each other in Messene at the house of Ortilochus, where Odysseus was staying to recover a debt owed by the whole people. The Messenians had stolen three hundred sheep from Ithaca and sailed away with them and their shepherds. To recover these sheep, Odysseus had taken a long journey while still quite young, sent on this mission by his father and the other chiefs. Iphitus had also gone there to try to get back twelve brood mares he had lost, along with their mule foals. These mares would be his death in the end, for when he went to the house of Zeus's son, mighty Heracles, who performed such incredible feats of valor, Heracles shamefully killed him, though he was his guest. He feared neither heaven's vengeance nor respected his own table that he had set before Iphitus, but killed him despite everything and kept the mares for himself. It was while claiming these mares that Iphitus met Odysseus and gave him the bow that mighty Eurytus had carried, which had been left to his son when he died. Odysseus gave him in return a sword and spear, and this was the beginning of a strong friendship, though they never visited each other's homes, for Zeus's son Heracles killed Iphitus before they could do so. This bow, given to him by Iphitus, had not been taken by Odysseus when he sailed for Troy. He had used it as long as he lived at home, but had left it behind as a keepsake from a valued friend.

Penelope soon reached the oak threshold of the storeroom. The carpenter had planed it smooth and drawn a line on it to make it perfectly straight, then set the door posts into it and hung the doors. She loosened the strap from the door handle, put in the key, and drove it straight home to shoot back the bolts that held the doors. These flew open with a noise like a bull bellowing in a meadow, and Penelope stepped onto the raised platform where chests stood containing fine linen and clothes laid away with fragrant herbs. Reaching up from there, she took down the bow with its case from the peg where it hung. She sat down with it across her knees, weeping bitterly as she took the bow from its case. When her tears had given her relief, she went to the hall where the suitors were, carrying the bow and quiver with its many deadly arrows. Her servants came with her, bearing a chest containing much iron and bronze that her husband had won as prizes. When she reached the suitors, she stood by one of the pillars supporting the hall's roof, holding a veil before her face, with a maid on either side of her. Then she spoke:

"Listen to me, you suitors who persist in abusing the hospitality of this house because its owner has been long absent, with no other excuse than that you want to marry me. Since this is the prize you're competing for, I will bring out the mighty bow of Odysseus. Whoever among you can string it most easily and send his arrow through each of the twelve axes—him will I follow, leaving this house of my lawful husband, so beautiful and rich in wealth. Even so, I'm sure I will remember it in my dreams."

As she spoke, she told Eumaeus to set the bow and pieces of iron before the suitors. Eumaeus wept as he took them to do as she commanded. Nearby, the cattle herder also wept when he saw his master's bow, but Antinous scolded them. "You country fools," he said, "silly simpletons! Why should you add to your mistress's sorrows by crying like this? She has enough to grieve her in losing her husband. Sit still and eat your dinner in silence, or go outside if you want to cry, and leave the bow behind. We suitors will have to compete for it with all our might, for we'll find it no easy matter to string such a bow as this. There isn't a man among us who is another Odysseus. I have seen him and remember him, though I was only a child then."

This is what he said, but all the time he expected to be able to string the bow and shoot through the iron. In fact, he would be the first to taste arrows from the hands of Odysseus, whom he was dishonoring in his own house—and encouraging the others to do the same.

Then Telemachus spoke. "Good heavens!" he exclaimed. "Zeus must have robbed me of my senses. Here is my dear and excellent mother saying she will leave this house and marry again, yet I'm laughing and enjoying myself as though nothing were happening. But suitors, since the contest has been agreed upon, let it proceed. It's for a woman whose equal cannot be found in Pylos, Argos, Mycenae, or even in Ithaca or on the mainland. You know this as well as I do—what need do I have to praise my mother? Come then, make no excuses for delay, but let's see whether you can string the bow or not. I too will try it, for if I can string it and shoot through the iron, I won't let my mother leave this house with a stranger, not if I can win the same prizes my father won before me."

As he spoke, he sprang from his seat, threw off his crimson cloak, and took his sword from his shoulder. First he set up the axes in a row, in a long trench he had dug for them and made straight with a line. Then he stamped the earth tight around them, and everyone was surprised to see him set them up so precisely, though he had never seen anything like this before. When this was done, he went to the threshold to try the bow. Three times he tugged at it, trying with all his strength to draw the string, and three times he had to give up, though he hoped to string the bow and shoot through the iron. He was trying for the fourth time and would have strung it, but Odysseus signaled him to stop despite all his eagerness. So he said:

"Alas! I must always be weak and powerless, or I'm too young and haven't yet reached my full strength to be able to defend myself if anyone attacks me. You others who are stronger than I am, try the bow and settle this contest."
With this he put the bow down, leaning it against the door that led into the house, with the arrow standing against the top of the bow. Then he sat down on the seat he had left, and Antinous said:
"Come forward, each of you in turn, going from right to left from where the wine server begins when he's pouring the wine."

The rest agreed, and Leiodes, son of Oenops, was the first to rise. He was the suitors' priest and sat in the corner near the wine bowl. He was the only man who hated their evil deeds and was disgusted with the others. He was now first to take the bow and arrow, so he went to the threshold to make his attempt. But he couldn't string the bow, for his hands were soft and unused to hard work, so they quickly grew tired. He said to the suitors, "My friends, I cannot string it. Let another try. This bow will take the life and soul from many a chief among us, for it's better to die than to live after missing the prize we've striven for so long and which has kept us together so long. Some of us are even now hoping and praying to marry Penelope, but when he has seen this bow and tried it, let him court and offer wedding gifts to some other woman, and let Penelope marry whoever makes her the best offer and whose fate it is to win her."
With this he put the bow down, leaning it against the door with the arrow standing against the tip of the bow. Then he returned to his seat, and Antinous rebuked him, saying:

"Leiodes, what are you talking about? Your words are terrible and intolerable—it makes me angry to listen to you. Shall this bow take the life of many chiefs among us merely because you cannot bend it yourself? True, you weren't born to be an archer, but there are others who will soon string it."

Then he said to Melanthius the goatherd, "Quick, light a fire in the courtyard and set a seat nearby with a sheepskin on it. Bring us also a large ball of fat from what they have in the house. Let us warm the bow and grease it—we'll then try it again and bring the contest to an end."

Melanthius lit the fire and set a seat covered with sheepskins beside it. He also brought a great ball of fat from what they had in the house, and the suitors warmed the bow and tried it again, but none of them was nearly strong enough to string it. Nevertheless, there still remained Antinous and Eurymachus, who were the ringleaders among the suitors and by far the strongest of them all.
Then the swineherd and the cattle herder left the hall together, and Odysseus followed them. When they had gotten outside the gates and outer courtyard, Odysseus said to them quietly:

"Cattle herder, and you, swineherd, I have something on my mind that I'm not sure whether to say or not, but I think I will say it. What kind of men would you be to stand by Odysseus if some god should bring him back here suddenly? Tell me which you would choose—to side with the suitors or with Odysseus?"
"Father Zeus," answered the cattle herder, "if only you would make it so! If some god were to bring Odysseus back, you would see with what strength and determination I would fight for him."

Eumaeus prayed in the same words to all the gods that Odysseus might return. When he saw for certain what their feelings were, Odysseus said, "It is I, Odysseus, who stands here. I have suffered much, but at last, in the twentieth year, I have returned to my own country. I find that you two alone of all my servants are glad that I should return, for I haven't heard any of the others praying for my homecoming. To you two, therefore, I will reveal the truth as it will be. If heaven delivers the suitors into my hands, I will find wives for both of you, give you houses and land close to my own, and you shall be to me like brothers and friends of Telemachus. I will now give you convincing proof so you may know me and be certain. Look, here is the scar from the boar's tusk that gored me when I was hunting on Mount Parnassus with the sons of Autolycus."

As he spoke, he drew his rags aside from the great scar. When they had examined it thoroughly, they both wept over Odysseus, threw their arms around him, and kissed his head and shoulders, while Odysseus kissed their hands and faces in return. The sun would have set on their mourning if Odysseus hadn't stopped them and said:

"Stop your weeping, in case someone comes outside and sees us and tells those inside. When you go in, do so separately, not together. I will go first, and you follow afterward. Let this be our signal: the suitors will all try to prevent me from getting hold of the bow and quiver. Therefore, Eumaeus, when you're carrying it around, place it in my hands and tell the women to close the doors of their quarters. If they hear any groaning or uproar as of men fighting in the house, they must not come out—they must stay quiet and remain where they are at their work. And I charge you, Philoetius, to secure the doors of the outer courtyard and bind them fast at once."
Having said this, he went back to the house and took the seat he had left. Soon his two servants followed him inside.

At this moment the bow was in Eurymachus's hands, who was warming it by the fire, but even so he couldn't string it, and he was deeply troubled. He heaved a deep sigh and said, "I grieve for myself and for all of us. I'm sorry that I must give up the marriage, but I don't care nearly as much about that, for there are plenty of other women in Ithaca and elsewhere. What troubles me most is the fact that we're so much weaker than Odysseus that we cannot string his bow. This will disgrace us in the eyes of future generations."

"It won't be so, Eurymachus," said Antinous, "and you know it yourself. Today is Apollo's feast throughout all the land—who can string a bow on such a day? Put it aside. As for the axes, they can stay where they are, for no one is likely to come to the house and take them away. Let the wine server go around with his cups so we may make our drink offerings and drop this matter of the bow. We'll tell Melanthius to bring us some goats tomorrow—the best he has. We can then offer thigh bones to Apollo the mighty archer and try the bow again, bringing the contest to an end."

The rest approved his words, and servants poured water over the guests' hands, while pages filled the mixing bowls with wine and water and handed it around after giving every man his drink offering. When they had made their offerings and drunk as much as each desired, Odysseus craftily said:

"Suitors of the illustrious queen, listen so I may speak my mind. I appeal especially to Eurymachus and to Antinous, who has just spoken so reasonably. Stop shooting for now and leave the matter to the gods, but in the morning let heaven give victory to whom it will. For the moment, however, give me the bow so I may test the power of my hands among you all and see whether I still have as much strength as I used to, or whether travel and neglect have ended it."

This made them all very angry, for they feared he might string the bow. Antinous therefore rebuked him fiercely, saying, "Wretched creature, you don't have so much as a grain of sense in your whole body. You should think yourself lucky to be allowed to dine unharmed among your betters, without having any smaller portion served to you than we others have had, and to be allowed to hear our conversation. No other beggar or stranger has been allowed to hear what we say among ourselves. The wine must be affecting you badly, as it does with all those who drink too much. It was wine that inflamed the Centaur Eurytion when he was staying with Peirithous among the Lapiths. When the wine got into his head, he went mad and did terrible things in Peirithous's house. This angered the heroes assembled there, so they rushed at him and cut off his ears and nose, then dragged him through the doorway out of the house. So he went away crazed, bearing the burden of his crime, robbed of understanding. From then on, there was war between mankind and the centaurs, but he brought it on himself through his own drunkenness. In the same way, I can tell you it will go badly for you if you string the bow. You'll find no mercy from anyone here, for we'll immediately ship you off to King Echetus, who kills everyone who comes near him. You'll never escape alive, so drink and keep quiet without picking a fight with men younger than yourself."

Then Penelope spoke to him. "Antinous," she said, "it's not right for you to mistreat any guest of Telemachus who comes to this house. If the stranger should prove strong enough to string mighty Odysseus's bow, can you suppose he would take me home with him and make me his wife? Even the man himself cannot have such an idea in his mind. None of you need let that disturb your feasting—it would be completely unreasonable."

"Queen Penelope," answered Eurymachus, "we don't suppose this man will take you away with him—that's impossible. But we're afraid that some of the common people, men or women among the Greeks, might go gossiping and say, 'These suitors are weak men. They're courting the wife of a brave man whose bow not one of them could string, yet a beggarly tramp who came to the house strung it at once and sent an arrow through the iron.' This is what will be said, and it will be a scandal against us."

"Eurymachus," Penelope answered, "people who persist in devouring the estate of a great chief and dishonoring his house must not expect others to think well of them. Why should you care if men talk as you think they will? This stranger is strong and well-built, and he says he's of noble birth. Give him the bow and let's see whether he can string it or not. I say—and it will surely be so—that if Apollo grants him the glory of stringing it, I will give him a cloak and shirt of good quality, with a javelin to keep off dogs and robbers, and a sharp sword. I will also give him sandals and see him sent safely wherever he wants to go."

Then Telemachus said, "Mother, I am the only man either in Ithaca or in the islands near Elis who has the right to let anyone have the bow or refuse it. No one will force me one way or the other, not even if I choose to give the stranger the bow outright and let him take it away with him. Go then into the house and busy yourself with your daily duties—your loom, your distaff, and managing your servants. This bow is a man's concern, and mine above all others, for I am master here."

She went back into the house wondering and took her son's words to heart. Then, going upstairs with her handmaids to her room, she mourned her dear husband until Athena sent sweet sleep over her eyelids.

The swineherd now took up the bow and was carrying it to Odysseus, but the suitors shouted at him from all parts of the hall, and one of them said, "You idiot, where are you taking the bow? Are you out of your mind? If Apollo and the other gods grant our prayer, your own hunting dogs will get you into some quiet place and tear you to pieces."

Eumaeus was frightened by all their shouting, so he put the bow down right there, but Telemachus yelled at him from the other side of the hall and threatened him, saying, "Father Eumaeus, bring the bow here despite them, or young as I am, I'll pelt you with stones back to the country, for I'm the stronger man of the two. I wish I was as much stronger than all the other suitors in the house as I am than you—I would soon send some of them off sick and sorry, for they mean trouble."

This made them all laugh heartily, which put them in a better mood with Telemachus. So Eumaeus brought the bow forward and placed it in Odysseus's hands. When he had done this, he called Eurycleia aside and said to her, "Eurycleia, Telemachus says you are to close the doors of the women's quarters. If they hear any groaning or uproar as of men fighting in the house, they must not come out, but must stay quiet and remain where they are at their work."
Eurycleia did as she was told and closed the doors of the women's quarters.

Meanwhile, Philoetius slipped quietly out and secured the gates of the outer courtyard. There was a ship's cable made of papyrus fiber lying in the gatehouse, so he fastened the gates with it and then came back in, resuming the seat he had left and keeping an eye on Odysseus, who now had the bow in his hands and was turning it every way, examining it all over to see whether worms had been eating into its two horns during his absence. Then one would turn to his neighbor saying, "This is some cunning old bow expert. Either he has one like it at home, or he wants to make one, judging by the skillful way the old vagrant handles it."
Another said, "I hope he's no more successful in other things than he's likely to be in stringing this bow."

But Odysseus, when he had taken it up and examined it thoroughly, strung it as easily as a skilled musician strings a new peg on his lyre and makes the twisted gut fast at both ends. Then he took it in his right hand to test the string, and it sang sweetly under his touch like a swallow's twitter. The suitors were dismayed and turned pale when they heard it. At that moment, Zeus thundered loudly as a sign, and Odysseus's heart rejoiced when he heard the omen that the son of crafty Cronus had sent him.

He took an arrow that was lying on the table—for those which the Greeks would soon taste were all inside the quiver—and laid it on the center grip of the bow. He drew back the notch of the arrow and the string while still seated. When he had taken aim, he let fly, and his arrow pierced every one of the axe handles from the first onward until it had gone right through them and into the outer courtyard. Then he said to Telemachus:

"Your guest has not disgraced you, Telemachus. I didn't miss what I aimed at, and I wasn't long in stringing my bow. I am still strong, not as the suitors mock me for being. Now, however, it's time for the Greeks to prepare supper while there's still daylight, and then to entertain themselves with song and dance, which are the crowning ornaments of a feast."
As he spoke, he signaled with his eyebrows, and Telemachus strapped on his sword, grasped his spear, and stood armed beside his father's seat.

chapters.title: Book XXII — The killing of the suitors—the maids who have misconducted themselves are made to cleanse the cloisters and are then hanged
paragraphs: Then Odysseus tore off his beggar's rags and leaped onto the great hall's stone floor with his bow and quiver full of arrows. He scattered the arrows at his feet and declared, "The contest is finished. Now I'll see if Apollo will grant me the power to hit a target no man has ever struck before."

With that, he aimed a deadly arrow at Antinous, who was lifting a beautiful golden cup to drink his wine, already holding it in his hands. The man had no thought of death—who among all these feasting men would imagine that one person, however brave, would stand alone against so many and kill him? The arrow struck Antinous in the throat, and the bronze point drove clean through his neck. He toppled backward and the cup fell from his grasp while thick blood gushed from his nostrils. He kicked the table away from him, scattering everything on it so that bread and roasted meat spilled onto the floor, all ruined. The suitors erupted in chaos when they saw a man had been killed. They all leaped up from their seats in panic and looked around at the walls for shields or spears, but found none. They angrily rebuked Odysseus: "Stranger, you'll pay for shooting people like this! You'll face no other contest—you're a dead man! The one you killed was the finest young man in Ithaca, and vultures will feast on you for murdering him."
They spoke this way because they thought he had killed Antinous by accident, not realizing that death hung over every one of their heads. But Odysseus glared at them and said:

"You dogs! Did you think I would never return from Troy? You've squandered my wealth, forced my servant women to sleep with you, and courted my wife while I was still alive. You feared neither god nor man, and now you will die."
They turned pale with terror at his words, and each man looked around desperately for somewhere to escape, but only Eurymachus spoke up.

"If you truly are Odysseus," he said, "then what you've said is justified. We have done terrible wrongs in your lands and house. But Antinous, who was the leader and instigator of all this wrongdoing, already lies dead. It was all his idea. He didn't really want to marry Penelope—he cared little about that. What he wanted was something entirely different, and Zeus has denied it to him. He wanted to kill your son and become the ruler of Ithaca. Now that he's received the death he deserved, spare your people's lives. We'll make everything right among ourselves and pay you in full for all we've eaten and drunk. Each of us will pay you compensation worth twenty oxen, and we'll keep giving you gold and bronze until your heart softens. Until we've done this, no one could blame you for being furious with us."

Odysseus glared at him again and replied, "Even if you gave me everything you own now and everything you'll ever possess, I won't hold back my hand until I've made you all pay in full. You must fight or flee for your lives—and not one of you will escape by fleeing."
Their hearts sank when they heard him, but Eurymachus spoke again:

"Friends, this man will show us no mercy. He'll stand right there and shoot us down until he's killed every last one of us. So let's fight back! Draw your swords and hold up the tables as shields against his arrows. Let's rush him together to drive him from the doorway and entrance. Then we can get into the town and raise such an alarm that his shooting will quickly end."

As he spoke, he drew his sharp bronze blade, keen on both edges, and with a loud war cry charged toward Odysseus. But Odysseus instantly shot an arrow into his chest that caught him in the nipple and lodged in his liver. He dropped his sword and collapsed doubled over his table. The cup and all the food crashed to the ground as he struck the earth with his forehead in his death agony, kicking at his stool with his feet until darkness closed his eyes.

Then Amphinomus drew his sword and rushed straight at Odysseus, trying to force him away from the door. But Telemachus was too quick for him and struck from behind. The spear caught him between the shoulder blades and went completely through his chest, so that he fell heavily to the ground and hit the earth with his forehead. Telemachus immediately sprang away from him, leaving his spear in the body, fearing that if he stayed to pull it out, one of the other men might attack him with a sword or club him down. So he ran quickly to his father's side and said:
"Father, let me bring you a shield, two spears, and a bronze helmet for your head. I'll arm myself too, and bring weapons for the swineherd and cowherd as well—we should all be properly armed."
"Run and get them," Odysseus answered, "while my arrows last, or when I'm alone they might drive me from the door."

Telemachus did as his father commanded and hurried to the storeroom where the weapons were kept. He selected four shields, eight spears, and four bronze helmets with horsehair plumes. He brought them quickly to his father and armed himself first, while the cowherd and swineherd also put on armor and took their places beside Odysseus. Meanwhile, as long as his arrows held out, Odysseus had been shooting the suitors one by one, and they fell in heaps. When his arrows were exhausted, he leaned his bow against the doorpost at the hall's end wall and slung a four-layered shield over his shoulders. On his noble head he placed a well-crafted helmet with a horsehair crest that nodded menacingly above it, and he grasped two formidable bronze-tipped spears.

Now there was a small door in the wall, and at one end of the stone floor was an exit leading to a narrow passage, closed by a well-fitted door. Odysseus told Philoetius to guard this door, since only one person could attack through it at a time. But Agelaus shouted out, "Can't someone go to the small door and tell the people what's happening? Help would come immediately, and we'd soon end this man's shooting."

"That's impossible, Agelaus," Melanthius replied. "The entrance to the narrow passage is dangerously close to the courtyard door. One brave man could keep any number from getting through. But I know what I'll do—I'll bring you weapons from the storeroom. I'm sure that's where Odysseus and his son have put them."

With that, the goatherd Melanthius went through back passages to Odysseus's storeroom. There he chose twelve shields, along with the same number of helmets and spears, and brought them back as quickly as he could to arm the suitors. Odysseus's heart began to fail when he saw the suitors putting on armor and brandishing spears. He realized the magnitude of the danger and said to Telemachus, "One of the women inside is helping the suitors against us, or else it's Melanthius."

Telemachus answered, "The fault is mine, father, and mine alone. I left the storeroom door open, and they kept better watch than I did. Go, Eumaeus, close the door and see whether it's one of the women doing this, or whether, as I suspect, it's Melanthius, son of Dolius."

While they were talking, Melanthius was going to the storeroom again to fetch more weapons. But the swineherd spotted him and said to Odysseus beside him, "Odysseus, noble son of Laertes, it's that scoundrel Melanthius, just as we suspected, heading to the storeroom. Tell me—should I kill him if I can overpower him, or bring him here so you can take your own revenge for all the wrongs he's done in your house?"

Odysseus replied, "Telemachus and I will hold these suitors in check no matter what they do. Both of you go back and bind Melanthius's hands and feet behind him. Throw him into the storeroom and lock the door behind you. Then tie a rope around his body and hoist him up to the rafters from a high beam, so he can linger there in agony."

They did exactly as he commanded. They reached the storeroom and entered before Melanthius saw them, as he was busy searching for weapons in the room's far corner. The two men positioned themselves on either side of the door and waited. Soon Melanthius emerged with a helmet in one hand and an old, rotted shield in the other—one that Laertes had carried as a young man but had long since discarded, its straps now loose and frayed. The two seized him, dragged him back by his hair, and threw him struggling to the ground. They bent his hands and feet behind his back and bound them tightly with painful bonds as Odysseus had instructed. Then they fastened a rope around his body and hoisted him up from a high pillar until he hung close to the rafters. And then you taunted him, swineherd Eumaeus, saying, "Melanthius, you'll spend the night on a soft bed as you deserve. You'll know very well when morning comes from the streams of Ocean, and it's time for you to drive your goats for the suitors' feast."

There they left him in cruel bondage. Having put on their armor, they closed the door behind them and returned to take their places beside Odysseus. So the four men stood in the hall, fierce and full of rage, while those in the main court were still both brave and numerous. Then Zeus's daughter Athena came to them, having taken the voice and appearance of Mentor. Odysseus was glad when he saw her and said, "Mentor, help me and remember your old comrade and the many favors he's done you. Besides, we're the same age."

But all the while he was sure it was Athena. The suitors from the other side raised an uproar when they saw her. Agelaus was the first to reproach her: "Mentor, don't let Odysseus trick you into siding with him and fighting the suitors. This is what we'll do: when we've killed these people, father and son, we'll kill you too. You'll pay with your life, and when we've killed you, we'll take everything you own, indoors and out, and add it to Odysseus's property. We won't let your sons live in your house, or your daughters, and your wife won't continue living in the city of Ithaca."

This made Athena even more furious, so she scolded Odysseus angrily. "Odysseus, your strength and prowess are no longer what they were when you fought for nine long years among the Trojans over noble Helen. You killed many men in those days, and it was through your strategy that Priam's city was taken. How is it that you're so pathetically weak now that you're on your own ground, facing the suitors in your own house? Come on, good friend, stand by my side and see how Mentor, son of Alcimus, will fight your enemies and repay your past kindnesses."
But she wouldn't give him complete victory yet, wanting to test his courage and that of his brave son further. So she flew up to one of the hall's rafters and perched there in the form of a swallow.

Meanwhile Agelaus son of Damastor, Eurynomus, Amphimedon, Demoptolemus, Pisander, and Polybus son of Polyctor led the fight on the suitors' side. Of all those still fighting for their lives, they were by far the most valiant, for the rest had already fallen under Odysseus's arrows. Agelaus shouted to them: "Friends, he'll have to stop soon, for Mentor has gone away after doing nothing but boast. They're standing at the doors unsupported. Don't all aim at him at once—let six of you throw your spears first, and see if you can't cover yourselves with glory by killing him. Once he falls, we needn't worry about the others."

They threw their spears as he ordered, but Athena made them all miss their mark. One hit the doorpost, another struck the door, and another's bronze point hit the wall. When they had avoided all the suitors' spears, Odysseus said to his men, "Friends, I say we should also let fly into their midst, or they'll add killing us to all the other harm they've done."

So they aimed straight ahead and threw their spears. Odysseus killed Demoptolemus, Telemachus killed Euryades, Eumaeus killed Elatus, and the cowherd killed Pisander. All these bit the dust, and as the others retreated to a corner, Odysseus and his men rushed forward and retrieved their spears by pulling them from the bodies of the dead.

The suitors threw a second volley, but again Athena made most of their weapons ineffective. One hit a pillar of the hall, another struck the door, and another's bronze point hit the wall. Still, Amphimedon managed to graze the top of Telemachus's wrist, and Ctesippus grazed Eumaeus's shoulder above his shield, though the spear passed over and fell to the ground. Then Odysseus and his men let fly into the crowd of suitors. Odysseus hit Eurydamas, Telemachus hit Amphimedon, and Eumaeus hit Polybus. After this the cowherd struck Ctesippus in the chest and taunted him: "Foul-mouthed son of Polytherses, don't be so foolish as to speak wickedly again, but let heaven guide your words, for the gods are far stronger than men. I give you this advice in return for the hoof you gave Odysseus when he was begging in his own house."

So spoke the cowherd, and Odysseus struck Damastor's son with a spear in close combat, while Telemachus hit Leocritus son of Evenor in the belly, driving the point clean through so that he fell forward face-first to the ground. Then Athena from her perch on the rafter raised her deadly aegis, and the suitors' hearts failed them. They fled to the far end of the court like cattle maddened by gadflies in early summer when the days are longest. As hook-beaked, sharp-taloned eagles from the mountains swoop down on smaller birds that cower in flocks on the ground and kill them—for they cannot fight or fly, and onlookers enjoy the sport—so Odysseus and his men fell upon the suitors and struck them down on every side. They made horrible groaning sounds as their skulls were crushed, and the ground ran red with blood.

Then Leiodes grasped Odysseus's knees and pleaded, "Odysseus, I beg you to have mercy and spare me. I never wronged any woman in your house in word or deed, and I tried to stop the others. I saw them, but they wouldn't listen, and now they're paying for their folly. I was their priest—if you kill me, I'll die without having done anything to deserve it, and I'll get no thanks for all the good I did."

Odysseus looked at him sternly and replied, "If you were their priest, you must have prayed many times that I would be long in returning home, and that you might marry my wife and have children by her. Therefore you will die."

With these words he picked up the sword that Agelaus had dropped when he was killed, which lay on the ground. Then he struck Leiodes on the back of the neck, so that his head fell rolling in the dust while he was still speaking.

The bard Phemius son of Terpes—who had been forced by the suitors to sing for them—now tried to save his life. He was standing near the small door, holding his lyre. He couldn't decide whether to flee from the hall and sit by Zeus's altar in the outer court, where both Laertes and Odysseus had offered the thigh bones of many oxen, or to go straight to Odysseus and clasp his knees. In the end he decided it was best to embrace Odysseus's knees. So he set his lyre on the ground between the mixing bowl and the silver-studded chair, then went up to Odysseus, grasped his knees, and said, "Odysseus, I beg you to have mercy and spare me. You'll regret it later if you kill a bard who can sing for both gods and men as I can. I compose all my songs myself, and heaven fills me with every kind of inspiration. I would sing to you as if you were a god—so don't be so eager to cut off my head. Your own son Telemachus will tell you that I didn't want to frequent your house and sing to the suitors after their meals, but they were too many and too strong for me, so they forced me."

Telemachus heard him and immediately went to his father. "Stop!" he cried. "The man is innocent—don't harm him! And we should spare Medon too, who was always kind to me when I was a boy, unless Philoetius or Eumaeus has already killed him, or he fell in your path when you were raging through the court."

Medon heard Telemachus's words, for he was crouching under a chair where he had hidden by covering himself with a freshly flayed cow hide. So he threw off the hide, went up to Telemachus, and grasped his knees.
"Here I am, dear sir," he said. "Hold back and tell your father, or he'll kill me in his rage against the suitors for wasting his wealth and foolishly disrespecting you."

Odysseus smiled at him and replied, "Don't be afraid. Telemachus has saved your life, so that you may know in the future, and tell others, how much better good deeds fare than evil ones. Go outside the hall into the outer court and stay out of the way of the slaughter—you and the bard—while I finish my work here inside."

The two went into the outer court as quickly as they could and sat down by Zeus's great altar, looking around fearfully and still expecting to be killed. Then Odysseus searched the entire hall carefully to see if anyone had managed to hide and was still alive, but he found them all lying in the dust, wallowing in their blood. They were like fish that fishermen have netted from the sea and thrown on the beach to lie gasping for water until the sun's heat finishes them. Just so the suitors lay all piled together.
Then Odysseus said to Telemachus, "Call nurse Eurycleia. I have something to tell her."
Telemachus went and knocked on the door of the women's quarters. "Hurry up," he said, "old woman who supervises all the other women in the house. Come out—my father wants to speak with you."

When Eurycleia heard this, she unfastened the door of the women's room and came out, following Telemachus. She found Odysseus among the corpses, spattered with blood and gore like a lion that has just been devouring an ox, with his chest and both cheeks all bloody, making him a fearsome sight. Just so was Odysseus smeared from head to foot with blood. When she saw all the corpses and such quantities of blood, she was about to cry out in joy, seeing that a great deed had been accomplished. But Odysseus stopped her: "Old woman, rejoice in your heart but restrain yourself—don't make any noise about it. It's unholy to gloat over dead men. Heaven's judgment and their own evil deeds have destroyed these men, for they respected no one in all the world, neither rich nor poor, who came near them. So they've met a bad end as punishment for their wickedness and folly. Now tell me which of the women in the house have misbehaved and which are innocent."

"I'll tell you the truth, my child," Eurycleia answered. "There are fifty women in the house whom we teach to do work like carding wool and all kinds of household tasks. Of these, twelve in total have misbehaved and shown disrespect to me and to Penelope. They showed no disrespect to Telemachus, for he has only recently grown up and his mother never allowed him to give orders to the female servants. But let me go upstairs and tell your wife everything that's happened, for some god has sent her to sleep."
"Don't wake her yet," Odysseus replied, "but tell the women who have misbehaved to come to me."

Eurycleia left the hall to tell the women and make them come to Odysseus. Meanwhile he called Telemachus, the cowherd, and the swineherd. "Start removing the dead," he said, "and make the women help you. Then get sponges and clean water to wash down the tables and chairs. When you've thoroughly cleaned the entire hall, take the women into the space between the round room and the outer court wall, and run them through with your swords until they're all dead and have forgotten about love and the way they used to lie secretly with the suitors."

At this the women came down together, weeping and wailing bitterly. First they carried out the dead bodies and propped them against each other in the gatehouse. Odysseus directed them and made them work quickly, so they had to carry out the bodies. When they had done this, they cleaned all the tables and chairs with sponges and water, while Telemachus and the two others shoveled up the blood and dirt from the ground, and the women carried it all outside. When they had made the whole place completely clean and orderly, they took the women out and penned them in the narrow space between the round room wall and the courtyard wall, so they couldn't escape. Then Telemachus said to the other two, "I won't let these women die a clean death, for they were insolent to my mother and me, and used to sleep with the suitors."

So saying, he fastened a ship's cable to one of the pillars that supported the round room's roof and secured it around the building at a good height, so that none of the women's feet would touch the ground. As thrushes or doves beat against a net set for them in a thicket just as they're heading to their nest, and a terrible fate awaits them, so the women had to put their heads in nooses one after another and die most wretchedly. Their feet twitched convulsively for a while, but not for very long.

As for Melanthius, they brought him through the hall into the inner court. There they cut off his nose and ears, tore out his genitals and threw them raw to the dogs, and then in their fury cut off his hands and feet.

When they had finished this, they washed their hands and feet and went back into the house, for everything was now complete. Odysseus said to dear old nurse Eurycleia, "Bring me sulfur, which cleanses all pollution, and fetch fire so I can burn it and purify the halls. Go also and tell Penelope to come here with her attendants, and bring all the maidservants in the house."
"Everything you've said is right," Eurycleia replied, "but let me bring you clean clothes—a tunic and cloak. Don't keep wearing these rags any longer. It's not proper."
"First light me a fire," Odysseus replied.

She brought the fire and sulfur as he had asked, and Odysseus thoroughly purified the halls and both the inner and outer courts. Then she went inside to call the women and tell them what had happened. They came from their quarters with torches in their hands and surrounded Odysseus to embrace him, kissing his head and shoulders and grasping his hands. He felt as if he wanted to weep, for he remembered every one of them.

chapters.title: Book XXIII — Penelope eventually recognises her husband—early in the morning Odysseus, Telemachus, Eumaeus, and Philoetius leave the town
paragraphs: Euryclea went upstairs laughing to tell her mistress that her dear husband had come home. Her old knees felt young again and her feet were quick with joy as she climbed to her mistress and bent over her head to speak. "Wake up, Penelope, my dear child," she cried, "and see with your own eyes something you've been waiting for all this time. Odysseus has truly come home at last, and he's killed the suitors who were causing so much trouble in his house, eating up his estate and mistreating his son."

"My good nurse," Penelope replied, "you must be losing your mind. The gods sometimes drive sensible people mad, and make foolish people wise. This is what they must have done to you—you were always such a reasonable person before. Why are you mocking me when I already have enough troubles, talking such nonsense and waking me from the sweet sleep that had finally closed my eyes? I haven't slept so soundly since the day my poor husband left for that cursed city. Go back to the women's quarters. If anyone else had woken me with such ridiculous news, I would have sent her away with a harsh scolding. Only your age protects you now."

"My dear child," Euryclea answered, "I'm not mocking you. It's completely true—Odysseus has come home again. He was the stranger they all kept treating so badly in the courtyard. Telemachus knew the whole time that his father had returned, but kept the secret so they could take revenge on all those wicked men."

Then Penelope sprang up from her bed, threw her arms around Euryclea, and wept with joy. "But my dear nurse," she said, "explain this to me. If he's really come home as you say, how did he manage to overcome all those wicked suitors by himself, considering how many there were?"

"I wasn't there," Euryclea answered, "and don't know the details. I only heard them groaning as they died. We sat huddled together in a corner of the women's room with the doors shut, until your son came to get me because his father sent him. Then I found Odysseus standing over the corpses lying all around him on the ground, one on top of another. You would have been thrilled to see him standing there covered in blood and dirt, looking just like a lion. But the bodies are now piled up in the gatehouse in the outer court, and Odysseus has lit a great fire to purify the house with sulfur. He sent me to call you, so come with me so you can both be happy together at last. Now your heart's desire has been fulfilled—your husband has come home to find both wife and son alive and well, and to take his revenge in his own house on the suitors who treated him so badly."

"My dear nurse," said Penelope, "don't celebrate too confidently over all this. You know how delighted everyone would be to see Odysseus come home—especially myself and the son born to both of us. But what you're telling me can't possibly be true. It must be some god who was angry with the suitors for their great wickedness and destroyed them. They respected no one in the whole world, neither rich nor poor, who came near them, and they've met a bad end because of their crimes. Odysseus is dead far from Greek lands—he will never return home again."

Then nurse Euryclea said, "My child, what are you saying? You've always been so stubborn and convinced that your husband would never return, even though he's in the house right now by his own fireside. Besides, I can give you another proof. When I was washing him, I saw the scar the wild boar gave him, and I wanted to tell you about it, but he wisely wouldn't let me and covered my mouth with his hands. So come with me, and I'll make this deal with you—if I'm lying to you, you can have me killed in the cruelest way you can imagine."

"My dear nurse," said Penelope, "however wise you may be, you can hardly understand the plans of the gods. Nevertheless, we'll go find my son, so I can see the corpses of the suitors and the man who killed them."

With that, she came down from her upper room, wondering whether she should keep her distance from her husband and question him, or go straight to him and embrace him. When she had crossed the stone floor of the courtyard, she sat down across from Odysseus by the fire, against the wall, while Odysseus sat near one of the pillars, looking at the ground and waiting to see what his wise wife would say when she saw him. For a long time she sat silent, as if stunned. One moment she looked him full in the face, but then again she was misled by his shabby clothes and failed to recognize him, until Telemachus began to scold her and said:

"Mother—though you're so hard-hearted I can barely call you that—why do you stay away from my father like this? Why don't you sit beside him and start talking to him and asking questions? No other woman could bear to keep away from her husband when he'd returned to her after twenty years away, after going through so much. But your heart was always as hard as stone."

Penelope answered, "My son, I'm so amazed I can't find words to ask questions or answer them. I can't even look him straight in the face. Still, if he really is Odysseus come back to his own home, we'll get to know each other better soon enough, for there are signs that only the two of us know, hidden from everyone else."

Odysseus smiled at this and said to Telemachus, "Let your mother test me however she wants. She'll make up her mind soon enough. Right now she rejects me and thinks I'm someone else because I'm covered with dirt and wearing such poor clothes. But let's think about what we should do next. When someone kills another man—even one who wouldn't leave many friends to avenge him—the killer must still say goodbye to his friends and flee the country. But we've been killing the pillars of a whole town, all the finest young men of Ithaca. Think about this carefully."

"Look to it yourself, father," Telemachus answered, "for they say you're the wisest counselor in the world, and no other mortal can compare with you. We'll follow you gladly, and you won't find us failing you as long as our strength holds out."

"I'll tell you what I think is best," Odysseus replied. "First, wash and put on clean clothes. Tell the maids to go to their rooms and dress properly too. Then Phemius will play a lively dance tune on his lyre, so that if people outside hear it, or any neighbors, or someone passing in the street notices, they'll think there's a wedding in the house, and no rumors about the suitors' deaths will spread through town before we can escape to the woods on my land. Once there, we'll decide which course heaven offers us seems wisest."

He spoke, and they did exactly as he said. First they washed and put on clean shirts, while the women got ready. Then Phemius took his lyre and filled them all with longing for sweet song and stately dance. The house echoed with the sound of men and women dancing, and people outside said, "I suppose the queen has finally gotten married. She should be ashamed of herself for not continuing to protect her husband's property until he comes home."

That's what they said, but they didn't know what had really happened. The head servant Eurynome washed and anointed Odysseus in his own house and gave him a shirt and cloak, while Athena made him look taller and stronger than before. She also made thick hair grow on his head and flow down in curls like hyacinth blossoms. She made him glorious about the head and shoulders, just as a skilled craftsman who has learned his art from Hephaestus and Athena—whose work is full of beauty—enhances a piece of silver by gilding it. He came from the bath looking like one of the immortals and sat down across from his wife in the chair he had left. "My dear," he said, "heaven has given you a heart more stubborn than any woman ever had. No other woman could bear to stay away from her husband when he'd returned to her after twenty years away, after going through so much. Come, nurse, prepare a bed for me. I'll sleep alone, since this woman has a heart as hard as iron."

"My dear," Penelope answered, "I don't want to seem proud or to put you down, but I'm not impressed by your appearance, for I remember very well what kind of man you were when you sailed from Ithaca. Nevertheless, Euryclea, take his bed outside the bedroom that he built himself. Bring the bed out of that room and put bedding on it with fleeces, good covers, and blankets."

She said this to test him, but Odysseus grew angry and said, "Wife, I'm very upset by what you just said. Who has been moving my bed from where I left it? It would be a hard task for even the most skilled craftsman, unless some god came to help him move it. No living man, however strong and in his prime, could shift it from its place, for it's a marvelous creation that I made with my own hands. There was a young olive tree growing within the grounds of the house, full of vigor and about as thick as a pillar. I built my room around this tree with strong stone walls and a roof to cover them, and made the doors strong and well-fitted. Then I cut off the top branches of the olive tree and left the trunk standing. I shaped this roughly from the root up, then worked it carefully with tools, making it straight by drawing a line on the wood, and turned it into a bedpost. I bored a hole down the middle and made it the center post of my bed, working on it until I finished it, inlaying it with gold and silver. After this I stretched a hide of crimson leather from one side to the other. So you see I know all about it, and I want to learn whether it's still there, or whether someone has moved it by cutting down the olive tree at its roots."

When she heard the clear proof Odysseus gave her, she broke down completely. She ran weeping to his side, threw her arms around his neck, and kissed him. "Don't be angry with me, Odysseus," she cried, "you who are the wisest of all mankind. We have both suffered. Heaven has denied us the happiness of spending our youth and growing old together. So don't be upset or offended that I didn't embrace you as soon as I saw you. I've been trembling with fear the whole time that someone might come here and deceive me with a lying story, for there are many wicked people around. Helen, Zeus's daughter, would never have given herself to a foreign man if she had known that the Greeks would come after her and bring her back. Heaven put it in her heart to do wrong, and she gave no thought to that sin which has been the source of all our sorrows. But now that you've convinced me by showing you know all about our bed—which no human being has ever seen except you and me and one maid, Actor's daughter, whom my father gave me when I married and who guards our bedroom door—stubborn as I've been, I can doubt no longer."

Then Odysseus melted in turn and wept as he held his dear and faithful wife. As the sight of land is welcome to swimmers making for shore when Poseidon has wrecked their ship with furious winds and waves—a few reach land alone, covered with brine, and are thankful to find themselves on solid ground and out of danger—just so welcome was her husband to her as she looked at him, and she couldn't take her arms from around his neck. Indeed, they would have gone on sharing their joy until rosy-fingered Dawn appeared, if Athena hadn't decided otherwise and held night back in the far west, while not allowing Dawn to leave Ocean or harness her two horses Lampus and Phaethon that bring daylight to mankind.

At last, however, Odysseus said, "Wife, we haven't reached the end of our troubles yet. I still have an unknown amount of difficult work to do. It's long and hard, but I must go through with it, for this is what the ghost of Tiresias prophesied about me when I went down to Hades to ask about my return and that of my companions. But now let's go to bed, so we can lie down and enjoy the blessed gift of sleep."

"You can go to bed whenever you like," Penelope replied, "now that the gods have brought you home to your own house and country. But since heaven has put it in your mind to speak of it, tell me about the task ahead of you. I'll have to hear about it eventually, so it's better I know now."

"My dear," Odysseus answered, "why do you insist I tell you? Still, I won't hide it from you, though you won't like it. I don't like it myself, for Tiresias told me to travel far and wide, carrying an oar, until I came to a country where people have never heard of the sea and don't even use salt in their food. They know nothing about ships or oars that are like a ship's wings. He gave me this sure sign, which I won't hide from you: he said a traveler would meet me and ask if the thing on my shoulder was a winnowing fan. When that happens, I must plant my oar in the ground and sacrifice a ram, bull, and boar to Poseidon. After that I should go home and offer sacrifices to all the gods in heaven, one after another. As for myself, he said death would come to me from the sea, and my life would ebb away very gently when I'm full of years and peace, and my people would bless me. All this, he said, would surely come to pass."
And Penelope said, "If the gods are going to give you a happier time in your old age, you can hope then to have some relief from misfortune."

That's how they talked. Meanwhile Eurynome and the nurse brought torches and prepared the bed with soft covers. As soon as they had arranged everything, the nurse went back into the house to rest, leaving Eurynome, the bedroom attendant, to lead Odysseus and Penelope to bed by torchlight. When she had shown them to their room, she left, and they came joyfully to their own old bed. Telemachus, Philoetius, and the swineherd stopped dancing and made the women stop too. Then they lay down to sleep in the courtyard.

When Odysseus and Penelope had satisfied their love, they lay talking together. She told him how much she had endured, seeing the house filled with a crowd of wicked suitors who had killed so many sheep and cattle on her account and drunk so many jars of wine. Odysseus in turn told her what he had suffered and how much trouble he had caused others. He told her everything, and she was so delighted to listen that she never fell asleep until he had finished his whole story.

He began with his victory over the Cicones, and how he then reached the fertile land of the Lotus-eaters. He told her all about the Cyclops and how he had punished him for so ruthlessly eating his brave companions. How he went on to Aeolus, who received him hospitably and helped him on his way, but even so he couldn't reach home, for to his great grief a storm carried him out to sea again. How he came to the Laestrygonian city of Telepylus, where the people destroyed all his ships and crews except himself and his own ship. Then he told of cunning Circe and her magic, and how he sailed to the cold house of Hades to consult the ghost of the Theban prophet Tiresias, and saw his old comrades and his mother who bore and raised him as a child. How he heard the wonderful singing of the Sirens, and went on to the Wandering Rocks and terrible Charybdis and Scylla, whom no man had ever passed safely. How his men then ate the cattle of the sun god, and Zeus therefore struck their ship with thunderbolts, so all his men died together while he alone survived. How at last he reached the island of Ogygia and the nymph Calypso, who kept him in a cave and fed him, wanting him to marry her and make him immortal so he would never grow old, but she couldn't persuade him to agree. And how after much suffering he found his way to the Phaeacians, who treated him like a god and sent him back to his own country in a ship, after giving him gold, bronze, and clothing in great abundance. This was the last thing he told her about, for here deep sleep took hold of him and eased the burden of his sorrows.

Then Athena thought of another matter. When she decided Odysseus had had enough of his wife and rest, she told golden-throned Dawn to rise from Ocean and shed light on mankind. At this, Odysseus rose from his comfortable bed and said to Penelope, "Wife, we've both had our full share of troubles—you here, lamenting my absence, and I being prevented from getting home though I longed to all the time. Now that we've finally come together, take care of the property in the house. As for the sheep and goats the wicked suitors ate, I'll take many myself by force from other people, and make the Greeks replace the rest until they've filled all my pens. I'm going now to the wooded countryside to see my father, who has grieved so long on my account. And to you I give these instructions, though you hardly need them: at sunrise word will spread immediately that I've been killing the suitors. Go upstairs and stay there with your women. See no one and ask no questions."

As he spoke, he put on his armor. Then he woke Telemachus, Philoetius, and Eumaeus, and told them all to arm themselves too. They did so and put on their weapons. When they were ready, they opened the gates and went out, with Odysseus leading the way. It was now daylight, but Athena still concealed them in darkness and led them quickly out of the town.

chapters.title: Book XXIV — The ghosts of the suitors in Hades—Odysseus and his men go to the house of Laertes—the people of Ithaca come out to attack Odysseus, but Athena concludes a peace
paragraphs: Then Hermes of Cyllene summoned the spirits of the suitors, holding in his hand the beautiful golden wand with which he closes men's eyes in sleep or wakes them as he chooses. With this he roused the spirits and led them while they followed behind him, whimpering and gibbering. Like bats that squeal as they fly through the hollow of some great cave when one has fallen from the cluster where they hang, so the spirits whined and squealed as Hermes the healer of sorrows led them down into the dark realm of death. When they had passed the waters of Ocean and the white rock, they came to the gates of the sun and the land of dreams, and then reached the meadow of asphodel where dwell the souls and shadows of those who can work no more.
Here they found the spirit of Achilles, son of Peleus, along with those of Patroclus, Antilochus, and Ajax, who was the finest and most handsome man among all the Greeks after Peleus's son himself.

They gathered around the spirit of Peleus's son, and the spirit of Agamemnon joined them, grieving bitterly. Around him were also gathered the spirits of those who had died with him in Aegisthus's house, and Achilles's spirit spoke first.

"Son of Atreus," he said, "we always believed that Zeus loved you more than any other hero from beginning to end, since you commanded many brave men when we all fought together before Troy. Yet death's hand, which no mortal can escape, struck you down far too early. It would have been better for you to have fallen at Troy at the height of your glory, for the Greeks would have built a mound over your ashes, and your son would have inherited your good name. Instead, you were fated to meet a most wretched end."

"Fortunate son of Peleus," replied Agamemnon's spirit, "for dying at Troy far from Argos, while the bravest Trojans and Greeks fell around you fighting for your body. There you lay in the swirling clouds of dust, all magnificent and huge, no longer concerned with your prowess in battle. We fought the entire day, and would never have stopped if Zeus had not sent a storm to halt us. Then, when we had carried you from the battle to the ships, we laid you on your bed and cleansed your fair skin with warm water and oils. The Greeks tore their hair and wept bitterly around you. Your mother, when she heard the news, came with her immortal sea-nymphs from the ocean, and the sound of great mourning rose over the waters so that the Greeks trembled with fear. They would have fled in panic to their ships if wise old Nestor, whose counsel was always best, had not stopped them, saying, 'Hold fast, Greeks, do not flee, sons of the Achaeans. This is his mother coming from the sea with her immortal nymphs to look upon her son's body.'

"So he spoke, and the Greeks feared no more. The daughters of the old sea-god stood around you weeping bitterly and clothed you in immortal garments. The nine Muses also came and raised their sweet voices in lament, calling and answering one another. There was not a Greek who did not weep at the dirge they sang. For seventeen days and nights we mourned you, mortals and immortals alike, but on the eighteenth day we gave you to the flames. Many fat sheep and cattle we sacrificed around you. You were burned in divine clothing, with rich oils and honey, while heroes on foot and horseback clashed their armor around the pyre as you burned, with the sound of a great multitude. But when heaven's flames had done their work, we gathered your white bones at daybreak and placed them in oils and pure wine. Your mother brought us a golden urn to hold them—a gift from Dionysus and the work of Hephaestus himself. In this we placed your bleached bones mixed with those of Patroclus who had died before you, and separately we enclosed those of Antilochus, who had been closer to you than any other companion after Patroclus was gone.

"Over these the Greek army built a noble tomb on a headland jutting out over the open Hellespont, so it could be seen from far out at sea by those now living and those yet to be born. Your mother asked the gods for prizes and offered them to be competed for by the noblest of the Greeks. You must have attended the funerals of many heroes, when young men prepare themselves to compete for prizes at the death of some great chief, but you never saw such prizes as silver-footed Thetis offered in your honor, for the gods loved you well. Thus even in death your fame has not been lost, Achilles, and your name lives forever among all mankind. But as for me, what comfort did I have when my fighting days were done? For Zeus planned my destruction on my return, at the hands of Aegisthus and my wicked wife."

So they talked, and presently Hermes came up to them with the spirits of the suitors who had been killed by Odysseus. The spirits of Agamemnon and Achilles were amazed to see them and went up to them at once. Agamemnon's spirit recognized Amphimedon, son of Melaneus, who had lived in Ithaca and been his host, so he began to speak to him.

"Amphimedon," he said, "what has happened to all you fine young men—all the same age too—that brings you down here under the earth? One could not pick a finer group of men from any city. Did Poseidon raise his winds and waves against you when you were at sea, or did your enemies kill you on the mainland while you were stealing cattle or sheep, or fighting to defend their wives and city? Answer me, for I have been your guest. Don't you remember how I came to your house with Menelaus to persuade Odysseus to join us with his ships against Troy? It took us a whole month before we could resume our voyage, for we had great difficulty persuading Odysseus to come with us."

And Amphimedon's spirit answered, "Agamemnon, son of Atreus, king of men, I remember everything you have said, and I will tell you fully and accurately how our end came about. Odysseus had been gone a long time, and we were courting his wife, who would not give us a direct refusal, nor would she bring the matter to an end, for she meant to bring about our destruction. This was the trick she played on us. She set up a great loom in her room and began working on an enormous piece of fine needlework. 'My suitors,' she said, 'Odysseus is indeed dead, but do not press me to marry again immediately. Wait—for I would not want my skill in needlework to go unrecognized—until I have finished a shroud for the hero Laertes, for when death takes him. He is very wealthy, and the women of the place will gossip if he is laid out without a shroud.' This is what she said, and we agreed. Then we could see her working on her great web all day long, but at night she would unpick the stitches again by torchlight. She fooled us this way for three years without our discovering it, but as time passed and she was in her fourth year, when the months were waning and many days had passed, one of her maids who knew what she was doing told us, and we caught her undoing her work. So she had to finish it whether she wanted to or not, and when she showed us the robe she had made, after it had been washed, its splendor was like that of the sun or moon.

"Then some malicious god brought Odysseus to the upland farm where his swineherd lives. His son also came there, returning from a voyage to Pylos, and the two came to town after they had plotted our destruction. Telemachus came first, and then after him came Odysseus, accompanied by the swineherd, dressed in rags and leaning on a staff like some miserable old beggar. He came so unexpectedly that none of us recognized him, not even the older ones among us, and we insulted him and threw things at him. He endured both the blows and the insults without a word, though he was in his own house. But when the will of Zeus who bears the aegis inspired him, he and Telemachus took the weapons and hid them in an inner room, bolting the doors behind them. Then he cleverly had his wife offer his bow and a quantity of iron axes to be competed for by us ill-fated suitors, and this was the beginning of our end, for not one of us could string the bow—we couldn't even come close. When it was about to reach Odysseus's hands, we all shouted that it should not be given to him, no matter what he said, but Telemachus insisted on his having it. When he got it in his hands he strung it easily and sent his arrow through the iron. Then he stood on the floor of the hall and poured his arrows on the ground, glaring fiercely around him. First he killed Antinous, and then, aiming straight ahead, he let fly his deadly arrows and they fell thick upon us. It was clear that one of the gods was helping them, for they attacked us with overwhelming force throughout the halls, and there was a hideous sound of groaning as our heads were smashed in, and the ground ran with our blood. This, Agamemnon, is how we met our end, and our bodies are still lying uncared for in Odysseus's house, for our friends at home do not yet know what has happened, so they cannot lay us out and wash the black blood from our wounds, mourning over us according to the rites due to the dead."

"Fortunate Odysseus, son of Laertes," replied Agamemnon's spirit, "you are indeed blessed in having a wife endowed with such excellent understanding and so faithful to her wedded husband as Penelope, daughter of Icarius. The fame of her virtue shall never die, and the immortals shall compose a song that will be welcome to all mankind in honor of Penelope's faithfulness. How different was the wickedness of Tyndareus's daughter, who killed her lawful husband. Her song shall be hateful among men, for she has brought disgrace upon all womankind, even the good ones."

So they talked in the house of Hades deep within the bowels of the earth. Meanwhile Odysseus and the others left the town and soon reached the beautiful, well-tended farm of Laertes, which he had claimed through endless labor. Here was his house, with a lean-to running all around it where the slaves who worked for him slept and sat and ate, while inside the house there was an old Sicilian woman who looked after him on this country farm. When Odysseus arrived, he said to his son and the other two:
"Go to the house and kill the best pig you can find for dinner. Meanwhile I want to see whether my father will recognize me or fail to know me after such a long absence."

He then took off his armor and gave it to Eumaeus and Philoetius, who went straight to the house, while he turned toward the vineyard to test his father. As he went down into the great orchard, he did not see Dolius or any of his sons or the other servants, for they were all gathering thorns to make a fence for the vineyard at the place where the old man had told them. So he found his father alone, hoeing around a vine. He wore a dirty old shirt, patched and very shabby. His legs were bound with leather straps to protect him from thorns, and he also wore leather sleeves. He had a goatskin cap on his head and looked very sorrowful. When Odysseus saw him so worn out, so old and full of grief, he stood still under a tall pear tree and began to weep. He wondered whether to embrace him, kiss him, and tell him all about his homecoming, or whether he should first question him and see what he would say. In the end he decided it would be best to test him with words, so with this in mind he approached his father, who was bending down and working around a plant.

"I see, sir," said Odysseus, "that you are an excellent gardener—what care you take with everything. There is not a single plant, fig tree, vine, olive, pear, or flower bed that doesn't show the trace of your attention. I hope you won't be offended if I say that you take better care of your garden than of yourself. You are old, unkempt, and very poorly dressed. It can't be because you're lazy that your master takes such poor care of you. Indeed, your face and figure have nothing of the slave about them and show you to be of noble birth. I would have said you were one of those who should wash well, eat well, and sleep comfortably at night, as old men have a right to do. But tell me, and tell me truthfully, whose servant are you, and in whose garden are you working? Tell me also about another matter. Is this place I've come to really Ithaca? I met a man just now who said so, but he was a dull fellow and didn't have the patience to hear my story when I was asking him about an old friend of mine, whether he was still living or already dead and in Hades' house. Believe me when I tell you that this man once came to my house when I was in my own country, and never did any stranger come to me whom I liked better. He said his family was from Ithaca and that his father was Laertes, son of Arcesius. I received him hospitably, welcoming him to all the abundance of my house, and when he left I gave him all the customary gifts. I gave him seven talents of fine gold and a cup of solid silver with flowers engraved on it. I gave him twelve light cloaks and as many pieces of tapestry. I also gave him twelve single-fold cloaks, twelve rugs, twelve fine mantles, and an equal number of shirts. To all this I added four beautiful women skilled in all useful arts, and I let him choose which ones he wanted."

His father shed tears and answered, "Sir, you have indeed come to the country you named, but it has fallen into the hands of wicked people. All this wealth of gifts has been given for nothing. If you could have found your friend here alive in Ithaca, he would have entertained you hospitably and repaid your gifts amply when you left him—as would have been only right considering what you had already given him. But tell me truthfully, how many years has it been since you entertained this guest—my unhappy son, if he ever existed? Alas! He has died far from his own country. The fish of the sea have eaten him, or he has fallen prey to the birds and wild beasts of some land. Neither his mother nor I, his father, who gave him life, could wrap our arms around him and shroud him, nor could his excellent and richly dowered wife Penelope mourn her husband as was proper at his deathbed and close his eyes according to the rites due to the dead. But now tell me truthfully, for I want to know: Who are you and where do you come from? Tell me of your city and parents. Where is the ship that brought you and your men to Ithaca? Or were you a passenger on someone else's ship, and those who brought you here have gone on their way and left you?"

"I will tell you everything quite truthfully," answered Odysseus. "I come from Alybas, where I have a fine house. I am the son of King Apheidas, who is the son of Polypemon. My own name is Eperitus. Heaven drove me off course as I was leaving Sicily, and I have been brought here against my will. My ship is lying over there, off the open country outside the town, and this is the fifth year since Odysseus left my country. Poor fellow, yet the omens were good for him when he left me. The birds all flew on our right hands, and both he and I rejoiced to see them as we parted, for we had every hope that we would have another friendly meeting and exchange gifts."

A dark cloud of sorrow fell upon Laertes as he listened. He filled both hands with dust from the ground and poured it over his gray head, groaning heavily as he did so. Odysseus's heart was touched, and his nostrils quivered as he looked at his father. Then he sprang toward him, threw his arms around him and kissed him, saying, "I am he, father, the one you're asking about—I have returned after being away for twenty years. But stop your sighing and weeping—we have no time to lose, for I should tell you that I have been killing the suitors in my house, to punish them for their arrogance and crimes."
