"If you really are my son Odysseus," replied Laertes, "and have come back again, you must give me clear proof of your identity that will convince me."

"First look at this scar," answered Odysseus, "which I got from a boar's tusk when I was hunting on Mount Parnassus. You and my mother had sent me to Autolycus, my mother's father, to receive the gifts he had promised to give me when he was here. Furthermore, I will point out to you the trees in the vineyard that you gave me, and I asked you about them all as I followed you around the garden. We went over them all, and you told me their names and what they all were. You gave me thirteen pear trees, ten apple trees, and forty fig trees. You also said you would give me fifty rows of vines with corn planted between each row, and they yield grapes of every kind when heaven's heat has been laid heavy upon them."

Laertes's strength failed him when he heard the convincing proofs his son had given him. He threw his arms around him, and Odysseus had to support him or he would have fainted. But as soon as he recovered and was beginning to regain his senses, he said, "O father Zeus, then you gods are still on Olympus after all, if the suitors have really been punished for their arrogance and folly. Nevertheless, I am very afraid that I shall have all the townspeople of Ithaca up here soon, and they will be sending messengers everywhere throughout the cities of the Cephallenians."

Odysseus answered, "Take heart and don't worry about that, but let's go into the house near your garden. I have already told Telemachus, Philoetius, and Eumaeus to go there and get dinner ready as quickly as possible."

So the two made their way toward the house talking together. When they arrived they found Telemachus with the cattle herder and the swineherd cutting up meat and mixing wine with water. Then the old Sicilian woman took Laertes inside and washed him and anointed him with oil. She put a good cloak on him, and Athena came to him and gave him a more impressive appearance, making him taller and stronger than before. When he came back, his son was amazed to see him looking so godlike and said to him, "My dear father, one of the gods has been making you much taller and better-looking."

Laertes answered, "Would that by Father Zeus, Athena, and Apollo I were the man I was when I ruled among the Cephallenians and took Nericum, that strong fortress on the headland. If I were still what I was then and had been in our house yesterday with my armor on, I would have been able to stand by you and help you against the suitors. I would have killed a great many of them, and you would have rejoiced to see it."

So they talked, but the others, when they had finished their work and the feast was ready, stopped working and took their proper places on the benches and seats. Then they began eating. Soon old Dolius and his sons left their work and came up, for their mother, the Sicilian woman who looked after Laertes now that he was growing old, had gone to fetch them. When they saw Odysseus and were certain it was he, they stood there lost in amazement. But Odysseus scolded them good-naturedly and said, "Sit down to your dinner, old man, and don't worry about your surprise. We have been wanting to begin for some time and have been waiting for you."

Then Dolius stretched out both his hands and went up to Odysseus. "Sir," he said, seizing his master's hand and kissing it at the wrist, "we have long been wishing for your return, and now heaven has restored you to us after we had given up hope. All hail, and may the gods bless you. But tell me, does Penelope already know of your return, or should we send someone to tell her?"

"Old man," answered Odysseus, "she already knows, so you don't need to worry about that." With this he took his seat, and Dolius's sons gathered around Odysseus to greet him and embrace him one after another. Then they took their seats in proper order near their father Dolius.

While they were busy preparing their dinner, Rumor went around the town and spread news of the terrible fate that had befallen the suitors. As soon as the people heard of it, they gathered from every quarter, groaning and wailing before Odysseus's house. They took away the dead, buried each man his own, and put the bodies of those from elsewhere on board fishing boats for the fishermen to take each to his own place. Then they met angrily in the assembly place, and when they were gathered together, Eupeithes rose to speak. He was overwhelmed with grief for the death of his son Antinous, who had been the first man killed by Odysseus, so he said, weeping bitterly, "My friends, this man has done the Greeks great wrong. He took many of our best men away with him in his fleet, and he lost both ships and men. Now, moreover, on his return he has been killing all the leading men among the Cephallenians. Let's act before he can get away to Pylos or to Elis where the Epeans rule, or we shall be ashamed of ourselves forever. It will be an everlasting disgrace to us if we do not avenge the murder of our sons and brothers. For my own part, I would have no more pleasure in life but would rather die at once. Let's go after them before they can cross over to the mainland."

He wept as he spoke, and everyone pitied him. But Medon and the bard Phemius had now awakened and came to them from Odysseus's house. Everyone was astonished to see them, but they stood in the middle of the assembly, and Medon said, "Hear me, men of Ithaca. Odysseus did not do these things against the will of heaven. I myself saw an immortal god take the form of Mentor and stand beside him. This god appeared, now in front of him encouraging him, and now going furiously about the hall and attacking the suitors, and they fell thick upon one another."
At this, pale fear seized them, and old Halitherses, son of Mastor, rose to speak, for he was the only man among them who knew both past and future. So he spoke to them plainly and honestly, saying,

"Men of Ithaca, it is all your own fault that things have turned out as they have. You would not listen to me or to Mentor when we told you to check the folly of your sons, who were doing much wrong in the recklessness of their hearts—wasting the wealth and dishonoring the wife of a chief who they thought would never return. Now, however, let it be as I say, and do as I tell you. Do not go out against Odysseus, or you may find that you have been bringing evil upon your own heads."

This was what he said, and more than half raised a loud shout and immediately left the assembly. But the rest stayed where they were, for Halitherses's speech displeased them, and they sided with Eupeithes. They therefore hurried off for their weapons, and when they had armed themselves, they met together in front of the city, and Eupeithes led them on in their folly. He thought he was going to avenge his son's murder, but in truth he would never return home and was himself destined to die in the attempt.
Then Athena said to Zeus, "Father, son of Cronus, king of kings, answer me this question—What do you intend to do? Will you make them fight still more, or will you make peace between them?"

And Zeus answered, "My child, why do you ask me? Wasn't it your own plan that Odysseus should come home and take his revenge on the suitors? Do whatever you like, but I will tell you what I think would be the most reasonable arrangement. Now that Odysseus has had his revenge, let them swear to a solemn covenant by which he shall continue to rule, while we cause the others to forgive and forget the massacre of their sons and brothers. Let them all become friends as before, and let peace and prosperity reign."
This was what Athena was already eager to bring about, so down she darted from the highest peaks of Olympus.

Now when Laertes and the others had finished dinner, Odysseus began by saying, "Some of you go out and see if they are getting close to us." So one of Dolius's sons went as he was told. Standing on the threshold, he could see them all quite near and said to Odysseus, "Here they are. Let's put on our armor at once."

They armed themselves as quickly as they could—that is, Odysseus, his three men, and Dolius's six sons. Laertes and Dolius did the same—warriors by necessity despite their gray hair. When they had all put on their armor, they opened the gate and marched out, with Odysseus leading the way.

Then Zeus's daughter Athena came up to them, having taken the form and voice of Mentor. Odysseus was glad when he saw her and said to his son Telemachus, "Telemachus, now that you are about to fight in a battle that will show every man's courage, be sure not to disgrace your ancestors, who were famous for their strength and bravery throughout the world."
"You speak truly, my dear father," answered Telemachus, "and you shall see, if you wish, that I have no intention of disgracing your family."
Laertes was delighted when he heard this. "Good heavens," he exclaimed, "what a day I am having! I do indeed rejoice at it. My son and grandson are competing with each other in courage."
At this Athena came close to him and said, "Son of Arcesius—dearest of all my friends—pray to the gray-eyed maiden and to Zeus her father, then aim your spear and throw it."

As she spoke, she filled him with fresh strength, and when he had prayed to her, he aimed his spear and hurled it. He struck Eupeithes's helmet, and the spear went right through it, for the helmet could not stop it, and his armor rang as he fell heavily to the ground. Meanwhile Odysseus and his son attacked the front line of the enemy and struck them down with their swords and spears. Indeed, they would have killed every one of them and prevented them from ever getting home again, but Athena raised her voice loud and made everyone stop. "Men of Ithaca," she cried, "cease this dreadful war and settle the matter at once without further bloodshed."

At this, pale fear seized everyone. They were so frightened that their weapons dropped from their hands and fell to the ground at the sound of the goddess's voice, and they fled back to the city to save their lives. But Odysseus gave a great cry and, gathering himself together, swooped down like a soaring eagle. Then the son of Cronus sent a thunderbolt that fell just in front of Athena, so she said to Odysseus, "Odysseus, noble son of Laertes, stop this warlike strife, or Zeus will be angry with you."
So spoke Athena, and Odysseus obeyed her gladly. Then Athena, in the form and voice of Mentor, made a covenant of peace between the two opposing sides.
